summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4, took a sample of Lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. The Public Analyst found that the sample contained nine living meal worms and he did not state that it was insect infested nor that it is unfit for human consumption. He also stated that it had been mentioned in the report that the contents of the sample were found to be present and that in the absence of any other evidence in support of the case, the respondent could not be convicted under section 7 read with section 16 of the . The High Court accepted this contention and held that the prosecution has failed to prove that the Lal mirch powder was adulterated. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Corporation that the Public Analyst had found in the sample only nine living meals worm, that the report of the Public analyst did not satisfy the requirement of section 2(1)(f) of the Act and as such the Public Food Inspector was not competent to say as to what extent of insectinfestation would make the article "adulterated" within the meaning of section2(1) (f). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was clearly wrong in its inter pretation of section 7(1), (f) and (g) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. [473F] 2. Section 2(ia)(f ) of the Prevention of food must be read disjunctively. The mere proof of the article of food being 'filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insect free ing, rotin, decomposing or disguntating, would be per se sufficient to bring the case within the purview of the word "ad adulterated" as defined in sub cl. (f), and it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfit for life because it consisted wholly or in part of any filthy, putative, diseased, decompose or disowested food or being ' insect impute ' or being " insect fraest ing, roast infested" or that on account of the presence of the meal wain wormings the sample was unfitfor human consumption.[473F G] 3. The expression "or otherwise unfit for live" in sub clause (f ) and it should be read conjunctively and not disjunctively, that is, in association with what precedes it. [474G H] 4.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3(2) of the order. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced it to one under section 49 of the Registration Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant produced a number of lease deeds executed by him in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it has to see whether they are genuine or not and whether an inference of innocence can be drawn against them. [90 D E] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the appellant could not be regarded as doing business as a dealer unless a series of transactions by him of sale were proved against him. [92 F G] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , followed. (iii)The presumption under para 3(1)(a) of order cannot be drawn from proof of storage only. It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a person though the words "as a dealer" are not there because storage has reference to business as such. The fiction in the second sub paragraph must be carried to its logical conclusion. [93 G H] Manipur Adminis tration vs M/s. Nilla Chandra Singh; , followed, (iv)The High Court was right that the presumption under Para 3(3) could not he drawn against the appellant.

The appellant was the lessee of a certain land in respect of which he had been paying rent to the Receiver. The lease was determined by a notice to quit and the suit was decreed by the trial court. On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the decree but on second appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court held that the lease was not a monthly tenancy for one year and that the appellant was entitled to a decree in his favour. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the lease being a monthly lease, the appellant could not be ejected in contravention of the terms thereof; (2) the suit had been filed by the respondent after the expiry of the first annual lease and therefore the appellant 's suit was bound to fail; and (3) even if two successive tenancies were created for one period each year, the facts admitted and proved would go to show that the tenant held over after the second annual lease. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i) A tenancy from month to month or reserving a yearly rent can be made only by registered instrument, as laid down in section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. Section 106 of the Act provides that where there is a contract between the parties for one month and the lessee under the provisions of section 116, transfer of property, such agreement may be express or implied, and the terms of the lease may be varied by writing. The terms of a tenancy are not to be confused with the terms and conditions of the original lease. [278 D E] (ii) A lease from month 'to month under section 106 Transfer of property Act is not one from month lo month to monthly rent under section 116 Transfer of the said Act. The contract to the contrary is not a mere agreement for sale but one for possession of land in lieu of the land in suit and the only question left open was whether payment to the lessee amounted to payment to him. [279 E] In the Second Appeal preferred by the appellant against the dismissal of his earlier suit by the lower appellate court, the High COurt held that as the lease had been created for a period of two successive years, no operative tenancy at any time after December 1926 could be created. The question whether payment of an annual rent was tantamount to payment of rent arose from the date of the notice and not from the subsequent annual lease or from the termination of the tenancy. [280 F] (iii) A contract for one term only is a creature of statute. It does not create any rights in the parties. The mere fact that the parties might have intended to create a lease for one years, did not make it a lease from year to month under the provision of section 106 of Transfer of Goods Act.

The appellant, a resident of Delhi, instituted a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722/86 against the defendants, M/s Dagi Ram Pindi Lal and Smt. Devi Prasad, who were partners in a firm, under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The defendants contested the suit on the ground that the plaintiff was not entitled to privilege by the Income tax Department for production of documents relating to assessment proceedings of an assessee summoned by the Civil Court. The Trial Court held that the defendants had failed to prove their case and decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit in limine. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Section 138(1)(b) of the Income ' Tax Act are mandatory in nature and do not affect the powers of the courts to summon the production of the documents from the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964 relating to an assessee as confidential from the courts and the bar with regard to the production or disclosure of any information therefrom. [556D E] 1.2 The finality attached to an order of the Commissioner under Section 138 (1) (b) has no relevance to the exercise of powers by a court to summon a production of document from the Income. Tax Authorities after April l, 1964 for the said purpose. [560F G] 1:3. In the instant case, the question is limited to the jurisdiction or lack of it of a civil court to seek production of certain documents relating thereto. The finality which has been attached to the order of Commissioner under section 138(i)(b), has no significance to the power of the Court to summon that record. [561G H] 1 :4. Section 138 of the Act does not affect its powers of a court.

The plaintiff appellant filed a suit for partition and possession of the property which he claimed as an heir under Muhammadan Law. The trial Court decreed the suit but the first Appellate Court did not accept it. In second appeal, the High Court held that the gift was made in contemplation of death and was voidable. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Mujtzal is living at the time of the gift in the house of his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for about two years after the celebration of marriage, had lived along with him, for after the anniversary of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; his gift included immovable properties and it was accepted by the mother who took over possession on behalf of her minor daughter. [557 B C] (ii) The appellant 's father had no authority to transfer the property to his minor daughter, because, he was not a legal guardian of the person of Seinaba. He could have made a declaration of gift and taken possession on his behalf. There is nothing in law which prevents him from transferring the property. [558 C D] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that there was a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammotty and to transfer it to the donee. If Mammottty had handed over the deed to his wife, the gift would have been complete under Muhammadans but for her husband 's power. [559 E F] (iv) The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's mother when the gift is from the husband to his daughter or not is a question of fact. It is only actual or constructive possession that completes the gift and registration does not cure the defect nor is a bare declaration in the deed that possession was given to a minor of any avail without the intervention of the guardian of property unless the minor has reached the years of discretion.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 (Act 19 of 1951) was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and endowments in the State. The Act provided that the Commissioner shall make rules for carrying out all or any of the purposes of this Act and not inconsistent therewith. Section 76(1) provided for imposition of a graded levy of contribution. The respondents were trustees of the Venkataramana temple at Mulki, District South Kanara District. They filed a petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand was illegal. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 63, 64, 69 and 89 as amended by Act 27 of 1954 were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of the Madras Religious & Charitable Endowments (Amendment) Act, 1954 were ultra vires the State Legislature and that the rules framed under the Act had been invalid. HELD : The High court was right in holding that appropriate rules were not in existence at the time when the demand for contribution was made and on that account the demand could be premature. [919 D] The Commissioner of Hindu Endowments, Madras vs Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, ; , followed. The order passed by the High court upholding the claim of the respondent temple on this part of the case must therefore be set aside.

The appellant, a contemner under the provisions of the (the Act), was issued a preliminary objection that no appeal lies to this Court under section 19 of the Act from an order rejecting prayer for stay of proceedings. The notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the proceeding is not barred by section 20 of the , but it was incompetent as a matter of right from any order or decision of a bench of the High Court if the order had been made in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. In appeal to this court, HELD: The preliminary objection raised on behalf of the respondents that no Appeal lies to the Supreme Court under Section 19 of Act from the order rejecting the prayer for staying the proceedings is not correct. [512 A] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court, ; , referred to. Section 20 of Act does not confer any appeal against the alleged contemner and cannot be said to be incompetent even at an earlier stage. The matter has to be decided either finally or, may be, even at a later stage, as even at the earlier stage an order is made which does decide a contention raised before the High court affecting the right of the party aggrieved. [511 B C] Barodakanta Misra vs Orissa State, ; and Baradikanta Mishra v Orissa High, A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 1206, referred to, The matter had to be considered either finally, or, as the case may be. even at any earlier stage, an order was made which did decide a question of its being barred under section 20.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 6(1 A) of the Act has no application to a case of a later amending Act inserting new provisions in an earlier Act, for where an earlier act is amended by a later Act, it cannot be said that the earlier Act applies, incorporates or refers to the amending Act. [760 B] (ii) Section 4 of the Repealing and Amending Act of 1952, which was introduced into the Act of 1949, provided for a different situation, namely, the repeal of an earlier enactment which had been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later statute. The section did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. [761 C] (iii) Section 7 of the Amending Act, 1949, has no applicability to a present amending Act, and the word " text " is comprehensive enough to take in the subject as well as the terminology used in a statute. [762 D] (iv) The words " unless a different intention appears" in section 6A of the are comprehensive enough. The object of the said Act is not to give it any legislative effect but to excise dead matter from the statute book. The word " language " is wide enough to include the amending act. [763 E] (v) Section 5 of the Punjab General Clauses Act, 1913, has nothing to do with the continuance of an existing law in which the repealed enactment has been applied incorporated or refered to. The independent existence of the two Acts is therefore recognised; despite the death of the parent Act, its offspring survives in the incorporating Act. Therefore, section 4 of, the Repealing & Amending Act does not affect the continuance and effect of the amending law.

The appellant was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930 and as Shebait he executed a Hatchita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty who died on April 1, 1928. The properties mentioned in Sch. Ka and Kha were put up to sale and they were knocked down to Srimati Oramba Sundari by the two decreeholders. The appellant 's case was that the property described in Schedule Ka was sold and knocked down in favour Of one Naniitosh Chakravarty, a son of the settlor, who died in April 1928, on the basis of which he received advances from time to time. The question for determination was whether the properties mentioned therein were really benamidars for another person. Held, that the sale deed dated August 27, 1941, was not a fictitious transaction and could not be said to have been executed by the settlor himself in favour as a mere benamidar for another. It was not correct to say that the appellant was a mere benami owner for another, who had been put up for sale and had purchased the properties in execution of the decree. The deed dated September 27, 1940, was a fictitious one and did not create any title in favour the appellant in respect of the properties. The order for restoration of possession made by both the courts below was illegal and improper. Renula vs Manmatha, , applied. Per Sarkar, J. The sale itself was not annulled but was set aside on the ground that it was a benami transaction. It is well settled that a new decree is passed only for the purpose and so far as it is necessary to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Act. The object of restoring possession of properties sold in execution proceedings is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues and not to relieve the debtor from any liabilities which may be incurred by any other person. It would be wrong to say, therefore, that it is only a device for the benefit of another person that the court has not only the right but is under a duty to make an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale, or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decree holder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b) of section 36(2). Renula v Manmathas, , followed.

The respondent, a Hindu inhabitant carrying on business as merchants and pucca adatias in bullion and cotton at Bombay under the name and style of Habib & Sons, was a Hindu resident of Bombay. In 1948 he filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7113 7 0 with interest at 6 per cent per annum from the date of the institution of the suit till realisation. The appellant contended that the respondent had not transferred the decree to him by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore he was not entitled to apply for execution. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the transfer was a transfer of the decree that was expected to be passed in future and that as soon as it was passed the respondent company became the transferees of the said decree and therefore the equitable principle came into play and that the appellant was not bound by the said equitable principle. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the transfer of or an agreement to transfer a decree that may be passed under Order XXI rule 16, Code of civil Procedure, was valid as it had been made by a person who had transferred his interest in the decree and not by assignment. Held, that the words "decree holder" in section 146 of the Civil Procedure Code mean a decree holder in fact and not an assignee of the judgment debtor. The expression "decreeholder" in Order XXI Rule 16 means a decreeholder in possession of the property which is subject matter of a suit without being in existence at the time of the assignment or to be executed in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as if the application were made by such decree holder. The words " decree holder" must mean a person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so, while a transfer is an agreement for transfer. The word "decree" in O. XXI, r. 16 means an agreement between the parties to the contract and does not include a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to claim the beneficial interest in it after it has passed. The rule of construction which operates on the decree as soon it is passed and applies only where there is no decree in existence. In the present case, the transfer in writing was made "application for execution under O. 21, r., 16" and not "decree". The respondent could not claim to be a transferee of the original decree because he had transferred the property to him.

The respondent submitted a tender for the construction of a building. The appellant offered to fit the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. The respondent 's bid was accepted and the contract was for sale of windows. The Sales Tax Officer held that the contract with the Executive Engineer was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of its manufactured goods undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for the service, and the High Court in appeal held that it was not a contract of sale as defined by section 2(6) of the . The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The object of the respondent was to enter into a works contract. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge and were to he "fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with rawl plugs in cut stone work". The rate quoted by the respondent did not represent the sale price for service, but was an essential term of the contract. [516 D E] (ii) The contract in question was of the second variety and the price was to be revised in the light of cost revision of the controlled price of steel supplied to the respondent. The contract undertaken by the appellant was to prepare the window leaves according to specifications with Glass plain or Ground as decided. The contractor was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows. [511 E F] Arun Electrics, Bombay vs Commissioner of Sales Tax, Maharashtra State, ; , followed. (iii) The High Court was right in holding that it could not be said that the respondent agreed to sell the window leave as described in the tender or did it as part of a works contracts nor was the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. [ 512 E F; 512 A] Arun electrics, Bom. vs Commissioner, Bombay, ; and Arun Electric 's Bombay vs Union of India, , referred to. (iv) The question whether a particular contract is one for sale or is a contract for work in which the use of materials isaccessory or incidental to execution of the work, or it may be a contract with respect to the installation of materials was a mixed question of law and fact.

The appellant State filed a revision petition against the order of the High Court quashing the charge against him. The High Court quashed the charges framed by the Presidency Magistrate against the appellant and allowed the revision petition on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Aggarwal was concerned, no case had been made out against him and the charges were consequently quashed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the report of Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agarwalla respondent because it was the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report, and that the part which was attributed to Raj Kumar was not the same as that of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar was no mention in the report which had been lodged by the prosecution. [279 B] (2) There is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the trial court as it has not been shown that the High court had interfered with the order passed by the Magistrate. [280 C D] (3) The fact that the appellant appeared on a scene only subsequently after the lodging report was made no reference to the name in which the part alleged incident took place. [278 E F] (4) There was no cogent reason for interference. [ 279 G H] (5) The judgment of High Court is set aside and the case remitted back to the trial Court for fresh disposal according to law.

The petitioner, an allopathic doctor by profession, had himself prepared and filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution in this Court for implementing the reports of the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees appointed by the Government of Kerala. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional obligation by the Railways adequate safety measures had been undertaken by them. The Union Government had appointed three high powered committees for investigation into the affairs of the Railways with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. The Court directed that the petitioner should visit the delinquent with proper punishment. The State Governments appeared before this Court and filed an affidavit stating that the State Government had constituted a committee in the post independence period for investigation of the accidents and that the Committee was not working well, with effect from April 1, 1966, a Railway Safety Work Fund has been set up and expenses are being met out of it. The Committee submitted its report on September 2, 1982. In the counter affidavit filed by the respondents it was stated that the Government had decided to appoint three high Powered Committees in the Post independence period namely, the Kunazru,olkar and Sikri committees. The committee had also submitted its recommendations for payment of Rs.22 crores as compensation to the victims of accidents. It was further stated that there were as many as 27233 unmanned level crossings on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of about Rs.23 crores would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs,44 crores will have to be met. The respondents have denied some of the assertions of the petitioner that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and that there was no accident in the running trains. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is true that the Central and State Governments are not bound by the policy of the Government but it is proper that this is worked out also in the Railways. The obligation cast by the Railway Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It is relevant to point out here that in the counter affidavits the respondents have stated that they have denied certain assertions of petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to the stand taken in the writ peti tion. [717C D] 1.2 The Court is alive to the fact that Government have limitations, both of resources and capacity, yet it is not prudent and we do not think it necessary to issue directions. It may be that the policy decision of the Court should have been examined. ordinarily the powers of the court to deal with a matter such as this which prima facie appears to be wholly within the domain of the Executive, should have be examined. [617D E] 1:3 The obligations cast by Railways Act and Rules under the it must he complied with.[718F G] 1 :4. It cannot be said that the fundamental rights of the citizens are violated by one and denied by the other. The petitioners have not been able to satisfy this Court that they had not been injured on account or that no loss has taken any of them. They have denied all the assertions. [700H; 700A] 1 5. It would be wrong to say that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. The Railways are approaching the status of an imperfect society where capability of maintaining elementary security in the streets, in the schools and for homes of our people is in doubt. [750B] Shaw vs Director Public Prosecution, has observed that "the obligation cast on the Railway Administration to ensure availability of situations, circumstances and environments in which every citizen can effectively exercise and enjoy those rights".

The appellants were holders of jagirs. They applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer, Baroda under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, in respect of their proprietary jagirs, which was granted by the State Government under section 12 of the Jagirs Abolition Act. The appellants contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and 24, 1961, they were time barred. The Tribunal held that they were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration should have been made within 30 day of the date of the said order of dismiss ment. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the orders of the Tribunal dated February 1, 1962 and March 3, 1961 were illegal and ultra vires because the Tribunal dismissed the appeals for non prosecution and there was no decision of the appeals on merits. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non Prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits and to record its decision even though there is default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal. [144 C] (ii) Section 20 of the jagirs Abolition Act makes a decision of Tribunal in appeal as final and conclusive and not to be questioned in any suit or proceeding in any court. The language of section 17(1) of the jagir Abolition Act is clear that it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss the appeal for failure to appear and even so, it is subject to the provisions of this Act and to the previous approval of the State Govern ment. [145 E] (iii) Section 18(2) of Jagirs Abolition act makes a provision for restoration of an appeal or application made under regulation 20. The words "decide it on merits" in Regulation 19(1), are wide enough to include in its scope and ambit an application for restoration to the appellant 's claim in all the four cases.

The appellant was the Mahant of a temple within which he was appointed as the manager. The respondent 's case was that the appellant had committed breaches of trust by offering to the temple certain properties and that he had committed breach of such trust. He also alleged that the temple was dedicated absolutely to the deity in the temple by his descendants. The trial court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village Telibandha for the temple and that the respondent had committed a breach of trust as a trustee of the temple. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree of the trial court and directed the trial Court to dispose of the suit after giving an opportunity to the parties to lead evidence. The appellant contended that the dedication by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 was not proper or legal and that it was confirmed by all the co sharers at the time of partition of 1897. Held, that the High court had rightly held that the plaintiff 's claim for a declaration that the villageTelibandha was held by him was not correct. The fact that Ramsaran Lal used to credit the income from Teli Oriyayat in the partition suit did not make any difference as he was himself led by the terms of the Bagchi award into thinking that the property belonged to the family with only a charge on it for the expenses of the Temple and did not create any absolute ownership of the Village to the appellant. The High Court had rightly found that the use of words "from the profits and income" as out weighing or neutralising the numerous other provisions which point to an intention that Ramsalan Lal would not have the absolute ownership, implied in the use Of the word "malik".

The appellants were convicted by the High Court under section 5(1) of the U.P. High Court 's Act, 1953. The High Court discharged them on the ground that they committed contempt of court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the contumacious conduct of the respondents amounted to contempt and that the High Courts had not properly construed the resolution passed by the Bar Association. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts were right in holding that since the resolution was passed under the Presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 1, he is as much guilty of having committed contempt as contemner NO. 2 was. [602 D] (2) The language used by them was unfortunate. They did not think it proper and it should have been passed in that manner. It was not proper to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumactive conduct of which they were adjudged guilty though they were not guilty of contempt. [600 E F] (3) The judgment of the High court is set aside and the appellants are discharged. [613 G] (4) The matter becomes clear when the High 's said "we do not propose to punish contemner No 2 for contumacious acts" and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeated". [603 A B] (5) The contempt notice issued by the appellants was not correct. [599 C D] In the instant case, the High. Court did not wish to proceed against the appellants. The judgment and order of the trial court is quashed and set aside.

The appellants and their eldest brother respondent No. 1 were entered into an agreement with the four brothers for partition of joint movable and immovable properties and a deed of conveyance was executed by them in February, 1927. The said deed provided that the executant would execute the sale deed within a period of two years from the date of its execution. On or about November 28, 1977 the appellants filed an application under section 14 of the Act before the Sub Judge, Hooghly for registration of the award. The Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitrators ' application to return the award to them. On May 1, 1978 the arbitrators made an application before the sub judge praying for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the Court in Misc. Case No. 74 of 1977. The appellants filed objection under section 30 of the . The Sub judge fixed the date for filing the award on 28th January, 1978 and fixed the next day the arbitrators presented the award before the Subordinate Registrar, Arambagh on 25th November, 1983. On 25th February, 1983 the arbitrators applied to return back the award with an application for returning it to them under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The sub judge ordered return of the Award to the appellants holding that the limitation for registration had already expired. The High Court in revision held that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo till the disposal of Misc. case No.74 of 1977 initiated by the appellant No.1, the award was presented within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely, 28th of January 1978 to 24th November 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under section 15 of the , and that the cumulative effect of sections 23 and 25 read together is that total period of eight months is available for registration if the conditions are fulfilled. The award was made on 28st January, 1979 and it was presented for registration to the Sub Registrar on 25 th November,1983. On 24th June, 1985 the arbitrators filed an objection under Section 30 of . The sub Judge fixed 20th December, 1982 for return of award but that was not done. The appeals preferred by the appellants were dismissed by the High Court. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 An act of the court shall prejudice no man. In the instant case, admittedly during the period from 26th July 1978 to 20th Decem ber, 1983 there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps.

The appellant was the owner of a building in Kalyan. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground that the appellant had sublet the building to him. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the grounds of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged was not bona fide. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed the decree holding that section 15 of the Act completely prohibited sub letting and under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the landlord had the right to evict the tenant on account of sub letting. Held, that the provisions of section 15 were not applicable to a case where the plaintiff asked the Court to afford him a remedy against one who by contravening section 15 had made himself liable to eviction and those cases where the Court was called upon to assist the plaintiff in enforcing an agreement the object of which was to do an illegal act. The suit for eviction was not brought within the mischief of section 13 (1) (e) as it was not a case of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 was prohibited and made illegal. P. VII of 1944, referred to. The provisions of sections 15 and 16 of the Indian Contract Act were intended to protect the interest of the landlord and unless there was in the Act itself any provision to the contrary such rights as far as they were personal rights may be parted with or renounced by the landlord.

The appellant, a private limited company, was appointed as a temporary employee of the respondent Board. The respondent challenged the appointment on various grounds including the ground that the Standing Committee had no power to take the impugned decision and that the procedure adopted by the Board in conducting the examinations was contrary to law and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the standing committee had no authority to take a decision, since the Standing Commit tee did not apply its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and quashed the cancellation order. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the impugned Standing Committee 's action was illegal and could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Standing Committee did not have power under Article 226 or article 136 to interfere with the decision of the authorities. It is only in cases where the requirement has been dispensed with expressly or by necessary implication, an administrative authority exercising judicial or quasi judicial functions is required to record reasons. [799B] 1.2 When the Standing Education Committee takes the decision on behalf of the Divisional Board to which they are members and the decision is taken on its own motion, it is acting on behalf Of the Divisional Boards. Therefore, when the Standing Educational Committee takes a decision in respect of the use of unfair means at the final examination conducted by the Divisional board, it cannot be said that the conclusion reached by the Standing committee that the examinees, parents or guardians are parties to the fabrication cannot be sustained for the reason that the regulation itself postulates that if the Committee disagrees with the Inquiry Officer then only it is obligatory to record its reasons. The crucial question, therefore, is whether the conclusions reached by such a body can be fairly supported by the evidence on record then the High Court or this Court has to uphold the decision, though as appellate court of facts, may be inclined to take different view on re assessment of those circumstances. [789D E] 1:3. The finding of the Single Judge that the inspection, parents and guardians were parties to fabrication cannot also be sustained because the Standing Committees itself did not record any reason in support of its conclusion that the examination conducted was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardian. It was only after the Standing Board 's taking the decision that the appellant had used unfair means in answering questions then it is not open to the High court under article 226 to itself evaluate the evidence and to quash the impugned notification. [788E F] 1 :4. The conclusion reached on the basis of the admission made by the respondents that the fabrication was done by either the examina tionees or their parents or the guardian was amply borne out from the record, is not correct. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [ 789E F; 791A] Shanti Prasad Jain vs The Director of Enforcement, ; , referred to. 1:5.

The appellants were charged with criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct by paying a sum of Rs. 2,000 to Madan Lal and in addition to this amount they also stood charged with an offence under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court found that the three accused had been guilty of the offence under sections 120 B, I.P.C., and convicted them. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the prosecution was barred by section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act. Section 5(1) of that Act provides for punishment for criminal misconduct in the discharge of his duty, and section 405 of the Indian Penal Code provides for penalties for abetment of criminal conduct by a public servant. The object of the Act as set out in the preamble is to make more effective provisions for the prevention of bribery and corruption. It is not necessary that each case should be tried separately from one another. A speedy disposal of corruption cases by special courts, the benefit of in vestigation by higher police authorities are some of the provisions intended for the protection of public servants prosecuted under the Act while they are subjected to a penalty prescribed by section 161 of the Code. The fact that the appellants were not charged with any offence under the Penal Code did not make them guilty of criminal conspiracy punishable under section 120 B of the Penal code. The prosecution was therefore barred by limitation. The case of Gian Chand did not stand on any different footing from that of the other appellants.

The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368/4/ with interest at the rate of 18% per annum from the date of the decree till realisation and future interest at 6%. The principal debtor executed a demand promissory note, Ext. 81 in favour of the Bank on September 16, 1957 and on the same day the principal debtor also executed a bond in favour off the Bank for payment of the amount due. The principal creditor executed a security bond in his favour in favour 'the Bank. On personal guarantee of the surety, the appellant bank executed a promissory note in favour the Bank. The appellant 's application for restitution under section 144 was dismissed by the trial court and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of letter of guarantee Ext. 31, even if it is found as a fact that negligence of the creditor bank was responsible for the loss of security of pledged oil tins, yet the surety would not be discharged from his obligation under the guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on the clear understanding that the principal creditor has offered security by way of pledge of goods and the goods were to be in the custody of the creditors Bank. Even if it was found as an fact that the negligence of creditor bank is responsible for loss of the security of the pledged oil, yet once the right of the sureties against the principal debtors is impaired by any action or inaction which implies negligence appearing from lack of supervision undertaken in the contract, the surety will be discharged under the combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Act. [923D E] 2. The respondent surety has made an application that in compliance with the decree made by the Trial Court he had paid the entire amount and he should not be exposed to second round of litigation for restitution of the amounts and that this Court should give a direction to the Bank as part of this judgment that the amount be returned with interest. [936F G] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the surety had agreed and had in fact pledged 5,000 tins of oil which even if sold at the then current market price would have satisfied the Bank 's entire claim. It is difficult to entertain a contention that section 141 would not apply and the surety could not be relieved from the obligation undertaken under the letter of Guarantee. [981G H] 4. The Bank has made a representation that in complying with the order made by it he had made an applica tion that in comply with the judgment of the High court.

The appellant was the holder of a jagir and was assessed to income tax for the year 1941. The respondent claimed that as a result of partition, the "patelki inam" lands were divided into two parts, one part being an inam grant and the other part being a grant of emoluments of his office. The claim was rejected by the Deputy Commissioner on the ground that the appellant had no right to hold the " patelki Inam" lands which were given as emoluments of the patel. The appellant then filed a suit for a declaration that the respondent was not entitled to hold "patels" in the jagir and prayed for a decree for possession. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal, the High Court substantially held that the lands were granted by the Government by way of remuneration or emoluments for the office of patel and that the grant was valid. Held, that the land was not "poli" within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1928, as it stood before its amendment in 1948. The grant was made by the sovereign authority which the Nazim confirmed in accordance with old judicial usage; but the grant did not confer any new right nor did it create a new title or create a fresh right in respect of the emoluments. The order of the Government dated August 28, 1922, was therefore valid and binding on the appellant. Venkata Jagannadha vs Veerabadrayya, I.L.R. (1943) Pat. 1, disapproved.

The respondent, who was the father of two respondents, died in 1955 leaving behind his widow and three daughters. The appellant 's son, who had migrated to Pakistan, filed a suit for partition of the estate of her husband, claiming that the entire property held by her was liable to estate. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed it holding that the respondent 's father had no right to succeed to the estate and that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondents were entitled to the properties. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a person is entitled as against a large number of persons who are not members of a joint Hindu family or of a deceased member of a Hindu Joint Family can be decided only by the courts in India and not by the High Courts. [241 G] (ii) The rule of devolution of property by survivorship was applicable to parties who were Cutchi Memons in the matter of inheritance and succession, including rules as to joint family property. The Act came into force on November 1, provided that all Cutchi memories shall in matters of succession and inheritance be governed by the Mahomedan law. [242 A] (iii) The Act was passed with a view to provide for the devolution of certain properties amongst Hindus. It was not proved before him that the cutchi Memon sect amongst the Hindus had acquired any interest by birth in the property inherited by his father from his ancestors. [243 B C] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that as there were no reported decisions on the position of the Cutchi members who had settled down in Madras, the Act came to an end and the Act would apply to the Cutch. [245 D E] (v) The definition of joint family does not include a Hindu law which applies to cutchi memons in matters relating to matters of inheritance. It is only when there are no reported decision on the question that it can be said that the accountable persons, having been born lone before 1948, had already acquired a right by birth. [246 B] (vi) The fact that the Cutchell Sait vs Ebrahim Hajee Aboo Bucker Sait, ; , referred to.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. The yarn so obtained is further processed in an integrated process in the said composite mill of the appellant No. 1 for weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not disputed that the yarn so purchased at an intermediary stage is subjected to the integrated process of weaving the said yarn. The appellant No 1, therefore, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid notification and the demand for excise duty. The High Court held that yarn obtained and further processed within the factory for the manufacture of fabrics could not be subjected to excise duty as it was produced at an inter state stage of the mill of appellants and subjected to integrated process for the purpose of weaving, and that the said goods were liable to excise duties in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The writ petition filed by the appellants was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High court holding that the retrospective effect given by section S l(1) will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. Hence this appeal by the appellant company. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The language of rule 9(1), which admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises appurtenant to the place of manufacture or production of the excisable goods. [707D] 2.1 The specification that is required to bemade under rule 9 (1) is of no consequence, because, so long as any product manufactured in such factory is not actually removed from the said factory, there is no removal and, therefore. such intermediate product although known to the market and comes under a particular tariff item yet, as there is nothing to show that it is only when the goods are removed from one plant to another it will be removal for the purposes of payment of duty. [077E F] 2:2 The expression "place of removal" in rule 9 contemplates the collection of duty levied on the production of a commodity at an appellate stage of an integrated activity of manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of the commodity at the intermediate stage to be removal from such place or premises of manufacture. It is not possible to say that the expression " place of removal", in rule9 contemplates only when there can be fictional removal as provided in the Explanation to rule 9. [807G H] 2 :3 The specification is not required to he made and, in our view, cannot be made of the place where the excisable commodity is manufactured or cured or manufactured or any premises ancillary thereto. It has been already noticed that the taxing event under section 3 of the Central Excise & Salt Act is the production or manufacturer of goods and not removal. [607H; 717A] 2I The contention of the appellants that without such specification there cannot be any deemed removal, fails. In view of section I IA of the Finance Act, 1982, the expression 'place of removing ' as defined therein does not contemplate any deemed removing, but a physical and actual removal of the goods from a factory or any other place or Premises of production or manufacturing or manufacture or a warehouse etc.

The petitioner, a holder of a permit issued under Chapter IV A of the Act to ply a stage carriage on Bulandshahr Siana Garh Bugrasi Brijghat Bhasians Shambha Nath Jadol Jahangirabad route in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner filed objections to the scheme and the State Transport Undertaking submitted its objection along with several others. After considering the objections, the State Government passed an order under section 68 C of the . The petitioner challenged the said order before the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by him since the jurisdiction was impliedly excluded. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a State Government (the hearing authority under section 69 D of the , is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining the hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing of the case and exercising its statutory functions. Whenever statute uses the expression that a decision of an authority shall be final, the jurisdiction is the jurisdiction which the jurisdiction has taken away. [544D E] 2. The jurisprudential concept of territorial jurisdiction is that it is created by the provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the Motor Vehicles Act for bringing jnto force an approved or modified scheme which would have the effect of excluding completely or partially other persons from operating motor service vehicles on any route or in any area. After the scheme became final, as provided in sub section (iii) of section 68 D of Act, the transport authorities concerned can issue permits only in accordance with the scheme, and the other provisions contained therein. This Court has gone through the plaint presented in this case.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellant had been convicted for an offence under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5 (1)(d) of that Act and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo further period of six months under section 6(2). The appellant was convicted by the Special Judge under section 165 I. P.C., and section 165 read with section 5. (2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and section 6 (2), and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for a period of two years. On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's R.I. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence within the meaning of section 5 of the Act and that the concealed facts disclosed that there was a gross abuse of his official position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case, the conviction under section5(2), was bad. HELD : The order of sanction must be set aside. (i) The order did not amount to an offence of 'any kind ' under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant has obtained money from Russel Nathaniel, it cannot be said that the accused had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act or for showing or forbidding to show in the exercise of his authority favour or disfavour to any per son. [186 G H] (ii) The appellant grossly abused his position as a police officer and extorted money from him by offering a gold ring from Ruscent Nathannyiel and his wife and also a gold chain from Roshan Lal. The charge against the appellant was established. [187 B C] Mahesh Prasad vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , followed. (iii) The sentence imposed is not excessive. The High Court was in error in holding that the conviction was bad as no reasonable explanation had been given by the appellant for his long and unexplained delay in lodging the first information report.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. The prosecution case was that on or about May 12, 1952, the appellant had accepted Rs. 100 as illegal gratification from one L and had accepted the sum as a motive or reward for showing favour to disapproval in seeing that a speedy and favourable settlement of the claim cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway was possible. The charge under section 161 I.P.C. was that he had accepted a bribe from L and gave the sum of Rs, 100 to the appellant in October 1951, as illegal reward for making a pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section 420 I. P. C. and for the offence of criminal misconduct by illegal and corrupt use of his official position as a public servant to obtain a pecuniary benefit for himself, punishable under s 5(1) (d) of that Act. The trial court found that the sanction accorded in this case was not a valid sanction but a valid one. On appeal the High Court held that the sanctioning authority had acted without jurisdiction and that the appellant could not be put on his trial in a court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 165 I.p.C., and convicted him accordingly. Held, that the order granting the certificate was not invalid because it was made by the Chief Commercial Superintendent who was competent to grant the sanction. The sanction clearly stated all the facts which concern the prosecution case alleged against the appellant with reference to his acceptance of Rs 100 from counterfeit and accepted a sum of money as a bribe for showing favourit to disapproval of the bribe by the appellant on May 12. 1952, in circumstances which, if established, would constitute offences under s 161 I P.C.; but it was not open to the High court to hold that the authority accorded his sanction was a valid order. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1924) L.R. 65 I.A. 129 and Gokulchand Badridas Morarshi vs The State of Bombay, ; , referred to.

The appellant was the holder of life interest in the property. He had two other properties, one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purposes. The tenancy under the landlord was admitted by the tenants there is also no question with regard to validity of the notice of eviction. The tenant filed a suit for eviction against the tenants on the ground that the building was bona fide required by him for demolition and reconstruction. The trial court held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of the tenants. On appeal, the High Court set aside the orders of the appellate authority and allowed the appeals to the extent that the landlord had no right to evict the respondents on the grounds of demolition and re construction. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard tO the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. [275E] In the instant case, the Act with which the High Courts refused to interfere in revision, was a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others; , followed. The Act withwhich the High courts were concerned is a self contain and complete Code for regulation and regulation of rights between landlords and tenants, as defined under the Act.

The respondent decree holder filed a suit against the appellant decree holder for the recovery of certain trees. The decree holder contended that after the coming into force of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. The executing court held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the Act in the State of Uttar Pradesh new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the , and therefore, the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force was provided in section 73 of the . The executing Court also held that the only course in which the respondent 's property could enforce the decree against trees in respect of any part of bhumidhari right, execution should have proceeded against trees. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after its coming into operation of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964, what can still be purchased by a mortgagee would have been held to vest under section 6(h) of the amending Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that after vested of all rights mentioned therein in the U .P. Act in State of U. P., new bhumidar 's groves are equated and groves were on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. [532B] 2. The definition of intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of U P. Zamindari abolition and Land Reform Act, 1951, is not applicable to the instant case since the respondent decree holders had no right to hold the property in any partof bhumidhari Rights, execution of all their rights mentioned under section 4 of the Abolition Act in respect thereof in the state of Uttar pradesh. [32F] 3. The position taken by the executing court that there is a distinction between trees and a grove and grove land should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the High Court (Lucknow Bench).

The appellants were charged with offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324, 326 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC. The prosecution case was that the first appellant and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW3 Devassothan turned hostile and did not support the prosecution case. The trial court convicted both the appellants under Section 302 IPC and each one of them was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court acquitted all the accused except the first accused and confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against them by the Sessions Judge. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there were some other known or unknown persons who had also been charged for the substantive offence of murder under Section 326/149 IPC and that the injuries inflicted by the first two accused were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the deceased. It was further submitted that the High Courts erred in holding that besides the four accused convicted by it, there were other known and unknown persons also who had been charged with the substantive offences of murder punishable under Section 307 IPC. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The effect of acquittal of the two accused persons by the High court and without the aid of Section 149 Cr. P.C., is that an assembly of less than five members is not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 and cannot, therefore, form the basis for conviction for an offence with the aid or Section 149 I.P.C. [94A B] 1.2 The effect and effect of the acquittal of two accused person by the trial court and the High COurt on the type of weapons with which they were armed and nature and seat of injuries inflicted in ordinary course would be that for all intent and purposes the two acquitted accused persons were not members of the unlawful assembly. Thus only four accused could be said to have been the members of a assembly but such an assembly which consisted of lessthan five members was not an illegal assembly within meaning of section 141 I.p. [95B C] 1:3. The effect or the acquittal by the Trial Court and without its being given the benefit of doubt, is that the conviction of the first appellants for an offences under Section 324 IPC is unwarranted and cannot be sustained. That apart, according to the medical evidence, none of the injuries allegedly caused by this appellant was either individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused by him, sufficient in his ordinary course to cause his death.

The assessee, Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd., is a non resident company having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. The assessee, a nonresident company, had its place Of business at Bombay in the U.K. In the year 1967 68, it had its branches at Copetral and its branches in the State of U.P. The question for determination was whether the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis for 1967 68 or 69 assessment if the books and balance sheet of such receipts were found to be maintained on cash system and directed fresh assessment on such basis. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal by certificate, it was contended that (i) since the Indian Company had credited to the assessee in its account books for the relevant years (accounting year for the Indian company), no part of the royalty amount has been received by it and therefore nothing is taxable; (ii) the assessee could be said to have received the royalty money only when it receives the same in U. K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own books at Co operative Society, and (iii) since it did not file any return under section 5(2)(a) of the Act, it could not be said that the assessee had received the amount. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "any person" used in section 145 is a word of wide import and includes all persons who are residents of U P. [105A] 2. In order to attract income tax under section 145(1) of Income Tax Act, 1961, it must be shown that the assesee was keeping his accounts in regard to a particular income regularly on the cash basis. It is not necessary to express any opinion on the question whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between section 5 (2) and section 145 of the Income Tax. [106B] 3. The word "income" has been used in the context of section 145 to mean income derived from the United States for paying its taxes in India, but it cannot be said so as to include income by the assessee because the expression "income from the U P." Section 145 was not applicable to this case. [107C] 4. The words "any other person" occurring in section 5 of the Indian Act have no application whatsoever and that section 5 is not attracted. [108D] 5. In view of the above, it is unnecessary for the Tribunal to express its opinion on question whether the assessee was entitled to receive the amount as claimed by the asses see. [109E] 6. The contention of the assessee that mere entry in the books of the assesses cannot amount to receipt and that the amounts cannot be assessed until they were actually paid over to the non resident companies or dealt with according to its directions, is not correct. [110F] 7. The fact that the Indian Companies were maintaining accounts on mercantile basis does not amount to receipts by the assessees. The practice evidently was that the I.T.O. assessed the amounts credited in the accounts of the assesseers as the income of the nonresident companies.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code read with section 34 of the Indian Penal code and sentenced to death. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars from the evidence of an accomplice and that the conviction was unsustainable, but confirmed the conviction. Held, that the evidence given by the approver was sufficient to convict him. The fact that the appellant had a suspicion that the deceased bad a liaison with his wife was not sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder under section 34 Indian Penal. The evidence of the approver in this case was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which the High Court relied. The circumstances proved by the prosecution were sufficient to sustain the conviction and the High court had rightly convicted him. Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, (1949) L.R. 76 I.A. 180, referred to. Held further, that in the present case the evidence was sufficiently supported for the appellant 's conviction. The conviction of an accused on the testimony of an approver could not be sustained. The law being that there should be corroboration of the accomplice in material details and qua each accused it is necessary for there being independent corroboration of his story that the first appellant made a confessional statement to his brother. Bhurboni Sahu v King, A.I.R., 1930 P.C. 308, referred. Held also, that under section 133 of the Evidence Act a conviction based merely on the uncorroborated testimony of the witness cannot be sustained unless he is corroborated in material parts.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. He was charged with having committed offences under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted him under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal by the State Government the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's R.I. The appellant contended that (i) the appellant was not a public officer within the language of section 5 of the Act, and (ii) the conviction was bad as it was not based on any evidence. Held:(1) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of Government within the terms of section 2 of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958. He could be deemed to be a public servants only when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of that Act. (2)The appellant could not be deemed as a public Servant within the mischief of section 3(1)(d) because he was not acting or purported to act on behalf of the State Electricity Board constituted under the provisions Of the . (3)The conviction was illegal and the appellant should have been convicted for the offences. The word 'officer ' in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal code means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances a delegated function of Government. (4)The words "public servant" in section 2(12) of that Code mean some person who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. The words "Public servant" are not defined in the Act. The expression "public servants" includes every officer in an service or post engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of a Government company as defined in section 617 of the . The word "officer" in the definition of "officer", there means some persons employed to do certain things and not necessarily in some circumstances. The definition of 'officer" there means an officer employed to discharge certain duties and are generally equated with those of a public authority. The distinction between a public official and a public employee is that they are immediately auxiliary to those of the public servant who isarmed with such authority or representative character; but, if their duties are immediately superior to the public representative character, then the charge of such duty would be immediately auxiliary. In the present case the appellant had been an officer of the Government and was in service of the Corporation as defined by section 21(9) of Act 54 of 1948. The question whether sanction of the government was required under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or not, therefore, was one of fact. The High Court found that the appellant 's appointment was not an "public officer" within the ambit of section 6 of the , and therefore a "public Servant" within section 21 (9) Of the Act could not have been considered as a Public servant within section 3 of the prevention of Corruption act.

The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1962. The High Court modified the sentences passed on him and instead of the sentences awarded by the lower courts sentenced him to imprisonment already undergone. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) was ultra vires because it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture is not ultra vires. Rule 141(1) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). If otherwise valid, they would have effect notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid they would be void. [273 G] The rule is within powers conferred on the Collector to seize stocks but does not enable the Court to forfeit the juar. In the present case the order of forfeiture was passed under section 133(2). It is true that the rule is in the following terms: "The provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect, notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act". The only provision contained in the Maharashtra Act is regarding forfeiture to the Government of packages, coverings or receptacles in which any stocks of jowar are found. This obviously does not entitle the Court, to order forfeiture of Juar. [272 G H] In the instant case the High court has modified the sentence passed on the appellant and instead it modified the orders of forfeiture. The appellant was therefore guilty of contravening the provisions of the two orders mentioned above.

The two brothers of the deceased, who were working as a lawyer and after finishing his work for the day, left the Fatehgarh Court along with the brother lawyers. The deceased was a practising lawyer and later on he succumbed to his injury at 5 25 p.m. On the following morning he went to the Fatehgarh court along with his brother and other persons. He was tried by the Sessions Judge under section 302 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Sia Lal and his companions were carrying guns and hockey sticks and therefore they would know that they had all gathered to commit the murder of Kunwar Singh. HELD: (i) The High court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court in favour of S, S,ia Ram. [626 B] (ii) The evidence shows that S was a lawyer who was working as an advocate with a doctor and he had stated that he had appeared for the complainant in a prosecution arising out of the murder. It is true that S, his companions could not say if he would be able to recognise Balister and that it was possible that he may not be able lo do so. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the crime, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder.[626 C D] (iii) The fact that S had been a practising advocate with Sia 's compounder but that might rather explain why he agreed to do so would not make him a party to the murderous design. [625 E F] (iv) The question whether S was aware of the nefarious design of S should be corroborated by evidence of identification.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted all the accused but convicted him under section 307 read with Section 34, I.P.C. In appeal by special leave it was contended that when three of the four named accused were acquitted they should not have been convicted under s. 302 readwith section 34, Indian Penal code and sentenced them to imprisonment. HELD : (i) The High court has rightly found that though accused 1, 3 and 4 were acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointly along with one of the named persons. There must be some foundation in the evidence that persons other than those named have taken part in the commission of the offence and if there is such a basis the case will be covered by the third illustration. In the first instance, the Court certainly can convict two or more of the said persons on the ground that their identity has not been established. But in the second illustration, the court certainly can acquit one of them on the basis of constructive liability. [683 E F] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. (ii) The appellant was rightly convicted under S. 302, read with s. 34, Penal Code for having committed the murder of the deceased jointly with the three accused who had been acquitted. The conviction of the appellant under section 3, I .P. C., for having commit ted the offence jointly with him, is set aside and he is convicted under that section. [684 E F; 683 A] Mohan singh vs State Of Punjab, , referred to. (iii) In the second instance, when three or more persons were acquitted either on the evidence adduced by the prosecution or after the High Court in appeal, the result would be the same, it would mean that they did not take part in an offence. [685 E F]. Mohan Singh v State of Bihar, ; and Mohan Singh V. State of Haryana, A.I.R.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of sheets, filed bills of entry on 30th July, 1984 for ware under section 59 of the . The goods were bounded on 7th August, 1984. The goods arrived at Bombay Port on 12th June, 1984 and were loaded in trucks. The petitioner was informed that the income tax authorities had imposed ban under section 132(1) of the Income Tax Act 1961. The Petitioner 's agent contacted the customs authority for clearance of the goods. The demand was arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional. The Assistant Collector of Customs rejected the claim of the petitioner on the ground that the consignments were not received by him as required by the petitioner. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee. In the Special Leave Petition to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that in view of the language used in section 15(1)(b) of Act, it is difficult to hold that the rate of exchange at which the goods name and address were cleared from the warehouse prior to the coming into force of the Ordinance would be the rate and valuation in force. Dismissing the Special leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The prohibition under section 15 (1)(a) of Central Excise Act, 1961 is not attracted. [626C] 2.1 The prohibition is not a penal provision. It relates only to the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part 111 of the Constitution. Unless a question of the enforcement Of a fundamental right arises, article 32 does not apply. There can be no question of infringement of a fundamental rights under Article 32 of the Constitu tion. [625D] 2:2 In the instant case, the petitioner as such has no fundamental right to clear any goods imported without payment of duties in accordance with law. The petition is accordingly dismissed. [526G] Smt.842 of the report as indicated hereinbefore clearly shows that the goods have been cleared pursuant to that order.

The appellant, who was the managing director of a company which went into liquidation, filed an application under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code for possession of certain properties belonging to the company.
