The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed that decision and held that the debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the share of the sons did not pass to the auction purchaser; and that what could legally be sold under section 156 of the Code was the right, title and interest of the defaulter. Held, that where a pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and (1) A.I.R. 1939 P.C. i.e., on the principle of pious obligation on the part of the son to discharge the debt of his father, the presence of the two sons coupled with their shares of their liability to be sold or be a means of reducing the efficacy of the attachment or impair the rights of the creditor is not necessary because they still have the right to challenge the sale on showing that immoral or illegal purpose of the debt has been discharged. The liability of the father to discharge debts of the deceased father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the appellants to discharge their debts of their father. The legal position in such cases is that where the pious obligations exist and partition took place after decree and the right title and interests of a judgment debtor are set up for sale as to what passes to the highest bidder, is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for auction sale.

The Delhi Administration and its officers were charged with offences under section 8 B of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The petitioners in this case were convicted by the Metropolitan Magistrate for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C. and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. The High Court dismissed their revision petitions against the orders of the Committee directing the filing of a complaint against them before the Committee. In the writ petition filed by the petitioners, it was contended that they were persons who fall under section 2(1) of the Act and have to be dealt with accordingly. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The orders of this Court directing the file of the complaints and the criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Metropolitan Magis trate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf of the committee should be quashed and they should be discharged. [521D] 2. The Committee 's own opinion formed in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, all those persons to whom notices under section 9 B have been issued have to he examined at the end of the inquiry. This is obvious from the order of the Commis sioner passed on 29th June 1988 after it was asked by this Court by its order dated June 2, 1988 to reconsider the whole question relating to the order in which the witnesses had to be examined in the case. [ 521E F] 3. The action of the petitioners in asking them to be cross examined at their end is discriminatory. Mere non issue of notices to them under section8 B ought not to make any difference if they otherwise satisfy the conditions mentioned in section 8B.

The petitioners who were the partners of a firm, and whose business was carried on by them in motor vehicles, challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, as amended by the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Rules, 1959. The petitions were dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Act did not impose any tax on fares and freights attributable to routes outside the State except in one instance which was contemplated by the proviso to sub section (1) of section 3 of the Act and therefore the Act was unconstitutional. Held, that the levy of a lump sum payment under the Rajasthan passenger transport business was justified on the ground that it was not obligatory, and a person can elect to pay tax calculated on actual fares and charges attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan. The tax is for purposes of State, and falls upon passengers and goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. The expression "shall" used both in Rules 8 and 8 A and the notification under section 3(1) does not cease to be a tax on passengers and Goods. The words "may accept". The two rules and the notifications are valid. The levy of lump sum in lieu of the tax is justified on a lump payment in lieu thereof and rules 8 and 9A and the Notification also do not cease as a tax. The State Government is empowered to grant exemption from the Act by general or specific order to any person or class of persons.

The appellant company was a private limited Company having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry. The raw material for its manufacturing process was tin plates. The appellant served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen, who were sought to be retrenched by the respondent employer, alleging non availability or raw materials to utilise the full installed capacity, power shedding limiting the working of the unit to 5 days a week, and also prayed for reinstatement with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures. The Labour Court held that retrenchment was invalid and directed the reinstatement effective from the day on which it was sought to take back the workmen. The High Court also awarded full back wages to the workmen, on its finding that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power sheding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and, therefore, the retrenchment had been illegal. The question whether the workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement was no more open to challenge. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Labour court has rightly held that the workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated and, consequently, the workman was directed to be reinstated effective from that date. [567F] 1.2 In the present case, the relief for reinstatement had been granted and the award had been implemented and the retrenched workmen were reinstated in service. The only question is whether the Labour Court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back Wages to the workman. [568G H] Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman, ; , referred to. 1.3 In the instant case, there was no material on record to show that the workman were always ready to work but they were kept away therefrom. On top of it, the were forced to litigation upto the apex Court and now they are being told that something less than full back wage should be awarded to them. When it was held that termination of service was neither proper nor justified, it would not only show that workmen were always willing to serve but if they rendered service they would legitimately be entitled to wages for the same. If the normal rule in a case like this is to award full backwages, the burden will be on the appellant employer (l) [1971] 1 Law Journal 327, 327 and Workmen of M/s. Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Limited, Calcutta vs their workmen, ; referred to 2.1 In the matter of retrenchment of workmen, the Supreme Court may in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry, direct scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too. [569B] 2.2 The award shall stand accordingly modified to the effect that the retrenched workman who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the amount paid to them as wages when recalled for work since the date of retrenchment and adjustment of the retrenchment compensation towards the amount found due and pay able. [570C] 2:3 In appropriate cases, the Court may, in the manner directed by this Court or disclosed such other exceptional circumstances that he may not survive to see the day when relief is granted. If after such a protracted time and energy consuming litigation during which period the workman just sustains himself, ultimately he is to be told that though he will be reinstated, he will he denied the back Wages which would be due to him, the workmen would be subjected to a sort of penalty for no fault of his and it is wholly undeserved.

The accused was charged with the murder of his wife. The prosecution case was that on the night of occurrence at about 10.30 p.m., Churi deceased had gone to the house of one Shri Sudershan Kumar Mahajan, a resident of village Gani. At about 10 P.M. when he was going to Kotkhai, the accused and his wife were seen together at the house. The accused asked the deceased to take Churl and the deceased told him that an accused had not been treating her well. The deceased told them that he had been illtreating Churi. The police party reached the house and the accused was seen by the witness with the deceased. The dead body of the deceased was recovered from the house, and a blood stained Khokhri and shirt were seized from the place of occurrence. The statement of the accused recorded by Shri Mahajan as well as other circumstances of the case showed that he was in possession of the stolen property. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted the accused under section 302 I.P.C. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the statement made by the accused to Shri Mahajan before the police regarding a murderer having come to the residence of Shri Mahajan was not admissible in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Evidence Act; (ii) the material on record showed that the accused had been in possession at the time when the crime took place, and (iii) the fact that the relations of the two accused with the victim were strained would not make any difference. HELD : (i ) The statement made to the police about a murderer being a result of his adulterous conduct cannot be accepted because there is nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder. Had the confession been recorded at a stage prior to the commencement of investigation, there would be no bar to the admissibility of such a confession. [437 B] (ii ) The fact that a person who was not a member of the family of the suspect had made an extrajudicial confession before a police officer cannot be considered as evidence against him.

The plaintiff sued the defendant for a sum of Rs. 80,000 and odd on the mortgage. The defendants pleaded that the mortgage was not a mortgage but a loan and so the suit was barred by section 43 of the Contract Act. Held, that the whole law of mortgage in India including the law of contribution arising out of a transaction of mort gage is statutory and is embodied in the Transfer of Property Act read with the Civil Procedure Code. The whole law is statutory. It is always open to a court to give a plaintiff such general or other relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in costs. In the present case the plaintiff was entitled to claim the balance of Rs., 80,507 7 4 and interest on the amount decreed by the trial court. The plaintiff 's only remedy is under section 92 of the Transfer Of Property Act and not under section 93 of the Indian Contract Act, but it is always subject to the provisions of sections 82 and 83 of the Act. The entire law of mortgages in India, including the Law of contribution arose out of the transaction of mortgage and was governed by the Transferof Property Act. In view of the fact that the plaintiff had not used the word "subrogation" he has asked for a declaration of charge and for a decree under Order XXXIV, Civil Procedure C.P.C. Held further, that in the absence of agreement be tween the parties as to the figures, the figures are ascertained and no prejudice is caused to the plaintiff ' s claim to which a subrogee would be entitled under the Transfer o Property Act, and the plaintiff has also asked for declaration of charges and a decree for sale.

The appellant No. 1 secured 29.50 marks out of 50 marks in the interview and 69.96 marks in all 91.23 marks out from 150. The appellants applied for the post of Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) for the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. Appellant No. 2 secured 52.40 marks out Of 50 marks. The appellant No 1 secured 24.83 marks in both the written test and interview. The second appellant obtained 24.1983 marks in interview and 66.40 mark in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out o the 150. In all 91,23 marks were kept at 100 and 50 for interview. Thus the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks. Applications were invited for the posts of Asstt., Engineers ( Civil) and the appellant No 2 obtained 24 marks in each of the written examination. The first appellant secured 2950 marks in every other Department according to the Rules of 1973 and was eligible to be appointed as Asstt. Engineer (Civil). Respondent No. 3, who was a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil), having secured 69.95% marks inalloto nal Engineering and both the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appel lant No.1 secured 24 marks outof 50 marks out af 150. Respondent No 2 secured 24,83 marks. Respondent Nos. 3 to 5 were not appointed in merit. Aggrieved against the aforesaid decision of the State Government, the appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33. 3% was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. S.C.R., 657, and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors, J.T. on 24th May, 1990, the High court dismissed the petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violation o the dictum laid down by this Court. In case of selection under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [497C D] 1.2 The Rules were clearly in contravention of the ratio laid down in Ashok Kumari Yadav & ors. vs state of Haryana and Ors., J. T. On a direction given by this court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the Selection Committee was produced before this Court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that a large number of candidates have been selected though they had secured much lesser marks than their appellants in the qualify examination but had secured very high marks in their viva voce out of50 marks kept for this purpose. Thus it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of tho total marks and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appellant were bound to be selected and a large numbers of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appel late appellants. In view of the fact that appointments under the aforesaid Rules were already made as it was back as the appellants had already joined the posts, this case is not considered as it has just and proper to quash the selections on the above ground.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the prosecution has failed to prove conspiracy and that he had been implicated in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As this Court pointed out in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , the confes sion of a co accused, is not formal evidence against another co accused person in the case but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. [408B C] 1.2 In the instant case, the prosecution had established that the appellant was regularly visiting Sadanand at the jail and that the story of bribing the jail officials had been introduced. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadanand on the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [413D E] 1:3 The confession of a Co accused is neither substantive evidence nor substantive evidence. It is well settled that the confession of co accused cannot be treated as substantive evidence in the trial. [414E F] Kashmira singh vs State, ; ; Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr.

The appellants were the workmen of the respondent company. They were the first appellant and its main activity was to invest money in manufacturing concerns. The last three companies were controlled by the first company, namely, Greaves Cotton & Co., in one way or the other and that is how the main activity came within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the . The Tribunal found that the appellants had not shown any capacity to pay the total pay packet in the appellant 's concern. It also found that there was a trend towards uniformity in the matter of scales of dearness allowance as between clerical and subordinate staff and factory workmen and held that the wage sales were in accordance with the recommendations of the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal further found that it had not considered the total effect of increase in the maximum packet including basic wages and dearness allowance and that had made the total wages (i.e. basic wage and dearness allowances) fixed by the Tribunal much higher in the case of the appellants than in comparable concerns. On appeal to this Court, HELD : The Tribunal was right in following the trend that has begun in the region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowances for subordinate staff. [365 E] (1) It is well settled that in applying the industry cum region formula for fixing wage scales the Tribunal should lay stress on the industry part of the industry and its capacity to work. The concept of 'industry ' has undergone a change from time to time. In the present case, the Tribunal had not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and the dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have done. [366 E F] (2) It was not correct to say that the Tribunal was wrong in applying its policy for fixing the wage scale. The fact that the appellant had not been able to make a comparison with the total paid up concerns, could not be said to be of no consequence. [367 G H] (3) The Tribunal has not specifically examined what the wages for these categories were in comparable concern and also took into account the trend in that region. It was therefore wrong in putting the subordinate staff in the same category on the same lines as those of the appellant. [368 A B] (4) The dearness allowance which is meant to neutralise the rise in cost of living should be paid to clerical staff, subordinate staff as well as factory workmen on the similar scales. [369 E F; 371 C D] (5) The fact of the trend towards the industry side was not of any consequence. The appellant had a high standing in that area and it had been usual to keep the same scales for clerical and inferior staff. It had also been urged that the dearness allowances which is intended to neutralize the rise, should be given priority over the dearness Allowance already paid to the factory workmen. [370 E F]. (6) The appellant has not shown that the capacity of the employees was very high or less than the lowest. It is true that the tribunal had not examined the total financial loss occasioned by misconduct in case of dismissal for misconduct. But it did not agree with the rate of dearness Allowance fixed by its award.

The appellants were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the decree was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code as Shiddppa had not come up to this court and therefore the decision of the Division Bench on a question of law was binding on the appellants. Held, that the appellants were entitled to succeed in their suit for redemption of the mortgages. The Rajinama executed by Shiddi in favour of the mortgagee, who executed a Kabuliyat, did not create any interest in the property and the appellants could not claim redemption of Shidda 's one half share in the mortgaged property. The mere assertion of an adverse title on the part of the appellants cannot affect the rights of other occupants or any particular occupant. The appellants had no right to redeem the mortgage property. Held further, that under Section 74 of Bombay Land revenue Code as shiddappa did not purport to file a suit for the redemption of a mortgage against the mortgagees and by reason only of his being the registered occupant, he could not himself give a notice of relinquishment but must give it by and through the registered occupants thereof. The registered occupant in the absence of any authority express or implied to be clearly pleaded and strictly proved, had no inherent or independent right to give any such notice so as to affect the interests of other persons. Lalchand Sakharam Marwadi vs Khendu Kedu Ughade, I.L.R. , approved.

The respondent company was a manufacturer of carbon paper, typewriters, ribbon, stepler machines and steplers despatches the said goods from its head office at Kanpur to its branch office at Allahabad. During the course of assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry 2 of the Schedule to the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, was liable to sales tax at the point and at the rate specified in the said Notification. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that carbon papers did not contain any chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of typewritory. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Sales Tax officer. In further revision to the High Court, it was contended for the respondent that carbon Paper did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes, and that the ribbon is not an accessory but an essen tial part of the typewriting machine taxed by the Sales tax Officer. The High Court held that carbon is not paper within the meaning of Entry 42 in the First Schedule to U. P. Sales tax Act, 1947, as it stood at the time relevant to the year 1966 67 and that it was not an integral part of a typewriter 's typewritten '. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The mere fact that the word paper forms part of tile denomination of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. The word "paper" in the common parlance or in the com plete means paper which is used for printing, writing or packing pur poses. [839C] 2.1 Carbon paper is not a part and cannot be a part thereof. It is a component which is derived from the name of reedy plant papyrus and grows ing into a compact web, made from linen and cotton rags, straw, wood, certain grasses, etc., which are macified into a pulp, dried and pressed; it is used in printing, or drawing on, for wrapping things in, for covering the interior of waxes, etc. [884C D] 2:2 The mere mention of ribbon also to which the above mentioned rule construction equally applies, does not attract tax as per Entry 18 of the Second Schedule to Act XV of 1948. [881D E] 3.1 carbon paper is a substance composed of fibres intertwined with and dealing in such goods.

The respondents were employed by the appellant as seasonal masons in the year 1946. The appellant was a seasonal magistrates and had been running them only for 2 years at Pilibhit. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager of the appellant ordered transfer of the respondents 1 to 4 from the appellant Mills to the new mill at Bulandshahr. The respondents challenged the order by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the right to transfer is implicit in every contract of service; and (2) the State Industrial Tribunal having held that both the concerns, i.e., the mills at Amroha and the mills, at Bulandshahr, formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Held: (i) The appellant 's right to have the respondents transferred the respondents to a new concern stared by him subsequent to the date of their employment was not an alteration of any service condition within the meaning of section 33 of the Act. (ii) The employer in the present case had no such right. It was not a condition of service of employment of the respondent either express or implied that the employer had the right under the terms of contract between them or by the terms necessarily implied therefrom. (iii) The Appellate Tribunal having found that both parties were different, it could not be said that each of them had the same rights as the employer.

The appellant company was formed in 1965 and went into production. The same year, the appellant company went into Production, but it did not produce any evidence to show that the company had paid the contribution under Chapter V A of the Employees ' State Insurance Act 1948 until the provisions of Chapter V of the Act were enforced in the area where the appellant 's factory was situated. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Ch. V A by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the contribution payable under Ch V A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the payment of contribution directed to be made by the employer under the or other similar payment or benefit under various other social welfare legislations must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the , is that the benefits which it provides should become available to the employees in all factories through out India as soon as circumstances make it practicable. When the whole Act is brought into force in the whole of India, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter. Therefore, the amendment provides that employers of regions to which the benefit clauses are not extended must also make their contributions though at a lesser rate. [1094C D] 2. The intention that such payment, contribution or whatever name is given to it should be so pigeon hold and fitted in stems from a misunderstanding of the scheme of our Constitution in regard to social welfare legislation. Apart from the preamble which promises to secure to all its citizens, "justice, social, economic and political", the State is enjoined by the Directive Principles of State Policy to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people. Both Parliament and the Legislature of any State, subject to conditions with which we are not concerned, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List llIl. [ 1094D E] 3. The Act is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children, but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. In fact, it may sometimes happen that the rendering of a service or its conferment of a benefit may only follow after the consolidation of a fund from the fee levied. The question of how soon a return may be expected or ought to be given must necessarily depend on the nature of the services required to be performed and benefits required to he conferred. This contribution goes to a fund known as the Employees" State Insurance Fund which is to be utilised for the benefit to be provided to the employee under the Act. The cost of these benefits will not be met from the general revenues of the state, but will be borne entirely from the aforesaid fund only. [1008C E] 4. In the instant case, the amount of contribution by an employer towards the premium (what else is it ?) of an employee 's compulsory insurance under the falls directly within entries 23 and 24 of List III of their own force enabling Parliament to make the provisions with respect thereto. The fact that the benefit of contribution may be to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas is not necessary to retained this Chapter.[1094D F] Basant Kumar vs Eagle Rolling Mil/s. ([1901] I.L.R. , referred to.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands were rejected by the management on the ground that they had been continuously working on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such there was not any question of regularising their services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [620D E] 2. The principles of regularisation are applicable to all the establishments to absorb the petitioners and accumulated loss to the establishment as on 31st March, 1988 is Rs. 10,29,40,583. A true copy of the balance sheet has also been enclosed with the counter affidavit. It shows the amount of retrenchment com pensation and the ex gratia payment offered to the 63 daily rated workers under this Scheme. The petitioners are included therein. [625E F] 3. In view of the offer made on behalf of respondent No. 2 in the counter affi davit, the Court directed that all the 63 casual labourers including the 54 petitioners herein mentioned in the aforesaid Annexure V to the counter affidavits be given the benefit of the voluntary retirement scheme framed by respondent No 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues.

The plaintiffs claimed title to and the recovery of possession of a property known as " Azamabad Tea Estate" which comprised about 2 1/2 acres of land in Touzi No. 911 of the Darjeeling Collectors, which was set out in Schedule A to the plaint. The defendants claim that they were entitled to the entire property as transferees from the National Agency Co operative Society Ltd., who had been impleaded as defendants. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree holding that the plaintiffs were precluded by 0. r. 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by them under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that in view of the decision of this Court in the case of K. C. Sen vs N. R. Sarkar, (1923) L.R. 58 I.A. 65, the plaintiffs had no right to challenge the validity Of the mortgage on the ground that it was not a transfer of property within the meaning of section 3 of the Crown Grants Act and as such could not be challenged under article 226 of the Constitution. Held, (per Das, C. J., Venkatarama Aiyar, section K. Das and A. K. Sarkar JJ.) that the suit was based on title to the full owner of the property and so could not have been decreed in favour of the plaintiffs. The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale was held to be real, the plaintiff would be entitled to a decree for a declaration that in addition to the 8 pies share granted to them by the High Courts, they would be enti tled to a further 2 as 13 gondas odd share belonging to K. The High Court had rightly held that the claim could not he accepted without careful scrutiny of facts.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction and sentence but on a reference under section 374(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court held that the provisions of sections 173(4), 207A and 207A were not complied with and that as a necessary consequence of those omissions the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. Held, that the omission by the police officer to fully comply with the provisions Of section 173(1) of Code of criminal Procedure was fatal and the irregularity in the trial was curable by reference to section 537 of the code. The fact that the appellant got the necessary copies of depositions of the witnesses in the Sessions Court before the statements of the eye witnesses were recorded by the Magistrate did not affect his case. Gurbachan Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; , followed. Held further, that it was not necessary for the prosecution to examine all the witnesses for the defence as they had been denied their complicity in the crime and that the irregularity was cracked by the trial court and the appellant could not be convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. The omission of the police officers to fully cross examine the prosecution witnesses did not render the proceedings including the trial before the Sessions judge wholly ineffective. Gurbyn Singh vs State of Bombay, ; and Gurbachan vs The state of Punjab ; , referred to. Held also, that in cases exclusively triable by a court of Session it is the duty of the magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry to satisfy himself that the documents referred in section 173 have been furnished to the accused and if he found that the police Officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that is done. The word "shall" used both in sub section (4) and sub section 3 of section 207A is not mandatory but only directory. Gurbervyn Singh V.

The appellant, a chemical works discharged effluent in very large quantities containing calcium, sodium and other chemicals. The respondent Municipality, however, refused to comply with the requisition of the appellant under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to it under the provisions of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of refusal on the ground that the provisions Of section 153 A were ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice issued by the Municipality was not valid because the existence of a nuisance in terms of sub section (1) was a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and beyond the scope of his enquiry. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective satis faction of the municipality as to the existence or absence of a disability which was purely a matter of the subjective opinion of the Municipal Committee. [395 G] The scheme is to permit the Municipality if it is satisfied that a nuisance exists and to agree to comply within the meaning of sub s.(1) (a) of section 153. If the reply to the notice given under sub section(1), objects to the requisition specified in the notice, is not denied by the owner or occupier of the factory, the Municipality may, with the previous approval of the Government, issue a written notice to the person on whom the notice is issued to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in such notice. The notice must be accompanied by an affidavit stating that the nuisance in question exists and that the occupier or the owner consents to comply therewith. [396 H; 396 A B] In the present case, the appellant had succeeded in proving that the Municipality had not been able to comply and report only as to its existence of nuisance. The scheme was therefore to leave the subjective satisfied the Municipality as to whether a nuisance of the kind alleged by the respondent Municipality existed.

The appellant was found to be in possession of railway stores which were used for the purpose of carrying goods. The appellant filed a complaint against him under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 alleging that he had failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods. He also alleged that he did not produce any evidence to show that the articles were sold by him in open market where goods of this kind were usually sold or that he bad bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the The appellant contended that the goods were railway stores within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 33 of the , did not arise. Held, that the prosecution must first adduce evidence to prove that the article seized were railway property within the definition of section 3 Of the Railway Rates (Unami Possession)Act, 1955. The mere description of the articles as new would not fulfil the requirements of section2(b). The mere fact that the description of goods as new was not enough to fulfil the requirement of section. 2(a) does not make it a case of seizure under section 31 of the Indian Railways Act. The prosecution must also prove that articles were being actually used or were intended to be used for by the railway. The possession of goods of any railway administration is not an offence. The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the good as in the case where they have become unserviceable or outmoded no person can be charged with an offence under section 2 in respect thereof.

The appellants were the tenants of the demised premises. The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The tenancy was terminated by a letter under section 108 of the Transfer of property Act, but she continued to remain in possession till date of the death of her husband. The appellants filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent landlord on the ground that on the death or death of the tenant in September, 1966 the appellants had no right to continue in occupation of the premises. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the suit holding that as the appellants were not carrying on the business with the tenant during her life time as family business they were not enti tled to the benefit of the amended definition of 'tenant '. The Letters Patent Appeal filed by the appellants was also dismissed by a Division Bench of the same High Court. In the appeal before this Court it was contended for the appellants that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of a tenant in Septem ber, 1966, the respondent had no rights to continue with the tenancy during her lifetime as family busi nesses. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The term 'tenant" has been defined under section 2(1) of that Act, thus, it is the same as in the present case on hand under clause (a) of Section 2(i) of the Act, which defines a person by whom or on whose behalf the rent is, or but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any accommodation and includes any person occupying the accommodation as a sub tenant. [10E F] 2. The word 'tenant has been used under section 3(vii)(b) of Act, in the context of the definition of "tenant" in Section 3(IV). It is a personal right to the tenant. A reading of the provisions of all the Rent Control Legislation shows that a contractual tenant on the termination of the contractual tenancy is by virtue of the provi sions of the Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land and he is entitled to remain In possession even after determination of the contract. [11D E] 3. The definition of tenant in Section 2 (1) has been given a wide meaning.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund Scheme to all its workers except those who are covered by the Act. The Employees Provident Fund Appellate Tribunal, Bihar and Orissa has made no effort at all to analyse the balance sheet of the Board to show the actual results of its working. It has made a detailed examination of the balance sheets of the appellant Board. The Tribunal has treated the whole matter in a very perfunctory manner. The main question for consideration by the Tribunal was whether there should be a contributory provident fund scheme on the basis of basic wage, or total wages. The appellant Board contended that this would impose additional financial liabilities which the Board would not be able to bear. It was further contended that no scheme run by the Board was running at a loss. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Provident Fund Act applies only to establishments which are factories. It could be applied to establishments where there is an industrial dispute between the employer and the employee. [47D] 2. The Board has made its own Regulations laying down the principles for determining the financial capacity of the employees. The Regulations laid down the principle that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the State. In the present case, the interest on loans advanced or deemed to be advanced to the Board under section 68 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948, had been taken into account. [48E] 3. The financial capacity and the fact that the burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer is to be taken into consideration. If it is not it would have to be met by loans on which interest will have to he paid and deduction of interest so paid will have been to be deducted from the interest so payable will have a bearing on the financial position of the employer. [49F] 4. The employees ' Provident Fund and gratuity are entitled to the benefit of the provident fund as well as other amenities. The employers ' contribution to the depreciation reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion while it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the deprecia tion reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed analysis of the finances of the board. [50B] 5. The interest on loan advanced or "interest" on stock not so guaranteed" will have no bearing on this question.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligations. The Magistrate rejected the application holding that the mere ground that the husband was not impotence was not a just cause for refusal of the wife to live with her husband and accordingly dismissed the application filed by the respondent under section 127 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973. The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court which also dismissed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to get maintenance from the husband, a wife is not entitled to live apart from her husband 's husband and claim maintenance on the grounds that her father was impo bent and incapable of discharging his marital obligation. [707B] 1.2 The High Court has rightly held that the appellant wife having been found to be impotency, this should be a just ground for the wife 's refusal to live in the husband '. [700F G] 1:3. In order that a wife may refuse to live at an earlier stage of her marriage, it is legitimate for it to take into account the relations between the husband and the wife, and the husband should be deemed to have deserted her and a roof over her head. If this could be a ground for divorce or for an action for restitution of conjugal rights, could it be said that it would not be a " just ground" for refusing to live along with her. [607C D] 1 :4. The courts cannot compel the wife in a proceeding under the section to prove, not indeed cruelty as a ground of separate maintenance but the conduct and acts of the husband from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife. This alteration gives a wider discretion to the court, which means that in passing such an order it is reasonable for it, to take note of the relations, between the parties, and, the husband "s conduct towards her". [708D E] 1 5.

The appellant filed a suit for possession of the suit property described in the schedule to the plaint. The first part consists of a large extent of vacant land which is referred to in the plaint as a plot of vacant lands which is described in para 2 of the plaint, and the second part consists in a small portion of vacant site which is stated to be a small area of vacant sites which is mentioned in para 5. The appellant contended that by virtue of the Resolution No 37 dated 19th January 1948 published in the Bhavnagar Darbar Gazette dated 24th January, 1948, the entire suit lands mentioned in the Schedule to the Plaint were vested in the Government and became its property. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the suit premises till 7th July 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of India to the State Public Works Department of the State of Saurashtra. However, on the ground that in respect of Rasala Lines the plaintiff have admitted that they did not own the buildings thereon, they are not entitled to recover possession of lands covered by the Survey numbers referred to above. The High Court allowed the appeal of the Union of India and dismissed the suit for recovery of possession. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court should have given a finding on title as Article 65 of the is applicable to this case since the suit was filed on 3rd March, 1964, and that on the finding of the Trial Court in favour of the plaintiff on the question of title in respect Of the suit lands, the defendants had denied title. On behalf of respondent No. 1 it was submitted that the suit is for possession based on title to a plot based on the title to that land and the defendants have denied title of the plaintiffs. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts ' decree should have been confirmed. [234B] 1.2 In the instant case, the suit itself was for possession basing on title and the plaintiff has not proved title. It is not open to the appellant to rely on the principle that possession follows title. In this view of the matter, it is not necessary for the defendant to plead or prove adverse possession. [235C] 1:3. The doctrine of adverse possession is applicable only to suits based on possession and not to suits in which possession has been handed over. The plaintiff has also admitted that the structures in Rasala Line are not shown to be that of the Municipality in the Municipal records and even in the pleadings they did so. [236D] 1 :4. In view of this, the Trial court 's decree should be confirmed. Since a number of Municipalities made representation to the Government to reconsider the same, the Government reconsider the entire case and decided that the right to sell plots of land given under Resolution No. 37 dated 9th January. 1948 by the State Government to all the Municipalities of Old Bhavnagar States and the right of the defendant in respect thereof shall be enjoyed by the Municipalities subject to the condi tions mentioned in this letter of the Govern ment dated 10th August, 1965.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged with having accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of the value of Rs. 150/ . The trial court convicted him under section 161 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively, on appeal by the appellant, the Judicial Commissioner acquitted him of that charge. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant was an officer in the service or pay of Government within the meaning of section 21(9) Of the Indian Penal code and being a public servant he fell within the definition of public servant contained in section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. The word "officer" used in section 21 (9) of the Indian penal Code meant some person employed to exercise, to some extent and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government. The appellant was not an officer of the Government within section 21, but was merely a contractor bound by his engagement but not by the terms of his office or employment to pay a certain proportion to the Government. Held, further, that when the appellant held the post of metal examiner he was not in the employ of the Railway Administration and was therefore a public officer within the protection of section 2 Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act 11 of 1947 and being such public servant fell within section 2(1)(d) of that Act. The words "public servant" in section 6, Indian Penal C.P.C., mean some person who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala for permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19, situate in village Ghagga, with a building constructed thereon. The auction sale was held for Rs. 1,38,000/ and the auction sale officer 's order was confirmed by the Additional District Judge, Sangrur. The Respondent filed an appeal to the District Judge who dismissed it with costs. The Appellant 's second appeal before the High Court was dismissed on the ground that the portion of the building standing on the said plot of the land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and, therefore, his said half share was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The opening words of sub section(I) of section 60 are "the following property is liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree". [847C] 2. Section 60 has no application to attachment & sale in any proceedings other than in execution. The provisions of section 61 of the Criminal Procedure Code do not apply to an attachment and sales under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said Act is concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. [848D] 3. Section 59 of the Civil Procedure Code provides that the following properties are liable to be attached and sold in execution thereof and the proviso thereto to sub s.(1)of section 60 sets out the properties which are not liable to such attachment or sale, namely: (i) to attachment; (ii) sale mentioned in sub section 1 of section60, that is, to attachment, and sale, in execution, of a debt. [884E] 4. Section 61 has no applicability to attachment. The words "such attachment or sales" in the said proviso refer to the attachment and the sale mentioned therein. The expression "such attached or sale" in section 60 means that the attachment is the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the ' suit and may be either preliminary of final. [854G H] 5. Section 58 of the Cr. P.C. provides that where a question is raised by an attachment, the same shall not extend to any property specifically charged with the debt sought to be recovered. The said section has no appli cation to attachment as regards all orany of the matter in controversy.

The respondent, a Hindu Undivided Family, acquired for the Synthetic Drugs Project Factory of the Indian Drugs and Pharmaceutical Ltd., by virtue of an agreement dated June 19, 1961 entered into with the appellant company. The Special Deputy Collector of Land Acquisition awarded compensation at Rs. 20,000 per acre for the lands acquired in January 1963 and by two separate awards both made on January 31, 1963, the Special Deputy Collec tor of Land Acquisi tion (Land Acquisition) Act, 1894 and the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act (Act No. 1 of 1964). The respondent as well as the High Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the land acquired in February 1963 and the subsequent awards made on February 31, 1970, the respondent was entitled to compensation at market value on the dates of the relevant notifications issued under section 59(a) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) since the lands were lost to the estate of the deceased before the relevant date, namely, May 7, 1965, the High court had no jurisdiction to enhance the value of the acquired land; and (ii) since in the instant case the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in question had not merely been acquired but even the compensation as determined under the awards made by the Special Dy Collector was paid to and received by the deceased and hence at the time of the death of the respondent, the initial right to receive compensation had already merged in those awards and the only right which the deceased had was the right to agitate against the correctness of the awards and nothing more. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has failed to take into consideration the relevant market value of lands acquired proceedings. [334E] 2.1 In the instant cases, the wards made by special Deputy Collector were not accepted by the heirs of the original owner and Land Acquisition Officer. They had no objection to the valuation made by them. They have also no objection if they are allowed to raise land references in Civil Courts. The only right is to receive the compensation for the acquired lands at their market value. [330G] 2:2 In the present case, the ward made by Special Deputy collector was not accepted and he had accepted without any protest by the respondent or his heirs such as the deceased, and therefore, the same were rightly rejected by the High Courts. [328B C] 3.1 The High Courts have failed to consider that the lands which were lost in the year 1962 could not be regarded as forming part of the estate. It is only after such acquisition that the Collector can determine the market value under section 11 and by the civil court under section 26 of the Land Ac t Acquisition Act, that he has no jurisdiction. [326C D] 3:2 The High courts have failed in their duty to consider the relevant valuation made on the basis of the valuation placed before them and examine the materials produced before them. It cannot be said that they have acted perversely or otherwise improperly in taking into account the market price of the lands adopted by the special Deputy Colle ctor. [324D] 3(i) The High court has failed in its duty to take note of the fact that the acquired properties still formed part of a State of the erstwhile State and that having due regard to glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the courts below, it was not possible for the respondent to estimate the market valuation of the properties on the date of death. [325E] 3.(ii) The respondent must resort to provisions of section 59 and proceed to make reassessment but such reassessment has to be done within the period of three years from the date when the original assessment under section 73 A of the Income Tax Act is made.

The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected as Director of the Bank from the Brewery. His election was not called in question by the Deputy Registrar, Cooperative Societies, Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development Bank, Nagpur, on the ground that he had defaulted in payment of the loan instalments as referred to in section 73FF(1)(b) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Banks Act, 1960. The appellant 's election was challenged by the respondent No. 1 on the grounds: (i) that section 73F(1) of Maharashtra State co operative Land development Bank remained in force even after the expiry of the period prescribed under section 73 F(1), and (ii) that the appellant having paid all the debts on 21.10.1986, he became defaulter under section 74FF(2) of Act, and rejected his nomination paper. The respondent No 1 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated 30.8.1989 passed by the Assistant Registrar removing him from the Committee of Directors of the appellant Bank holding that Section 73F was applicable to him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 74F(2)( generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, and would apply only when a defaulter is defaulter under Section 73FF. In the appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i). the disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the respondent society and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellant being disqualified to be elected or to continue as Director or Executive Committee member of the Executive Committee under section 72F(l)(b), he having ceased to be a defaulter, was lawfully removed and the fact that he repaid the loan before the notice was issued would not make him liable to be absent from the committee. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant had already ceased to he a Director and his seat already fell vacant. This has to be interpreted in the context of the provisions in the section. [683F] 1.2 In the instant case, the emphasis is on the appellant ' s default in payment on account of his being defaulter and disqualified for being elected but it has been addressed to the appellant as Director. The expression "makes default" or "stands disqualified" being in present the default must have been committed after the coming into force of section 73G(1). [683H; 684A] 1:3. In this view of the matter, there could not be any infirmity either in the notice or in the impugned order of removal. No doubt there is reference to the appel lant 's having been a defaulter and disqualification for being a member of a committee and his vacancy deemed to have fallen vacant.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on September 1, 1977. After his retirement the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's explanation was accepted by the State Govt. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the order dated December 4.1982 on the ground that the State government had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The validity of Rules 188 and 189 of the Act was not challenged either before the State or before this Court. In this view the Government has power to reduce the amount. [189D] 1.2 The validity is not challenged before the Court or before the Supreme Court. [188E] 1:3. The validity cannot be questioned either before a High Court or in an appeal against the judgment of the High court. [187F] B.J. Shelet vs State of Gujarat & Ors., ; and State of Uttar Pradesh vs Brahm Datt Sharma & Anr., ; , referred to. 1.4. In the instant case, the purpose of the enquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent "s pension". The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 & 189 of Bombay Civil Service Rules. [186F] 2.1 Rule 184 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or after the completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government servant depend upon the good conduct of the Government servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part thereof if the pensioners are found guilty in grave misconduct whilst he was, in service or thereafter after completion of their service. [185G H] 2:2 The State Govt., had power to reducing the pension payable by 50% permanently under rule 188 of Bombay civil Services Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules. This Rule further provides that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part or of the pension is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note 1 to Rule 33 of the said Rules.

The U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, was passed by the State Government in exercise of its revisional powers under section 3(3) of the Act. The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction against the respondent tenant on the ground that he needed the premises for his own use and occupation. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on the view that the appellants suit was incompetent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The bar created by section 3 (4) of Act III of 1947, excluding the jurisdiction of the civil courts to entertain the question about the correctness, legality or propriety of an order passed by a District Magistrate under the relevant provisions of the , is not attracted in cases where the plea raised before the civil court goes to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to the conclusion that the impugned order is a nullity. [560 C D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 2(4) was invalid in law. [559 E] (iii) The words "any other pleas" used in section 3 of the U. P. ( Temporary) Control Act, 1946, are clear and unambiguous and they indicate that the jurisdiction conferred on the State government by section 7 F is very wide. In other words, whenever it is brought to the notice of the State Govt. either by a party aggrieved by the order passed under section 16(3), or otherwise, that the order was passed without notice to the party affected by such order, it would be open to the said party to contend that an order made in violation of the principles of natural justice is a null and void order. [561 G H] (iv) The question as to whether such a plea can be raised before a civil court in relation to orders passed under the Act can be a plea which, if sustained, would render the order wholly invalid and as such, a nullity and a nullity in law, must be decided on the merits. [562 A B] (v) The fact that an application for permission to file a suit against the tenant is dismissed by the Rent Controller does not make him a party to the proceedings before the appellate authority. It is only when he satisfies the court that the appellate order is passed without any notice to him, it will be open for the said authority to reject the application on the grounds of the exclusion of the jurisdiction or the jurisdiction which has been exercised by the appellate court. [563 E F] (vi) The provisions of section 3 1(4), read with section 16 of the Uttar Pradesh (Temporary), Control of Rents and Eviction) Act,1947, do not intend, even prior to the amendment of 1954, to limit the jurisdiction to cases where irregularity or illegality has been committed by the District Magistrate in granting or refusing to grant permission. The result is that the appeal is allowed, the order of the High court in the Letters Patent Appeal is set aside and that of the District Court restored with costs throughout.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was charged with having committed an offence under section 3(1)(a) read with section 5(2)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to various terms of imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the provisions of article 317(1) were not applicable to the case as the expression "any other person" in article 317 had been used in the context of the Act; (ii) the words "such person" occurring in article 318(1), which confers power on the President to remove the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commissioner for reasons mentioned therein, are not relevant for the purpose of deciding whether the allegations made against him were proved at all. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i). The expression "such persons as may be specified" in Article 317(2) is not relevant to mean that after deciding which witnesses should be summoned and examined, evidence must be recorded by this Court itself. [640C] (ii). The words "any person" used in article 316(1). are of a wide import and have to be understood in the light of the context. They are intended to convey the immediate or proximate connection between the acts done by the public servants and their employment, and the consequences that follow from such acts. [643D] (iii) The expression 'such person ' occurring in Article 318(2), which is in point, has to be read as "any one" and not "a disability". This provision confers a requisite power on this Court to summon witnesses, but nothing contained therein can be read to mean the examination in chief of the respective witnesses. [641E] (iv) The word 'person ' occurring under Article 317 is used in a sense which means a person who has been heard against the decision of the Court. It is impossible to accept that the Supreme Court in one case and the Parliament in the other case are entrusted with the limited power of determining whether the facts found by some other body establish misbehaviour or incapacity in one Case and guilt or innocence. [651G] (v) The words 'such persons ' occurring therein cannot be read in a narrow sense which is to say that after considering the nature and gravity of the matter referred to it, the Court is entitled to summon and examine witnesses but nothing in Article 316(2). [642C D] (vi) The power of the President under article 317 is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some one else. It will be open to him to ask for a copy of the evidence which he has produced before the Court and which may be considered necessary for the disposal of the case.

The appellants were the deity installed in the temple. The temple was declared to be a public temple and a trust and the endowment was held to be of a public nature and, therefore, was to be governed by the Act. The respondent (Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments) filed an appeal against the decision of the Subordinate Judge which was heard by the Division Bench of the High Court. The High Court reversed the decision holding that the temple and the deity were not entitled to pass orders for its management. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has not properly construed some of the important features contained in the documents and the evidence and has in fact overlooked certain important aspects which completely negative the fact that the endowment is of a private nature. [832E] 1.2 The High Courts have not properly interpreted some of these important features. It is well settled that under the Hindu law, however, it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the founder is to instal a family deity in the temples and worship the same in order to effectuate spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and their descendants. [821F] 1:3 The High courts have not correctly construed some important features in the document and the oral evidence produced in the case. It has been held that the mere fact that members of the public are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members of a family had a right to worship in the Temple.

The appellant Bank was a contractor to the military and other authorities. The appellant bank was required to pay certain sums under the contracts in respect of the supply of stores to the respondent. The contract provided that all powers hereby granted were and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorneys against, the bills for supplies under the contract were pending. The respondent filed objections in the execution proceedings. The objection was dismissed by the trial court but on appeal the High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no transfer of the decree or of the claim which was the subject matter of the pending appeal as the appellant had an interest in the fund and therefore there was a valid equitable assignment of the monies due under the bill in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Bank that there could be no transfer by the respondent of the bill and the appellant was not entitled to recover the monies as the respondent had an equitable assign ment of the funds by way of security. HELD: The contract was a revocable mandate. It gave the payee no interest in its fund. An assignment creates an interest In the fund, and is not revocable. Read in the light of the power of attorney the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the moneys receivable under the bills and amounted to an equitable assignment. [596 B C] Palmer vs Carey, , referred to. The High Court was in error in holding that the respondent was valid equitable assignee of future debts, see Palmer 's case, [777 E] Palner vs carey, ; , referred.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. The appellant, who was the Manager of a tea estate under the management of a company, was assessed to income tax on the basis that he 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but on further appeal to the Tribunal the tribunal held that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary had to be considered as salary and not as an accretion to the assessee. The High Court answered the reference against the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered a salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17(3)(ii) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income Tax under the head "income from other source" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E '. In computing the income for the purpose of section 17(1)(iv) all receipts of profits in the lieu of, salary have to be consider as salary. But then the question is what is meant by "profits in lieu Of salary". [439 C D] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the receipts of Rs 27,949/ by way of interest on any investment are not income.

The Madhya Pradesh Legislature passed the Madhya Pradesh and Berar Animal Preservation Act, 1949, which was extended to the State of Bombay. The Act provided for the regulation of slaughter of animals of all ages and calves of cows and cals of a cow and the male calves and buffalo calves. Section 4(1) (g) of the Act provided that no person shall slaughter a cow or female calves except under a licence issued by the appropriate authority in this behalf. The petitioners who were the owners of cattle, challenged the validity of the Acts on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that the Act violated articles 19(1)(g), 31 and 31 of the Constitution; (ii) that it was not reasonable to impose the restrictions on the slaughter of the animals as they were not within the protection of article 19(6); (iii) that section 16 of the impugned Acts infringed articles 19 (1) and (g). Held, that the provisions of the two Acts violated article 19 (i)(g) and 31 (ii), and that the impugned Act was constitutionally valid. The Bihar Act in so far as it prohibited the slaughter Of a cow of all age and calve rides of cows, male and female, was valid. It was not possible to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on the slaughtering of she buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) which were useful as milch or breeding or working animals and strike down the ban in so insofar as it prohibits the slaughter except under the provisions contained in article 19. The entire provision banning the slaughter was therefore void. The State of Madras vs R. M. Sarkar, ; , followed. Held, further, that a total ban on slaughter of a cattle of all years and caleves of buffaloes, male or female, could not be justified as reasonable restriction on the right to carry on their occupation or business. The provisions in the Act were not discriminatory but were only discriminatory and did not violate article 19 of the constitution. The impugned Acts were therefore unconstitutional and void.

The respondent was a "workman" within the meaning of the , and an employee in the appellant company. The respondent filed a complaint against him alleging that he had been receiving illegal gratification from him for wrongful dismissal. The trial Magistrate held that the charge against the respondent was proved, but on appeal the High Court set aside the order of the trial Magistrate holding that the respondent had committed a breach of the statutory provision and that the appellant was not an employee within the definition of the "workman". On appeal by special leave: Held, that the complaint was maintainable under section 30 of the . The words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in the departmental musters " occurring in Standing Order No. 18, which provides for penalties for misconduct, and submit ted to the Labour Commissioner for approval, do not mean that the Standing Orders apply to the respondent. The Standing Orders do not apply to a person who is employed in any industrial establishment to do any skilled or unskilled manual or clerical work, nor does they apply to persons employed in an industrial establishment. The definition of "workman " in section 2(1) of the Act includes such categories of employees as may from time to time be declared to be workmen by the management and Standing Order NO. 18 provides for punishment for misconduct. The word "employee" is used in the widest sense, and it means such categories or classes of employees who are not 'workmen ', but all persons employed on any industrial establishments to do an unskilled or unskilled, manual or supervisory work, work or clerical, labour for hire or reward, but does not include any member of the armed forces. The expression "workman ", in section 30, means such category of employees, as may be declared by the company and includes a member of a armed forces, but it does not mean such categories as may, from time lo time, be declared as workmen by an employer. The essential content of the definition is employment in the office, Mains Department, eta., of the Company either at Nagpur or Wardha, and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the Company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order 18, is not an essential characteristic of an employee.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen of the respondent company claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 66 on the ground that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect whereof separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained. The Tribunal held that alloy steel project could not be treated as separate establishments because under the Act a company is itself an establishment which has been in existence for a long period and has been even earning profits, so that exemption could not he granted to this Company in respect thereof. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because Alloy steel Project is owned, managed and managed, by Hindustan Steel Ltd., it had to be treated a separate Establishment; (ii) the Act does not apply to new departments or undertakings or branches set up by existing establishments; (iii) the expression "establishment" in section 3 of the Act means an establishment in which there are two departments or units. The word "establishment " is used in the context of the definition of "establishment".
