The Tribunal found that though the Company, Hindustan Steel Limited, had a number of undertakings, separate accounts were kept for each separate undertaking and after such consolidation, profit and Loss account were maintained for each distinct unit; (iv) the fact that the Company was treated as an establishment newly set up did not affect the principle to be applied to the separate units for which separate accounts, separate balance sheet and separate profit and losses statements were maintained; and (v) the question whether the Alloyel Project is a separate one for purposes of computation of bonus under the payment of Bonus Rules, 1965 was not raised in this Court. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding on the basis that all theoy steel projects were treated as a separate establishments newly setup in the year 1961. [633 G] (i)(a) The Tribunal went wrong in treating the Alloys Project as a 'establishment ' and held that even if Alloy II Project is treated as one of the units for purposes, for purposes Of computation of Bonus under the , it lays down in section 6(d) read with the Third Schedule that the deductions to be made from net profits will also include dividends payable on preference share capital. [625 B C] (b) The expression " establishment" in the definition in section 2(a) means an establishments newly setting up, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, and includes all factories which are set up for a period of six years immediately before the commencement thereof. [613 E F] (c) The word 'establishment " in the inclusive part of section 3 cannot be construed as including all different departments, undertakings and units set up under that clause. [517 B C; 613 D] (d) The definition of 'establishment in section 4(1) is not to be read as a whole but it must be given its plain meaning. It is clear from the definition that the expression 'establishment includes all different Departments, undertakings or units set out in the Act. [600 E F]. (e) The words "establishment in a public sector" in clause (a) of section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act refer to all departments, undertaking or branches and are not confined to any other department for purposes which is clearly mentioned in the expression.

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution with a view to control the pollution of rivers and streams which has assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urbanisation. The Act provides for levy of cess on water consumed by persons carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed, by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corre sponding Entry in column II thereof as the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. The Cess Act is a fiscal enactment, and is intended to ensure that the domestic and industrial units are not allowed to be discharged into water coarses without adequate treatment. The cess is payable by every person carrying on the industries specified in Schedule I. The Water ( Prevention and Control) Act provides that the cess shall be levied on all persons falling within the Schedule. The appellant State Board for Prevention and control of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd., and others, ; , was a public sector company which had established a public undertaking under the . It also filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy and collection of cess. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products industry". The appellant has preferred this appeal by special leave against the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Cess is a taxation on goods specified in schedule I to the Central Excise and Salt Act. It has been defined as including the preservation of such products as canning, freezing, drying, salting, smoking, peeling or filleting or any other method of processing which the authority made by notification under the Act specified in this behalf. [529C] 1.2 The term "vegetable" has been used in Entry 15 of Schedule I to Act. The word 'vegetables ' gives a definite colour, meaning thereby all that belongs to the world of plants would come under Entry 15. [540D E] 1:3. The expression "veg etable products" is generally understood as referring to edible plants as opposed to edible crops and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry No. 15. The term vegetable in taxing statutes is not products of manufacture unless there is a mention of any and every kind of plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule 1 like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and even Chemical industry which were covered by the other entries can also be bring within Entry, 15. Therefore, the word 'cameg etcea ble ' has been employed in the context in which the word "vege" is used in entry 15.

The respondent, an Advocate, filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who contended that the practice of profession was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a) (iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds that he requires the premises bona fide for the purposes of carrying out his profession. The Rent Controller held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for carrying on the profession as a advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction. In revision, the High Court set aside the order and directed the Rent Control Tribunal to dispose of the appeal afresh in accordance with law. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The expression business occurring in Section 10 (3) (a)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or the profession of an advocate.[14H] 1.2 In a broad sense it is taken to mean any house or hut or a part of a house or, let separately for residential or nonresidential purposes. It is not a sound principle of construction that meaning of words and expressions used in one Act with reference to their use in another Act should take their colour from the context in which they appear. [14H; 15A] 1:3 The expression 'business ' has not been defined in the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. It has been defined as meaning any house, hut or part of an house or a hut, let or to be let separately, for residential, nonresidential or non residential purposes. [15D] 1 :4 The expression "business" is used to mean everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the pur pose of lndia. It does not include the practices of the profession which are generally defined in a broad definition. [16E] 2.1 A lawyer who is a member of the legal or medical professions and who requires the same for carrying out the practice, of his profession should be wholly debarred from obtaining possession of the premises. It would indeed be anamolous to hold that all the provisions of the Act including section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and Section 10 of the Andhra Act bars the eviction by landlords against tenants who are not in occupation of the same premises. [17H; 18A] 2:2 A lawyer, undoubtedly does not carry on trade or business when he acts for his client or advises him or pleads for him, if and when pleading is permissible to him. " The expression Business occurring in section 10(1) (g) is intended to mean the business which is carried on by a person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building on his own account or on behalf of another person etc. Tenant is defined as a person by whom or on whose account rent is payable for a building. Section 10, therefore. expressly said that the word may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. [18B C] 2 :3 A lawyer undoubtedly does no carry on business when his client is engaged in trade or profession when he act for his clients or advices him or plead for him if and whenever pleading is permitted to him or pleaded for him.

The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 with the appellant and also paid interest at 6/9 per cent on the amount due from him under an agreement that the same would be paid on demand. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the said amount but the trial court decreed the suit in favour of the respondent. On appeal by the respondent the High Court held that the respondent was entitled to recover the sum as it was advanced under an arrangement and therefore the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The appellant 's contention that the statement made by the appellant in his letter dated 29th September 1942 (exhibit 7) showed that he had never any payment of money in cash and adjustment entries were made in the books of the appellant cannot be accepted. [577 F] The mere fact that the appellant did not pay money in the year 1943 under an earlier agreement would not make the respondent liable to pay return of the amount deposited. It is precisely because of the then inability of India Supplies to repay the money immediately. It was not a case of the res pondent giving loan to the appellant for the obvious reason that the history of the transactions between the appellant, the respondent and the respondent showed that the amount was deposited with the appel lant. [578 G H] The agreement in question was between the parties and the appellant was entitled under it to recover from the respondent a sum which was advanced by him to the respondent under an agree ment that the said sum would be payable on demand, but the agreement did not state that it was a case where money was deposited. [579 A B] The respondent 's case was that the transaction was between appellant and the respond ent for the purpose of having the use of money by way of deposit. The transaction was in the nature of deposit and was not covered by the award.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under section 3(1) of the . The grounds of detention stated that he was a "detenu" and that he had been orally directed to attend the office of the District Magistrate, Burdwan. He made an application to this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging his detention on the ground that the period of parole granted by the detaining authority to him was not added to the period during which the petitioner was in custody and that the order of detention was illegal as he had already been arrested on 27th February, 1986. The petitioner contended that the grounds of his detention were vague and did not indicate any compelling circumstances against him to raise those points against his detention. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1.1 Section 3(i)(a) does not preclude the authority from passing an order of preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground thatthe detaining authority was aware of the fact that the detenu was already in custody. [843C D] 1.2 The mere circumstance that the petitioner is in custody does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining author ity in making an order for preventive detention, and the principle enunciated by this Court must apply but where the offences in respect of which the detenu is accused are so interlinked and continuous in character and are of such nature that these affect continuous mainte nance of essential supplies and thereby jeo pardise the security of the State, then sub ject to other conditions being fulfilled, a man being in detention would not detract from the order being passed for preventive deten tion. [851D E] 1:3 The fact that detenu is in detention does not taken away the juris diction of the appropriate authority in making the an order under section preventive detention and that it is necessary to detain him in such a situation, cannot be said to have been prejudice to the detenu on account of the authority 's withholding the summons. [852E] 2.1 The fact of the detenu being in custody when the order was made, yet he was satisfied that his preventive detention was necessary. [853F] 2:2 In the instant case, there is no material to show that the detaining au thority was aware about the fact of his having been in custody before the order for detention became necessary. The fact is that the detenue is in jail for at the most one day. Therefore, he has been detained under the National Security Act.

The petitioners are working as casual labour in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. Their grievance is that even though many of them have been working for the last ten years as casual labourers, they have been denied the benefits such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc., which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. They have produced a order of the Director General, Posts & Telegraphs, Department bearing No. 28 II/77 SR/STN dated 15.5.1980 prescribing the rate of daily wages for casual labour employed in the Telecommunication Wing of the Department. The petitioners have produced the order of Director General Posts and Telecommunication Department bearing NO. 28 11/77 RTN dated 5.2.1986 which prescribes the rate or rates of wages payable to casual labour as and when they occur. They are being paid wages far less than the minimum pay payable under the pay scales applicable to regular employees belonging to corresponding cadres. The grievance of the petitioners is that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are being treated as casual labourer in the Department from 1.4.1975 or earlier and have been engaged as casual Labour for nearly ten years. They cannot be denied the same benefits which the regularly recruited employees are enjoyed. [602C D] 1.2 In respect of categories (ii) and (iii), i.e., for those who had completed seven years of service, the revision of wages is done as and whenever DA/DA is paid to casual labourers working under the P & T Department. But in respect of category (ii), i .e., the petitioners have been subjected to hostile discrimination. It may be that the casual labourer has agreed to work on such low wages. But there are several types of work such as road making, railway construction, house building, irrigation projects, communications etc. which have to be undertaken on a large scale. [503D E] 1:3 The petitioners who have not been regularly recruited but many of the respondents have been worked continuously for more than a year in the department and some of them are engaged as Casual labourers for nearly 10 years. The arrears of wages due to them from 1st April, 1975 to 30th September, 1980 on which date the first of the two petitioners namely, Writ Petition No. 805/86 and Writ Petition (C) No. 36/87 were paid have been increments paid to them. They should not be discriminated against in respect thereof. [403E F] 1 4.

The assessee, a partner in a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the accounting year 1945 46. The Income tax Officer did not act on this return but on February 27, 1950, he issued a notice under section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act calling upon him to submit his return. On February 27. 1950, the Income tax officer served a notice on the assessee under section 22(2) of the Act calling for a return of his income. The assessee submitted a " voluntary " return on January 5, 1950 and the assessment was made on March 31, 1951. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the notice issued by the Income Tax Officer was valid in law. Held, that the notice under s. 34 of Act was not a valid notice within the meaning of cl. (c) of sub section (1) of section 28 of the Income ' tax Act and therefore the assessee could not be allowed to raise any question of limitation under section 23(2). The expression "assessment" in section 22 of the 1922 Act means assessment proceedings commenced before the end of the assessment year. The word "assessment " is used in its ordinary sense, but it does not mean a proceeding which is completed before the assessment. It is only when the return is made that the Income. tax Officer can take any action under section 28(2), and he has to issue a notice for making such an order. In the present case, the assessee had submitted a voluntary " returns on January May 5, 1951, and the IncomeTax Officer did so after issuing a notice of demand under section 24(2); but before the benefit of the extended period could be claimed by him, he filed a return in July 1952, which was completed four years after the end Of the relevant assessment year; and the assessee submitted his voluntary "assessment on January 4, 1950" and the demand for tax was made within one year of the date of service of the notice. The notice under S.24(2)(a) was issued on February 5, 195o and the benefit thereof could not possibly be extended in this case. The assessment proceedings commence with the issue of a public notice and the period during which action could be taken is the extended one of eight years. The only question is whether the assessee was entitled to make a "penalty" for the assessment made on January, 5, 1952. If it is held that the return filed by the assessee in July 1953, was a return under section 20(2A) of Act, then the conditions under the first sub section of section 34 obtained and the second proviso thereto are satisfied. The second proviso to section 28 (1), however, does not apply to a case where the return has been made before the expiry of the period mentioned in the proviso. The proviso is applicable only when a return is filed after the expiry Of the assessment years in question. The words "assessment proceedings commence either with a notice or during the pendency of the proceedings" in the first proviso are not relevant and must be read as meaning "a return of income which has escaped assessment for any year". The expression 'assessment ' in section 28 means assessment proceeding commenced before an assessment completed under the Act, and does not include a return filed under section 27(3). The word 'assessment " in section 23 (1 ) of the , is used to mean assessment proceedings initiated before the commencement of the law. The expression is used for the purpose of determining whether the income has escaped assess ment or not. It would be for the legislature to decide whether a return should be made showing an income below the taxable limit. If the return was filed belatedly under section 21(3), it could not have been treated as such a return. The remedy is for the Legislature to amend the law suitably.

The first petitioner, a registered Central Trade Union, filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry 's Office Memorandum dated 23 8 1982 ( Annexure A). The second petitioner also challenged the Circular dated 23rd August, 1982 (Annexure B) issued under Section 9 of the Act on the ground that it violates the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act 1970. The petitioners contended that the circular is contrary to the letter and spirit of the Scheme inasmuch as it cuts at the root of the representative form of selection for appointment to the Board of Directors as contemplated by the statute. The second respondent contended that there was no justification whatsoever in issuing any such circular for the very object of the legislation, namely, to encourage democratic selec tion of the Directors who will truly represent the interests of the various categories of persons mentioned in the Act. Allowing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of Section 9 is to empower the Central Government to make a scheme for the constitution of the Board so as to include representatives of the employees and other speci fied categories. The policy of the legislature is to give the Board a truly representative character so as not to reflect the genuine interests of various persons manning or dealing with the bank as an industry and a commercial enterprise. [857C D] 1.2 The object is to confer on the Central Govern ment the power to make scheme for its constitution, and to include representation of employees and others who are employees to be appointed by the Central Gov ernment as appropriate mode of appointment in respect of various categories. [884D E] 1:3. The Act requires the Central Govt. to make the Scheme in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India. The Central Government must, therefore, continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repre sentatives of the concerned employees and if election were to be construed to be the appropriate mode for choosing the representatives of employees, appointment by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen as the case may be would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election.

The appellant was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961 for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The Appellate Tribunal declined to order any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) By virtue of section 220(6) the power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal has been given to the Income Tax Officer only when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Tribunal. [69 E] (ii) The Tribunal 's powers in dealing with appeals are of widest amplitude and have in some cases been held similar to and identical with those of section 221(6). [69 G H] (iii) The power of the High Court under section 254(1) is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It will always be open to the Tribunal, for instance, to decide whether to stay recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matters of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in the disposal of appeals by the Appellate Tribunals. [70 E F] (iv) The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Assistant Commission must be held to have the power to pass such orders for staying proceedings as would prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. A certain apprehension may legitimately arise in the minds of the authorities administering the Act that if the Appellate tribunals proceed to stay the recovery of tax or penalties, payable by, or imposed upon the assessees, as a result of which the assessee is prejudiced because of inordinate delay, the Tribunal will be putting to great losses because of this inordinate delay.

The respondent was a constable in the U. P. Police Force and on his return to the District Magistrate, Gonda, he was placed under suspension and on an enquiry being made by the Superintendent of Police, he found substantial complaints against him. The Superintendent of police made a report to the Superintendent that the respondent had been guilty of dishonesty, corruption and misbehaviour in that he had on nine occasions watched the matter with a strong opposition in this new charge. The respondent was dismissed from service with effect from February 18, 1953. On appeal by the respondent to the Deputy Inspector General of Police the Deputy Inspectors General of police directed the Sub Divisional Magistrate to make an enquiry into the allegations and submit his report. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal on the ground that the Superintendent was not competent to dismiss him since an order in such circumstances could only be made by a Police Officer senior in rank to a Superintendent; that the trial was vitiated by a number of serious irregularities and that the specific acts with which the appellant was charged were cognizable offences and therefore the Superintendent had no jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph (1) of para 486 of the Police Regulations. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The order proposed by the High court did not express its opinion on other questions raised and argued before it. It was substantially the same and therefore it was substantially in the same terms as the report of the Superintendent. [677 E] The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect the question whether substantially the subject matter of the departmental trial was cognizable offences. It is well settled that para 486 does not apply to a case where a magisterial inquiry is ordered; and that a Police officer can be departmentally tried under section 7 of the police Act after such a magical enquiry. [678 B C] The State of U.P. vs Babu Ram Upadhya, ; , followed.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Medical Department of Health and Family Planning on September 9, 1966. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971. The post of Professor in Medicine at the time of his appointment was vacant on September 10, 1966 and he was holding a post in categories 'C ' and 'D '. On September 9 1966, the appellant was promoted as Professor in medicine in the year 1971 and held a post of Director in Medicine in the Health Department. The appellant challenged the promotion of respondents 4 to 24 though they were junior to him. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellant had not been properly treated in the matter of promotion to super time grade II because he was in no way likely to be benefited by this bizarre exercise. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) when a post is created in a certain grade, category or cadre and it is to be filled in from amongst those who may be promoted from 'General Duty Officers Grade I because General Duty Officers grade I are also promo ted to super Time grade II; (ii) once an unspecified Specialists ' grade post was converted into a specified post and assigned to a speciality, he being the seniormost and otherwise qualified for being promoted to that speciality and (iii) the appellant having not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' Grade I was eligible for promotion to the super time scale II because his appointment to the said post would be one who is eligible to be appointed to that privilege and not some one who was on top of the general seniority list in Specialists Grade II. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not qualified for promotion as he was not fully qualified for the post of director of Health Services. [53E] 1.2 In the counter affidavit filed by the Central Government it is stated that the 19 unspecified specialists posts were meant only for promoting category 'C clinical Specialists to super speciality II and that as it was assigned to Ophthalmology speciality, the post was not filled in by promotion but by way of promotion which in fact was done in this case there is any violation of the rule. [54F] 1:3 The appellant being conscious of this position tried to circumvent it by saying that he was senior to him as Professor and was not entitled to be promoted to the post from that date. He, therefore, cannot be considered eligible for promo tion to super hoc grade II in February 1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for the said promotion. [55F] 2.1 It is true that the word 'exists ' has been used in a wide sense and it includes all persons who are eligible for consideration. But, it is implicit in this arrangement that the person to be so appointed would be either promoted or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. In the instant case, the unspecified 'specialists ' posts were converted into 'dak ' category 'and that as they were not qualified, they could not be promoted. [56A B] 2:2 The appellant is entitled to promotion from the date on which he refused to accept the promotion to a post for which he was selected. He is not qualified and, therefore. he must be considered for promotion from that day on which the respondent refused to receive his promotion to another post. [57B C] 3.1 In the present case, it was not shown that the respondent junior to the appellant in the speciality was promoted.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) was enacted to bring about agrarian reform. The object of the Act was to provide for the rehabilitation of tenants ejected and landless persons in excess of the permissible limit. Section 19B provided that every person who has been evicted by voluntary transfer, shall hold no more than the permissible area and the surplus land in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transfers or involuntary operation of law will go to feed the surplus pool. The Act was enacted with a view to see if it would be a large holder, but by inheritance or bequest he may acquire lands in excess Of the permissible limits. Section 10A provided that the surplus area shall be at the disposal of Government for utilization under section 10 A. The appellants who were tenants of land and peasant proprietors created a surplus pool of land which was taken over for settling ejected tenants and others. The respondents challenged the validity of the provisions of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1962 on the ground that they contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they had not been given any opportunity to make their representations. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that section 19B read with section 10A did not affect the petitioners ' rights and that section 9B was not affected by the provisions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Act violated article 14 inasmuch as it deprived them of their property, (2) the gift made by the land owners who exceeded their permissible area having come by additional lands by inheritance were to be ignored or taken into account when computing the surplus areas in their hands, having regard to the specific provision in section 19 B providing life to the tenants and (3) the provisions in sections 10A and 19B did not offend article 14. HELD: (1)(a) The Act is enacted because the High Court took the view that area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 was not hit by the ceiling set and land acquired by an heir by inheritance is saved from utilisation by the State. [632 B] (b) Section 19 B provides that even if the source of the excess area is inheritance, bequest of gift, the capacity to own is conditioned by the permissible limitation. Indeed section 19 had to be enacted because, the High Courts took the stand that area was not covered by the Ceiling Act having come into force on April 15 1953.

The appellants were the proprietors of Dhanora and other jars. The respondent claimed that he was entitled to receive compensation in respect of Malguzari lands received by them from the Government. The claim was rejected by the Compensation Officer on the ground that the jars had no proprietary rights over the Malguna lands. The appellants filed a suit for possession of the properties and mesne profits and also for recovery of the amount of compensation. The trial court held that the respondent was entitled only to the Zamindari as he was found suitable to hold the Zamindari and the decision of the Compensation officer did not operate to deprive him of the right to those lands or compensation payable in respect thereof; that the suit with regard to Malguazari lands was not barred by the decision. The High Court confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the Land Acquisition Officer under sub section (1) of section 14 of the Act was binding on the appellants and the respondent had no right to claim the compensation paid or payable in the lands. [337 B] (ii) The High Courts were in error in not reducing the amount awarded by the Land Tribunal as it was not shown that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of his power under section 14(1). That is also clear from the terms of section 35(7) of Act 1 of 1951 which provides "The payment of compensation under this Act to the creditors of a proprietor or to the proprietor in accordance with the prescribed manner shall be a full discharge of the State Government from all liability to pay compensation for the divesting of proprietary rights, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect Of such rights to which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom compensation has been paid as aforesaid. [330 G H] (iii) The provisions of section 15(7)(a) and (b) of the , are mandatory and do not affect the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. The order passed by a Land Acquisition officer under sub s.(1) is binding on all authorities to determine rival claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3 of the . [330 B C] (iv) Section 14(2) does not invest the Compensation Officers with jurisdiction to determine competing claims of person claiming proprietary right to the land vesting in Government by virtue of section 5. A question regarding the proprietary right may in ordinary course be raised only in a claim against the State, and if that claim is decided against the claim or in a summary inquiry held by the compensation officer, a suit to set aside the decision must be filed within two months from the date of the order. That is equally clear from section 35 (7) which provides for the payment of interest on the amount deposited by the State under section 3.

The appellant tenant was in arrears of rent for more than six months. The respondent landlord filed a suit against the appellant terminating the tenancy on the ground that he had failed to pay standard rent and that the provisions contained in section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 were not applicable to the suit. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the provision contained in sections 11 and 12(1)(b) of Act did not apply to the case because the provisions of section 12 (3) were not attracted. On appeal the High Court held that the dispute as to standard rent was one which must have been raised before the expiry of one month from the date of service of notice under section 12. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the suit was governed by the provisions in section 11(3)(a) and (b) and that, therefore, there was a dispute as regards standard rent which could be raised before expiry of the period of one months after notice under Section 12. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court erred in holding that section 12 was applicable to suit. [633D] 2. The expression "in any other case" occurring in section 2(3), (a), (b), and (c) of section 11 of the Act is not confined only to a dispute raised within one month of the notice as contemplated in section12(3). The words "any question relating to standard or permitted increases" are used in the context of the expression "any other case". [634E] 3.

The respondent company was a company incorporated in Canada, held a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2(21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940. The Aluminium Ltd., a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and its subsidiary, a company which had a controlling interests therein, was assessed to tax on its ordinary or extraordinary general meeting of shareholders. The respondent company paid the controlling interest to its subsidiary at certain rates and in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1941, December 31 and 1942, December 1, 1942 and December 31 , 1942, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondent company. One of these directors was Mr. L. G. Bash who was then the managing director of the company. The other directors also gave notice to the Aluminium Company that they would be a director of another company nominated by the Aluminium company and the other directors had between them during the chargeable assessment periods ending December 31 1941, and December 1 , 1942 and January 1, 1950, respectively. The Income tax Officer held that the directors of respondent company were not liable to pay tax on their shares as directors but only as a director. On appeal by the respondent Company the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the decision of the Income tax officer. In further appeals to the Tribunal the appellant contended that the Directors of the Aluminium had no controlling interest therein and that they could control the affairs of the Respondent company and that in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10% per annum and not at 8%. Held, that the decision was correct. The decisions of the Bombay High Court in British American Tobacco Co. Ltd. vs Commissioners of Inland Revenue, , Commissioner of Income tax vs Bipin Silk Mills Ltd., ; and Commissioner of Inland Reve nue Tax vs Jamed Hodgkinson (Salford) Ltd., , relied on.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st October, 1957 he was allotted to the new State of Karnataka with effect from 1st November, 1956. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former state of Mysore, and on 1st April, 1969 he was promoted as Accounts Superintendent on his having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to him were promoted on their having passed the SAs examination while promotion was denied to them. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the order dated 1st Octo ber, 1968. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High court erred in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that the Board was exempted from passing the Departmental Examination before qualifying for promotion. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The Board 's interpretation of Regulation No. 79(c) does not apply in the present case as the Regulations framed by the Board under section 79(C) are silent regarding the allottees and is not made applicable to them.[511B] (1) The Regulations framed under section 80(c), prescribing the passing of the examination, were not relaxed by amending the Regulations. [511D] (2) The resolution dated 19th May 1969 was not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the Resolution the inference that the allottees are exempt ed from passing of Departmental Examination is not justified.

The petitioner, a retired Government employee of the State of Orissa, was taken from his home in the police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No. 6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, who was detained under section 3(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed theft and detained at the Police Outpost near a bridge at some distance from the Jarai Check Post. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of his detention on the ground that he had been taken in police custody after he had managed to escape from police custody by chewing off the rope with which he had already been tied for being detained at Police Out post, and that his death was unnatural as a result of multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police lock up. The State contended that the evidence adduced during the inquiry did not support the defence of respondents and there was no reason to reject the finding of the District Judge that the petitioner had died in police confinement as a consequence of the multiple injuries imposed to him, while he had himself managed to escaped from police arrest by chewing off the ropes with which the petitioner was tied for be detained at police Outpost. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of detention passed against the petitioner on the finding that it is a case of custodial death and Suman Behera 's torture is not acceptable as it is well settled that in a petition under Article 32 or 226 of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights, the court has the right to be indemnified by and take such action as may be available to it against the wrongdoer in accordance with law through appropriate proceedings.

The petitioner, a prisoner under the sentence of death, was sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by him were dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that if the petitioner wanted to interview the prisoners, he would be interviewed only by a matron or a female warden and not more than one hour on the whole, there would be no justification for the petitioner to have an unrestricted access to means of information. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the press, to have a unrestricted access through its medium. [1187G] 2. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentence of life imprisonment and the petitioners, therefore, are entitled to be allowed to interview them. While there is no data either that they are not willing to be interviewed and, indeed, if it were to appear that the prisoners themselves do not desire to be heard, it would have been impossible for this Court to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be allowed interview them.[1187B C] 3. The right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of a Press, which includes the freedom of press, is not invade the rights of other citizens and which does not violate the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order, decency and morality. [1108C D] 4. The Supreme Court cannot overlook that the press is entitled to exercise its freedom of expression by publishing a matter which does no invade its rights of others and which did not violate their sovereignty and authority. [1087D E] 5. The Press is entitled 'to exercise its right of speech, and expression by publication in the jail Manual. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore it cannot be said that the Press is an absolute freedom nor indeed spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the press. [1018E F] 6. The Court cannot ignore that the Supreme Court can overlook that right of the press to have the unrestricted access, to means and not to more than two hour on its whole. There is a provision in the rules that if a person who desires to interview a prisoner is a female, she can be searched only by the matron personally and for not more then one hour. [1008F G] 7. The fundamental right of freedom of Press is not absolute but indeed does not confer any rights on the Press to havean unrestricted access. [1000B C; 1087G H] 8.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., on January 19, 1950. On January 20, 1950, the appellant entered into a surety bond in the sum of Rs. 50,000 in favour of one R. M. Goswami, District Judge, Agartala, his successors in office and assigns. The appellant 's application for damages was heard along with the mortgage suit. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he allowed the respondent 's appeal against that order. On October 4, 1961, the respondent moved an application asking for damages from the Receiver and the appellant filed a reply to that application. The trial court decreed the same on May 1, 1956. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellant on June 29, 1970. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that under the terms of the surety bond the appellant was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire and therefore the suit was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The surety bond was executed both be the Receiver as well as the Subordinate Judge. [359 B] (2) Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. The surety bonds were executed both before the transfer of the suit and the transferee Court. [360 C] (3) Under the terms Of the bond, the appel lant rendered itself liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the court. Therefore, the order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver could be executed against the appellant to the extent to which it rendered itself personally liable under the term of the bond. [361 E F] (4) Under Section 150 of Code of Criminal Procedure, the Subordinate judge was entitled to exercise the same power in the matter of the enforcement of the bonds as the District Judge himself. Section 145(c) of the code of Civil procedure provides that where any person has become liable as surety for an fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of the Court in any suit or in any proceeding consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed by the transferee to the amount to which he has rendered himself personally liable.

The appellants were dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat by them. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat, by taking into account the sale price of the wheat by the appellants and rejecting the contention that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. The order was confirmed by the Additional Commissioner (Judicial) who held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning of the U .P. Act, 1948. On appeal the Assistant Commissioner (judicial) Sales Tax held that there was a sale within section 2(h) of the Act and the tax was payable by the assessee. The appellants appealed to the Appellate Tribunal which held that under the definition of 'sale ' in section 2 (h), the dealer was obliged to sell to the State Government 50% of the quantity of wheat purchased by him at the commencement of the Order, and that the sale was not a sale ' within the contemplation of the legislature. The High Court also rejected the contention of the appellants that the transactions were sales within the definition in section 3(h). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the transaction was not one of sale but only an agreement to sell; (ii) the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax, because, the State had treated the transaction as a sale and levied tax thereon under the Act under the , and (iii) the expression 'sale of goods ' in the Constitution must be understood in the same sense in which it is used in the Indian Sale of Goods Act. HELD: The High court was right in holding that there could not be any contract between the assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the term of section 2 of the Indian Contract Act. [50 F] The expression 'Sale ' in article 366(29) means a transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment, a transaction in which an obligation to supply goods is imposed, and which does not involve an obligation on the part of the seller to enter into a contract, cannot be called a sale. [51 F] In the instant case, the transactions entered into by the appellant with the Regional Sales Tax authorities were not sales within section 3 (h) but in the statutory order. The State Government was therefore directed by the Order to pay tax on the turnover of the goods sold within it. [52 G H] The High Courts had rightly held that despatches of sugar pursuant to directions issued under a State Act would be taxable as sales. [53 A B] Ram Bilas Ram Gopal vs State of Madras, ; , followed.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him and he was informed that he was not actually released from prison. He was also not arrested in connection with some other case. The Advisory Board considered his representation and passed its report on September 26, 1986. The appellant was thereafter taken into custody. The order of detention was challenged by the appellant in a writ petition before the High Court. A Division Bench of the High court dismissed the petition holding that there had been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22(4) of the Constitution and therefore the appellant was entitled to be set at liberty. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there has been a violation of the Constitutional protection afforded to him under Article 22(1) of ' the Constitution inasmuch as he was required in connection therewith to appear before the Advisory Board within three months from the date of the order of deten tion and his representation was not considered by the Advisory Committee within the period contemplated by section 11 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the Court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The procedure under the Act has been strictly complied with if any value is to be attached to the liberty of the subject and the constitution al rights guaranteed to him in that regard. If a reference to an Advisory Board is to he made within three weeks, it is no answer to say that the reference, though not made within 3 months, was made before the hearing of the case. If the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it was no answer tO say that his representation, although not made in three months, were disposed of before the hear ings. [209C D] 2. The mandatory requirements are: (a) the procedural requirements must be strictly complied; (b) the reference though not making the report within three month, was a time barred; and (c) the constitution rights guaranteed under article 22 (4) were to be strictly followed.

The petitioner, a father of the respondent, filed a suit for setting aside an award made in his favour by the arbitrator. The arbitrator entered upon the reference and passed an award. The petitioner preferred an appeal against the judgment and decree passed in the said award. A revision application was also dismissed. In the meantime, the petitioner filed a civil revision application against the order of the Civil Judge raising practically all the disputes which had been raised by him in this civil revision petition. The High Court dismissed the civil revision applications. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to the arbitrator, and that he made an award, and therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. [538C D] 1.2 The conduct on the part of the petitioner that there is an arbitration clause and by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th August, 1978 (Exhibit 40) the respondent had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20th January, 1977 and that they made an Award. All these are in writing and signed by all the parties. This, in our opinion, is not a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of the Act. [540D E] 1:3. The Civil Court had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the award under sections 14 and 17 of the . This question had come up for consideration before the Judicial Committee in Rajah Amir Hassan Khan vs Sheo Baksh Singh, ; , where this Court observed that interminable time consuming, complex and expensive court procedures impelled jurists to search for an alternative forum less formal, more effective and speedy for resolution of disputes avoiding procedural claptrap and this led them to the . However, the way in which the proceedings under the Act are conducted and without an exception challenged in Courts, has made lawyers laugh and legal philosophers weep. This Court further observed that experience shows and law reports hear ample testimony that the proceedings u/s 14 and17 of the , are conducted by all parties. [541F G] 2.1 In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that both the parties have agreed to referred the dispute for arbitration to the Arbitrator. The award was signed by both the par ties, about which there is no factual dispute, reiterated the fact that the particu lar proceedings were without jurisdiction.

The appellant, a mortgagee in a mortgage of leasehold interest, was appointed receiver of that estate in the suit. The receiver applied to the Court for striking off the execution case against him on the ground that he had failed to discharge his obligations under the decree and that the Court may pass an order directing him to exercise all or any of the powers conferred on it by section 36(1) of the Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953. The application was dismissed by the Subordinate Judge but the High Court in appeal held that the order made on January 30, 1937, was not a proceeding in execution and as such could not be reopened. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words and that he bad not received the notice referred to in cl. (a) of sub section (1) Of section 28 make it plain that an assignee of a mortgage debt is within the sub section, since section 28, sub section(1), is concerned only with assignment of debts '. [586 B C] (ii) The expression "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in the passage quoted above, means "all rights of a mortgagor" and not merely "all his rights". The words "all such rights of an assignee" are used to denote all the rights which are of a suit to which this Act applies. [596 C D] (iii) The word "decree" is not defined in section 2(22) of 'a suit to be instituted or filed on or after that date and includes a proceeding arising out of execution of a decree. The words used by them are "all those rights of any assignee". They are not defined either in the Code of Civil Procedure or in the Act. [606 D] In the present case, the order of January 30. 1937, which purported to dismiss the respondent 's execution case for non prosecution while continuing the attachment was made and was pending after January 1, 1939, when the application for striking out the execution was filed. The expression 'all the right of the assignee ' used by its Lordships in Promode Kumar Roy vsRupees ', Pat. 1, referred to.

The appellant was the karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided into three equal shares, namely, the undivided interest in the joint family properties and the undivided share of the appellant. In 1947 he transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint Hindu family. In 1954 he transferred those properties to the respondents. He also instituted a suit for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 15, 1946, were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court dis missed the suits. On appeal the High Court confirmed the decree in O.S. No. 62/54 but held that the transfers were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transfer was by way of gifts and not in consideration of the past cohabitation, and that the transactions were void as they were made in consideration for past illicit cohabitation. HELD: The transfers were without consideration and were by way off gift. The gifts were therefore invalid. [46 B] (i) In the present case, the transfers are without consideration. They were by the appellant in favour of the respondents and they were invalid because they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubine for her past services. [47 C D] Balo vs Parbati, A.I.R. 1940 All. 370, approved. (ii) The transfers are invalid. The gift was without consideration by way or gift and as such was valid.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of Nagput, was the wife of the deceased husband. The Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to the Manager of the Life Insurance Corporation of India (the respondent) for payment of interest on the amount of policy which had matured much earlier on 14.9.72 and 28.12.75. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice under Section 226(2) of Income Tax, 1961. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice was not valid as it involved the risk of exposing the L.I.C. or its officer making the statement on oath under section226(3)(vi) of 'the Act and that the failure to perform its statutory obligation under section 26(3), 1961, on the part of the Ll.C., in issuing the notice, amounted to an act which required the appellant to pay to the respondent. The appeal by special leave was filed against the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The question whether a notice under this sub section is governed by Section 244 of the Act or not has to be decided on its own facts and circumstances. [104G] 1.2. The expression "any person" in sub section (3) means any person who holds or occupies any share or interest in any newspaper or newspaper or whose business is carried on with the intention of earning income or property tax dues. The word "person" has been defined to mean a person who held or occupies property or interest and includes a company or other body corporate which may be carrying on any activity as an agent, trustee, receiver or otherwise in respect of any debt or claim or liability. [105A B] 1:3. The words "any such person" have been used in the context of section 244(1) to mean "a person who is a person against whom a notice has been issued by the Income tax Officer under sub section 3 of section 226". The expression 'person ' has been interpreted to mean any person whose duty or obligation to pay income tax dues of the assessee arises by virtue of the provisions of the Indian Income Tax and Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1975. [106B C] 1 :4. The term "person", in the definition of "person". In the context, it is clear that the expression "person ' includes a person whose income or claim for compensation or property taxes dues or property dues or any other person, then, nothing contained in this sub Section shall be deemed to require such person to pay any such sum or part thereof as the case may be. [107C D] 1 5. The liability of the appellant in these circumstances is not covered by section 244 of Income tax Act,1961.

The appellant, who was the owner of certain lands in Bombay, filed a suit against the respondent for possession of those lands on the ground that they were not liable to pay the arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal by special leave, Held: (1) that article 156 of Schedule 11 of the Limitation Act does not apply to an appeal under the Burma Courts Act, 1947 and as such the application for a special or local law is not governed by that Code. The words "where any special or other law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the First Schedule" occurring in article 156(2) of the Indian Limitation Act are wide enough to include a suit, Appeal or application for which no period of time is prescribed in the first schedule but a period Of limitation has been prescribed by a special law. (2) that the words " where any special and local law prescribes a period within the meaning of article 29(2), the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18 and section 22 shall apply only in so far as they are not expressly excluded by such special or special law" and since the suit was filed more than one year after the coming into force of the limitation Act, it was governed by section 29(1) of that Act. (3) that even assuming that article 158 of Schedule II of the Act did not prescribe a period for an appeal to the High Courts under the Code of Civil Procedure, the question arises whether sub section (2), will apply to such appeals and if so, whether it was sufficient if the procedure for filing the appeal and the powers of the court for dealing with the appeal were governed by the Code.

The appellant, a bus operator, was charged with the offence of having driven a bus stand at Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stands. The District Magistrate passed an order under section 76 of the , directing that the bus stand of Baldev ( MATHUR) be taken over by the District Magistrate. The respondent challenged the said order before the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76 was not applicable to the permanent bus stands which was a sort of radiating centre of all the bus traffic in the town. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 76 of The Act has nothing to do with the fixation or alteration of a bus stop and the power to issue a notification fixing a bus Stand is implied in section 68(2)(r) of the Act. [717B] 1.2 In the instant case no order has been passed by the Regional Transport Authority, Mathura to determine the area in question as a Bus stand and the District Magis trate cannot be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under the Act.[718C D] 1:3 The High court was in error in upholding the impugned order passed by District Magistrate, since section 76 has nothing ties to do. [700F G] 1 :4 In the present case no such order has ever been passed either by the State Government or by any authority authorised in this behalf by the respondent State to determine whether the area is a bus scheme or a bus stood. The Regional Transport Author ity, Mathura had made bye laws under the provisions of section 358(7)(f) and (m) read with section 349(ii) of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act 1961. [617C D; 700D] 1 5 2.1 The High Courts have rightly held that section 77 of the has nothing lo do with fixation or altering a bus service and the powers to issue such notification fixing the bus stands are implied in Section 68(1)(c). It is not disputed that in the instant cases no order had been passed under section 77.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the . The prosecution case was that on October 19, 1961 Sub Inspector of Food and Supplies Department was present at Smalkha Barrier along with Head Constable Badan Singh and others. On October 18, 1961 the truck carrying 75 bags of paddy was intercepted at Samalkha Barriers which was 32 miles from Delhi. The truck was intercepted by the police and it was found that the consignment of paddy had been booked from Lakerkotla on October 18. 1961 by Qimat Rai on behalf of M/s Sawan Ram Chiranji Lal. The goods were seized as also the bags of rice. On appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction of the appellants but convicted them under section 3(1) of the and sentenced them to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellants that there was an attempt on the part of the appellant to transport paddy to Delhi and so there was no export of paddy outside the State in this case. HELD : The fact that the truck with the loaded paddy was seized at Samalskha BarPost which is 32 miles away from Delhi cannot be said to be such that if the offender changes his mind and does not proceed further in its progress, the acts already done would be completely harmless. [667 B] In order that a person may be convicted of an attempt to commit a crime he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit the offence, and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the actuarially reus is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt lo commit it. If a man buys a box of matches, he cannot be convicted for attemptedarson however clearly it may be proved that he intended to set fire to a haystack at the time of the purchase. Nor can he be convicted under s.7 of the , if he approaches the stack with the matches in his pocket, but if he bends down near the stacks and lights a match which he extinguishes on perceiving that he is being watched, he may be guilty of an offence if he approach the stroke with the match which him extinguishes.

The Sassoons of the respondent company were the Managing Agents of a company which was incorporated under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The managing agency commission was payable in respect of services for an entire calendar year and not for a portion thereof and therefore no remuneration was payable to the Sassoon till the end of the year. The question for determination was whether the remuneration for the broken periods accrued to the respondent as a result of the assignment of its Managing Agency to the transferees under the agreement dated March 31, 1943. Held, that the managing agency remuneration for each of the four years was the income of the assessee company and not of the company and therefore the remuneration was not liable to tax in respect thereof. The Managing Agency commission was paid by the respondent on its accrual and not by the transfer of the managing Agency to it. The liability of the assignor to receive the entire remuneration did not depend on any specific term between the assignors and the assignee but on the fact that what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that fell due after the date of assignment. Held further, that in computing the taxable income of a person for the purpose of taxation of the assigned agency the true nature of the functioning of a Managing Agent where it is, a firm or company, which so functions, has been previously held by this Court in Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son vs The Government of Hyderabad, ; , referred to. Held also, that though the managing agent was liable to pay the entire sum of remuneration for his broken periods of actual services rendered by him to the respective Mill Companies for broken periods, he was not entitled to any part of the remuneration as per this agreement.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the courts below held it to be true; (2) the defence version that the soliman assented to him was not a admissible piece of evidence, and (3) the deceased and the accused had some quarrel on the Janmashtami day in the evening. HELD: The High court was right in holding that the statement made by the accused under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should have been communicated to another before it could be used to corroborate the testimony of another witness. [89 D] (1)(a) The evidence Act places them in the category of relevant evidence, presumably on the ground that as they are declarations against the interest of the person making them, they are probably true. The probative value of an admission or a confession does not depend upon its communication to another, though just like any other piece of Evidence, it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. [90 F] (b) A statement whether communicated or not admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But, there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional solil acknowledgments are exceptions to the hearsay rule. The Evidence Act places it in the categories of relevant Evidence, presumably, on the grounds that as the they are declaration against the interests of the persons making them they are certainly true. [91 G H] (c) It is not a necessary ingredient of the term that it shall be communicated to other than the person proposed to be proved. The expression "confession" is not defined in the Code. What the Legislature has done is to give effect to the circumstantial evidence adduced in the case. [92 B C] Pakala Narayana vs R. section Rajagopalan, A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 310 and Pakala Venkataswami vs State of Bombay, A I.R., 1960 S C. 311, referred to. (2)(a). The expression 'confession ' is not used in the sense that it is stated 'and the element of communication was not necessary before "something that is stated" became a statement under that section. [93 B] (3)(b) The expression means 'the act of stating, reciting or presenting verbally or on paper '. The term 'statement ' is used in section 133 of the Evidence Act to indicate what are the exact words used by the appellant. Even if so much was established, prudence and justice demand that such evidence cannot be made the sole ground of conviction. It may be used only as a corroborative piece ofevidence.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. The general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. The appellant was kept under suspension from August 9, 1973 pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973. In response thereto the appellant submitted his reply on deci sion dated June 13, 1974. While dropping the proceeding the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The respondent challenged it in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee 's service whether permanent or temporary" which shall be decided by the Board" is susceptible of two interpretations. The one interpretation put up by Sri Ramamurty is that the Board may unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there is no need for the services of a particular employee, in given facts and circumstances, though the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. [225B C] 1.2 The expression 'in the case of the society not having no further need ' has been defined thus: "in case of a society not being having any other need" it is susceptible o two interpretations, namely, that the board may unilaterally & arbitrarily decide to abolish the post, in consequence the service of the officer/employee occupying couched in Rule 5 also is capable of that interpretation. [226C D] 1:3 The expression `in the possibility of the employee ', whether permanent, or temporary, which shall he decided by Board" was susceptible of both the interpretations. [227D] 2.1 In the instant case, the Board of Management did not abolish the Post but put an end to the service. Therefore, it is not necessary to deal with other contentions or decisions cited across the bar. The High Court has rightly held that Rule 5 does not become arbitrary. [228E F] D.T.C. vs D. T.C., Mazdoor Congress & Ors., 225; referred to. 2.2 In view of this settled legal position, the question emerges whether the language in Rule5 would be capable of two constructions. It is settled law that there was a presumption of constitutionality of the rule. The Court ought not to interpret the statutory provisions unless compelled by their language, in such a manner as would involve its unconstitutionality, since the legislature of the Rule making authority is presumed to enact a law which does not contravene or violate the constitutional provisions. Therefore the rule is valid.

The appellant State issued a notification under section 6 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915, for the grant of exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell country liquor. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notification dated August 19, 1970 issued under section 29(2) of the Act was ultra vires the Act as it was issued for the purpose of getting over the High court 's declaration in O.J.C.No. 357 of 1970 that rule 103(1) of Board 's Excise Rules was ultra rites and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The State has the exclusive right to privilege of manufacture and sale of liquor. It is not a privilege of a citizen of the State, and it is not an absolute right of a citizens of the state. [814 D] A citizen has a fundamental right to do business and deal in liquor with the utmost possible care and caution that he may use for his trade or business. The State cannot be said to have reserved any right to manufacture or sell liquor. [850 E] In the instant case, the State had no authority to issue a notification fixing the amount of consideration for the granting of a license for the exclusive privilege of retail vend of country spirit. The High Court was wrong in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector was not for the same purpose as the power of the Government under section 22 of the Excise Act. [851 F G] A.K. Roy vs State of West Bengal, ; , referred to.

The appellant was charged with having entered into a criminal conspiracy with the approver Dinkar Sakharam for committing the murder of Narendra. The prosecution case against him was that he had entered into criminal conspiracy to commit theft of articles in the house of Dr. Nanavati and disposed of the property so as to induce him to commit the theft of article in the House of his grand father. The appellant was tried along with other accused for having committed the murder. The trial court convicted him under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence of death to rigorous imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder and that the evidence against the appellant was not corroborated by the evidence of the approver 's own witness. HELD: (i) The evidence of Dr Nanavati was sufficient to connect accused No. 2 with the crime. [621 B] (ii) There was no motive for the appellant to commit a theft in the room of his house. He was seen alive in the company of accused No 2 and Dinkar. Accused No.2 and 3 were known to him by face and the third was a boy of 14 or 15 years of age, wearing khaki shorts and a shirt. The shirt and the chain were identified by Dr. M. Nanaji and his wife to belong to Narendra. [625 E F] (iii) There is no corroboration in regard to the approver. He had seen accused No 1 and 2 going together for the sale of cycle carrier to Rupvate. The evidence on record established that he was seen last seen in the Company of accused NO. 2 and his son. The discovery of the chain which Narendra wore found in the godown of accused no. 2 was as a result of a statement by accused No, 2. [613 E F; 614 A] Lachi Ram 's case, approved. (iv) There were material particulars in regard tO the appellant not only with the offence of theft but also with murder. He did not have any motive to commit that crime. The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that there is sufficient corroboration of his evidence. [516 B] Lachmi Ram ' case, referred to.

The appellant, a lessee of a Hindu undivided family, was the lessee. On July 4, 1967, the Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 50 per sq. The total compensation awarded was Rs. 3,31,455. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Town planning officer. The Town Planning officer enhanced the compensation by his order dated November 4, 1971. The respondent preferred an Appeal. Section 34 read with section 32(1) of the Act provided that the amount of compensation payable to an owner for loss of land has to be determined on the basis of the market value of the land at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. The appeal filed by the appellant was dismissed by the Town plan officer. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Act specifies a principle of compensation, and (ii) the rate fixed for the purpose is not excessive or unreasonable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that enactment of a rule determining payment or adjustment of price of land of which owner was deprived by the scheme estimated on the marketvalue on the date when the declaration of the intention to making a scheme was made. [92F] 2.1 The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating compensation payable by an owner of land who has not been given a plot in the final scheme and also provides for a case where the amount payable to the owner exceeds the amount due from him. Section 71 is as follows: "The owner of any property or right which is injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme shall be entitled to obtain compensation from the local authority or from any person benefited or partly from the Local Authority and partly from such person as the Town development officer may in each case determine."
