[92G H] 2:2. The Act contained the necessary provi sions for estiming the compensation payable. The expression "person interested" as defined in section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act is the generally accepted meaning of that expression and it is not relevant for the purposes of this appeal.

The appellant was the brother of one of his sons. He had a brother in law and a son who died in 1934. The widow made a will on October 4, 1927 bequeathing all her properties to the daughters. The appellant 's father made a gift of the properties to his daughter. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the property according to the custom of 1925 which was decreed by the trial court but the High Court held that the will was for the benefit of the widow and not for the daughters to make the selection. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The testator 's intention was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees making the selection in the order in which they were named in the will. [975 B] (ii)The words "he shall give to the female children" in section 89, are not used in the Act for the purpose of giving preference to the testator. The intention of the testator was clearly expressed by him in the Will and he could have given them a share in the properties bequeathed to the two daughters. [945 B] Narayanasami Gramani vs Hindle (I.L.R. , approved. (iii)The will was not intended to be a will for the reason that it was for a collateral purpose. The testator had indicated the selection or appointed a third person to make it. It is clear that the testator intended that each daughter should get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. If that were the intention of a testator he should have given him a share which could be taken into account in computing the area to be allotted to the daughter. [946 B C] (iv)The High Court was right in holding that the direction of the will did not amount to an appointment of selection to the legatee and it was not necessary for the testator to give them a larger share in his properties. The words " he shall give" in the deed were intended to cover only those items which are mentioned in the document. [947 E F] (v)The intention of testator was clear that he intended that the daughters would get their land after taking account the bad quality and had quality of land. The will was therefore not a will within the meaning of section 89.

The appellant, who was the widow of one Syed Laek Husain and defendants No. 1 and 2 were his brothers. The respondents filed a suit for joint possession over the land in dispute on the ground that they were co bhumidars, because after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 the plaintiff appellant was dispossessed from the land. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendants were in separate occupation of the land or plots in dispute and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. On appeal, the District Judge reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit for a joint possession of the share of the property from the hands of the defendants. The High Court also held that the plaintiff 's name was suddenly deleted after 1359 Fasli and there was no order of any authority or court to show the circumstances under which the plaintiff was suddenly removed, nor were there any judicial proceedings under which he could be dispossessed. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the defendants had committed fraud; (ii) the suit was barred by section 49 of the Act because the defendants did not have any concern with the consolidation authorities and were assured by the defendants that they would take proper care of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The possession of defendant No. 2, apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of plaintiff. Apart from this, the fact remains that the District judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the respondents or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. [867D E] 2. The mere non participation in the rent and profits of the landlord does not amount to an ouster so as to give title by adverse possession to the other co sharer in possession. Indeed even if this fact be admitted, then the legal position would be that Mohd. Basir and Mohd. Rashid, being co sharers of plaintiff 'Souza, would become constructive trustees on behalf of the appellant and the right of the respondent would be deemed to be protected by the trustees. The learned counsel appearing for the respondents was unable to contest this position of law. [886G H] 3. The fact remains as it is absolutely correct that mere non participating in the rents and profits cannot amount to a suit on the basis of title, the courts will not easily infer a bar of suit to establish the title of the parties.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The Chief Minister of Haryana took the oath of Prime Minister and filed an affidavit on behalf of Union of India stating that he had been sworn into office as the Chief Minister. The High Court held that the oath register is by virtue of section 75(4) of the Constitution and that the petitioner was still functioning as the chief Minister. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The oath register has to be read along with Form VII A pursuant to which the petitioner 's name is one which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, he is a Minister of the Union and there is no separate form even for the Prime Minister. Since the petitioner himself is described as Deputy Prime Ministers, he takes the same oath as the other ministers are required to take. He maintains that yet in view of the fact that the Constitution describing him as Deputy Chief Minister, while being sworn into Office, he describes himself as Prime Minister but the description of him as the Deputy Prime Minis ter does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers along with his other submis sions. [1269C D] 1.2 The oath registers are by virtue and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Minister does not conferment on him no powers of his Prime Minister, alongwith his otherSubmis sion, but the name of the Deputy Chief Minis tors does confer on them any powers oy of the Chief Prime Minister along with their other subse quent submisions. The oath Register is by incumbent signed as Prime Ministers and all others sign as representatives. He also indi vates that description of Shri Devi Lai as Deputy Lok Minister doesnot confer on the petitioner any powers or privileges of the President, alongwith the other sub stars. [1369G H] 2.1 In view of clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as the Dy. Prime Minister he cannot press it. [1470A B] Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant company was a strike which took place in the night of 1st November, 1948. The strike ended completely and the workers were not entitled to any holidays with pay as provided by the Act. The dispute between the workmen and the management related to the period for about 2 to 4 hours in the circumstances of this case. The Tribunal held that the continuity of service of the workers was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that the workers had failed to take back their wages with pay. Held, that the appellant company could not be denied the right to a reasonable opportunity of being heard on the ground of non permitted absence as a result of the strike. The principle of natural justice is applicable only in cases where the interruption in service is brought about by an illegal strike. But in the present case the strike was not a continuous and continuous one and the appellant had no discretion not to regard it as a strike. Held further, that in view of the facts and circumstances detailed in the adjudicator 's award this contention cannot be sustained. The question whether the workers should be reinstated or not depends on the construction of the rules and this in volves a substantial question of law. It is not necessary for an individual worker to plead that the stoppage of work on 1st, November,1948, amounted to a strike, because, if it could be denied that the stopped work was not as a consequence of the illegal strikes, the action of the workmen on the night intervening 1st and 11th November, 1949, fell within the definition of the word "strike" in section 2(q) of the .

The appellant, actor, photographer and distributor of the film, was charged with offences under sections 292 I.P.C., 79 I. P.C. and section 292 I P. C. for having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censors. The prosecution alleged that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and he had a feeling of hatred because of the exhibition of the films. The trial court, after examining some witnesses, took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused. Thereupon, the producer, namely, the appellant moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P C. on the ground that the criminal proceeding was an abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censor and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious would not be an offence under section 292 1.P C. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 79 I P C is general, the is special. The scheme of the latter is deliberately drawn up to meet the explosively expanding cinema menace if it were not strictly policed. No doubt, the film is a great instrument for public good if geared to social ends and can be a public curse if directed to anti social objectives. But all freedom is a promise, not a menace and, therefore, is subject to socially necessary restraints permitted by the Constitution. [515D E] (2) The High Courts have rightly held that the facts stated in the complaint prima facie attract the offence under sections 293 I.p.C.[516F G] (3) Section79 I. p. C., as it stood at the relevant time, was not considered by this Court because the facts were admitted and the question of law is whether the film has been given a certificate by an authority competent to heavy investments in films. [511B D] (4) The finding that one had sufficient reason for doing that which i.e. is called to answer, is not correct. The film was a great document with millions of viewers and many people were rich in the impression that it was a public trust. It is an antinomy to say that under section 79 I .p. C, the Board certifies a film as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292 l.p., to punish such exhibition unless the ground covered by the two laws be different. [ 512D E; G H] (5) The certificate issued thereunder is not binding on the Court. It was issued under article 19(2) from the angle of public order, decency or morality. These concepts are themselves dynamic and cannot be whittled down to stifle expression nor licentiously enlarged to promote a riot of setta display. Anyway, the appeal must succeed and extinguish the prosecution by the order.

The petitioner, a practising advocate for the Patna District, was appointed as an Advocate on July 1, 1970 and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He also alleged that his client 's claim as the sole representative of the Government Pleader for the first time in the Patna High Court was not accepted by the Supreme Court or at least flawed in law which is fraught with manifest injustice, there being no legal right to appoint more than one lawyer except u/s 16(2) of the Bihar Public offices (Prevention, Control and Appeal) Act, 1970. The petition was contested on behalf of the State Government contending that his clients were not entitled to seek lucrative offers for a lakh of rupees. It was further contended that the petitioner 's client ' is an independent legal representative for his persistent litigation, May be it through court or by any other litigant, and that he has no locus standi to file the petition under Article 32 of the Constitution or at any rate flawed with the procedure prescribed in law. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition holding that the Government pleader was not entitled for a just ad valorem enormity of the work done by him and that the court had no other open sea of litigation. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly pointed out that the State is an inclusive one and, therefore, it cannot be said that lawyering in India needs a National level bulk of the total volume, it is not necessary to sacrifice speedy conduct of cases by not appointing more than two Government Pleader. [764G H] 1.2 The High Courts have rightly pointed to the fact that the Advocate General has been appointed by the State on remuneration paid from the public exchequer and having regard to various functions and duties to be performed by him in the due exercise of that office, most of which are of an independent and responsible character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [766B C] 1:3 The High court has rightly observed that the Court ordered about a Government Pleader is obnoxious but nothing savouring of such conduct is made out although it may affect the legality of the action and subvert the rule of law itself. After all, a Government pleader and, in a sense, every member of the legal profession has a higher dedication to the people. [765C D] 1 :4 The Court has also pointed out the view that the conclusion that the office is a public post is irresistible.

The appellants held out of a total issue of shares of the Bank of India. At an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the bank held on May 6, 1948, a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the company to Rs. 50 per share for every three shares held by the shareholders. The Directors of the Mills passed resolutions approving the increase in the share Capital and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of one new share for each new share. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and also undertook to pay Rs. 100 per share as capital and Rs. 500 as premium per each share. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors of Mills passed a resolution on May 25, 1948 increasing the shares to Rs, 50 per one ordinary share held in this company. The question for determination was whether the distribution of the right to apply for the shares amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the distribution was not distribution of capital and that the resolution was not a distribution of its capital. The resolution was therefore not justified having regard to the form of the question which expressly related to the distribution. The face value of the new share was Rs.50 but the shareholders had to pay a premium of Rs. 10,000 as premium for acquiring the new shares out of 1,666 shares offered by the Bank. The old shares were quoted in the market at more than Rs. 200 and the difference between the amount payable for acquiring them under the right offered by it and the market quotation of the shares was indisputably the value of 1.666 shares.

The appellant was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly. The respondent filed an election petition under section 81 of the Representation of People Act, 1951 for setting aside the election of the appellant. The High Court refused to examine him on the ground that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered was not mentioned in the list and therefore, the election petitioner could not be permitted to examine more than one witness whose names had not been mentioned in that list. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant could not have been allowed to examine only those witnesses whose names were mentioned in a list prepared under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the election petition was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The obligation to supply the list as well as the gist of evidence of each witness whose name is entered in the List has to be carried out in respect of those witnesses for procuring their attendance. [532B] (1)(a) The obligation under these provisions are conjointly read and properly analysed, it clearly transpires that the obligation to provide the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub section (1), of Order XVIII is in respect only of witnesses who are mentioned in List II. Sub rule (3) confers a discretion on the Court to permit a party to summon through court or otherwise any witness other than those whose names appear in the lists prepared under subsection (1). [533B C] (b) The mandate of these provisions is that the failure to supply a list of the witnesses within time prescribed by sub rule(1) should be viewed as directory and not mandatory. If mere omission to mention the name of a witness in the Lists envisaged by sub section(1), the party would be entitled to examine such witness, Rule 1A would have given a clear legislative exposition in that behalf and the marginal note of Rule IA clearly negatives this suggestion. [525C D] (c) The requirement of these provi sions are mandatory and not directory. If a party wants the assistance of the Court for producing witnesses on being summoned through the Court, it is obligatory on the party to file the list with the gist thereof. [500D E] (d) The provision of Order XVII of the Civil Procedure Code enables the court for reasons to be recorded in writing to refuse to examine any witness or witnesses if it is of the opinion that the evidence of such witness or witness is not material for the decision of the petition or that the party tendering such witness is doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. [511D E; G] (e) The proviso to section 87(1)(d) confers power on the court to permit the party who may be examined by the party, to produce evidence or to produce documents without applying for summons under Rule 1.

The appellant, a double M.A., was appointed as Principal of the College by the Committee of Management of the college. The Selection Committee consisted of Shri Shankar Shukla, Principal and Shri Phul Deo Pandey, Principal of Sri Nath Intermediate College, Jaunpur and Dr. Gauri Shanker Misra, Principal, Sri Ram Dularey Tripathi, Principal in the College. The appellant submitted his application for appointment to the post of Principal. His name was included in the panel prepared by the Selection Committee on April 12, 1981. He was required to present himself before the Manager of the institution and take over charge within 10 days of the receipt of this letter failing which he would be deemed to have been appointed as the Principal of his college. On May 1, 1981, the appellant wrote a letter to the Manager that as permitted by him he had assumed charge of the post and was required by him to present personally before the manager of the Institution and take up the charge within ten days of receipt of the order of appointment failing which the appointment would be void. The Manager sent a reply on May 1 1981 stating that as per the radiogram dated April 7,1981 contained an order of the State Government suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore he was required not present himself at the time when the order was passed. The manager of his school filed a writ petition in the High Court praying for a writ of mandamus directing the 5th respondent to hand over charge to him. The High Court held that the radiotry dated April 8, 1981 contained an Order of the Government suspending the appellant 's appointment and directed the State Govt. to take immediate steps to fill in the post as Principal and to pay salary. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) The order of suspension having been passed without giving an opportunity of being heard to the appellant, the order dated May 1. 1981 was not valid; (2) The State Government had no power to make the appointment and therefore the Committee 's order suspending or withdraw power of appoint ment of teaching Staff including Principal could be sustained; (3) The High court erred in holding that the Executive Committee had no right to select the appellant nor the Committee had any power to do so; (4) The letter dated May, 1 1981 which has been extracted above clearly shows that on April 7 1981 the institution had received the order that the power of appointing Principal has been withdrawn or suspended. The order contained in the radiolram was communicated to the manager and the appellant was asked to hand back charge to the Principal. The State Govt., therefore, enjoys the power to appoint the appellant as Principal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order dated April 27, 1981 is not received by the institution. It is only an interim order passed in favour of the management. [975B] 1.2 The order was not received back from the Manager who was the appointing authority. The letter was sent to the Management of a college which was topless and an unfair advantage is being taken of this situation by Jagannath whose credentials to be appointed as principal are still to be investigated. It was, therefore, imperative that the State Govern ment should direct the Commission to take necessary steps to filling in the posts of Principal of College. [986F G] 1:3 The situation is that the powers of appointment conferred on the Committee under regulation on Committee of management of all non government aided institutions were withdrawn or suspension. The Committee of the Management had no authority to make any consequential order. [987B C] 2.1 It is imperative that a State Government should direct its Commission to takes effective steps to comply with the provisions of the Act as it deems necessary and in particular, may by such order modify or rescind or make any other order consistent with the provi sions of the act as it deem necessary and, in particular.

The respondent assessee is a manufacturer of tyres. The goods manufactured by the petitioner were assessed to sales tax under the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954. The contention of the respondent was that the goods were exempt from taxation. The Sales Tax officer rejected these contentions and held that the respondent had wrongly escaped assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order. The High Court in a reference made at the instance of the petitioner held that since the goods sought to be taxed are not the "end product" it must be deemed to have been exempted under the Act so that the appellate authority could go into the whole evidence and decide disputed questions of fact. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Courts were right in not interfering with the decisions of the taxing authorities at this stage. [502 D] (i) The word "textiles" has a wide meaning. The first instance of such a product is: "a manufactured material". It is true that the term fabric has a broad meaning. But, against pushing this point of view too far it may be urged that in the technical and commercial parlance it is not just the skeleton of a textile. But against paving this point, it must necessarily follow that if the goods are manufactured in the same way as cloth is woven on looms, they would fall under the definition of "textile" given in the Oxford Dictionary. [500 E F] (ii) The words "toollen fabrics" do not contain any definition and the word "fabric" has been used to give the exact meaning of the term "f Fabric". It may be that the "lyre cord fabric" is so well established a category of rayon "fool", it could have found mention specifically in item 22 in the New Encyclopaedia Britannica, and the description in the preceding entries seem to be very wide. [504 E F; 505 A] (iii) The context in which the entry occurs shows that it is meant for "totton fabric" fabrics and not for any kind of fabric. Therefore even if the tyre cord fabric may be the end product for the Delhi Cloth Mills, the crucial question is: Does this product constitute a fabric entitled to exemption. [506 B C] (iv) The High court was right in holding that the product for which the Delhi cloth claims exemption Is a textile fabric and not any other kind of fabrics. Having indicated the nature of the enquiry which must by undertaken by the taxing Authorities, the Court is not bound to decide whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric as such or as merely cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric This is really a technical question. [ 506 E F]. (v) The definition of 'textiles ' in section 2(c) of the Rajasthan Act shows that the word 'textile ' has a wider meaning and the first instance may be a question on which two views seem possible on apparent facts. It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, of the composition of the "tyre cord fabrics" and an evaluation of opinion of experts on the subject, to be able to decide the question satisfactorily.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal, and was caught red handed while carrying 55 pieces of electromagnetic clutch plates kept concealed in the tool box of his scooter. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred to Labour Court for adjudication. The Labour Court registered the case as a reference case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance before the Labour Court and filed their respective pleadings. The State Government, in exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , transferred the proceeding from the Labour court, Dhanbad to Labour court Patna for speedy disposal. The High Court did not agree with the contention of the appellant that it was expedient to withdraw the case from the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workman and transferring the case to Labour Courts, Patna should have given an opportunity to the management to give a notice to him before making an order under section 33 B; (ii) the State Government had no power to transfer a case on the basis of allegations of one party without giving reasonable opportunity to other party to represent its point of view. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement about the statement of reasons to be recorded must be complied with both in substance and in letter. [302E] 1.2 In a democratic polity wedded to the rule of law, the State or the Legislature does not intend that in the exercise of their statutory powers its functionaries should act unfairly or unjustly. It is only when administrative officers are concerned, the duty is not so much to act judicially as to act fairly and justly. [303G] 1:3 The requirement regarding the statement before the Government for transferring a case from one Labour Court to another without hearing the assessee is a fatal flaw to the decision of the Government. [304B] 1st Respondent has withdrawn the pending proceeding from Labour Court, Dhanbad and transferred it to another Labour Court at the distant District of Patna on the representation of the workmen without getting it veri fied from the management. The order of transfer in that case was quashed for not communi cating reasons to the Government which had acted as a prudent check on abuse or misuse of power. [305C] 2.1 In the instant case, the Government has withdrawn its pending refe ration from the labour court, Patna and transferred the case. The Government has stated that the workman is having his residence at Hajipur and it would be therefore inconvenient for him to attend the labour Court regularly at Dhanbad. Reference may also be made to a letter dated September 8, 1988 (Annexure E) of the Headmaster of the School in which the children of the work man are studying. Reference might also be make ted to a Letter dated September8, 1988 issued by the Headmaster. [306D] 2:2 The Government was misled by the representation and transferred to Labour courts Patna. The labour court has stated in its letter dated Sept 8,1988 (Annexure D) that the workmen is having their residence at Hazipur and that it would therefore be inconvenient for them to attend t he labour court regularly at bay of Dhanbad. [307E] 2 :3 In view of the fact that the Government had withdrawn the earlier pending proceeding, the transfer order dated September, 1988 transferring the cases from the Court of Labour Court Patna to the Labour Courts Patna is quashed and set aside.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of its employees. The dispute between the hotel and its workmen related to the terms of employment, but the management did not make any reference under the , as required by section 10(1) of the Act. The company applied for leave to appeal to this Court against the order of the Tribunal on the ground that the reference was incompetent. Held, that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer and its employees and it went to this length that the hotel decided to dismiss a large number of workmen on October 7, 1955. The words " as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " in the order dated January 13, 1956, meant "as represented by such and such union in the dispute". The words were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy (A.I.R. 1953 S.C. 334) referred to. Held further, that there was no force in the contention that even if the workman is entitled to be represented by an officer of a trade union, the reference in this case did not mention any officer of the trade union but mentions the union itself. The fact remains that the parties to the dispute are clearly specified, namely, (1) the management which is the management of the hotel, and (2) its workmen.

The appellant is a manufacturer of rod bushes and parts thereof. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 281 Cus/76, dated 2 8 1976 issued under Section 3 of the . The appellant 's appeal before the Customs Excise and Gold Control Appellate Tribunal was dismissed by a common order dated 1 9 1976. The appellant contended that the said notification did not mention "the parts" of internal combustion piston engines, but only mentioned in Heading No. 84.06. The Tribunal held that the bushings and bearings are the same and as the bearings come under the heading No.84.06 they are not entitled to claim any exemption under the said Notification. Hence this appeal by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification grants exemption in part from payment of Customs duty in respect of articles specified in column (2) of the Table and falling under Heading No 84.07. [225B] 1.2 The intention of the notification is clear enough to provide that the parts of the engines, mentioned under Heading Nos. 8406.06 not only contemplates the engine or engines, and also the parts thereof.[225C D] 1:3. The Notification will apply to parts of a engines mentioned under heading No., 84.05. [226D] 1 :4. The intention is clear and manifest. It will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the Notifications and not to extend its benefit to the parts. [227E] 1 5. The notification will apply only to parts which are parts of such engines. When, therefore, the intention is obvious and manifest, it will be reasonable to take the narrow view that the words "parts" referred to in Heading Nos., 8406, 84.04, cover parts of internal fire pistons falling under heading 84.08. [228F] 1 6. The object of the exemption is to provide for the articles specified therein mentioned under a Heading other than Heading No.,84.07, and not a few parts thereof, and that though the parts are not mentioned under Entry No.

The first appellant, the plaintiffs in the suit, was the founder of a Muslim Wakf. He had two sons and one daughter. The first appellant was the eldest son of the first respondent. The second appellant was his eldest son. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants for declaring their right to be in management of the Dargah. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were entitled to be appointed in the office of Mujawar on the ground that they had been given only to male members and not to the females. The High Court, however, held that if really the rights of Fathima Bee had become barred by limitation, then the plaintiffs would have no independent right to claim any right of management or share in the offerings in the Dargah and even if they were entitled, they would be lost as a result of ouster. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was wrong in holding that if the rights had become extinct by reason of ouster, then succession would not have been barred by limi tation. On behalf of respondents it was submitted that the suit was barred by time and the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathina Bee had lost their right by ouster. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts in India committed a serious error in reversing the finding and in taking a wrong approach in holding ouster on the basis of judgment and decree given in Suit No. 116 of 1909 and on the grounds that Fathita Bee had not made a demand or asked for her share of the hundial collections at any point of time till her death in 1957. The only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High Courts were right in holding the ouster on this basis. [526B C] 1.2 In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathuma Bee or the plaintiffs, it was neces sary for the defendants to plead that they have asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoy ment to the knowledge of Fatina Bee.

The 1st respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. He was charged with house rent allowance for the period from 1st November, 1947 to 31st March, 1948. The 1st appellant 's case was that he became entitled to the allowance of Rs. 10 per month as part of his wages and that therefore he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowances. The authority rejected the claim on the ground that the house rent was "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the , and held that the 1st Respondent was entitled to a house rent Allowance. On appeal, the Appellate Authority confirmed the order. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the terms of the contract between the parties included the rule quoted above and therefore the position in law is that there is no absolute right in the 1 st respondent to claim the house allowance; (ii) the 1St respondent had been allotted railway quarters for his accommodation and he refused it, but that even so, the appellant was not enti tled under the Rules to any House Rent Allowance. HELD : (i)(a) The rule does not make it unconditional and absolute in terms. It is only when a person has been offered suitable house accommodation and has refused it he ceases to be so entitled whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. [1349 F] (b) Rule 3(i) of Chapter III of the Railway Establishment Code, which deals with "wages", makes it clear beyond all reasonable doubt that there was no absolute rights in the employee at all places wherever he may be posted and in all circumstances irrespective of whether or not he has been given Government quarters. [1449 G] (c) The definition of "wages ' under the Act cannot include the value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee; otherwise it would not be a legally permissible deduction from wages. It does not create an indefeasible right in an employee at ail places wherever lie may be posting and in All circumstances irrespective, of whether he has actually been offered Government quarters or not. [1549 G H] (d) The appellant 'rejected the claim for house rent on the basis that the House rent allowance was "payable" to him under section 7(2)(b) of Act. The High Court was right in holding that the grant of house rent does not created an indefeasible Right in the respondent at all. [1649 B] (e) The house rent agreement clearly showed that the employee posted at any one of those places would be entitled to house rent and that he actually occupied the quarters allotted to him, and that the appellant 'was not entitled to withhold the house Rent allowance.

The detenu was detained under the provisions of the . The grounds of detention were served on him on February 16, 1980. He filed a writ petition in this Court challenging his detention mainly on these grounds: (1) The order of detention purported to have been signed by Shri Salvi, Secretary in the Home Department, to the Government of Maharashtra, was void because the concerned Minister of State never applied his mind to the earlier statements of four persons from whom he claimed to have acquired the gems in question and in which they had on the basis of documentary evidence supported the contention of the detenus; (2) The detaining authority never applied its mind to these facts and there was thus unreasonable delay of more than three months in supplying the copies of the basic materials and documents relied upon in the grounds for detaining the detenu; (3) The detenu 's representation dated March 24, 1980 made to the State Government was considered by the Minister on April 3, 1980 and rejected on April 8, 1980; (4) The representation dated February 18, 1980 of the detenu was considered only on March 27, 1980, after more than one month. This delay of nearly three months was explained by the detaining authority in his counter affidavit filed before this Court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. "The constitutional imperatives enacted in Article 22(5) of the Constitution are two fold: (i) the detaining Authority must, as soon as practicable after the detention, communicate to the detenu the grounds on which the order has been made; and (ii) the detenue must afford the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the detention order. The mere fact that the grounds of deten tion served on the detenu are elaborate does not absolve the detaining authori ty from its constitutional responsibility to supply all the basic facts and materials relied upon by the Detaining Authority. [352B C] 2. "the vital link" in section 3(1) of COFEPOSA is that the detaining au thority must, within three months, communicate the grounds to the detenue. The detenu has to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. In the instant case, the detaining autho rised authority never intended to pass any order of detentiOn. It did not do so in public interest. [353E F] 3. "Some of the statements" recorded by the four persons mentioned in the ground for detention were not supplied to the detenus.

The Gujarat High Court, in a joint appeal by the State against several accused persons tried jointly, held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeals by several accused. The High Court also recorded a finding that the Scheme of Chapter XXVI of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules (which are applicable to proceedings in Gujarat High Courts) was inconsistent with Chapter XXX of the code of Criminal Procedure, with the result that a joint Appeal by several persons convicted at one trial must be upheld. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that r. 6 of Chapter XXVII of the Act dealt with "criminal business" and r.6 did not apply to a joint trial in a Joint trial. HELD : (i) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the joint appeal against several persons acquitted at a joint Trial was not maintainable. [875 B] (ii) Section 419 of the Criminal Procedure Code provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal, empowered the State Government to direct the public prosecutor in any case to present an appeal from an order of acquittal. This section does not seem to indicate any bar as is suggested by the order of the High Court. [888 C] (iii) The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Courts by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C. and r, 6 does not appear to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code.

The assessee firm was a registered firm carrying on business in India and its income from the properties owned by it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The assessee firm claimed that having regard to the severance of joint family status, the income of the family from April 13, 1938 to June 2, 1938 was not liable to be taxed by reason of section 25(3) and (4). The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that there was no discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 26(3), but held that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25 (3) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the income from these properties could not be taxed under the 1918 Act because the assessee had been assessed on remittances received from and out of the profits of the foreign business and there was nothing in the assessment order which would justify the claim for relief under Section 25(4) of 1922 Act. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the applications and held that there were discontinuance of business within section 25 by reason only of the transfer of the interest in the foreign partnership to the assessee and that the entire profits were assessed to income tax in the hands of the assessee under the 1922 Act, and that it could not therefore be said that the foreign income was liable to tax. The High Court on reference held against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The assessee was not entitled to the relief under s 25(2) of Income tax, 1922 Act with regard to rental income from house properties owned and sold by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. [910 B] (a) The High Courts were in error in holding that foreign business of the assesses was not charged under the provisions of the 1918 act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the assessee from the foreign company and not the foreign concern itself. [936 C D] (b) The income derived by the asses see was in relation to a business and therefore the assessment of the income must be treated as an assessment of that business. No doubt under the Act the charge was made on the receipt of income in British India and as the income received by it, was derived from the Indian business, it must be taken that there is an assessment to tax on the foreign activity within the definition of section 2(22) of that Act. [810 G H] (c) The question whether the assessee is entitled to claim relief under the section depends upon the facts found by the appellate Tribunal in this case and the High Court was right in holding otherwise.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of Capital Project, hundhinagar. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959, on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax to determine whether the supplies of bricks by the assessee to the Public works Department were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of bricks was not sales within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Act and accordingly he assessed the said supplies of kiln burning bricks to tax under section 10(2)(vi) of that Act. The respondent appealed to the Tribunal which held that as the supplies were made by the appellant to the public works Department, the transaction envisaged by the contract was a works contract and not a works contracts. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction contemplated by the Contract to which the appellant was a contractor was a contract of sale and not an execution of the contract. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was right in distinguishing the present case from the decision of the Supreme Court in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of orissa and others, ; that the decision in Chandra Mohan Gosain 's case was clearly distinguishable on facts; that the contract in question was a work contract and therefore the transaction was a sale of works contract; that even if it was held that there was a transfer of the property in and the delivery of the possession of a chattel as a chatte for consideration, the contract did not fall within the purview of section 4(6); that the agreement to brick produced was a composite one and it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special features and characteristics of the contracts that the contracts were sales; and that the question whether the transaction involved in the present appeal was a "works contract" or not must depend upon the true construction of all the terms and conditions of the document when there is one. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contract in this case is a contract for sale and cannot be said to have been transferred as a property of the chattel. All the above terms relate to a stage in the process of proper and efficient manufacturing of bricks and are not inconsistent in a contract or transactions of sale. These terms do not negate the concept of a contract, of sale of the bricks that are ultimately manufactured. The true test in this ease is whether in making the contract to brick produce was transferred as an chattel for consideration and we are clearly of opinion that this has taken place in this Case. [163E F] Chandra Bhanj Gosain & Ors. vs State Of orissa & Ors., ; , referred to. 2. The question whether a particular transaction is a works Contract depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case, the property was entirely of the assesses. The essence of the Contract was, therefore, the delivery to the assessee after manufacture.

The President of India promulgated on March 3, 1976 the Emergency (Extension of duration) Act, 1976. The President of the India 's Legislative Assembly was dissolved and the President passed the General Elections Rules, 1975. The validity of the said Rules was challenged by the petitioner in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the two Proclamations of Emergency were validly issued, and that the proclamation of Emergency as required by clause (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution had ceased to be in operation on March 31, 1976 because the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament approving each of them had not been published in the official Gazette. The petitioner contended that the Proclamation of Emergency was duly issued by the President and approved by the resolutions of two Houses of the People (Extension to the period between the time when the resolutions were moved in each of the two Houses and the time which was to come into operation on the expiry of two months from the date on which each of these two Houses was issued as the resolution of the Houses of both Houses. The Union of India contended that even though the said Proclu sions had been validly issued the Proclamation could not be questioned in view of the provisions of Article 353 of the Constitu tion and since the two proclamings of Emergency had been duly revoked by the two Con clamations, the proclamation was not valid. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the President 's assent to the two resolutions had ceased as in the meantime the House of the people (Extension) Act 1976 was passed by Parliament and therefore Parliament was entitled to extend the period of the House for a period not exceeding one year at a time. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The two Pro ceedings of emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions dated March 3rd, 1971 and January 29, 1976 which were issued by Vice President acting as President of Indian National Assembly on March 23, 1971. [445C] 2. The production of the Lok Sabha Debates though after some short delay is adequate publication of the resolution passed by the Houses. It is not a condition precedent that a proclamation of emergency should be published in an official Gazette and that such a proclamation should have been published for the very same reason which compelled the Government to publish the said resolutions in the Official Gazette. [441D] 3. The effect of the Proclamation has been duly published in two Houses, namely, the President ofIndia Danappa Jatti, Vice President, acting as the President in the year 1977 and the State Legislatures 'Decreements were kept In force by the same date. The proclamation of the Emergency was not made in the course of the period during which the resolutions in question had been passed. [442E] 4. The publication in the Parliamentary Debates thoughafter some short time delay is sufficient publication of a resolution of Parliament as required under clause (c) of section 102 of the Government of India Act, 1935. Since the two Legislative Memoranda were in force when the House was dissolved or the dissolution of the Assembly was given effect to, amounts to proof of the same. [443F] 5.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the property in dispute was his private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the authorities. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the premises were not a public temple and set aside the decree. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court and held that the properties were not private property but were the private property of the family and therefore was incapable of valuation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was not one for a market value and that cl. (b) of article 133(1)(a) could not apply as the judgment of the High court had reversed the decision and decree passed by the trial Court. HELD: The appeal must be allowed. The question whether the property is private or public temple, it was incapable or not, was a question of fact to be determined with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the respondents the property was a private or a public Temple, it could have no value. [156 B] In the present case, the suit properties were admittedly private properties and that the appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit had to be ascertained with reference tO the claim of the plaintiff. Since according to him the property belonged to the Thoguluva family, his share could not be determined. [157 C] The question as to whether the properties are private or private was a mixed question of law and fact. It is not in dispute that the site of the Mandapam and the structure standing thereon was originally the property of one Kuppaiyan and his undivided sons. The appellant ' s case was accepted by the Trial Court but was rejected by the High. Court on the ground that the disputed properties were private properties.

The appellant, a railway employee, was awarded a gratuity of Rs. 40/ per day and the respondent company paid him a sum of Rs, 570 as compensation for the loss caused to it by reason of the re employment of retired persons. The appellant claimed that the practice started by the appellant of re employing retired persons should be stopped. The Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical staff should be paid As. /8/ per month wages in lieu of the tiffin arrangements made by the company. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant 's grievance against the direction in the award that as the company gave assurances to its employees that it would consider the quantum and value of free tiffs be paid to them in that behalf, the Tribunal thought it unnecessary to make any such directions. That is how the present claim has been allowed by the Tribunal. [573 E] (ii) The fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appel lant could have no material bearing in dealing with the point. In the very nature of things, the said re employed person is bound to support the appellant. The result is that the Tribunal has overlooked the fact that it was an implied condition of service that in addition to the wages and dearness allowance, a provision for tiff in respect of the payment of gratuity was an amenity to which the employees were entitled. That being so, there was no justification for the appellant ' s grievance against direction in award that As. [574 E F] (iii) The Tribunal thought that the company had refused to make a reference on the ground that only 4 cases of re employment had been brought to its notice and so, the problem did not call for any consideration at that stage. Therefore, it thought it necessary to make an order in respect all those cases.

The respondent, a subscriber to the State Bank of India, applied for transfer of his money decree against the appellant. The Union of India claimed immunity from attachment of the cheques on the ground that they represented provident fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune from attachment. The claim was resisted by the Bank on the grounds (i) that the money represented provident Fund money and was immune under section 3(1 ) of the . (ii) that it was not immune from attached to the account of the respondent, but only from being proceeded against for non payment of the amount due under the cheques. Held, that the moneys in the hands of the Reserve Bank of lndia had ceased to be provident fund property within the meaning of section 3 Of the , and were liable to attachment. Section 60(1)(k) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that where under these Rules any payment is to be made to the subscriber in sterling, he prior to the date on which payment is required, shall send written instructions to the Accounts Officer intimating the place at which payment was to be paid and the payment was required either under the first intimation at Liverpool by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the bankers of the Bank of Browne in England. The respondent had not been a subscriber for conversion of the amounts into sterling and was not liable to be attached. Held further, that section 60(l)(k), as it stood before its amendment by Act No. XXXVII of 1956, imposed upon the Accounts officer an obligation to send the amount through a bank for payment at the place where payment was deemed to have been made.

The appellant was a pump manufacturing enterprise, issuing a notice under section 10(1) of the , terminating his services with effect from December 31, 1965. The respondent contended that the action being a simple termination without a sting, the order of termination was illegal and an act of victimisation. The Labour Court held that the termination was not a camouflage but merely a camouflage to cover up what really was an order of dismissal and dismissed the petition. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The appellant had no merit in the contention that the respondent 's action was bona fide. The management could not have terminated the services without notice or without giving any opportunity to the workman concerned. The termination was a colourable exercise of power and was bad. (ii)The Labour Court was right in holding that the order terminating the services was not one of dismissal as and by way of punishment. The appellant was given two extra increments, in addition to normal increments. These were the facts and circumstances which led to the conclusion of the respondent that the appellant was divulging secrets relating to his business. (iii)The question whether or not the employer had lost confidence in the employee was essentially one of fact aadmittedly a Court of construction, simply this does not amount to an order for dismissal as it is a sinister intent to punish as a guileless order based on mere suspicions and surmises. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former, although circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of the power of simple termination. There, a termination simpliciter may be bow fide, not colourable but merely an act done by the employee or though circumstances may arise which justify such a genuine discharge. (iv)The appellant had not only the ipse dixit of the employer that he was suspecting since 1968 that the appel lant was divulged secrets in his business and that the enquiry was held to be bonafide, but without any stigma attached to it. The High Court was therefore right in dismissing the appeal.

The petitioners, who were the victims of the medical mishap, filed a writ petition in this Court praying for directions to the Indian Medical Council and the Union of India to initiate appropriate action against those responsible for the tragedy. The petitioners contended that the victims had suffered irrev erable damage as they had suffered a irrevory injury; that Government did conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered a medical misadventure of such a scale possible and evolve proper guidelines for the conduct of eye camps in sanctioning permission for the course of treatment of eye camp; that the State should be directed to initiate suitable action against persons concerned and that, indeed, a criminal case has been regis tered against the responsible officers of the Government who had failed to ensure obedience to the norms; and that appropriate legal action be instituted against those who were not guilty of any negligence. Disposing of the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Revised guidelines issued by the Union Government on 9.2.1988 arrived at after a careful study of all aspects of the problem are quite comprehensive. However, it is desirable that some monitary relief by the State Government should be afforded some monaster relief by way of interim relief. [246B] 1.2 In regard to the quantum of relief, learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the Court would not interfere with the right of the victims for damages on the footing that the persons who organised the 'eye camp ' were acting pursuant to and under the authority of Government and that on humanitarian consideration, the victims should be given some moneto ry relief by this Court. [245C D] 1:3 The Revised norms issued by Union Government dated 9. 2.1988 came into force after a thorough study of the various aspects of problem. However the limited scope of the proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine of State action. [247D E] 1 :4. In regard t he quantum of reliefs, learned Counsel for the victims submitted that this was a wholly avoidable mishapp and is entirely the result of the composite negligence on the part of the surgical team and the authorities of the U.P. Government who failed to take steps to ensure observance of norms. [248E] 1 5. The State would indeed be willing to render help to the victims within the constraints of its resources. These matters would have to be gone into in the criminal and other proceedings that may be pending or in the contemplation of the government.

The appellant was elected to the State Legislative Assembly in the year 1984. The appellant challenged the action taken by the State Government under the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984 on the ground that the management and administration of the Samiti were run by nominated members and by this order all persons except respondent No. 1 were appointed as members and the appellant was not elected. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned action taken under the Act was in accordance with law and that the office of Adhyaksha of the Parishad was being run by nomination members and therefore the office was not validly constituted. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word "State" in section 3 of the Act includes the State of Assam Rashtra bhasha prachar Samiti, the President of the District Council and the Karyapalika Sabha which normally used to be an elected body. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The impugned action and the action issued under the statute taking over the management of the Rashtra Bhashapra Panchayat Samiti could not be accepted to be in accordance wi th the Constitution. Apart from this it is also clear that although when the Act talks of a temporary measure in fact, the Act does not provide for as to how when the temporary measures came to an end the elected Byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalikika Sabha are functioning and they had sufficient time to go on and in this view of the matter it is necessary to decide upholding the Constitution and right of association conferred under Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution.[175G H] 2. The word " State" in Section 3 of Act takes care of the situation where the elected by nomination or aasthapikika and byabastha pika Sabha duly elected are functioning, and they have sufficient time for going on and the Society shall be run by group of per sons nominated by the Government, about the persons no norms have been laid down.

The appellant was the son of a Hindu widow. The respondents, who were her sons, filed a suit for a declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10, 1940 executed by Sumitra Devi in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on the reversion. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the question whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be judged according to the state of the family at the time of the gift, the extent of the property of the reversioner and in pursuance of the ante nuptial agreement made by Sumitra, the widow had for spiritual benefit of Ram Gopal Lal Sao and that therefore the gift was binding on her. Held:(i) The question whether the deed of gifts was valid or not would have to depend upon the facts of each case. (ii) A final settlement of the terms of a marriage was made at Deoghar and the terms which were settled between the parties were: (a) that the widow would give four houses at Asansol, (b) that she would give 4 houses at asansol in lieu of the maintenance of her husband at the rate of Rs. 2/ per month; (c) that if the widow Thaiyyu Ammal, who was a Hindu qualified owner, had authority to make such a gift, it would be binding on him and it was not essential to make a gift at the date of the marriage but it may be made afterwards in fulfilment of the promise.

The first respondent was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The appellant challenged his election by a petition in the High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he had committed corrupt practices under section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice were clearly proved and that the appellant had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the first respondent that (i) the allegation of corrupt practices committed by Tej Singh has been clearly proved; (ii) the appellant has not shown that he was a person who was only a candidate who can defeat the Congress; and (iii) the evidence adduced by the parties is false. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The allegations of bribery indulged in by Tej singh have been clearly established. [419B] 2.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123), between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to the appellant cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [416D E] 2:2 The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubts that Tej singh had indulged into corrupt practices particularly when the printing of the posters by Tej. Singh has not been established. Therefore, it is clear that the allegation in the election petition was false and there was no evidence to prove that the poster was circulated by a strong inference that the voters polled in favor of Rup Lai would have go to Avtar Singh cannot be accepted. [414F G] 2 :3 The appellant had proved beyond doubt that the posters were circulated by him and he was not collected with the printing, of the poster. Therefore it is difficult to hold that Tej Kaur had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collecting the posters from the voters of the constituency wherein they had mentioned that Ruplal: had withdrawn and any vote given to him would be considered as a vote given in all probability the votes would have went to the appel lant.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was defeated in the legislative assembly election held in 1982. The said candidate, who had been political and personal relations with Shri Bhajan Lai, was personally very keen on giving him an office of profit. In order to achieve this objective, the appellant got an Ordinance being Ordinance No. 44 of 1982 promulgated by the Governor. The Ordinance inter alia provided that the constitution of a Forest Development Board shall be constituted with a view to appoint its Chairman. It was further provided that such Board should consist of a Secretary to the Government of India and one other person nominated by him. The appellant, who was an officer of the State Government, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the Ordinance on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The Single Judge dismissed the application holding that there were circumstances to indicate that it had been not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court exercises its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitu tion when it imposes a punishment for contempt. When no punishment is imposed by the High court, it is difficult to say that the High Courts have exercised their jurisdiction or powers to punish for contempt.[893C] 1.2 In considering a question whether the alleged contemnor is guilty of criminal contempt, the Court must always be borne in mind that in a contempt proceeding there are only two parties, namely, the court and the contemnor. It may be one of the reasons which weighed with the Legislature in not conferring any right of appeal on the petitioner for contempt, but it does not mean that when the HighCourt erroneously acquits a contemnor guilty of civil contempt,the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the Court will not be without remedy. Even though no appeal is maintainable under section 19(1) of the Act, the petitioner in such a case can move this Court under Article 136 of the constitution.

The respondent was the daughter of one R. The appellant, who owned two inam lands in Poona district, filed a suit for ejectment against R on the forfeiture of a lease. The trial court granted possession to the appellant but the appellate court found that the lease was not for the plaintiff 's benefit and decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the statutory provisions of section 111(g) as well as section III(g), were applicable in this case, and (2) the period of limitation for ejectment should be calculated from the date on which the right of re entry accrues to the landlord. HELD : The provision as to notice for determining a lease for non payment of rent was not based on any principle of justice, equity or good conscience and could not govern leases made prior to the coming into force of the , or to leases executed prior to 1st April 1930. [1011 B] (a) The provisions of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939, as amended in 1929, were applicable to the present case and there was no reason why the period for determining the lease should not be calculated under section III (g). The provision in section 111 (g) was a matter which even today in English law is considered as a matter of justice.

The appellant, a contractor, was charged with having committed an offence under section 5(1) (d) of the , and was dismissed from service. The Labour Court held that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the workmen to show cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. 17. The award was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Labour Court had erroneously construed the certified Standing Order NO. 17 as requiring a second opportunity being given to a workman at the conclusion of the enquiry into his misconduct and before inflicting upon him the punishment of dismissal; (ii) assuming that the Arbitrator had power to interfere with the punishment in the instant case having to the facts and circumstances he was not justified in setting aside the dismissal order on the ground that while focussing the strike the conduct of the employee was more grave than that of a workman; (iii) assuming without affording an opportunity to showcause against the proposal for punishment before issuance of the Standing Orders, the Labour court had no jurisdiction and power to consider both the aspects and the punishment therefor became open and the Arbitrator could not have entered into merits of the case or interfered with the penalty of dismissal inflicted upon Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan; (iv) assuming the enquiry was vitiated for the reason mentioned by the Arbitrator even though he had recorded his findings on each one of them, it was not open to him to interfere in the punishment order unless the punishment was so harsh as to smack of victimisation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that since the enquiry got vitiated the entire field of determining the mis conduct as also the punishment thereof became open, the Arbitrator has jurisdiction and powers to consider whether the punishment is so harsh or not. [368E] 2.1 The scope of the reference to a domestic inquiry is very limited. It is clear from the provisions of section 5 of the that the opportunity spoken of by para 3 OE S.O. 17 is the opportunity to be given to an workman to offer his explanation. In other words, it is clear to us that the procedure laid down in the Act for the purpose of dealing with the misconducts against a delinquent, first holding of a departmental inquiry into the charges where principles of natural justice must be implied and second the infliction of graver punishment before awarding which opportunity to ' show cause has been provided for; but the plain reading of the standing order read as a whole does not warrant any such assumption and, therefore, it would be clear that the only ground on which inquiry was held to be invalid by the arbitrator and by the same High Court must disappear. [369E F] Hamdard Dawakhana vs Badri Das & Ors., ; , referred to. 2.2 The word 'opportunity ' is to be read as an aid to giving a right to a delinquent to offer any explanation, which suggests that the same is to he called for prior to the recording of finding that the delinquent is guilty of misconduct. It would be difficult to attribute any intention to the framers thereof to provide for a second opportu nity being given by him and not the proposed penalty. [370E F; 371A] 2:3 The word `opportment ' is used in the last part of the section, which must mean that a workman who has been dismissed from the service or proceeded against on an enquiry or otherwise, would be entitled to have his dismissal order set aside and he would be visited with such punishment after giving him an opportunity of being heard. [372B] 2 :4 The word "opport ment" is to mean a right of representation in respect of a matter which has been considered by the appropriate authority and not merely a right which the workman has been given a hearing.

The appellant was the owner of certain land in Malabar to which the provisions of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 were applicable. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that they were entitled to be paid compensation under the Kerala Revenue Reforms Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the benefit of section 7D would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin and not to persons m unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible entry. The High Court in appeal took the view that the bene fits of the above mentioned section would apply even to persons who were in occupation of the land of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believed it to be competent to grant such leases or had come into possession with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7 D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". In the present case the finding of fact entered by the High Court is that the appellant had come to possession of the lands by trespass. His plea before the Courts below was that he was himself the owner and had prepared to pay to him a sum of Rs.50,000 as ex gratia payment in full and final settlement of whatever claims the appellant may have towards the value of the rubber trees standing in plots. A, B and C or in any other respect. [114D E] 2.

The appellant was convicted under section 135(b)(ii) of the . He was found in possession of certain goods. The goods were confiscated. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption contained in Section 123 of the Act corresponding to Section 128(A) of that Act was sufficient to enable the prosecution to ask the court to presume that the appellant knew that the goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had not produced evidence to show that the gold found in the circumstances stated above had been imported without payment of duty. [542 B] 2. Section 123(1) of Act only lay down a procedural rule and they could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969. Indeed, the complaint itself was filed on 30 10 1968. It is immaterial that the appel lant was found to have been in possession or was not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory; and, therefore, the appellant had been convicted only under section 136(1)(ii). [542 E F] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove innocent possession of these goods upon which the appellant was prosecuted. [543 G] 4. Section 106 of the Evidence Act only lays down a procedure for applying when the cases come up for Trial before the Magistrate who actual decided it. It does not require any other person to be examined to show the goods were legally brought into India. The onus of proving innocent possession rests on the appellant. [541 G H] 5. Section 103 of the provides that no presumption shall be raised against a person from whose possession the goods are seized unless he is in possession thereof. The prosecution has not produced any evidence to prove that the said goods were actually smuggled or brought into the country without payment or that duty, if leviable was not P d on them. [544 G H; 545 A] 6. Section 112 of the , only lay lays down that procedural rule can be applied where the case comes up for a trial before a Presidency Magistrate. The complaint itself is filed on the 30 10 68. It cannot be said that the accused had been found in posses sion of the goods on 21 4 1967 there was an innocent receiver of such goods without knowing that they were illegally imported or smuggled he may have had a chance of getting the benefit of doubt. [545 B C] 7. The fact with which the High court has held that the onus to prove the innocent possession is upon the appellant, does not mean that the evidence adduced by him was sufficient for conviction.

The appellants were the President of a Hindu undivided family. The members of the said family formed themselves into an Association to collect the quota of cloth to be allotted to them and sell it on profit wholesale and retail. The Association was registered under the Madhya Pradesh Co operative Societies Act, 1935, and its members were authorised to receive their share in the profits from the beginning of the month of April 1946. The appellants filed a suit for accounts and claimed that they had become entitled to the amounts due to them as the Association was not registered as a company under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1936; but the trial court decreed the suit holding that the other members were not entitled to participate in the profit made on the sale of the yarn. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Held, that the appellants had a right to bring a suit within the meaning of section 4(2) of the Rewa Act and the suit was maintainable for recovery of the contributions made by them and also for accounts. Section 4(1)(a) of that Act being prohibitory in nature could not be excluded from consideration even though the bar of that provision had been raised at this late stage.
