The provisions of section 5(2), (3) and (4) of Madhya Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act were mandatory in character and did not contravene article 14 Of the Constitution. Section 7(1) of Act No. 1 of 1936, being prohibitory, was not excluded from considera tion even though it was mandatory. The suit was therefore maintainable for a declaration that the Association had become a legal association of which accounts ought to be taken.

The respondents were charged with offences under sections 447, 429 and 379 IPC read with section 54 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognizance of an offence under section 9(1) read with sec. 51 of the wild life (Protection) Act, 1973 against the respondents. The respondents filed a Criminal Misc. Petition in the High Court challenging the proceedings before the Magistrate contending that the Magistrate acted contrary to the provisions of sec. "The second ground was on the merits of the complaint and the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of process against the accused. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the Respondents holding that the learned Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of offences and ordering issuance of summons. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 2(16) of the Act defines "any act or omission" to include any act or omissions which constitutes an offence against the Act. The expression "any acts or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act ' in section 56 of the Indian Penal Code merely imports the idea tat the same act or omitted some of the ingredients. But, where as here cognisance can be taken only in one way and that on the complaint of a particular statutory functionary there is no scope or occasion for taking cognisance more than once and, accordingly, section 210 has no role to play. [466D E] 1.2 The expression 'any act ' in sec. 56 of Act means an offence which includes acts or omissions mentioned in secs. 56 and 54 but does not say 'there the act alleged to constitute such contempt is an offence. In order that the prohibition is attracted the same acts must constitute an offence u/s 500 IPC and at the same time constitute an offences under any other law. [409F G] 1:3. The ingredients of an offense under sec. 9(i) readwith section 50(l) of 'the Wild Life (Protection ) Act, 1986 require for its establishment certain ingredients which are not part of the offences under secs 56 and 56 but are not parts of the same offence. [411B] 1 :4. The ingredient of an act under sec tion 9(I) read along with section 50 is much wider than Sec. 56. An act or an omission can amount to and constitute an off an offence if the acts or failure constituting an offence underss. 62, 59 or 60 are punishable as an offence as contemplated by sec. 2(11). [446C] 1 5. The words "any Act or omission ' which constitutes such an offence" in section 9 (1) of Chapter IV of the Penal Code require for their establishment certain ingredient which are non existent.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the trial court. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment on the ground that he had been in jail for a non bailable offence either as undertrial or as convict who has appealed or sought special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. In our country, personal liberty is not a necessary element of the criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deter mination against flight. The system is brought out in the Report: "The evil of bailment is that either the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties for providing bail or suffer pre trial detention. In one case the poor, accused is fleeced of his moneys by tins and professional surety and sometimes has even to incur debts to make payment to them for securing their release; in the other he is deprived of his liberty without trial and conviction and this leads to grave consequences, namely, loss of property or injury to the community. " [343 G H] 1.2. The law is being followed in the United States of America since then. In India, the law has been that the accused should ordinarily be released on bail on his own bond without sure proof of furnishing bail with sureties as it will only compel him to be in custody with the consequent handicaps in making his defence. [344 A B] 1:3. The practice which is now being followed by the Government in the U.S.A. is that the person in jail should ordinarily he released on his bond without sureties, but, if the court decides to grant bail with surety, what criteria should guide it in quantifying the amount of bail and also for a maximum period of time, the court should not reject the surety 's application on the basis of the substantive part of the law, unless there is substantial risk it is appearance or there are circumstances justifying imposition of conditions on release. [343 B C] 2.1 The law in India is that a person who has been too poor to find sureties, cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place. It is not necessary for juvenile delinquents to provide him with court, for redress of grievances in any language used in the Union of India. equality before the law implies theat even a vakalat and affirmation made ill any State language according to the law in that State must be accepted everywhere in the territory of India save where a valid legislation to the contrary exists. This divagation has become necessary to still the judicial beginnings, and to inhibit the process of making Indians aliens in their own homeland. [345 B C; 346 A] 2:2. In this case, the appellant was too poor than the accused who had been convicted under Section 302 I P.C., and sentenced for life imprisonment. The sentence of death covers both release on one 's own bond with or without sureties. He may not know any one there and might have come in a batch or to seek a job or in a morcha. [346 C D] 2 :3. In the instant case, it was not necessary to read ' arrests ' in the Punjab Jail. The appellant had been keeping a large sum of money with him for securing his release. He could not be permitted to have a job and in fact he had no means of earning his livelihood.

The assessee, a registered firm, had at different places in India branches one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity. In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of six% of its capital employed in the undertaking as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of capital invested for the purpose of section 15 C. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle Amritsar, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not been computed and included in the assessment of the assessee. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The finding of the Tribunal was based on the inference arising from non inclusion by the Income tax officer in the assess ment in question of the income of the appellant. [431 D] (i) The Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at its conclusion and it had not considered the other questions whether the constitution and ownership of the two businesses were the same. The finding was based upon the inference that in the previous year to the year 1951 51, the income from 'Castle ' had not actually been computed, and included the income in the capital employed for the purposes of section 5 C. [ 430 E] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the finding of fact was one of fact as it was based only on the conclusion of the Income Tax Officer that in view of the finding covering all essential matters, the Tribunal had misdirected itself in law in arriving at the conclusion.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was impleaded as a party in the writ petition filed by him. The Minister concerned filed an affidavit stating that he had dealt with the matter directly and by passed the Secretary 's order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the Minister concerned should file his affidavit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in directing that the respondent be impleaded as party in a writ petition and that the Secretary should file an affidavit in regard to allegations made in the petition. HELD: The direction for impleading of the Minister as a respondent was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made against him. [972 B] (i) The High court was in the nature of a writ of certiorari and it was not necessary to interfere with the order made by the Court in regard thereto. [963 C] (ii) The direction regarding impleading of a Minister as an independent party is given by this Court with a direction that the minister concerned should be impleaded. [942 D] (iii) The Secretary 'S, who was also directed to file his affidavits, could not file affidavit in respect of allegations made by him in the present case. [953 C D] In the instant case, the High Commissioner heard the petition and made a speaking order on Feb. 29, 1974 affirming the previous seniority list, but did not issue any notice to the Minister. The Secretary was directed to be impleaded in his personal affidavit.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application for recovery of arrears of rent under section 259 of the Act was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala Cantt., on January 7, 1960. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereafter the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge who following certain earlier decisions of the Lahore High Court took the view that rent under a lease could not be recovered under section 258 of the , as it was not payable by the Board under the provisions of the . The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 259 of Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 does not bar the right of the Board to recover rent on land and buildings let out by it even by suit if the rent in the section refers only to rent directly claimable under the Act or the Rules. The words "rent on land" are used in the context of the present case as they occur in section 259. Therefore, the rent which is payable by a Board under section 260 cannot be said to be claimable by the respondent under any express provision of the statute. [347 B C] (ii) Section 258 does not affect the right to recover arrears of land revenue on land or buildings leased out by the appellant even by suits for recovery. The first is that proceedings before the Magistrate were not one under the Code of Criminal Procedure and, therefore, neither could a reference be made by him to the High court under section 438. [346 C D] (iii) Section 257 does not in any way affect the rights of the parties under the . It only provides for recovery by suit or by application of the provisions contained in the Act. The right of a Board to claim rent only arises after the execution of the lease.

The appellant was terminated from service on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. The appellant challenged the said order before the Labour Court by way of a writ petition which was dismissed in limine. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of the services of the appel lant by the respondent company was legal and justified. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The finding of the Tribunal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the labour Court. [474G] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant was employed to do canvassing and promo tive sales for the company. From perusal of the records produced before this Court, it is seen that the appellant is required to supervise the work of the local salesmen and local travelling salesmen appointed in the area of his operation as well but it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promoting the sale of the product of the company in the four districts allotted to him. [473B C] 1:3. The finding that the appell lant is not a workman is also not correct. [475C D] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah shell Management and Staff, ; , D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, ; and Burmahuri Shell Oil storage and Distribution Co. Ltd. vs Burmahu Shell Management and staff; , , referred to. 1:4. The findings of the Labour court on the question whether the appellant has been a workman employed for manual, skilled, unskilled or clerical nature are not sustainable in law. [476D] Burmaah Shell Oil storing and Distribution Companies vs Burmaha Shell Management & Staff ; , referred tO.

The respondent company was a Government lessee within the meaning of section 181 of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Samvat 1999. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed a suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Additional Collector passed an order dated 1.10.1977 holding that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a ' Gair Maurusi ' tenant. The Company filed an appeal before the Collector, who dismissed the same holding that it was not covered by section 181 and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms thereof. The respondent preferred a revision petition before the High Court which held that the Company did not have become a 'Pakka tenant ' under section 54(vii) of Part II of Act 177. The High Court also held that it had not become a `pakkar ' tenant ' and that it could not be evicted by summary proceeding provided for under that section. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Company it was contended that the company did not acquire the status as a 'Tarka ' within the definition of Section 181 and that the respondent was not an occupancy tenant under Section 185 of the Act. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the High court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [179F] 2.1 The High court had found in the earlier proceeding held that there was a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable for being questioned in these proceedings. His finding shows that large amounts are due and payable by the Company as rent and that rents have remained unpaid for a period far in excess of three months from the dates on which they became due. In either event, the company has been holding the land from the State Government. This is so whether or not the Company is deemed to be holding over under the old lease or holding upon termination of that lease under and in terms Of the fresh conditions agreed upon between the parties to enable the Company to remain in possession of the land as a lessee. [180G H] 2:2.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 was passed by the State of Orissa in exercise of its power under section 1(3) of the Act. The Act provided for payment of compensation to persons who were in possession of land and related matters. Section 2 of the said Act defined "landholder" as a person who held after the commencement of the Amendment Act, any land comprised therein. Under section 3 of the principal Act, it was provided that no person shall hold after the date of the final statement referred to in sub section (3) unless he fixes the amount of compensation payable under the provisions of the Principal Act. Section 4 provided for the payment of interest on excess land held by a tenant and related to the procedure for determining the ceiling area. The petitioners who were tenants of certain lands filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of section 47 of the Orissa Land Reform (Amendment) Act, 1965 which provided that compensation in respect of the interest of the land holders medi cally or immediately under whom the surplus lands were being held shall stand extinguished and the said lands shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that section 47 was inconsistent with article 31 A of the Constitution, as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act 1955, which provided for compensation not based on market value of the lands but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that: (1) the impugned Act was inconsistent and violative of article 31 B; (2) the provisions in Ch. IV of the , were ultra vires as they contravened articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31 A and 31 C of the Constitu tion; (3 ) the Act was not a law providing for compensation but only provided for acquisition by the Government under section 45 of the amending Act; (4) the Act did not provide for the compulsory acquisition of land within the meaning of article 19(2); (5) the State Legislature had no power to enact the impugned legislation which was inconsistent therewith and (6) the provision in Ch IV of Orissa Land Revenue Act, 1 965 was inconsistent. HELD: (i) The expression "law" in section 2 of this Act includes a law made by Parliament under Entry 54 of List I of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The State Legislature could not be said to have intended to restrict the ceiling limit and to vest the surplus land in the State Government under s 45 as amended, there was no ceiling limit applicable to the landholders under any law providing compensation for the property so acquired and either fixes the compensation or specifies the principles on which, and the manner in which, the compensation is to be determined and given. [594 B C] (ii) The Act was enacted by the Legislature of the United State and was not in force when the Act came into force. It was therefore not a 'law ' within the contemplation of article 13 of the Consti tution. [495 G H] (iii) The provisions of Ch. II of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Amendment ) Act, 1964 were inconsistent with or take away or abridge any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the constitution and were therefore void.

The widow of her husband, who had died in the year 1938, instituted a suit against the widow for possession of certain properties belonging to the last male owner. The widow resisted the suit on the ground that she was entitled to recover possession of the properties belonging only to the widow during the life time of the widow from persons who acquired title to the same by adverse possession against her prior to the date of surrender and these rights would, in law, endure during the entire period of the husband 's natural life. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) as the widow had no interest in the property which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversioner, her surrender would not affect the rights of persons acquired by grant from the widow or by prescription against her subsequent alienations made by the widow; and (2) as there were other circumstances justifying the taking of possession of properties belonging either to the husband or to the reversioners, the widow was entitled only to possession so long as the widows remained alive. HELD : The suit must be dismissed. (i) A surrender is a voluntary act on the part of the wife and she is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. [346 B] (ii) In the present case, the surrender was not an alienation of an interest of the reversioners in favour the reversioner but only a relinquishment by the reversioner. The right of surrender by a Hindu widow could and ought to be exercised only when the widow has already parted with her interest in her property by a voluntary acts of her own or her rights therein have been extinguished by adverse posses sion of a stranger acquiring title by adverse Possession against her. [347 C] (iii) The mere fact that a surrender is made subsequently by the husband, does not affect his rights which he had already created. In the case before us no equitable considerations at all arise. [349 E] (iv) A transfer of property by one Hindu widow in excess of her powers, though not binding on the inheritance, creates in the alience an interest commensurate with the period of her natural life and does not amount to a surrender by the transferee from her prior alienations. [350 F G] Per Hidayatullah, J. The effect of a surrender under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act is not to spilt up the husbands estate into two parts or to give to the alienee an interest necessarily co extensive with her life. It is only when such transfer is made by a widow that the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. [351 G] (v) The effect is to destroy the widow 's estate in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death. If the effect of surrender, as explained above, is to destroying the widow "in excess of its powers", though not expressly conferred on her, then it will be a condition precedent to the vesting of the estate in him. [352 C] Per Sarkar, J: (i). The right to recover Possession of property during the widow"s life time without any justifying necessity or in the case of a person acquiring title under an heir against her the interest created is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender was made subsequently, by the wife, the surrenders must take effect from the death of the transferee. [353 B] Per Subba Rao, J., dissenting) The widow 'son has no legal right in the properties left by her husband except for the surrender made by her widow. She is under a legal or legal obligation to transfer her estate into one of her absolute and absolute rights. [354 C] The widow, her self may be incapable of derogating from her own grant and disputing the alienation which she has herself made; but as the reversioner does not derive his title from her, there is no principle of law under which the acts of the widows could bind him.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile State of Uttar Pradesh. It held a special general meeting of the Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Ltd., which was to consider and if thought fit, to pass with or without modification the following as ordinary resolutions: "Out of the 10 lakhs shares of the Polytex Company held by the Cotton Mills company, the attachment of the shares of all the five lakh shares held by it shall be made in accordance with the order of the High Court". The appellant company filed a writ petition in the Allahabad High Court challenging the validity of an extraordinary general meeting dated February 11, 1984 and the confirmation of the said resolution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the extraordinary general meetings had not been validly called since the Cotton mills Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the polytex company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver in respect of the ten lakhs shares held in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the extraordinary General meeting had not properly called since no notice under section 284(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 had been issued; and (ii) the special resolution dated February 1, 1984 had not validly been passed by the Collector in respect thereof. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The order of confirmation of a extraordinary general body has no effect on the voting rights of the Cotton Mill Company. It is also significant that the Directors of the erstwhile Cotton Mills Ltd., who were parties to this appeal have not questioned the correctness of the judgment of the Allahabad Court. One other subsidiary contention urged on behalf Of the appellants relates to the effect of an order made by the Central Government on April 13, 1978 under section 18AA(1)(a) of Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 taking over six industrial units of the cotton Mills Company held in trust by the erstwhile Textile Mills Company. The order was passed in the nature of a charging order. [875E F] The Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs Union of India, ; , followed.

The petitioners filed a suit in the representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure for a declaration that they were owners in possession of the suit land along with some others. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. The Trial Court framed an issues regarding the maintainability of the suits. The petitioners filed revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat deh. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamlat or not and whether it belonged to the Panchayat or not. [834D E] 2. The plaintiffs could not by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration, that the lands in question were shamlat ter confer jurisdiction on the civil courts when by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 the jurisdiction of civil courts to try such suits had been taken away. [884F G] 3. The Gram Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. It was therefore not possible in law to make any declaration in respect of the land which the Commissioner had wrongly claimed that it belonged exclusively to the Gram Panchayat. [851B C] 4. The plaintiff could not, by drawing his plaint cleftly by seeking a declaration from the civil Courts that the plaintiffs were owners along with certain others of the Suit land had avoided to seek a declaration. [864D E) 5. The defendant could not have by drawing the plaint cleffault in the suit filed by him.

The respondent Board, a public limited company, had been granted a licence to operate additional security but the licence was not renewed. The respondent Board issued a notice to the respondent Board demanding additional security for the period of three months from 1st April, 1985 to 31st March, 1985. The Board refused to grant the additional security and demanded interest at 3% per month for non payment of bills within the stipulated period. The appellant Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the demand. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent had no power to charge interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Board in terms of clause 20(a) and (c) of the General Conditions of Supply. The Division Bench held that the Board was in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumers in trust with the respondent to secure the Board against default in payment of interest. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board is clearly in the positions of a Trustee in respect to this money. It is not necessary that the board should have an upward revision of the consumption security deposit since it has a direct bearing on the level of supply in consumption of electricity. [251E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent has failed to pay the charges for the consumption of the security deposit within the specified period. For supply of such electricity, the Board has to borrow and make payment of the interest. The security deposit is not only a part of the money which is payable to the Board on the bill being raised against the consumer. [250G H] 1:3. The terms and conditions of supply of Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar provide for payment of Interest at certain rate in case of default in making payment of advance tax. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security is a condition of Supply and if there is a revision in the rate of tariff there has to be an upward revisions of the demand security deposit. [249A B] 1 :4. In the present case, it was not in dispute that the appellant Board had been conferred statutory power under section 49(1) of Act to determine the conditions on the basis of which supply is to be made. The conditions of Supply requiring a Consumption security deposit have a direct impact on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. [ 250C D] 1 5. The question whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) and 31(g) of Constitution is not a matter for consideration in this case. It depends upon the nature of consumption security deposits, it cannot be doubted that Section 59 requiring the Board to adjust its tariffs for the purpose of Board 's finance is to ensure that the intentions of Parliament shall not be defeated. [252E F] 1 6. The term "interest" has been defined in section 2(g), in the context of which it is used, to mean interest payable on fixed deposit. It cannot be said that the expression "interest " must be construed as including any interest. It does not mean interest. Interest is a charge for payment and is intended to be appropriated for the satisfaction of any amount liable to be paid by the Board. [253B C] 7. The expression " interest" in section 4(2) (g) means interest payable by way of consumption or deposit. The clause relating to non payment does not contemplate appropriation but only a deposit in cash to safeguard recovery of electricity dues for the energy supplied to the consumer on credit, but also a security for payment or satisfaction of other dues. [254C D; 255D] 8.

The petitioners in these petitions were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre in the Telenganga Research Centre. They were recruited in four batches in 1965, 1967 and 1973. The Class I posts of Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I were filled by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission. In response to a notice issued by the Government under Article 309 of the Constitution of India, the petitioners applied for recruitment and they were selected for appointment to the post of S&T. They challenged the selection and appointment of the persons who were likely to be affected by the decision of this Court in Randhir Singh vs Union of India and Others, ; The High Court dismissed their petitions holding that the direct recruits (direct recruits) could not be appointed as S& Ts merely because they had to perform functions for which they were recruited while on the other hand, the officers drawn from the ITS cadre, when posted in TRC. Allowing the petitions, HELD: 1. The direct recruits are entitled to the Special Pay at the same rates at which it is paid to the transferred officers working in that centre with effect from the date from which the transferred officer has been drawing the Special pay. [1011D] 2. The petitioners belong to the category of S & Ts and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is not deputation allowance. It was paid for the transfer officers to perform duties, which are not in their general line. In other words, there is no justification to deny the Special Leave Petition amounts to viola tion of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion of India. [10lB C] Randhir Singh & Ors. vs Union Of India & Others, , referred to.

The appellant, a munshi in the Bidi factor at Bhandara, was employed as a muna in the appellant 's Bidi industry. The appellant had framed a charge sheet against him and after considering his explanation, dismissed him from service with effect from August 1, 1965. An appeal to the State Industrial Court was unsuccessful. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed for reinstatement. HELD: (i) The scheme of Chapter VIII seems to be that in regard to any "change" in an matter there must be compliance with the provi sions of that Chapter. In other words, effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of matters covered by section 42 (1) or an employee desiring a change in the respect of any order passed by the employers under standing orders which would of necessity include an order of dismissal to see whether it was possible to come to any agreement and an application to the labour court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at. [737 B C] (ii) The Scheme of ChapterVIII seems to have been that in respect to any 'change ' in an matters there must he compliance with section 84 of the Act. In the present case, the Statement of Objects and Reasons (A clause 31 of the Bill which later resulted in Act 22 of 1965 shows that the underlying dea was to enlarge the powers of the Labour court.

The appellants filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif claiming that they were the successors in interest of the lessor company. The respondents contested the application contending that the appellants had formed a partnership, as a result of which a new month to month tenancy was created, and the respondents, therefore, were not liable to eviction. The Munsif held that the respondents were the heirs and successors of the original lessor company and the legal representatives of late S.M. Ganguli who had executed a registered lease deed in favour of one S. M. Ganguli, who on his death was succeeded by his legal representatives. The appellants filed a revision application before the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi which was dismissed. The respondent moved the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution and contended that the order of the Munsif was not maintainable as the allegations contained therein were incorrect, and that the applications under section 13(3) of the Act were not maintainable. The High Court allowed the revision application holding that in absence of a month 's notice under section12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not competent. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that both the remedies, i.e., by an application u/s 12 of Act were open to a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term tenancy and it is for him to choose which course to follow. On behalf of respondent No. 1 it was submitted that the application under Section 12 was not one under section 11 of the Code, as also by way of a suit. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proceeding arising out of the appel lant 's application before tho Munsif should be treated as a suit and his decision as a decree in that behalf.

The appellant, a registered society, filed a suit for declaration that the office bearers of the Society were not elected as the Secretary and had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the appellant 's application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. The High Court in appeal held that the trial court had committed several serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the elected Secretary of the society and entitled to prosecute or withdraw the Suit, on several grounds. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the application under Section 15 1 was not competent because the trial Court had committed many serious errors which vitiated the impugned decision. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High court was right in holding that only remedy of the appellant is to file a fresh suit. [238F] Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483, referred to. In the instant case, the case has to go back for reconsideration of the evidence on this point. The case has been rightly held by the High Court that the only remedy was to file fresh suit, and the High court should have exercised its revisional power on the ground that the Trial Court had failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in it by law. [239G H] Sadhukhan Rai and others vs Anant Raj and Others, AIR 1923 Pat 483, approved. Sadho Chaki Raman vs Vayalil Kochu, 27 Madras Law Jour nal Reports 172, referred.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 read with section 4 of the Ordinance read with sections 5 and 6 of the Defence of India Act, 1935. The appellant contended that as soon as the declaration that the emergency was at an end was made on April 1, 1946, the original position was restored and the Ordinance in question which had been promulgated on April I, 1946 was repealed by the Ordinance and it was not necessary to make any limitation on its duration for the continuance of the ordinance in question. Held, that the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" in section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India (Amendment) Act, 1940, were intended to be used in a different sense and the words 'for the space ' meant only the place where the Ordinance was passed and not the place of its promulgation. The words "for the time being" in the section did not mean that the Ordinance had been repealed or superseded by any other enactment. The effect of such repeal was to continue in force until it was repealed. The Ordinance having continued in operation even after April 1. 1946, was saved by article 372(3) of the Constitution and could be controlled or superseded only by any Act passed by the Indian Legislature. The provisions of section 72 were not intended to operate retrospectively but only to extend the period of the duration of the Ordinances which had to be determined having regard to the provisions of s. 72 as they stood with the omission of the words, " for a space of more than 6 months from the promulgation" and the effect of the saving provision was not to continue the duration during the period specified in section 3 of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act 1940, but was perpetual in its duration with the result that it continued in force till it was repeal.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi. The High Court confirmed their convictions and sentences. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) Section 302 I. P.C. is not a law declared by this Court as unconstitutional by this court; (2) section 302 I P. C. is constitutionally invalid because the discretion to impose capital punishment is vested in the Court, and (3) section 303 I.p.C.; was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sentence of death passed by the Addl. Sessions Judge is set aside and he is directed to consider whether the death sentence should be awarded or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case. [1065B] 2. Section 302 IPC gives a choice while section 354(3) of the Code merely requires 'special reasons ' to the indicated for imposing the death penalty. In the absence of any specific indication in that behalf 'special reason ' would relate both to the crime as such but in the great enthusiasm for doing so, the pendulum has swung to the other extreme and the guideline given is that the 'specialreason ' must relate "not to the criminal as such, but to the Criminal. Law declared by the legislature. The legislative intent behind section 302 IPC is to save the death of a person from being at large. [ 1065D E] 3. Section 303 I P C. gives a discretion while section 302 does not confer any power on the Court to impose death penalty for an offence of murder and the Court has to choose between a sentence of life imprisonment and a sentence for life; while under section 354 (3), Cr. P C., 1973, the Court is enjoined with a duty to record special reasons in case the extreme penalty is awarded. But the question whether the capital punishment should be imposed or not need not be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend on the facts of each particular case. The only thing in a Judge decision binding on him is the principle upon which the case is decided and for this reason it is important to analyse a decision and isolate from it the ratio decidendi. [1106G H; 1066A] 4. Section 304 I.PC. gives power to the Court a discretion in the matter of the punishment to be imposed for an act of murder, and while under Section 354(1) Cr.P C., the Court was enjoined with the duty to recording special reasons 'in case the death is awarded, it would be impermissible for any Judge to advocate its abolition in judicial pronouncements. [1166B] 5. The discretion vested in this Court regarding death sentence to be exercised for an accused person is not arbitrary or capricious and is subject to judicial review. It is neither feasible nor desirable to define or describe the manner in which the discretion has to be determined. [1266C D] 6. Section 301 I.A.C.[1166D] 7. The decision of a sentence passed by a Sessions Judge does not depend upon any specific expression in that section. In this case, the High Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of Cr. Procedure Code being satisfied that there were "special reasons" within the meaning of section 354, sub section (3). [1267D] 8.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Clerk in the State of U.P., when he was prematurely retired. He challenged the order of compulsory retirement on the ground that the order passed by the Commissioner of Income tax, Lucknow, on 2nd April 1956, reducing him to the rank of an Income Tax Officer, and that the said order was also barred by rules of natural justice. The appellant contended that a fresh enquiry into the same charges was not permissible under the Departmental Rules and was also denied opportunity to produce nine witnesses in defence with some documents. The departmental authorities rejected his application for a certificate of fitness on the view that the evidence did not support the charges levelled against him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the delay in making the enquiry was not justified as the appellant had been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries. HELD: (i) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural Justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental proceedings. [584 E] (ii) The appellant was entitled to have his case considered by the Departmental authorities, which had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he had suffered some injustice which to be set right. He had been given a second opportunity by the punishing authority before it inflicted the punishment of demotion. And, therefore, the order refusing to grant special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court must have been passed after hearing arguments of the parties. [585 E F] (iii) The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the departmental proceedings unless such point could be raised and decided by this Court. [586 A B] (iv) The plea that the appellant has been subjected only to a number of submissions was rejected by this court. It was for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental Authorities, which has looked into all relevant questions raised before them upto its stage, that the High Court did not deal with a number sought to be raised by it were not argued at the time when the first appeal was heard by the High court. [583 E F; 584 A B]. (v) The contention that the departmental enquiry was null and void is without substance. The plea of mala fides or would have affected the final decision. It cannot stand in the way of the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed and fully inquired into by officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged. [ 584 E F]. (vi) The doctrine of laches does not apply to a case where an order of dismissal or removal from service purports to be made under the rules of the Court. The rule of estoppel does not give any right to a party to challenge the findings in the departmental proceeding or the punishment inflicted upon the Government servant even if these are erroneous. [ 585 A B; 584 C D] (vii) The fact that the enquiry officer has been found guilty of misconduct which had not been argued at all before the High Courts, does not render his decision ineffective.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. The appellants contended that their contracts were identical with the M/s. Eastern Tractors (P) Ltd., and that they were not the last purchaser but the MCOB was the last buyer within the State, and therefore, the MFA was liable to be taxed. The Sales Tax Authorities rejected the contention of the appellants and held that the contract between the appellants was a composite one and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export of manga ness. The High Court also held that there existed a bond between the contracts of sale entered into by the appellants with M.C., and the actual exportation of the goods, and that the contracts were not integrated activities in the way of export. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the sales were inter State sales within the meaning of section 5 of the . Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The contracts between the Mecco B.T.,C. and the foreign buyers are different contracts and it is the S.T.(M)C. which entered into independent contracts with their foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis. Under the contracts between a dealer and the State Trading Corporation, the merchants were required to bring the goods on board the ship. The sales tax authorities considered only one contract. The transactions between the appellant and the MCCC were different contracts. The MFA did not fall within the scope of section S.5 of the Act. [445B C] 2.1 The fact that the MF.C was a party to the contract, does not make the two contracts either inte rised or the contract in the present case void. The only sale which can be said to cause the export is the sale which itself results in the movement of the good or is in the progress or process of export.[445G H] 2:2. The fact of the appellant in the sale of manganese ores from the MOCC and the other exporters does not render these contracts either void or unenforceable. [444B C; 445E F] 3.1 There cannot be two last purchasers in the sales of same goods within the same State. Similarly, there cannot be both exportation and sale in the same state. The taking of the consignment from the merchants ' place to the ship is completely separate from the transit pursuant to the export sale (See Serajuddin vs State of Orissa, [1975] Supp. S.C R. 169; Seraju vs State o/Madras, ; and Serajul Islam vs Commissioner of Commercial Taxes Bangalore, ; , referred to. 2.3 The law is this. It has to be found out whether the contracts in the instant case between the merchants and the Corporation are integrated contracts in tho course of the export or they are different. If they are differ contracts, as they are in the State of Karnataka, the Madhya Pradesh Act will apply. [ 445C D] 2 4. The correct law is laid down by this Court in the Coffee Board case and Serrajuddin 's Case. The law was this.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974. The respondent moved for setting aside the termination order and seeking permission to participate in the proceedings, which was granted. The Labour Court held that the termination of the appellant 's services was illegal and/or unjustified and that the service was not terminated during or at the end of the probationary period on the ground of unsuitability, but a discharge of a temporary servant, constituted retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with section 25F of the Industrial Dispute Act. The High Court also held that there was nothing in the two clauses of the contract of employment between the appellant and respondent which could justify the removal of the employee on successful probation during the initial or extended period of probation, and therefore the termination in this case, according to the Labour Court, would not constitute retrenchment within section 2 (oo) of the Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the respondent was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, the period of probationary being extended upto 8th September, 1974, and on the expiration of this extended period, his service was liable to be terminated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service of the respondent is ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits. [530D] 2.1 The termination is abruptly void and unenforceable. He must, therefore, be deemed to be In continuous service for one year if he satisfies the conditions in clause (a) of sub section (2). [531E] 3.2 The termination was not termination simpliciter but a declaration follows that he continued to be under an employer for a period of one year and that his services were terminated during the extended period.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet on the ground that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and had demanded Rs. 30/ as bribe from one Ude Singh. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet but the Deputy Commissioner without considering the explanation of the appellant passed an order dated March 17, 1955 directing that services of the respondent be terminated forthwith and in lieu thereof he was asked to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him if the allegations in the charge sheets were proved. The Deputy Commissioner by his order dated April 17, 1965 ordered that the services of respondent be terminate forthwith and that in lieu of notice be will get one month 's pay as required by the Rules. The order was confirmed on March 17. The respondent filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of dismissal on the grounds (1) that the order was not passed by the Enquiry Officer in exercise of his authority delegated to him and (2) that there was no reasonable opportunity to showcause against the order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was a temporary servant and had no right to hold the post he occupied and therefore the order terminating his services was invalid. In appeal by certificate, Held: (1 ) The protection of article 311(2) of the Constitu tion applies as much to a temporary public servant as to permanent public servants. By virtue of article 310 of the constitution the appellant is not liable to be dismissed or removed from service until he has been given reasonable opportunity against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The enquiry against the respondent was for ascertaining whether he was fit to be confirmed, and a penalty was imposed on him because it put a stigma on his competence and thus affects his future career. (2 ) The fact of holding of an enquiry is not decisive of the question. What is decisive is whether the order is by way of punishment in the light of the tests laid down in Parshotam Lal Dhingra case.

The appellant State Government issued a notification dated November 15, 1968 under section 133 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir inviting applications for appointments to posts of Professors in the colleges. The Commission was consulted by the Commission on the recommendations of the Public Service Commission and it was approved by the Government. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's Order dated November 1, 1968. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 133(2)(b) was not applicable because the various sealed covers containing the date on which selections were made had not been received from the High court; that the Commission was also consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another, and that the State Govern ment had acted mala fide in favour of some of the members of the Commission. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court erred in holding that the Government was not consulted in the manner required by section 133. [875 B] (2) Section 133(1)(b), which is a self contained code, provides for appointment of Professors and transfers to other universities and institutions and section 133 provides for appointments of Professors from one Service to another. The State Government at first framed rules on November 15 1968 for selections to be made to posts in the Colleges. By notification dated June 2, 1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professor. [873 E] (3) The Commission had not followed the procedure prescribed by section 132 of the Act and that it was not necessary for the Commission to consult the Commission before making the promotions in question.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, has the fundamental right to publish and publish in the State Legislatures all the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons of the United Kingdom at the commencement of the Constitution. The question for determination was whether the privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the provisions of article 19(1)(a) of the Constitu tion. Held, that the privileges and immunity given to the House under article 19 (1) (a) are not those of the House or Houses of Commons but are those of Parliament and the members and committees thereof must be like the powers of the Legislative Assembly of a state. The privileges and privileges of a House of the Legislature cannot be said to infringe that right. The privilege conferred by article 19 is preserved even though it does not extend to the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by article 194(3) of India. Article 194(1) is not made subject to any law made by Parliament prescribing reasonable restrictions within the ambit of article19 (2). The privileges, immunities and immunities of a member and the committees of a Legislature of the State cannot be confined to those privileges which are expressly made subject under article 194 (3) and are therefore outside the scope of article 194. The fundamental right conferred on a citizen by article 14 is preserved notwithstanding the fact that it infringes the fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 19(2). Article 19(5) gives freedom of publication of proceedings of Parliament, while the second part of article 105(3), deals with the powers and immunities and privileges enjoyed by members and the Committees of a Legislative Assembly. The first part says that the powers privileges and allowances of a house of the legislature of a Province and of the members of the committee of a Municipality shall be such as may from time to time be defined by the Legislature by law, and until so defined shall be those of that House of Parliament of the U.K. State. The second part says, that even if the privilege was not expressly made, subject to article 19 of the constitution, the privileges, privileges or immunities of the Houses of the Legislatures of a province of a Union Territory and of members and Committees thereof shall be so defined by law. The petitioners were citizens of India under the Constitution and their fundamental right under article19(1), (a), (b) and (c) of that Article was preserved despite the provisions in article 194, and (b). The second contention of the petitioner was that the privilege granted to him by the Speaker of the Assembly for publishing its proceedings without the authority of the Speaker to be a breach of privilege under article 13(2) and the third contention was that it was not open to the Speaker or the Speaker, as the case may be, to make any action in respect of the said publication. Held further, that though the privileges conferred on members and officers and committees of the Municipality of a Part C State and of those Committees and the Legislatures thereof were not expressly saved by article 13 (2) of this Constitution, the fundamental freedom guaranteed under article 14 was preserved notwithstanding anything contained in article 19, and the second contention must be negatived. The right to freedom of expression includes the right to move freely throughout India and the right of the member and committees and committees to vote and to vote at all the meetings of the Council of Ministers of a United Kingdom and its members and committee of such House and Committees as are mentioned in article 105 (3), on a reasonable classification having regard to the nature of the fundamental freedoms guaranteed by Article 19 (2); and the privileges or immunity conferred by articles 2, 3 and 4 of the Covenant of Association of the States, which were not made under any of the provisions Of the Constitution, must be held to be protected by article 31(5). The right conferred by the said Articles was preserved even after the Constitution came into force. The petitioner 's fundamental right was preserved because the privileges of the Committee and the committee had been expressly saved.

The appellant, a private college affiliated to the Andhra University, was taken over by the Government in pursuance of the decision of the Govern ment. The State Government took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971. The appellant was appointed as Reader in the said college on ad hoc basis for a period of six months with effect from 1st September, 1971 or till the appointment is made in consultation with the Orissa Public Service Commission whichever is earlier. The respondent No. 2, who was working as Reader, was drawing salary at the rate of Rs.600/ per month. The Government prescribed qualifica tion for appointment as Reader by a Circular dated 23rd March, 1971 addressed to the Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education) Orissa which provided that in case of candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, who had not less than 8 years of teaching experience as a Lecturer, their names were not referred to the Public Service Commis sion for consideration. The respondents filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the said Circular on the ground that they were drawing as Reader salary of more than Rs. 600/ per year and that the post of Reader was filled up by promotion subject to the satisfactory performance and conduct of the officer as a lecturer. The High Court accepted the Writ Petitions and held that the respondents were entitled to be considered for appointment in terms of the Circular dated March 23, 1971 and directed the State Government to take into account the experience of teaching in a recognised private college. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since they had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Readers and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the take over and five of them were even confirmed Readers, their services could not be considered by the Public Services Commission for appointment to the post. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The only differentia was, therefore, the salary drawn by the Readers on the date of taking over. That action based on the salary aspect under the said circular had to stand the test of Article 16 in the High court, as well as before this Court. [778C] 2.1 The only difference between eligibility and suitability is that the salary was drawn by a teacher on the day of take over. It is apparent that the employees had to join the new service under the Government for the first time, and so could be in that sense, fresh entrants. But to say that the teaching experience of the Readers in the private college is completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible, on the plea of absence of teaching Experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment, is a seriously grim issue. [777D E] 2:2 The only distinction was, however, made by the High School Tribunal taking recognition of the service in the Private College in the case of two (1) ; and the other (2) the scale for teaching experience which is needed for eligibility for appointment. [779E F] 3.1 In the present case, the respondents had to be promoted as Reader on 4 5 1969 and was drawing Rs.660/ on the dates of takeover. That was done by the State in the first instance. The fact that the appellant had all along been promoted as a Reader would not make him ineligible for appointment since Government may not undertake to take over all the employees by maintaining the billabong of a status quo ante. [780G H; 778A] 3:2. The question is entirely different when, as in the present ease, the Respondents do not fulfil the qualifications, experience and other requisite conditions, they may not be eligible for appointment because Government maynot undertake to takes over all those employees by maintain the bill which will be considered without any objection from the State.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority granted three temporary permits to ply their vehicles on Khurja Animals valid for a period of 3 years. The applications of the Corporation for grant of three temporary permit were rejected by the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition filed in the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) Section 68 F (1 C ) confers power on the State Government or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be, to grant temporary permits for the exclusion of any other operator; (2) section 68F(1 D) confers power upon the State Road Transport Corporation or the State Authority to grant such temporary permits. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The correct approach would be that keeping in view the strength of the vehicles fixed by the competent authority, the authority should first examine the application for number of temporary permits made by the Corporation. If the Corporation has made an application for temporary permit covering all the vacancies the matter ends there. But if the Corporation does not apply for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation had made no application for the temporary permits and section 68 G(1 A) would be squarely attracted. [985C D] 2. The true scope of the provisions of Chapter IV A of the Act is that keeping In view the existence of the three vacancies for temporary, permits, it is an admitted position that the Corporation was able to provide only one vehicle and therefore applied for only one permit, according to the State transport authority as well as the High court no temporary permit can be granted to any one else. [986F G] 3. The Authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling public. While interpreting the provisions Of Chapter IVA of the it is undoubtedly true that the corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits. The authority under the , must not always lose sight or the power left in the State to grant permanent permits to any person. [985B C] 4. The authorities under the Motor Act must be given an opportunity to make all available temporary permits, and they should also have to exercise their discretion in public interest. It is common ground that the strengths of vehicles on the route in question were raised from 13 to 20.

The appellant was the son of a grandson of his mother who died in 1947. He sold the equity of redemption to the mortgagee, Shibba, who died on March 22, 1927. The mortgagee filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the equity and for setting aside the sale. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the property inherited by the widow was not ancestral property qua the appellant and dismissed the suit. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Courts had wrongly decided in favour of the appellant on the ground that the properties inherited by her were not ancestral properties as they belonged to a Hindu father who died before the coming into force of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1951. Held, that the decision of the first Full Bench of the Lahore High Court was correct and must be affirmed. The doctrine of stare decisis is in applicable only where there are two or more decisions of the same court which have been followed for a long period of time, and before this character can be predicated of any property in the hands of a male owner it must be found that it has descended to him from a male ancestor in the male line. The rule of stare finality is thus stated in Halsbury 's Laws of England (4th Edn.) Vol. 2 p. 951, that it is now well settled that a decision which has been followed by the community since 1895 should be taken to have been overruled by the courts below. The principle of stareoppel is in respect of property which more secure. It may be conceded that the question as to whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral or not, does not arise for the decision in this case; but it is significant that the words used by Lord Collins in describing the true position under the Hindu law in regard to the character of ancestral property are emphatic and unambiguous and this statement has been made while dealing with the case governed by the customary law of the State.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under section 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of the 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them armed with dagger struck him down his knees and the other three held him down. Fortunately, the injury inflicted on Ebr Ali did not prove fatal. The Sessions Judge accepted the verdict and convicted all under sections 449 and307/34 I.P.C. On appeal by the appellants the High Court acquitted them of the charge under section 307 read with section 34 I. P. C. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "in order to" have been used in section 449 of the Code are not to be interpreted as meaning "with the purpose of". If the purpose in committing the house trespass is the commission of an offence punishable with death the house construction of which is to be adopted would be proper to say that he has committed the house offence punishable under section 450 I.p.C., and that he had committed the 'house trespass in order to the commit the offence indicated in those sections. Whether or not the purpose was actually accomplished is quite irrelevant in these cases. [982 F G] (ii) The fact that the murder was not actually committed will not affect the applicability of section 449 Of the Indian I.I.P., I.T. Act. The second contention that no charge under s.307 read with s. 34 of the I.L.R. is sustainable in law, appears to proceed on a misreading of the effect of the provisions of section 34 of I.l.P,.C.

The appellant was the daughter of one of the Sarswat Brahmin. The respondent filed a suit for declaration of his title to the properties in dispute on the ground that the appellant had been in possession of tenants, that the property in dispute being in possession thereof was not ancestral and that there was no custom whereunder the collaterals of the father who was the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree holding (i) that the parties were governed by Hindu Law, and (ii) that there is a custom according to which a collateral could not claim any collaterals. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the courts below had erred in law in holding that the respondent was entitled to succeed to her father 's ancestral property in preference to collaterals even though they were within the fourth degree and therefore the appellant was a collateral of the deceased. HELD : (i)(a) The custom as recorded in Rattigan 's Digest of Customary Law is not a record of the wishes of the persons appearing before him as to what the custom should be, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom set up by the persons who appear before him. [153 B] (b) The High Court was right in holding on the basis of the evidence that the custom as well as the evidence adduced by the parties had been correctly accepted and that the High court had rightly held that the case was not governed by the Hindu Law. [154 C D] (c) The question whether there is custom in the Gurdaspur district governing the parties under which a relation can be recognised or not, has to be determined on principle, the general rule is that the daughters are excluded by the widow and male kindred of the joint family properties. If the Riwaj i am lays down a custom in consonance with the general agricultural custom of the province, very strong proof would be required to displace that presumption; but where on the other hand, the custom is opposed to the custom generally prevalent, the presumption will be considerably weakened. [155 E F] (d) The evidence as to the succession to property of a person who was born in Punjab and who had been born in the State of Punjab at the time of his death was not admissible under section 8 of the Indian Evidence Act. [156 G H] (e) In the present case, the appellant has failed to discharge the onus that was cast on him by producing in evidence the Rws showing that the collateral of one Harnam Singh who was also a Sarshatra and whose father had been last male owner excluded the collateral from succession. [157 B C] (f) The fact that the daughter did not contest the succession of the collateral to her husband 's property would not make any difference because in order to enable the appellant to displace the general custom recorded in the Rdaj i Am of Punjab, it was necessary for the appellant who had failed to do so. [158 E] (g) The appellant has also failed to produce a Riwaji am of the Gurdas pur chaser who was not present at the scene of occurrence as to how the appellant came to the scene. The evidence on record shows that the R ws were in possession and the property which was in the possession of the appellant in preference 'to collaterals, even though it was within the 4th degree.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company which was acting as an agent of several companies. The Managing Director executed two deeds in favour of one person, and another in favour Of another. The first deed provided that if they were completed in more than one instrument, not all of them were liable for the duty specified in the second deed. The second deed provided inter alia that if the first deed was executed by one person he fills several capacities and the authority conferred is general, there would be distinct delegations in respect of each of those capacities and that the instrument should bear the aggregate of stamp duty payable in respect thereof. The respondent filed a suit for adjudication of the duty payable on the two deeds. The trial court held that the two documents were not chargeable with the duty as the first one was a power of attorney and the second was a deed of trust which was executed and registered by the Managing Committee of several Companies, as an authorised agent of certain companies jointly and severally to act for them in all the capacities specified in those Schedules. The High Court on appeal held that though the two instruments were executed by the respondent, if he filled several capacities, they were not distinct matters within section 5 Of the Indian Stamp Act and that therefore the proper duty payable thereon was Rs. 2,000/ . Held, that the words "distinct matters" in section 5 of the Indian stamp Act must be construed as a single power of agent liable for a single duty under article 48(d) (1) of the Schedule to the Indian Registration Act and not as a matter of law and without regard to the contents of the instrument, to comprise a single matter. The words "contrary to the provisions of the Act" in the section mean that the person who executes a power must be considered as distinct matters. The word "distinction" used in section 4 of the Registration Act means one matter which is capable of performing and which he appoints his attorney to do for him and in his name and on his behalf.

The assessee, a resident in the State of Saurashtra, was carrying on business in Bhavnagar. In 1948, the Raj Pramukh of the newly formed State of Bombay, promulgated an Ordinance called the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949, which came into force on April 1, 1949. The Ordinance was repealed by the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and the assessee 's claim for deduction under section 10(5)(b) of the said Ordinance was rejected by the Income tax Officer. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner as also the Tribunal held that this expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian income tax Act had in force" in section 13(5) (b) applied and that it was not necessary for the assessee to make any deduction under this bead. The High Court on reference, however, held that the words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be read as "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating thereto". In appeal to this Court it was contended that the word "or" occurring in the said paragraph had been used in the context of section 13 (5) and not in the terms of the provisions of the Act. HELD: The words "of a Part ' State" in para 2 of article 31(1)(a) must be given their natural meaning, so as to include all depreciation actually paid under any law or rules or orders of a part B State. It is not possible to think however that when making this Ordinance the Raj Pramatha Nath, the Ruler thought that if the British War Profits Act was in force a proper claim would ordinarily have been made and whatever was allowable under it, if the Income Tax Officer had to apply the provisions Of section 10 (5)(a), he must be satisfied that in certain cases difficulties have actually arisen in giving effect to the provisions. The appellant was a contractor of the respondent Corporation. He had been awarded contract by the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation to the Mysore Construction Co operative Society Ltd., an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka in favour of the Mysore construction Co operative Societies. The contract was for the construction of a Main Station Building of a Power House at an estimated cost of about Rs. 1.8 crores. The appellant had submitted a certificate from the K.P.C. itself that it had done 35,000 cubic metres of work and they were capable of mobilising the work force required for the work. He took the view that the pre requisite for supply of tender forms was only the three conditions set out in para I of the N.I.T. and that all the documents referred to in para V were only for information and were such they could be met before the opening of the price documents, and that the appellant had no other alternative but to accept the tender form. The respondent Corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award of contract by it. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the requirement of para I was only para I and not para V sets out the pre conditions set forth in para IV of the National Building Code, and as such the appellant could not be said to have satisfied the preliminary conditions Tendering it eligible to tender for the contract. The Division Bench also held that the respondent had failed to satisfy the preliminary condition No. 1 and that there was nothing unfair or arbitrary about the award. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that para V could not have been arbitrary as it was only Para I which could be read with para I in isolation and treated as the only condition precedent for supply. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of Para I is only para II that stipulates the prequalifying conditions. It does not require that the candidate must fulfil the pre quali fied requirements set out therein. [231D] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant did not satisfy the main condition No I and was much better qualified for the Contract. The comparative merits of the appel lant vis a vis M.C.(M.C.) are, however, a matter which it is for the KPC to assess. [232E] 1:3. The question whether the course adopted by the K P C.C., has caused any real prejudice to the appellant and other parties who had already supplied all the materials in time and sought no extension at all, does not arise. [234F] 1 :4. The High Court was right in holding that while the rule in Ramana 's case would be readily applied by Courts to a case where a person complains that a departure from the quali cations has kept him out of race, injustice is less apparent where the attempt of the applicant before court is only to gain immunity from competition.
