[235G H] 1 5. The requirement in para II of theNational Building Code is only Para II and not Para V sets forth the general procedure which the K .P. C. had been following in regard to N.l.T., and it further clarifies that while tenders will be issued only to those who comply with the pre qualification, any deficiency in the general requirements will not disqualify the applicant from receiving tender documents and that data regarding these requirements could be supplied later. [236B] 1 6.

The appellant was the owner of a house in Lahore. He was put in possession of the said house on 10th October, 1947. In pursuance of that exchange, he took possession of his house and started cultivating possession thereof. The appellant filed an application under section 5 A of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, for confirmation of the order of the Custodian or Additional Custodian. The Custodian General rejected this application on the ground that the order was not appealable under section 27 of the Central Act. The respondent thereupon filed a revision petition before the Custodian General which was also dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the orders passed by the Custodian were without jurisdiction as the orders were without Jurisdiction and (2) the revisional power could not be exercised when there was an appeal provided under section 54 of the Act. HELD : The order of confirmation passed by an Additional Custodian General is final and conclusive. Under section 27(4) of the , the Custodian can exercise revisional powers "for the purpose of satisfying himself as to the legality or propriety of any order of an Custodian". But in the present case, the orders under appeal were not appealable but only those orders which were passed by him. The orders under appeals were therefore without jurisdiction and must be quashed. [1137 B C] (a) The power conferred on the Custodian under section 4(2) of East Punjab Act XIV of 1947 is a quasi judicial power and it cannot be exercised where there was no appeal provided for in that section. The order under appeal is one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the Custodian. [1103 B C, F] (b) The orders are not appealable unless they are quasi judicial. The scope of revisional powers is limited to matters covered by section 27 and it is not necessary for the purpose to decide whether such orders should be passed or not. It is only when there is an appeal that the High Court can exercise its jurisdiction under section 25(4). [1105 C D] (c) The order passed by a Custodian General under section 8 of the West Punjab Evicuees (Administration Of Property) Ordinance, 1949, was not open to appeal or revision but became final and binding.

The appellant, a locality in Bombay, was a locality where the respondents were working as workmen. The claim for bonus for the relevant four years was founded on tradition or custom or condition of service and in that light the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these terms: "Many other workmen less than the statutory minimum of 20 workmen are paid by the employer to their workmen of small amounts for a number of years prior to 1965 when trouble began. The workmen, in their statement before the Tribunal, have asserted that bonus had been paid for several years prior thereto and what transpired at the conciliation stages is clear from the letter of the Commissioner of Labour dated May 29, 1965 addressed to the appellant. " The respondents ' plea was that a scrutiny of the accounts of the firms was unnecessary since the demand for Puja Bonus could not be considered as a matter of implied agreement between them. The Tribunal made a short shrim in the demands and made shortshorths of the workers 's claim on the basis of which bonus had to be paid. The appellant contended that the claim put forward by the appellant before the tribunal was unsustainable on the short ground that what was pleaded was profit based bonus only and, therefore, fell squarely within the Bonus Act. The respondents also urged that the dispute raised by the workmen in their statements before the Labour Court was not based on profits or the financial results of the employers but was based on custom. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish that the demands were based on profit based and therefore, fall squarely within its definition of "employee" under section 2(s) of the Bonus act. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The bonus Act speaks of a case of profit bonus urged under the by two sets of workmen. It is silent on, and cannot be annihilated by implication, other distinct and different kinds of bonus such as the one oriented on custom or conditions of service. [605 D] (2) The definition of 'employee ' in section 2 (s) does not include an employee who has entered before May 29. 1965 into an agreement or settlement with their employers for payment of Puja bonus, or that even where no implied agreement can be inferred it may be payable as a customary bonus, this Court in the said decision specifically dealt with such a case. [505 E] (3) The Bonus Act speaks and speaks as a whole Code on the sole subject of profit based wage but is silent as to how the employer has to pay bonus. It does not say that the bonus has been paid even in years of loss. In case of such customary or traditional bonus, the question of profit may or may not arise at all and such customary and traditional bonus will depend on the content and terms of that custom or the practice on which the claim for Bonus is made. [600 E F] (4) The fact that the payment was called ex gratia by the employers when it was made would make no difference in this regard because the proof of custom depends upon the effect and terms thereof. It may be that the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which case other types of bonus are left untouched.

The petitioners were officiating continuously in the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab as Additional District and Sessions Judges for two or three years prior to their appointment to the Superior judicial service. The control over district courts and subordinate courts vested in the High Court by article 235 of the Constitution. The Governor of Punjab amended rule 12 by providing that seniority of members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined with reference to the respective dates of confirmation. In regard to the rule of seniority, the position as it obtains in the two States is distinct and vital. Rule 12 provides that seniority shall be fixed on the basis of continuous service on a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation, and that unless there are exceptional circumstances attaching to each individual case, a direct recruit cannot be confirmed from a date earlier than the date on which he has satisfactorily completed his probation of to years. The petitioners who were officiating in the superior judicial service as Additional district and Sessions judges for two/three years prior thereto filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitu tion challenging the validity of the amended rule, which was allowed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the seniority of the members of judicial Service is so integral and vital to the control of the High Courts over them, that any erosion thereof would both be violative of Article 235 of Constitution and equally run counter to the settled concept of the independence of judiciary which is now coming to be recognised as the basic feature of the constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The rule of rotation cannot implicitly be read into the quota rule prescribed by Rule 8 of the Punjab Superior Judicial Services Rules. [1050B] 2.1 Rule 12 of the Haryana Superior Judicial service Rules is similar to Rule 12 which was in force in the State prior to its amendment on December 31, 1976. However, on a plain reading of Articles 235 and 309 of the Con stitution, it is clear that the power to frame rules regarding seniority of judicial officers by laying down rules of general application cannot be exercised in a manner which will lead to interference with the control vested in High Court under Article 235. [ 1051C D] 2:2 The High Court was not justified in applying the rule as of rotation at the time of confirmation of the promotees and direct recruits as District and Session Judges.

The respondents Nos. 4 and 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, were appointed as Junior Assistant to the post of Senior Assistants in the Andhra Pradesh State. The appellant No. 1 was a direct recruit to the said post. He was promoted as Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal seniority of Warangal local area comprising of Warang and Karimnagar districts. The respondents Nos 4 and S filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated April 1, 1982 passed by the State Government in exercise of its power under cl. (5) of Article 371 D of the Constitution. The High Court allowed the said writ petition holding that the zonal seniority was the criteria. Aggrieved by the decision of the High court, the appellant No 2 filed an appeal before this Court. During the pendency of the appeal, the State issued a notification dated February 18, 1986 under cl.(5) Of Article 371D declaring that the Zonal seniority in the local cadres would be determined on the basis of the length of continuous service for different parts of the State and allot ing in accord ance with such principles and procedure as may be specified in the order, the persons holding such posts to the local cadre so organised shall be treated as the local area (i) for direct recruitment to posts in any local cadre under the State into different local cadres for different part of the state; (ii) for promotion from the local Cadre to the cadre of Senior Assistant and Assistant Commercial Taxes Officers, which are zonal posts common seniority of the Junior Assistants working in all the four revenue districts shall have to be maintained and promotions made in accordance with the Minister 's Order dated April l, 1982 and the Andhra pradesh State Government. The appellants filed a Writ Petition before the Andhra High Court contending that the local areas were not to be treated to be zone and the divisional seniority maintained by the department was bad in law. The learned Single Judge allowed the Writ Petition holding that since the zonal list of Commercial Taxes Department for the purpose of recruitment, seniority, promotion, transfer etc., of local cadres is co terminus with the zone V of the Presiden tial Order, the order of the Division Bench was illegal and void. The State Government preferred an appeal to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the learned Single judge. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order passed by him, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants for Adilabad and Warangal Divisions is illegal, contrary to Order issued in G.O.Ms. No. 2 dated April I, 1982. [574D] 1.2 The State Govern ment shall have the power under para 3(1) of the Order to organise any local cadres within a zone where a local cadre has been organised in respect of any class or classes of posts in the Civil Services of and class or class of civil posts under the state into different Local cadres. [575F] 1:3 The State Govt.

The appellant was the owner of Gadi Sirampur and he executed a simple mortgage in favour of the Bank. The Bank purchased certain properties from the appellant. After the mortgage had been executed, the Bank filed a suit against the Bank for enforcing the mortgage and obtained a decree for possession of the mortgaged property. The appellant contended that the mortgagee was not a party to the suit and that the Bank was entitled to recover khas possession of Gatabari property so as to bind the Bank and that he was entitled only to recover possession of those properties. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to the decree for recovery of possession of his lands. The mortgage deed did not prohibit the grant of a permanent lease in favour the appellant 's father. The question whether the mortgagor had power to lease the mortgaged properties has to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management. The fact that the mortgagor was not bound by the acts of the mortgagee with reference, to the mortgaged Property does not affect the question whether he possesses any larger powers of leasing it out to the mortgagee. Nor does it affect the rights of a mortgagor who has been granted a lease without the concurrence of the mortgage. The right conferred on the mortgagor in possession is only a limited one and not a limited right. Held further, that as long as nothing took place which impaired the value or impede the operation of the mort gage, the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term.

The petitioner filed an arbitration suit in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for a declaration that the respondent had committed breach of contract. The respondent filed an application under section 5 of the Arbitration Act for appointment of an arbitrator. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. On appeal the Division Bench set aside the order of the Single Judge and directed the matter to be referred to arbitration. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment by the Court and thereafter the same cannot be revoked except with the leave of the Court unless a contrary intention is expressed in the agreement; (ii) clause 68 provides that if the arbitrator refuses to act upon or omits to refer the dispute to arbitration within 15 days from the date of receipt of notice, then it is open to him to approach a Civil Court for reference to the arbitration. The question was whether the High Court was justified in permitting the respondent to rescind the contract of Arbitration provided in clause 68 of contract and not for a period of 5 years as stipulated in the contract. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Clause 68 provides for arbitration by the court and thereafter it cannot be said that the Court would be justified to permit a contracting party to rescind an agreement or the court can revoke the authority to refer disputes or differences to arbitration [368C D] 1.2 In mercantile reference of the kind in question it is an implied term of the contract that the arbitrator must decide the dispute according to the existing law of contract, and that every defence which would have been open in a court of law can be equally proponed for the arbitrator 's decision unless the parties have agreed which is not suggested here. [368D E] 1:3 The Court has the power under sections5 and 12 to grant leave to the applicant in exceptional circumstances to revoke the contract or the Court can revoke, the authority of the arbitrator. [369E F] 2.1 In mercantile refer ence of the kinds in question, it is not possible to say that the court would be reluctant to grant a contracting parties to rescind a contract or to revoke its authority to agree to relieve the party from dispute or difference and to order that the arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect with respect to the dispute or differences. [370F G] 2:2 In the mercantile reference, at page 436 it is stated thus: "In an appropriate case leave should be given to revoke, either expressly or by necessary implication, the contract between the parties, and relieve the parties from arbitration agreement. " [369G H] 2 :3 The proceedings before the arbitrator are like civil proceedings before a court within the meaning of section 14 of the Limitation Act, by consent of the parties.

The appellants in this appeal obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of section 2(1) and the notification issued under section 3(1), of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, was published on June 18, 1958. The appellants contended that the objection raised by the judgment debtors was barred by the principles of res judicata and further that the bar of section 4(d) of the Act was not tenable because the objection as regards execution proceedings in which the decree holder sought to proceed against the estate of the judgment debtor was barred under the provisions of the Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1951. Held, that the preliminary decree passed by the trial court on June 25, 1958, was a nullity and could not be set aside on the principles laid down by this Court in Raj Kishore Pratap(1). The decision of the executing court was affirmed by the High Court in appeal. The judgment of the High Courts in India had been affirmed by this court in State of U.P. vs Ram Saroop Singh, ; , and State of Uttar Pradesh vs Gauri Kumari Devi, A.I.R. 1954 All. 829, approved. Maharaja Radha Parshad Singh vs Lal Sahab Rai, A, I. R. 1953 All. 946, disapproved. The effect of the vesting of an estate in the State absolutely, was that where a suit was wholly or partly dismissed under rule 8, the plaintiff would be precluded from bringing another suit for the same relief on the same cause of action. The consequence of the notification under section 4 of the said Act was that claims of the creditors had to be submitted before the claim officer and the decision of claims officer or the Board has been made final by the Act.

The respondents in the appeals were allocated to the Indian Police Service, Group 'A ' and I.P.S. and who have appeared in Civil Services Main Examination of a subsequent year under the interim orders of the Tribunal for the Civil Services Examinations 1988 or 1989 and have succeeded are now being given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the C.S .E. Rules, 1987. The respondents in all these appeals were allotted to the I.A.S., Group 'B ' and 1.P S.S.; and they were permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to so appear at the next Civil Services Examination. They filed a writ petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of C.P .S.E. (Recruitment) Rules, 1988 introduced by Notification No. All those candidates who have been allocated to any of the Central Services Group ' A ' or I. P.S.(including the respondents in this appeal) and who had appeared in civil services Main Examination for competing for IAS, IFS, IPS or Central Services, Group B, and who were permitted by the Tribunal to abstainfrom the probationers in order of merit, were not given benefit thereof. The Tribunal allowed the writ petitions holding that the second Proviso to Rule 17 is in no way ultra vires clause (iii a) of Regulation 4 of the Civil Service Examination Rules, as it does not contain any provision for relaxation of age limit and thus has been violated by the second provisos to Rule 7 of C .S .A. Rules. The High Court allowed the Writ Petitions filed by the respondents and quashed the orders dated 20.8.1990 and 5.10.1990 passed by the Central Adminis tration, Principal Bench, New Delhi. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Under Article 73 of the Constitution, subject to provisions of the Constitu tion, the Central Government in exercise of its executive power can regulate the manner in which the right of a candidate in appearing for the competitive examination is to be exercised and, therefore, the restriction imposed by the proviso to rule 4 of Civil Services ( Examination) Rules is in force. [79F G] 1.2 The proviso to r.4 of CS.A Rules is not only placed on the candidates who on the basis of the result of the previous CSE had been allocated and appointed to IPS or to a Central Services group 'A" but also on the candidate ap pointed in the higher echelon of Civil Service, which is a category distinct from those specified in Regulation 4 as well as in the case of other candidates who are not otherwise eligible. [80G H] 1:3 The proviso imposes an onerous restriction that they should first resign in order only for those appointments.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The grounds of detention were that he filed a petition requesting the Advisory Board to permit one Mr. Sundararajan, a retired Assistant Collector of Central Excise to assist him as a friend. The Board rejected the request and ordered his release on bail. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the appellant had requested the Board to allow him to represent the case of the detenu. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Advisory Board has no justification to refuse assistance of a person who is not a friend in the normal sense could be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. [790B] 1.2 In the instant case, on 25th November 1986 while the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central excise, the detenu was denied the assistance of the Deputy Collector of Customs. On the recommendation of the Advisory board, the detention order was confirmed. The appellant is a clearing and forwarding agent at Madras and is said to be a young man aged around 26 or 27 years. The case before the Board involved certain facets which require acquaintance with legal provisions and the procedure and practice adopted by the customs authorities. It is the case that on 25.11.1986 while the detain ing authority was engaged by a person, who was denied permission to assist the appellant his case would have been better placed before the Advisory Committee. In this connection, two aspects have to be examined (1) whether the appellant was entitled to the assistance; and (2) whether when the detaining author ity was assisted he could be represented by a retired assistant Collector of central Excise. [789D E] 2.1 It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial. This Court has reiterated the position that matters relating to preventive detention are strict proceedings and warrant full compliance with the requirements of law. In view of the position of law and the facts of the case, it must hold that the refusal by the Advisory Boards to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan as a lawyer was bad and continued detention of the appellant became vitiated. [788E F] 2:2 The question whether the detaining authorities or the Government should have the facility of appearing before the advisory board with the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser would be in breach of Article 14 if a similar facility is denied to the detenu, has been decided by this court in Nand Lal Bajaj vs State of Punjab, [1982] 2 SCR p. 874. The Advisory Boards have no justification for refusing assistance of an Advocate on the ground that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist his case as a representa tion was bad, and continued detained of the appel lant became vitiated by reason of such refusal. This court has reiterated its position in the present case. [781E F; 782B] 2 :3 The Advisory board has no power to refuse to permit an authority or the government to do indirectly what they cannot do directly; and no one should be enabled to take shelter behind the excuse that such officers are not "legal practitioners" or legal advisers.

The appellants were the owners of certain premises in Calcutta and were carrying on business as agents for the respondent mills. The goods were delivered to them by endorsement and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they related. The delivery orders were served on the managing agents of the mills as such there was no service of any notice of acquisition on them. The appellants contended that the property in the goods passed to the respondents only when they were actually appropriated to the particular order and not when they had been delivered, and that the delivery orders did not amount to a service of the order on them and therefore there was a service as provided by r. 75 A (2) of the Defence of India Rules. Held, that the provisions of rr. 75A and 75A of the Rules were applicable to the case. The words "any person interested in the property" in r. 2(a) of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure are wide enough to include all persons who have interest in the properties being affected by it and those who have a right to be heard, and the word "person interested" in the rule means not only the owner of the property but also the person who has a right of being heard. The word "persons interested" is used in the sense of "any persons interested". In the present case the appellants were not given any notice as required by r, 75 A(2) and therefore no acquisition under r. 1 was valid. Held further, that it was not necessary to serve them with notices under rr. 2 (a), 2 (b) and 5 of the Indian Rules. The provisions of r. I of Order 21 of the Civil Procedure Code as to the manner in which documents may be served on a company or a corporation are very wide enough for the purpose of requisition and publication of such documents.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. The assessee company claimed that the sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer did not agree with the matter and held that no action could be taken against the assessee under section 23A of the Act. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the income tax officer. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax under section23A was made on or before the date relevant to the assessment year 1963 64, the said amount cannot be treated as a provision and a reserve. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions made by the Income tax Officer in its books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under section 23 A) were not a reserve, and the assessee itself called it a provision. [113B] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , referred to. In the instant case, the High Court took the view that no such order was passed with respect to the assess year 196364 and therefore the said sum cannot be included as a reserve for the purpose of the Wealth Tax Act. [114C] Metal box Company ofIndia Limited vs their Workmen, [1963] Supp. 2 SCR p.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Assistant Engineers (on a later date) by the Railway Board, pursuant to an advertisement issued by the Railways inviting applications for recruitment to temporary posts of Engineers. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said appointment on the ground that they had been discriminated against and denied equal opportunity to them in the matter of seniority. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions holding that the classification of persons into those that were recruited on the basis of the competitive examinations was not discriminatory, and that the principle of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Katyani Dayal 's case. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the principle laid down by the Supreme Court in Kat yani Dayal vs Secretary, Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors., ; and (ii) the principles of constructive Res judicata would not bar the retried persons from claiming equal rights. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The distinction between the two services was well marked in Kattyani Dayals case (supra). It is not in the interest of service to unsettle a settled position. [1023D] 1.2 In view of the dismissal of the main matters, no orders are necessary on all the C.M.Ps. 1022/82 and 1024/83. The cases aforementioned relied upon by learned counsel for the petitioners do not remove this hurdle, however broadly may be considered and expanded. [1123F] 1:3. In view the dismissal in Kat Yani Dayal"s case, no order is necessary on the strict principles of res judicata as also in the rule of constructive constructive resjudicata. The case aforesaid relied upon was not removed by the High Court. [1105B C] 1 :4. The distinction and the classification between the three services was equally well marked. [111C D] Katyni Dayal 'S case, ; distinguished.

The Saurashtra State Public Safety Measures (Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1949, was promulgated by the Governor of the State on April 1, 1949. The preamble to that Ordinance stated that it was intended to amend the Saurashtra State public safety measures and to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State. Section 11 of the said Ordinance provided that a Special Court shall try such offences or classes of cases as the Government of the United State of Saurashtra may by general or special order in writing direct. The appellant who was convicted under section 3(1) of the Act, was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . He challenged his conviction on the ground that the impugned Ordinance violated article 14 of the Constitution as it contravened articles 14 and 19 of the Constitu tion. Held, that the provisions of the Ordinance were discriminatory in character and violative of article 14 Of the Constitution. The object of enacting the Saurashtra Ordinance was to provide a speedy remedy for public Safety measures and preservation thereof. The Act did not contravene article 14 because it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) of that Constitution. It was not open to the State Government to direct any class of cases or offences to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the Act. The Ordinance was a temporary measure and the State Legislature could not make a law for the purpose of securing public safety. The provisions of article 19 were not discriminatory but were only intended to protect the fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 14, 19(i)(f), 21 and 22 of the constitution. The fact that the maximum punishment prescribed by the Act was less than the minimum prescribed by section 5 (1) Of the West Bengal Special Courts Act did make it a valid classification. The State Government could direct any one or more of these categories to be considered as based on some intelligible differentia distinguishing the offences grouped together from other offences and that differentia must have a reasonable relation to the object of the statute as recited in the preamble. The impugned Ordinance was not therefore invalid because it contravened article 14. The ordinance was not discriminatory and did not offend article 14, because it was passed by the State legislature after consultation with the Advisory Board constituted under section 5(1).

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentences. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1) the evidence of P.W. 2 who had been injured in the house and who had received injuries at the hands of the assailants and could see what had taken place in the light of the lantern as well as the moon; (2) the fact that no property out of the properties looted from the house of the deceased was recovered from the appellants and that it was not possible to identify any of the culprits, and (3) the conviction under section 302 I. P.C., and the sentence awarded to them by the learned Sessions Judge were illegal. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses is corroborated by the evidence on record. [581D] 2. The reasons given by the High Court for rejecting the evidence are not convincing. It is not possible that all the 9 appellants were in the eastern kotha of the house at the same time and it was also not improbable that these appellants entered the house, and assaulted her husband fatally and that some of them caused injuries to her and committed dacoity by looting properties worth about Rs. 2,700/ from her house. [583E F] 3. The fact that Mauji Lal was murdered and property from his house was looted on the night of 16/17th February 1968 and in that occurrence Mauji Lai 's wife P. W. 2 and her children were sleeping during the night and that P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 were injured in their house left the place and that they had received as many as 19 injuries during the course of the occurrence which had gone on for about 15 20 minutes. The presence of the appellants at the scene of occurrence was also doubtful. [584F G] 4. There is no reason whatsoever for rejecting evidence of PW 2 who undoubtedly was in the western kothas of the family of the appellant and his wife. It cannot be said that there were some other persons who had got up on hearing the noise and that he did not reach the spot and did not see the occurrence with his own eye. The prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily and beyond all reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the appel lants for the offence under section 395 I.p.C.[584F H] 5. The reason given by PW 2 for rejecting her evidence is not convincing because she had intentionally made improvements in his version about the occurrence. [585B C] 6. There was no reason whatever for rejecting his evidence altogether. The conviction of appellants for the offences under section 398 I.e. with imprisonment for life cannot be sustained. The Sessions Judge has rightly rejected their evidence and there is no ground to interfere with the same. [586C D] 7. The appeal must accordingly fail.

The appellant State Road Transport Corporation created under a State Act, entitled the Transport Corporation to run its bus service. The respondent was employed as a driver on probation for two years and such probation could be extended by an order of discharge from service. On the ground that he had unsuitability for being appointed in the service, the appellant terminated his employment. A writ petition filed by him challenging the termination was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court holding that the order of termination amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance with section 25F. The Division Bench also held that the termination of service was bad, because, it was not a case of disbanding surplus labour force and, therefore, did not amount to retrenchment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly come to the conclusion that in these cases the order terminating the services was bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour Court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief. [790B] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent terminated the employment of a workman on the ground of unsuitability and it was therefore not a fit case for interference under Article 136 of the Constitution. [788C D] 2.1 It is well settled that the expression "retrenchment" must include every termination of the service of a workmen by an act of the employer. The underlying assumption, of course, is that the undertaking is running as an undertaking and the employer continues as an employer but where either on account of transfer of the undertaking or on account or on the closure of the Undertaking the basic assumption disappears, there can be no question of "ret retrenchment" within the meaning of the definition contained in section2(oo). [791D E] 2:2. The expression "termination of service for any reason whatsoever" is used in the definition discharge from employment or termination of services of a probationer. It is not the case of the respondent that termination in the instant cases was a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. [789E F] 2 :3. The question whether the discharge of the employee on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was justified, depends upon the terms of the agreement between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf, and termination of such service is not a retrenchment within the definition of " retrenchment" under section 2 (oo). It is the effect of the expression 'retrenchment ' and posed the question whether it would be retrenchment. [ 789E F; 789A] 2 .4. The word `termination ' means the discharge by the employer of the services of the workman for any reasons whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment imposed by way or disciplinary action of a employer. [ 788G H] 2 5. The termination of an employee on transfer or closing down of an Undertaking is treated by Parliament as retrenchment within section 2 of the Act and not as a case where such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or lay out of the business. [ 791A B] 3.1 In the absence of any compelling words to indicate that the intention was even to include a bona fide closure of a whole business, it would not be correct to say that the word `retrenchment " must include all termination of employment of such workman by an Act of the legislature. The concluding words in section 25 F of the Industrial Disputes Act are not mandatory and do not stand on a different footing from the language used in section 10F of the . [787B C] 3:2 In view of the decision of this Court in Sundara Money 's case, it is clear that the stage has come when the view indicated in money 's Case has been "condemned" and there is no scope for putting the clock back or for an anti clockwise operation.

The assessee, South Eastern Railway disposed of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. The assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of registration as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the disposal of unclaimed or unconnected goods was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities. He held that the sale effected by the assessee was sales under the Act and that the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the activity of so disposing of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment under the West Bengal Finance Act, 1942. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The activity of the so disposed of the good came within the purview of the Bengal Act. [781E] 2. The activities of so disposed are adjunctive to the principal activity of carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. It seems to South Eastern railway was a "business" for the purposes of the Calcutta High Court 's decision in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In the instant case, the assessee Eastern Railway disposing of unclaimed, and unconnectedgoods lying with it, was not a " dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the West Benjamin Act, 1940. The High Court was right in holding that the respondent Railway in each case is a "manufacturer" for tho purposes of as sessment under the Calcutta Finance ( Sales Tax)Act, 1941 enabling it tO sell the goods.

The appellants were convicted under section 120 read with section 409 I.P.C., and all of them were sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of rigorous imprisonment for six months. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the purchase and sale transactions were genuine and that the appellants had no knowledge of the details of the working of the company, that they had authorised the Directors of the Insurance Company to purchase and sell securities and that therefore the transaction was not a false one; that the transactions were bogus and fictitious and that they were not authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf of the Bank. HELD : (i) The transactions were not genuine and were not voluntary transactions. The transactions did not amount to a false statement as they had been made by the appellants themselves in answer to question No. Raghunath Rai stated that he had no authority to deal with them. It was not possible to believe that the Directors had given any instructions to the appellants for the purchase or sale of securities and the transactions amounted to genuine transactions. [336 B C] (ii) The fact that the transaction took place on September 16, 1955, and it was not alleged by the prosecution that the amount was paid through the brokers without mentioning that the securities were purchased on behalf the Insurance company did not make any difference because the appellants were not aware of the transactions. They had to deal in accordance with the instructions given by Dalmia. [329 C D] (iii) The mere fact that a person who has signed blank forms is not required to sign them does not mean that they are not signed by him. It is only when he says that they have been signed by some one else that they can be used for the purpose of signing them. If they do so, they must be attested by some other person and they cannot be said to have signed them. [429 F G] (iv) The evidence showed that the money was received in cash and not through transfers which were made with the help of the brokers. It could not have been possible for the prosecution to lead direct evidence about the source of the money from the funds of the insurance company to show that the moneys were really paid by the brokers to the Insurance Companies. [529 G H] (v) The High Courts had rightly held that the purchases and sale of the securities had taken place on the date following the receipt of the advice from Dalmia about the purchase of those securities. The fact, however, that the appellant had not signed the documents in question did not affect the correctness of the entries made by Dalmia in the books of the companies. [540 G H; 541 A] (vi) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is that the person who makes a false declaration has to be examined as a witness and he must be able to see that such statement was made with due care and attention. If he does not do so he can be convicted for an offence under section 409, I. P. C., [541 G H]. (vii) The appellant had no motive to purchase the securities and it could have been known that the shares were purchased by him or could have raised money on its credit. It would have been difficult for the appellant to lead any direct evidence of the purchase, sale or other transactions. He had to be given an opportunity to cross examine the brokers and to explain the transactions in his own way.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial branch of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956, they were transferred to the Secretariat of the Government of Gujarat and assigned duties in connection with the Secretariat service. The appellants were allotted to serve in connection therewith. In 1957, the State Government issued an order to the effect that the question of regularising the appointment to various posts in Secretariat Service on and after 1st May 1960 of the prepared persons was under consideration of Government for some time. On August 19, 1966, the Government issued another order to that effect. The respondents challenged the validity of this order by a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States Secretariat personnel to the Gujarat Secretariat per se was not open to objection. HELD : (i) The order dated August 19. 1966 was invalid. [522 B] (ii) The State Government had the authority to transfer subject to the Constitution and the rules made under article 309 any public servant to render service which by his training and aptitude he was competent to do. Transfer of the personnel from the States of Saurashtra and Gujarat States to the secretariats in the Secretariat could not be challenged, and that because they were posted between 1956 and 1960 in the Districts they would not be deprived of their statutory right under section 115(7) proviso. [422 D E] (iii) The High Court was wrong in holding that the order dated 8th September 1966 purported to amalgamate the former State with the Gujarat States Secretariat Service contrary to the terms of r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules and the Government had no authority to vary the method of recruitment provided by the statutory rules.

The petitioners were dealers in goods manufactured by them and sold at the very first instance. The tax was levied on the taxable turnover of the petitioners under section 3(1) of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The petitioners challenged the levy on the ground that the tax was not a tax on the sale or purchase of declared goods but only a tax which was imposed on the goods sold at a very first sale and that the transactions were made liable for tax. The High Court held that the levy was not in accordance with the provisions of section 5(2)(a) of Act, that the purchases of the same item of declared good were made taxable under section 4(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the expression "taxes on goods" used in section 3 (1) includes not only the first purchase but also the first sale. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The levy is not at all leviable on the first purchases and the second sales are made taxable only when they are sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce. [553 B] Section 5(3)(a), negatives the assumption that the normal rule under the Act in respect of declared Goods is to levy the tax on first purchase. If a person sells cotton and sells it after the period provided for in section 5 (2) (a) he can never be taken into account at any stage, for the purpose of calculating or arriving at the taxable turn over and for levying tax. [554 E] The Act has been amended in the year 1956 by the Amending Act which came into force on April 1, 1967. It is not necessary to decide whether a person who is not liable for payment of tax at all, at any time, the collection of a tax from him with a possible contingency, of refund at a later stage will not make the original levy valid; because if particular sales or purchase are exempt from taxation altogether they can never he taken into consideration at any stages for the purposes of calculating and arriving at or revising the taxable price and for imposing tax. Therefore, the levy is beyond the competence of the legislature. [555 E F] The State of Andhra Pradesh vs Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, ; , followed.

The appellants were the representatives of three original plaintiffs who instituted a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain amount due from them on the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed that decree holding that the appellants were entitled to have their debts scaled down under the Agriculturists ' Relief Act, 1938. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the mortgage bond was not binding on the appellants or on their shares in the joint family property; and (ii) the debt if scaled had been split up, and in any event, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to be paid by defendants 2 to 7. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that it was not possible for the appellants to have sold the properties scaled under the provisions of the Agriculturists Relief Act. [297 E] Arunachalam Pillai vs Seetharam, I.L.R. , Arunachalam Chettiar vs Seetaraman, I,.L. R. and Arunachalam vs Ramachandra, I., L. R., , approved. (i)(a) The fact that in a mortgage debt when the loan has been advanced to more than one person, if one of the debtors happens to be an agriculturist while others are not, the agriculturist debtor would certainly be entitled to get the benefit of the relief which has been granted to his agriculturist co debtor under the Act. But there is no provision in the Agriculturists Act which prevents a mortgagor from denying the liability of the interest which he owns in the mortgaged property to satisfy the entire mortgage debt and if the respondent gets any benefit thereby, such benefit would be merely incidental or consequential in its nature. [298 E F] Arunachalaswami Pillai vs Ramachandra (I.L.,R. referred to. (b) The decree in the present case should not only have stated the amount payable by defendant No.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of rent in respect of certain premises on the ground that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The City Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit holding that there had been no lawful subletting by the first respondent of the premises to the second and third plaintiffs as the provisions of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 were not applicable to them. On appeal the City Civil court held that the City civil court had jurisdiction under section 28 to entertain a suit but that the High Court was in error in holding that the suit filed by the appellants could not be entertained by the City 's Court. Held, that the Bombay Rent Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1946, was applicable to the City of Bombay and the City Magistrate had jurisdiction thereunder to try the suit. The Bombay Rents. Hotel and Lod House Rates Act, 1949, was a law relating to eviction of tenants and not to suits for eviction which were governed by the provisions Of section 28 and no other. The suit filed in the City Court was one relating to possession of premises which did not arise out of the Act or any of its provisions. The Act specifically provided that nothing contained in section 28 or section 29 shall be deemed to bar a party to a suit, proceeding or appeal mentioned therein, in which a question of title to premises arises and is determined from suing in a competent court to establish his title to such premises.

The appellant was appointed managing director of a private company. He was appointed the managing director in his place from the date of his appointment and his successor was appointed by the will of the company. The respondent, who was one of the directors of the Company, was appointed as the managing directors of another company. On the question whether the appellant had been validly appointed as a managing director, HELD : (i) The word "assignment" in section 312 of the new Act means "appointment". It is legitimate to infer that by using the word "appoint", the Legislature intended that a certain number of directors would be the chosen representatives of the shareholders. But it did not prevent a director from appointing his successor. [334 C] (ii) The proviso to section 86B does not indicate that it was intended that the word 'assignment ' in the main part of the section would include appointment. It is only when there is an assignment by a director that section 312 can be rendered infructuous by a person including one who holds the office of a director. [333 C] In the present case, the appellant was not appointed as managing director but had to be given by the articles and the proviso to s 86B did not indicate any policy in the Act or of section 312 which could be said to be liable to be defeated by the appointment of the successor of such a director by him. [332 D] (iii) The appellant was validly appointed the Managing Director of the respondent company. It was not correct to say that the proviso would apply only where there is no policy in writing or otherwise indicating that there should be no perpetual management. Therefore, section 312 was not applicable to the present appeal.

The appellants were the partners of a partnership firm. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, in the Court of Small Causes, Madras against the appellant and one another partnership firm for unauthorised occupation under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop to the said M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart and were liable to be evicted for contravening sub clause (i) of section 10 of the Act. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. In second appeal, the High Court held in favour of the appellants on the ground that the eviction petition was filed against the firm and one of the partners, M/ s Adeshwar glass Mart without joining any of the partner of the firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence the eviction order was not maintainable. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that the petition must be set aside as the eviction petitions were filed against M/S Adeshwar Chettiar and one others without joining anyone of the three partners of the said firms as respondent or serving the appellants as partners. [420D] 2.1 In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise this contention at this stage at all. The contention that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellant had sublet the premises to M/ S. Adeshwar Excise Mart, which would justify the finding that the firm had sublet it to M from M/ Smt. Adeswar Glass Mart is not one which would have been fatal to eviction petition. Had this contention been raised in the Trial Court or even in the first appeal before the High court, it would have be open to him to amend the eviction Petition and join the partners as re spondents. [426E F] Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm and others vs Shikharchand, In that case an eviction order passed against the tenant was set aside by the appellate authority on the grounds that the tenant had unlawfully or without the permission of the landlord sublet the said shop let out to the appellant from the premises. The appellate authority dismissed the said appeal upholding his finding of subletting. [416F G] Chh Mahalal Pyare Lal, the partner in the partnership Firm and others v Shikhar Chand, In this case no such objections were raised at any stage before the trial court or even by even in second appeal.

The Andhra Pradesh Act was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its power under Entry 25 of List III of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The validity of the Act was challenged on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it made a discrimination between minor son and minor sons, while excluding minor son from the definition of "vacant land" in the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned Act did not have the effect of invalidating the whole of the Andhra State Act but only validating the entire Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the landholders that (i) the Andhra Act sought to impose ceiling on land in urban agglomeration other than land which is mainly used for the purpose of agriculture and agriculture, and (ii) the definition in section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Central Act was an inclusive one and any area with a population of more than one lakh could be notified as an urban agglomerations under section 2 (n)(B) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Andhra Pradesh Legislature had no legislative competence to enact the impugned legislation. [1155E] 2. The definition of 'vacant Land ' in section 3(f) of Central Act is an inclusive definition and any land which comes to the share of a divided minor son would be liable to be assessed as on 1st January 1975 under the Andhra Area (Abolition) Act, 1976 and only land within the ceiling area will be allowed to remain with him. [1105F G] 3. The expression 'vacants land ' in the definition clause includes raising of grass, dairy farming, poultry farming, breeding live stock and cultivation or the growing of such plants as may be prescribed by the Rules. The word 'vacancy ' is not defined in the Act but it is used in the sense of a mere possibility. [1055G H] 4. The term "vacants" has been defined in section 4(1) to mean any land held by a person in excess of the ceiling limit, and includes raising or raising grass, Dairy farming, cattle stock and cultivated such other agricultural produce as may from time to time be prescribed. [1255H; 1256A] 5. The definitions of ' Vacant Land" in section 1(f)(1) of Act 3(j) are not exhaustive but only illustrative. It is a general rule that if the definition is inclusive, then it would apply in relation to land situate within such area. [1357B C] 6. The State Legislature was competent to enact a law relating to ceiling on vacant land in the whole area of the State of Andhra Pradesh. [1455C] 7. The Act came into force on 1.1.1975 and it was with reference to this date the surplus holding of land in excess thereof was required to be determined and if there was any surplus it would have to be surrendered to the State Government. It could not therefore be said that merely because an area may possibly in the future be notified to be an urban land, the Central Legislature would cease to have competence to legislate with respect to ceiling. [1557D E] 8. The power of the Parliament to enact legislation on vacant lands in urban areas other than those specified in section I(f), is not restricted by the Andhra area which is included within the definition. It will thus be clear that the Central Legislation enacted by the A.P.

The appellant company was ordered to be reinstated with full back wages. The company terminated the services of all other workmen on the ground that they had turned up on or before October 2, 1953, and that the Company refused to employ them without any condition. On September 23, 1953 the company issued a second notice to the workmen stating that unless they voluntarily recorded their willingness to do normal work they would be considered as no longer employed by the Company from February 24, 1953. The workmen contended that the said notices were illegal because they had been suspended for misconduct and were not entitled to reinstatement. Held, that the appellant company had failed to produce satisfactory evidence of its absence and that was the reason why it should have refused leave to the workers. The Industrial Tribunal found that the services were rightly terminated by the appellant. Chattoraj there being a suspension order against him, the company could not be said to have abandoned the services. The fact that the workmen had been discharged by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute as in this case, did not affect the finding of fact. The Tribunal was right in holding that the company had decided to terminate the services and that it could not have interfered with the decision of the Company unless it found that its decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. Chatturbhuj vs The State of Bombay, ; , followed. Held further, that there was no reason for interfering with the order of suspension passed by the Industrial Tribunal unless it was shown that the decision was malafide or amounted in violation of any statutory provision or principles of natural justice.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Urea Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list but was not selected. Dr. Nathawat, respondent No. 1, filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challenging the appointment of Dr.Urea Kant as Professor in the department of Bot any. The Single Judge held that the constitution of the Selection Committee was valid but as regards the appointment to the post, it was held that once a person selected by the Selection Commit tee had joined, that post is filled and some vacancy is caused thereafter a fresh selection committee should have been constituted and no appointment on such post could have been made from the reserve panel. The Division Bench also held that since the appellant Dr. Uma Kant was selected by a Selection Committee, he was not entitled to be appointed against a future vacancy. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had committed a clear error in restricting the scope of the reserve List only against the post for which the selection was made and which according to the High Courts was inconsistent with section 5(1) of the Act, and that the appointment was therefore void. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was wrong in taking the view that a regular vacancy of Professor having arisen on the retirement of Dr Nathawar on 30th September, 1989 again a fresh Selection Committee should have be constituted and the appointment made by it is exhausted and the reserve select list is of no avail and becomes extinct. [426F] 2.1 The High Courts were wrong in holding that a irregular selection of teachers was not justified. The proper course for the selection of a teacher was to fill up the vacancy by following the procedure prescribed under section 6(2) of Act of 1974. [420B] 2:2. The Syndicate in its Resolution dated 10th July, 1978 had resolved that the reserve lists recommended by the Committee shall be valid upto six months from the date of approval of the Syndicate which was subsequently extended to one year instead of six months in a resolution passed on 3rd December, 1983. [416D] 2 :3.

The petitioners challenged the validity of sections 4 to 16 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, on the ground that they infringed their fundamental rights under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the provisions of sections 14, 15 and 16 were ultra vires the Constitution as they contravened articles 14 and 19(i)(f). Held: (i) The combined operation of sections 3 to 17 of the Act is not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authority but a Municipal Commissioner himself or the Chief Officer of the Municipal Borough or a person exercising the power of an Executive Officer of any local authority. When the power had to be exercised by one of the highest officers of the Local Authority intimately connected with the preparation of the development plan in all its stages, it is difficult to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. The preparation of a tentative plan or the final development plan was not something that was left for the pleasure of the municipal authority. The preparing of the tentative plan and the final Development plan were not something more than the Municipal Commissioner 's power to deal with his land as he pleased, but a discretion had been conferred in a manner which is legal and constitutional. (ii)The preparation of tentative plan was an integral part of the process of development and it could be made in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 4, 5 and 6. The scheme was not a mere paper but a whole and was a whole. The word 'may ' used in section 17(1) of Bombay Town planning Act, 1953, is used to convey a discretion to the local authori ty to make a town planning scheme in respect of the whole or any part of land referred to in section 2 1. (iii)The power conferred on the local autho rity by section 13 of the City Improvement Trust Act, 1956, was not an arbitrary power and could not be exercised arbitrarily. The use of the word 'shall ' in section 11(3) of that Act showed that it was a matter of no moment for the authority under section 13 is no less than the municipal Commissioner himself, or the chief Officer of a Municipal Borough, or a Municipal Corporation or a Corporation exercising the powers of an executive officer of any Local Authority. When power had been to be conferred in respect only before its final development scheme was made, it could not have been a ground for invalidating the law.

The appellant, a Ruler of Kutch in the State of Gujarat, was granted by the Government of India, to the Dominion of India certain rights in the territory of the State. The appellant challenged the validity of the grant on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution and was not saved by article 31(2) of the Consti tution. Held: (i) The award of the Tribunal is binding on the Government and no constitutional amendment is necessary. The award does not purport to nor does it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. The claim of the Government to exercise fundamental rights in respect of the territory in that sector may be entertained only if it be established that the territory is found to be originally governed by the Maharao of Kutch. In the present case, the dispute was between the appellant and the State Government which was set out in the resolution of the Govern ment dated February 24, 1914. The dispute was not one relating to the territory over which the Maha Rao had sovereign rights but only to the State which had exercised sovereign rights. The decision to implement the award by exchange of letters, treating the Award as an operative treaty after the boundary has been marked in this area is within the competence of the Executive wing of Government and therefore no constitutional amendments are necessary. (ii)The award does no more than define on the surface of the earth a boundary which has at all material times remained indefinite and by the award of Tribunal the true boundary of India and Pakistan is determined: the award does nothing more than defines on the basis of the surface in the pre partition maps, which are not sporadic but consistent and effective. (iii)The appellant 's claim that in implementing the award, territory which was Indian was now declared foreign territory, was involved, and the executive was incompetent to cate any part of it.

The mortgagor borrowed Rs. 5,500 from one M and executed a deed of mortgage whereby he agreed to repay the amount with interest at the rate of Rs. 1/8/ per mensem and also undertook that in default of payment, the mortgagee shall be entitled to recover the amount due by sale of his interest in Mauza Bahaldih in equal instalments. The mortgagor failed to pay the amount within the stipulated time and the mortgagee did not execute a sale deed. The mortgagee filed a suit for recovery of the amount on July 12, 1946, but the trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred by limitation because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, she could still maintain the suit relying upon the dispossession of M. The High Court in appeal held that the mortgagor 's interest in Mauzas Bansjora was not extinguished by the sale of Mauza Bahab or on April 14, 1925, and that the mortgagee had never lost his interest therein. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922, was partly simple, partly usufructuary and even if it be assumed that the two Mauzis alone were mortgaged, the mortgagor having lost his interests in Mauazas Bans jora could not operate to extend limitation under section 20 of the Limitation Act; (ii) the suit filed by the plaintiff was for enforcement of payment of money charged upon immoveable property and money sued for on the later mortgage had become due on April 1, 1937, and therefore the suit to enforce that mortgage was barred under article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act. HELD: (i)(a) The right conferred by section 68 is again not a right to enforce the mortgage but a right which is again subject to limitation. [642 B] (b) The suit filed on July12, 1946 was for the enforcement of the payment of the money charged on immoveable property as well as for interest and costs by selling Mauzhas Bansjore simitanr and Simitanr. The plaintiff 's claim to enforce this mortgage dated August 27, 1922 was at the date of the suit not barred by article 120 but only a right of appeal against the order granting the relief. [643 C] (c) The mortgagor ' interest in the mortgaged property Bansjor could not be enforced under article 119 of the Act.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees, the appellants provided transport facilities for their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages. The appellants provided Transport facilities to the employees from Pimpri or Khed or Vadgaon or Vadgod and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly, for transport facilities provided to the workers from PimPrior to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back, the appellant further averred that these amounts were realised by them only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. In the course of arguments it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, the employees would be provided free transport as in the case of supervisory staff. The Commissioner rejected these contentions and held that the appellants were liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the appellant against the order imposing the tax. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that even if a nominal charges are realised from the employee that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, and that the transport vehicles provided to their employee by the company would be a public services vehicle within the meaning of the charging Section. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'public ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employee of that company. Thus qua public the employees form a separate class and cannot be said to be public as contemplated by rule 2(i). On the other hand, the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act 1958 clearly indicates that vehicles which could not be termed as public service vehicles fell beyond the ambit of the taxing provisions of the Bombay Act. [362G H; 362A B] 2. The words 'public service vehicle ' have got a very wide connotation and mean a carriage, to which no member of tho public can has free access, on payment Of the usual charge.

The appellants, who had objected to the grant of a licence for a "no objection" certificate, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court challenging the validity of the order granting a licence. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the District Magistrate was not influenced by any extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence had been re opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a "temporary cinema licence" and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Govt. on being satisfied that there was an impediment to the granting of such a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and therefore it was not a fit case for interference by the High court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that if before grant of the "no objections" certificate and the appellants ' objection were heard, the District Magis trate as the licensing authority was persuaded to accept the objections and reject the application for a no objection certificate and thereafter when under section 5(3) of the Act respondent preferred ar.a revision petition against the refusal of the licence, the appeal was decided at the back of those who had not only filed objections but whose objections had prevailed with the licensing authori ty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order granting the no objection certifi cate is violative of the principles of natural justice. [799B] 2.1 A detailed provisions for the grant and renewal of a license at three distinct stages by the licensing authorities in the process of licensing a cinema houses, viz., (i) no objection Certificate for the site on which the cinema house is to be constructed; (ii) appeal is provided against the order of a licensing authority only at the instance of a person aggrieved by the decision of the licensing Authority refusing to grant a licence; and (iii) an application for renewal of licence under Rule 102 is without prejudice to the right of the licensee to refuse a cinema licence under rule 102. [899C D] 2:2 The appellants did not file any objection at that stage "no objecting" certificate. When any person desires to erect a cinema meaning thereby a place where an exhibition by means of cinematograph is to he given, he must apply for a No objection certificate in respect of the site where the cinema houses are to be built. [800D] 2 :3 The appellants were not entitled to challenge the grant or renewal of the cinema licence on the ground that there were mosque, a "madarsa" and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the Cinema house is situated. The appellants had not raised any objection to the renewal of such an order. When the present appellants objected to it, they opposed it on the grounds that there is a mosque, and a Temple in the adjoining locality and that the cinema, if permitted, would constitute an obstruction and annoyance to the local residents. [900E F] 2 .4 The appellants failed to raise any objection as to the validity or otherwise of the grant. The appeal must fail. [901F] 2 5. The application for licence is for a quasi permanent cinema license.

The respondent entered into a contract with the appellant for the supply of float iron lying in the mining area and gave them the right to win and remove the iron ore. The appellant refused to do so. On the question whether there was a concluded contract, HELD : (i) The letter written by the respondent to the appellant did not amount to an acceptance of the offer. The letter was not an acceptance. There was no other acceptance either oral or in writing. Mere mental assent of the plaintiffs to the defendants proposal is not sufficient. [583 E F] Bloxam 's case, referred to. (ii) The plaint was not a suit for specific performance of the contract. Before the present suit for Specific performance could be instituted, the offer had been withdrawn. [584 G] Blitz vs Ayerst, , relied on. Bloxom vs Akerst, ; , relied upon. Bloys vs Alerst, (1893) 6 Madd. 316 and Bloxmull vs Aierst, [1923] 1 K.B. 318, referred. Bliton 's Case, L.J. pointed out that the letter written on September 2, 1957, was in point of law an offer only. The acceptance of a tender by serving a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons was not sufficient to enable the appellant to obtain the necessary sanction of the Central Government and the approval of the central government. [585 E F; 584 A] Blockon vs Aasterst, I.L.R. , relied.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K.G. Sugar Mills Ltd., (Lauriya). A complaint was filed against them under section 3(1) of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 alleging that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The appellants contended that the investigation which was being carried on against them was in accordance with law and therefore the investigation was not liable to be quashed. Held, that the complaint did not disclose a cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of that complaint. Section 3(2)(b) of Act provides that if the Central Government is of opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing supplies of any essential commodity or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices, it may, by order, provide for regulating or prohibiting the production, supply and distribution thereof and trade and commerce therein. The power conferred on the Central Govern ment under section 33 of the Act cannot be challenged as invalid. Ch. Tika Ramji and Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , referred to. Held further, that there was no substance in the contention that the impugned order contravened the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens under article 19(1). Ch.Tika Ramji & Ors. v The State Of U. P., ; at page 432 and Ch.ika Ramji 's case, referred to, Held, also, that section 3 of the , was a specific mandate.

The Government of Karnataka issued a notification dated 12th January, 1977 under which the Government of India was committed to a policy of rapid industrialisation and that the Government had on 30th June 1969 issued directions indicating incentives for starting new industries in Mysore State. The Government of Mysore issued another order dated 12.1.1977 giving certain concessions to entrepreneurs starting new industrial units in the Mysore State, but later on, by an order dated 11th August, 1975, it was directed that the said concession would be given to entrepreneurs start new industries and in pursuance thereof, the Government issued directions specifying incentives for the entrepreneurs starting existing industries in the Bangalore State. On 12th February, 1977, the State of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialization and that, in pursuance thereto, the government had on 31st March, 1966 issued directions stating that the incentive would be granted to entrepreneurs from 1 5 (five) years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concessions being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce.
