The appellants who were manufacturers of new industrial undertakings in Mysore, challenged the validity of the said order dated December 30, 1974 passed by the State Government on the ground that the concession granted under the said orders was not a promissory estoppel against the Government on account of which they acted by starting new units requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order dated January 12, 1977. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it Was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government that the concessions granted under orders dated 30th May 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same; (ii) the concession given by the earlier order had been withdrawn by the appellants on the grounds that the grant of concession constituted a promissory est estoppel against them; (iii) the concessions were in fact granted to the entrepreneurs, and (iv) the said concessions were of no legal effect as there was no statutory provision under which such concessions could be granted and the order of 30th July 1969 was ultra vires. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegation that they caused the death of one Madda Lakshamandas by stabbing the deceased with a stick. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 1 to A 3 under Sections 148 and 307 read with 149 I P.C., but set aside their conviction and sentences of imprisonment on applying Section 149 IPC. Allowing the appeals by the appellants, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.p.C.[8D] 2.1 The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A 1 and A 3 were armed with spears, A 4, A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 was armed with a sticks. All the accused persons were armed by A 3 to A 7 who had come on parole. They were also given beating by legs. The deceased died instantaneously on the spot. It is in evidence that the complainant and the accused belonged to opposite factions and there was long standing enmity between them. During the last 30 years, there had been murders and rioting between the two factions. The case from A 1 was that he named persons formed the Unlawful assembly. A 4 to A 6 having been acquitted, the remaining three appellants cannot be convicted under Sections 302 readwith Section 34 I. P. C.[8E F] 2:2. It would be safe to accept the evidence of PW 3 that the common object of the unlawful assembly was to kill the deceased.

The assessee, a registered firm, was carrying on business of sale and purchase of certain properties. The assessee had purchased the property from its managing director and had also paid a sum of Rs. 48,500 to the managing director. The price of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of the consideration declared by the assessee in respect of the transfer by an amount equal to 15% of the value so declared. The Income tax officer assessed the sum of RS. 48.500 to tax on the ground that it was not a condition precedent for attracting the applicability of section 52(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 or that it should be deemed to have been under statement of consideration in respect thereof. On appeal by the respondent assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the income tax officer. The Tribunal held that in order to bring a case within section 52 sub section (2), it was necessary for the Revenue to show not only that the fair market value of capital asset transferred by the assesee as on that date exceeded the Full value of Rs, the transfer was not at all necessary that there should be under statement or disclosed the true value of consideration declared. On a reference made by the High Court, the High court held that the assessee could not be said to have purchased the land in question when it was found that the market value was more than Rs. 45 lakhs and that the difference between the fair price of Rs 48, 500 and Rs. 46,500 shown by the Income tax Officer were only Rs. 50,000 and that therefore the fair and reasonable construction of section 51 sub section(2), would be to read into it a condition that it would apply only where the consideration for the transfer is under stated or in other words, shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by the assesses. On the question whether the High Courts were right in holding that the respondent was not entitled to claim deduction of Rs 50,00,000 under section 52 (2) on the basis that the value of transfer and the balance of consideration were not disclosed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in its view that the provisions of section 54(2)(a) of Income Tax, 1961 were limited to cases where there was under statement by the appellant assessee and in most of the cases if not all, it would have no application in case of a bonafide transaction where the full market value had been disclosed or disclosed by the appel lant. [653E] 2.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 16(1)(a) (i) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, for having adulterated Til seeds to the Food Inspector. The prosecution case was that the appellant had gone to "a shop to make purchases", without giving either the name or the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. Under cross examination he stated that he did not know who made the payment but only told him that he would write on the cash memo, that he had no knowledge as to what was being done by him and that he was told that he should write on it. The trial court found that the version of the appellant that there was a tall, about the actual purpose for which the Til seeds were kept in the accused 's shop, but did not find anything material. On appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what was kept by the Food inspector was "food" at all and that the use of the word "gift" meant for human consumption was not entirely irrelevant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "fruit", and that it was presumed from the nature of the article itself or the circumstances and manner of offering it for sale. HELD: (i). The use of article 7(1) in the present case, did not amount to a partial admission that they were used for Pooja. Therefore, the view taken by the High court that they could be consumed by people after the performance of pooja rests on bare conjecture. There had to be credible evidence to show that black Tils were ordinarily used as food. If that were so, the burden would have shifted on to the shoulders of the accused to prove that what he had stored was not really food meant for his human consumption but an article kept for a special use. [357 B C] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that they had been consumed by persons who were in the shop at the time when the seeds were sold by the appellant to the food Inspector. [330 G] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to.

The appellant, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966. He filed an appeal before the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31.8.1966, but the order of dismissal was communicated to him on 19.9.1960. The appellant 's suit for declaration that the order dated 13.6.1969, merged in the appellate order dated May 7, 1949, and both the orders were in fact passed simultaneously, was decreed by the trial court on 2nd January, 1966. The appeal filed by the respondent was dismissed by the Divisional Commis sioner and his order was confirmed by the High Court in second appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit had been filed within a period of three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The cause of actions shall be taken to arise not from the dates of the original adverse order but on the date of preferring of the appeal or making of the representation shall be the date which when cause is preferred or representation was made. [54F] 2.1 In every such case only when the appeal and representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of a remedy shall first accrue. The Civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore, as far as Government serv ants are concerned, Article 58 may not be flouted in view of the special limitation.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittoor for his half share in the properties which were described as 'A ' and 'B '. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienations effected by his father as well as sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in those properties could not be affected by them. On appeal, the High Court reversed the trial court 's decree holding that the appellant was entitled to a half share of the properties covered by the alienations. The appellant then applied for special leave to appeal to this Court. Held, that the High Courts had taken a contrary view and were in error in taking a different view. It is well settled that where two courts have concurrently found that the appellate decree has been varied in favour of the intending appellant, it is not necessary to disturb such findings on the merits. The question whether the appellate court has jurisdiction or not must be decided on its own facts and circumstances. In the present case the High court had taken the view that an appellate decree which makes a variation in favour was one of affirmance and so the finding of the trial Court could not affect the character of the appellate order where it made variation in respect of the award, interest which was entirely in the discretion of the Court under section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Chittam Subba Rao vs The State of Andhra Pradesh, A.I.R. 1953 Mad. 946, approved. Chitranjan Das vs The Collector of Chittoon, A I. R. , distinguished.

The provisions of section 115, Code of Civil Procedure read with section 115 of the Code of civil Procedure, 1908, are applicable to the State of Uttar Pradesh. The High Court has exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in cases arising out of original suits of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above. Section 115 provides that any amendment made or provision inserted in the Code by a State Legislature before the 1st February, 1978 would stand repealed except insofar as such amendment or provision was consistent with the Code as amended by the said Amendment Act. The appellant, who was the owner of certain properties, filed a suit for recovery of Rs, 20,00,000 on the ground that he had been in possession of the property during the pendency of the original suit and had been dispossessed from it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the High Courts ' exclusive jurisdiction was not vested in them by section 115. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the High court possesses revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, read with Section 115 of Code of Criminal Procedure, and (2) the District Court had exclusive jurisdiction to exercise revisional power under section 25 in respect of an order of the District Judge under section, 115. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 115 are applicable only to cases decided before 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising from original suits or other proceedings instituted before 1st August, 1978; (2)(a) The High Courts have exclusive jurisdiction in respect cases arising under the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, disposing of a revision petition. [38B] 2(b) Section 115 is not applicable to cases pending before 20nd September, 1973 and also the revisional jurisdiction was concurrently shared between the High courts and the District court.

The respondents, a company registered under the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, applied to the State Government for acquisition of certain lands belonging to them under section 52(1) of the Act. The State Government issued a notification under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act on February 8 , 1984 for acquiring the said land for public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme at public expense viz., the Civil Lines Extension Scheme. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi on the writ petition were not maintainable as the same had been filed beyond the territorial limits of the Calcutta high Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under section 51(1 ) of the Rajasthan Act arose within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the State High Court at the Jaipur Bench. [602D] 2. The notification dated February 8, 1984 issued by the State Govern ment under section 5(1), or the notification issued by it under section 18 B , Brabourne Road , Calcutta i. e., within the geographical limits of that State of West Bengal could not give rise to a cause of ' action within that territory unless the service of such notice was an integral part of the cause of the action. The whole cause of actions culminating in acquisition of land under Section 52( 1 ) of Act arose in the State, i.n., within its territorial jurisdiction. [600F G] 3. The High Court had no jurisdiction to issue a rule neces sary exparte prohibitory order restraining the appellants from taking any steps to take possession of the acquired land acquired.

The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant from the premises in dispute on the ground that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises by a co operative housing scheme of the State Bank of India. The claim was resisted by the appellant on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that the building in question was constructed in 1968 and that it was covered by the new Rent Act; (ii) that rent had been cleared upto 6th April, 1977 and there was no default in the payment of rent; (iii) that since the building was not ten years old on the date of suit, the respondent could not get any protection of the new Act. The trial court dismissed the suit for ejectment as also the appellate court. The High Court allowed the appeal in part and set aside the decree of the trial court relating to the recovery of Rs.3158 30 as arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the premises were exempt from the operation of the old Rent Act on two grounds: (i). that the buildings in question had been constructed by a cooperative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the Judge that the construction of the building would be deemed to have been completed on 1st October 1971 was manifestly erroneous. The respondent contended that the new rent Act would not apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court has rightly held that the tenant could not be evicted under section 20 of the Act. [334B] (2) Section 2(2) contemplates that the old rent Act will not apply if ten years expired during the pendency of the litigation. The building was subject to assessment therefore it would be a deemed to be completed on the dates of assessment which was 1st November, 1971. [340C D] Om Prakash Gupta vs Dig Vijendrapal Gupta ; , followed. (3) The landlord could not seek the benefit of section 20(2). Section 20 of Act stipulates that in any suit for recovery of possession on the basis of a decree for eviction on the allegations mentioned therein is satisfied. It is, therefore. open to the tenant to contend that the Act would be attracted if ten year 's period was expiring from the commencement of the suit and not from the first date of the decree. [341D E] (4) The suit was filed more than 10 years old during the penden cy of the proceedings. Therefore, the question assumes importance in the present case. [343F G] (5) The appellant in the instant case only seeks the protection of section 39 and not to the appellant. Section 20 is a bar to a suit. It does not give any benefit of the newly added new Rent Acts or create new cause of action. [344G H; 344A] (6) The Act provides a bar against a suit in respect of eviction on grounds mentioned in cl. (a) to sub section (2), viz., arrears of land revenue, rent if at the first hearing of the suits the tenant in default pays all arrears of rents to the landlord or deposit in court the entire amount of rent, and damages, for use & occupation of the buildings due from him, such damages for user and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the plaintiff 's cost of the Suit in respect thereof after deducting there from any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section(1) of section 30, the court may, in lieu of passing a decree of eviction, pass an order relieving the tenant against his liability for eviction.

The appellant filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of an award. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent it to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed objections to the award on various grounds. The appellant raised the objection that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant time. The trial court passed a decree against the appellant and the High Court confirmed the decree. Held, that the award was valid and the appeal must be dismissed. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated by notification in the Official Gazette but there is nothing in section itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person, and when that is established the requirements are satisfied. In the present case the arbitrator sent a copy of the award signed by him and a third copy also signed by the appellant was sent to the court. The copy of it was not a certified copy but a copy thereof. It was therefore the original and not a copy. The judgment of the High court was set aside and the decree passed in terms directed that the appellant should execute the agreement. The award was not invalid on the ground that it did not conform to the requirements under section 175 (3) Of the Government Act, but only as a certified copies of the same. The order of the trial court was therefore illegal and inoperative.

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab. On various dates he was placed orders for purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and other places. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. In 1980 some complaints were received against him pertaining to the purchase of the sign boards. Vigilance enquiry was instituted against him under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The respondent was charge sheeted for offences under sub clauses (i) and(ii) of clause (b) of Rule 2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, 1955. In the meantime, the respondent retired from service on September 30, 1983. The First Information Report was lodged against him in the Police Station, on August 28, 1985. The Respondent applied for quashing of the First Information report on account of which challan could not be filed and it was only when the challenge to the First information Report was repelled by the High Court that a challan was filed on August 29, 1985 in the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Punjab. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the said rule placed an embargo on prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i). the view taken by the trial court was correct and in view of Rule 3(b) the said Rule cannot be interpreted to mean that the rule placing an embargo is a rule regulating the conditions of service of such a person; (ii) the expression "any other law" in clause (a) of sub rule 2 of Rule 4 of the Criminal Service Rules has been used in the substantive clause of a rule or in the proviso thereto. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The intention of framing the said rules was not to grant immunity from prosecution to a government employee if the conditions mentioned therein are satisfied. [917C] 1.2 In view of the language used by the legislature in its wisdom it cannot be said that an assurance to an employee that he shall not be prosecuted after his retirement would amount to a rule prescribing an exception to the right conferred on the government by the substantive provision if the condition mentioned therein is fulfilled. This purpose can be achieved if the said proviso by adopting the rule of reading down is interpreted to include even an express prohibition against prosecution. [936D E] 1:3. The object of the third proviso thereto is not to place an embargo upon prosecution. It was further contended that the third Proviso to clause (4) of the Rule 2 has not been framed for that purpose but has been framed in exercise of the power conferred on him by the first part thereof. [981F] 1 :4. The second proviso to clause(b)(b) is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the Rule has been created.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. In September 1936 the respondent company sold its shares to the appellant company which later became a public company under section 23 A of the Income tax Act, 1922. The respondent company took over the business conducted by the company for Rs. 5,50,0001 paid in the form of 2,500 ordinary and 3,000 preference shares. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to vote at the meeting of the company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings of the respondent assessee company the Income Tax Officer found that for three years ending March 31, 1948, March 31 and March 31 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the income tax officer but reduced the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the respondent in respect thereof to Rs. 1,000/ . On further appeal the Tribunal held that the undistributed portion of the assessable income of the appellant as computed for income tax purposes and reduced by the amount Of income tax was not taxable. The High Court on reference held against the assessee company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (1) the Explanation to sub section (1)(a) of section 23A of the Indian Income tax, 1922, as it stood at the material time, no order could be passed in respect of any company in which the public were substantially interested; and (2) where the public are substantially interested, the provisions of the Explanation would apply. HELD: The Explanation to section 23(1)(b) is not applicable to a case where the Public are substantially interest. In terms, however, the Explanation raises a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of the Company carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power are held by persons other than the controlling group. [51 F] (a) The Explanation has no operation. Whether inview of the third proviso the company may be regarded as one in which public are substantial interested is a question to which no attention was paid by the Tribunal. Whether in fact there exists such control interest in the hands of one shareholder or a group of shareholders as would render the company one in whom the public is substantially interested. [52 F] In considering whether shares carrying not more than twenty 5 per cent.

The first appellant was a registered joint stock company. The first appellant and the second appellant were partners in two firms, the first appellant 's firm and the third appellant. The second appellant was the Director of the Mills. The third appellant was also the Managing Agent of the first respondent. The firm was dissolved on March 31, 1947, and its managing agent was appointed as the purchaser. The last appellant was appointed a managing agent of the second respondent. On February 3, 1947 the first appel lant sent a return signed by him stating that he had received payment in advance from the Mills at the rate of Rs. 20,000 on each of the bales and that the 13 bales were delivered to him on January 21, 1947. The appellant submitted a return on October 30, 1947 and accepted the money from P. C. Vora who was the managing agent. The case of the appellant was that the first two appellants had received the payment in February 1947, the amount paid by them to the purchasers with whom they deal direct. The High Court held that the godown belonged to the first appellants but that the goods were sold to the second appellants and accepted their money from the mills. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that the delivery of the goods was not by way of delivery but by way or actual delivery of them, and (2) that in any event the delivery was not with the permission of the purchaser and as the first 2 appellant had no title to them, they were entitled to a decree for Rs. 10,000. HELD : The High court was right in holding that this was a true and correct return. The fact that the second appel lateer was the Managing agent of a firm did not make any difference because he was responsible for the price whatever happened between him and the Mills when delivery was made. [833 B] Dwarkadas Khetan could, in the circumstances given above, be described, without any straining of language, as the person to whom the goods are actually delivered. The goods did reach the quotaholder in the end, or rather his proper agent, and it cannot be said that the agent was not in physical possession. [ 834 C] Dwarakas Khetan vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , followed.

The appellant was a Senior Lecturer in the College. He was appointed as an Examiner for Physics practical examination for the first year B.Sc. and was later promoted to the post of Assistant Professor. The appellant was also a resident of Jamnagar. In April 1964 he was appointed an Examiner to examine him. On the basis of the report made by the Examiner, the appellant was charged under section 161 I.P.C. for having committed the offence of criminal misconduct in that he accepted gratification of Rs. 1,000/ and gave him a sum of Rs, 500/ as bribe. The trial court acquitted him but on appeal the High Court held that the last part of the Ninth clause of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code was not attracted to the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the ninth clause did not apply to the present case because the ninth cl. (a) of the first clause had been omitted from the definition of a public servant as given in section 21, Indian Penal code; and (ii) the words "corrupt or illegal means" in the second clause meant criminal breach of trust by a public officer. HELD : (i). The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of a receivers one may accept money, that if offered, or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion, in each case, lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public servants. [319 D E] (ii). The use of the word "corruption" on the first cl. of section 5(1)(d) is not conclusive and it would be unreasonable to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. According to the High Courts, the abuse of position as public servant would be essential whether the means are corrupt or illegal or are of the nature covered by the word ' otherwise '. [320 E F] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration ; , followed. (iii) The use in clause (a), (b) and (c) of section 1 65, if it is habitual, is comprised in cl.

The petitioners, who were casual labourers engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the construction Department of Signal Unit in Northern Railway, challenged their claim before the Central Administrative Tribunal contending that they were entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The Senior Signal & Telecommunication Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the respondents, contending that the Administration was requiring continuous service for purposes of eligibility, and that the Railway Administration, respondent herein, had not treated them as temporary servants and had applied discriminatory rates of wages. It was further contended that since the petitioners have put in more than 360 days of service, they are now entitled to all the privileges as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. The respondents contested the claim on the ground that the petitioners were project employees and do not belong to the open line. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1. It is the stand of the Railways that no pensionary benefits are admissible even to temporary Railway servants and, therefore, that retiral advantage is not available to casual labour acquiring temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc. Service prior to the absorption against a regular temporary/permanent post after requisite selection will, however not constitute as qualifying service for pensionary benefits. [144G H] 1.2. The benefit of Discipline and Appeal Rules is also applicable to casual labourers with temporary status and they are allowed to carry forward the leave at their credit to the new post on absorption in regulation service. [145B C] 1:3. In the Signal and Telecommunication Construction organisation under which the petitioners are working, according to the Railway Establishment Manual, casual labour is entitled to the same pay as is 1) admissible to others either in the project or in the openline. That would take away inequality which is main grievance of the petitioners. The Respondents shall have a direction to consider the claims of each of the Petitioners promptly and make appropriate orders for their regularisation. [146C D] 1 :4. There is perhaps slackness in enforcing them.

The Forward Markets Commission, in exercise of its powers conferred by section 12(1) of the Act, framed bye laws for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the , and issued a notification under section 12 of the . The appellants challenged the validity of the said bye laws on the grounds that they infringed their fundamental rights guaranteed to them under articles 19(1)(f), 31(2) and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned bye laws were not ultra vires the State Legislature as they contravened article 14 Of the Constitution and were therefore void. The power conferred by the Act was a legislative power and the Central Government had no power under section 11 or 12 to make bye laws with retrospective effect. The provisions of section 12 (1) did not confer any such power on the Commission. The object of the legislation would be defeated if the provisions in question were held to be invalid. The words "under the Act" in section 12 Of the Act meant that the Central Govern ment had no authority under section 1(4) to make a bye law with retrospective operation and therefore the new bye laws made on January 21, 1956, in so far as they applied to hedge contracts were not void. It was not correct to say that unless retrospective operation was given to the provisions Of section 12 the objects of the Legislation would be frustrated or the purposes for which the power was conferred could not be fulfilled. The Act did not provide any machinery for the enforcement of the rights conferred by it and therefore, the new Bye laws made under section 18 of the were invalid.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The shares were declared as dividend and compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declaring as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of long term leases was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assessee from other sources. The Appellate Tribunal held that the entire sum for each year was income in the hands of the asses see and hence, it was liable to be grosned up. In second appeal, however, the High Court took the view that part was assessable as dividend, but interest which is statutorily payable on compensation was income and not capital gain. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: The order of the High court is set aside and the case remanded to the High Tribunal for disposal according to law. [34 C] (1) The scope of enquiry in this group of cases in view of the form of questions is more extensive. In appeals Nos. 737 to 739 of 1968 and 1621 of 1968 which arose out of Reference No. 131 of 1961 and other references, decided by this Court on July 25, 1969, the only question of law raised was whether distribution of dividend out of capital gains was taxable. [35 D] (2) The High Court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain and whether any part of compensation received for compulsory acquisitions of land was capital gains.

The appellants were charged with offences under the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short 'the Act '. The prosecution case was that Sandalwood oil was not wood oil as defined in section 2 (f) (1) of the Act. The jurisdictional question for determination was whether Sandal Wood Oil is forest produce within the meaning of section 2(f)(i) of Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'wood oil ' used in section2 (f)(1) must receive its colour from its context and connotation. When the legislature used the word 'that is to say 'the wood oil and other natural growth referred to in the definition it would only mean natural bye product directly drawn from the trees. [502C D] 2. The dictionary meaning of the word is "to be construed according to the intention expressed in the Acts themselves". It cannot be restricted in a narrow circumference as was done by the learned Single Judge so as to defeat the object and purpose of the . [503D E] 3. The expression 'wood Oil ' used therein includes the following: (i) the wood oil; (ii) other natural produce; (iii) the following when found in or brought from the forest as a raw material; (iv) the use of the timber charcoal, charcoal etc., being an essential oil would include wood oil. [506F G] 4. The restricted meaning canvassed by the counsel would defeat the purpose and purpose for which the oil is used. [500B C] 5. The definition of 'agricultural produce ' in section 3(f) of Kerala Forest (Vidarbha Vasava & Ors. vs State of Gujarat & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code but was acquitted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court set aside his conviction and acquitted him on the ground that there were no compelling reasons for reversing the judgment of acquittal. Held, that the High Court should not have interfered with the findings of the trial court because the conclusions on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused differ from those of the High court. The Supreme Court has held in the case that the evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could be drawn from it. The judgment of the Sessions judge was based on a misreading of the evidence and was not liable to be set aside. The evidence in this case was not of such a quality as would justify interference with the concurrent findings of fact. The conviction of the appellant under section 307 I.P.C. could not therefore be sustained. The mere circumstance that the deceased was to be produced as prosecution witness and because he was prevented from taking his turn of water, did not amount to compelling reasons. The statement of the deceased recorded by the doctor in the hospital was not admissible in evidence. The fact that the doctor was asked to mention it at the time of recording the dying declaration was also not relevant for sustaining a conviction under section 300 I. P. C. The medical evidence showed that there was no such compelling reasons as were put to the doctor and that he had been asked to give his opinion on the dying declarations. The doctor 's evidence was corroborated by the statement of one of the eye witnesses, who was in all probability not there.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar there were establishments in the State of Bihar and its workmen represented by their union called the Indoxco Labour Union. The dispute between the management of the appellant company and its employees employed in the factory at Jamshedpur was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal found that the constitution of the said Indox Co. was duly amended on January 6, 1963 and that as the workmen of the factory were represented by the Indian Oxygen Workers ' Union which represented also workmen employed in that factory, the reference extended to them also and the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the union 's constitution was duly altered on either January 6 or 21, 1963 or that therefore, it made no difference that the name of Indoxo Labour Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the agreement and the said statement and not that of the Indian oxygen Workers Union is erroneous. The appellant company appealed to this Court by special leave against the award of the Tribunal. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make its award operative not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at their other establishments and that in doing so it acted beyond jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal 's conclusion is not justified in obliging the appellant to grant special leave demanded by the union. [558C] (2) The award of Industrial Disputes (Bihar) Rules 1961 is operative in respect of the workmen in the appellant 's other establishments. The reference extended only to those workmen who were asked to work beyond 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours. Therefore, no reliance can be placed on the provisions of that Act for the company 's contention that it cannot be called upon to pay for overtime work anything more than its ordinary rate of wages if the workmen do work beyond 48 hours but exceed 48 hours work a week. [559D E] (3) The Industrial Disputes Act is a self contained code and does not require any elaborate procedure. It is only when there are more than one union in the company, the representatives of all such unions would be bound to give special leave with pay to the union concerned. Therefore the Tribunal 'may make an award in respect Of those workmen of a company ' 's factory at Ranchi and not the workmen thereof. [560F G] (4) The appellant Company could not be asked to pay more than their ordinary rate for overtime wages as provided by the Act which is applicable only to workmen of tho appellant company '.

The assessee was dissolved on March 31, 1939. In the assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm M/s Hakam Mal Tani Mal Toni Mal had been dissolved on April 1, 1939 before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force and the first succession to the business after April 1. 1939 was in March 1943. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to M/S HakamMal Tani was not a valid one and that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4). On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the appellant was carrying on business when Act 7 Of 1939 was brought into operation and was on that account entitled to the benefit. The High Court in reference held that it was not necessary for the Income Tax Officer to give to the asses see the benefit under section 5(3) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The assessee was constituted to carry on the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1 , 1939. The timber business was an old and running business and an intention to maintain continuity of the business and its transactions may reasonably be attributed to the assesses. It must therefore be held that in the absence of other evidence, it may be held, that the business of M/Tani Mal tani TaniMal Toni was not carried on at the commencement of the Income ' tax (Amend ment) Act, 7 of 1940. [646 B C] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the respondent commenced doing business immediately after the dissolution of the firm Messrs Hakam M/ Tani and R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala, Abdullapur from April I 1939.

The appellant was granted stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimogal. The Secretary to the Regional transport authority, Shmogal, also issued a permit on the same day. Against the order of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal, the appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the issue of the permit was made beyond the prescribed period of limitation under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules 1963 and that the grant of the permits was only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant Of the permit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appeals before the State Government and the further appeal to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal are not competent under section 64 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeals and interfere with the order passed by the State Road Transport Appellate Tribu nal. [189D] (1) Section 64(11)(a) of the does not confer any power on the State transport authority against the grant o. a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Trans port Authority granting the permit, but only requires that the Regional Authority has to give such person and the original authority has no jurisdiction. [190E] (2) The High Court was right in dismissing the writ petition of the appellant. [191F] (3) The order granting the permits is only a supervisory act necessarily followed the grant ing of the same.

The appellant was declared elected to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in 1967. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground of corrupt practice as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was guilty of corrupt practices as he had been denied the opportunity of meeting that case. HELD: (i) There is no violation of the provisions of section 100(2), Code of Civil Procedure, because, under sub sections 2(3A) and 3(4) a meeting was organised by the supporters of the Congress Party. Therefore, there was not an appeal to vote for a person on the grounds of religion nor was there any appeal to votes for a candidate on the basis of his religion. [897 G H] (ii) The evidence in the present case shows that the appellant had been shown to have participated in the meeting at Hapur on 7 February, 1967 and the voters were told by him that the meetings were held on 7 2 1967 and 9 3 1967. There was no complaint by the appellant to the Election Commission or to the Chief Minister or his election agent. The evidence of the appellant was that he had seen the party office in Hapur and the people from Ghaziabad would be insulted and they should remain there. [889 H; 897 A B] (iii) The High court rightly came to the conclusion that no notice was given to the respondent before the meeting. There is nothing on record to show as to what effect the election of the respondent had been held. The appellant failed to prove that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri committed any corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the candidate.

The appellant decree holder in execution of the final decree for mortgage himself purchased the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978 the judgment debtor filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions were filed by one Chiranji Lal and another by one M/s. Abhey Kanwar. The learned District Judge held that in view of Article 136 of the Constitution the application was not barred by limitation as contended on behalf of the judgment debtors. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order dated December 12, 1980 and remanded the matter to the District Judge for disposal afresh. The District Judge took a similar view and after considering the evidence led by both parties held that the application filed under Order 21 Rule 95 was not within time as prescribed by Article 134 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on his behalf that (i) in view Of Article 136, the application for setting the sale was maintainable and not barred under Article 134; (ii) in any event, the period of limitation under Article 135 would apply. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 134 will apply to an application filed within three years from the date on which sale became absolute as prescribed under Article 180 of that Act but under Article 136 it may be made within one year from the order passed by the executing court either allowing or dismissing the application will be final and effective subject to an appeal that may be preferred under the provisions of the code. [361C D] 2. Article 135 will apply only where there is a conflict between the two statutes. The words "any other law" in article 134 will not include an application for execution of a decree so as to apply 12 years ' period of Limitation as prescribed in Article 136. [362D E] 3. Article 137 will apply even if an application is made and disposed of, the sale will become absolute after the disposal of such application, even though the application is not one as contemplated by Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the Civil Procedure Code. [363E F] 4. The period of three years under Article 133 would be computed from the dates of dismissal of the second application for set aside on the ground of fraud and not from the first confirmation. [364F G] 5. Article 136 will apply in an appeal against a decree passed ex parte. But if an order is passed ex prece dure, it will be subject to appeal that might be made under the provi sions of the C.P.C. [365G H] 6. The suit terminated in a compromise decree on August 15, 1944 and the application under O. XXI Rule 90 was made by the decree holder on August 14, 1947, that is, within one month from July 21, 1979. It was subject to the disposal thereof, even if the application were not one. [366H; 367A] 7. Article 133 will apply where there are two different procedures and each procedure has to be followed separately. The periods of limitation prescribed by article 134 would apply to applications under O XXI Rule 92 of the CPC. [367C D]. 8. In the instant case, the order of the District judge confirming the sale on August 13, 1944 was binding not only on the judgmentdebtor but also on all other parties to the execution proceedings including the 4th judgment debtor.

The appellant was the candidate of the first respondent. The first respondent filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from the State Assembly on the ground that the appellant had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court recorded a finding that the said wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appel lant 's election agent. It further recorded a findings that the first Respondent had reasonably calculated that the voters or at any rate the voters in and about the locality where the theatre was being put up, had knowledge of the fact that it was being constructed by the respondent for an offence of harbouring the accused in that murder case. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was filed on the basis of a certificate granted by the High Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the first respond ent had not seen the wall poster together with exhibit P 1 being pasted near the wall posters. It is therefore difficult to understand as to how this witness could have seen the walls of the poster together. [732B] 1.2 The High court has recorded a concurrent finding that exhibit P1 was pasted at the behest and with consent of appellant ' s election agent and hence it attracts all the requirements of section 100(1) of Representation of People Act. [764C D] 1:3. In the present case, there is no reference to the election agent in this connection anywhere and the reference to him was not only all his witnesses had stated that he had seen the said act of pasting. It would thus be seen that in the petition it is the case of the second respondent himself that exhibit PW 1 was printed and pub lished only a day prior to the date of election. The evidence of this witness also shows that he has not seen any such act of previousing.

The respondent No. 5, a society registered under the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, was purchased by the appellant 's father in the year 1966 and after purchasing the land, the respondent No 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for construction of a five star hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal Council, however, rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the appellant filed an appeal before the Minister of State for Urban Development, who rejected the same on the ground that the whole of the said building should be kept reserved for a green belt or recreational ground in the interest of general public. The respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner and directed sanction of the scheme to the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order granting permission to the respondent to construct a hotel on the said plot. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that after the Municipal Commissioner had decided to revise the development scheme, no appeal would be competent to the State Government under section 47 of the Act. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the Municipal Commis sioner was entitled to take into consideration other relevant facts including the contemplated revision of plan and having regard to the position that in the sanctioned plan of 1966, the said plan was not inconsistent with the draft revised development plan. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The ground for rejection of permission is that the Bombay Municipal Corporation had decided the revision of 1966 plan in accordance with the direction of the respondent NO. 2. [924D] 1.1 The respondent no. 2 directed sanction for the development of plots as per plans submitted by appellants be granted by the M.C.B. and the permission for development of plot No. 2 be granted. The Municipal Commissioner was not justified in merely relying upon a proposal for the preparation of a draft revised plan. [936E] 1:2. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved is a fraud on the Urban Land Ceiling Act. It is, therefore, apparent that in granting permission, the Respondent No. 3 had violated the relevant guidelines and also the provision of section 20 of the Urban Ceiling Act.[924F] 1 :3. The contention of the appellants against the validity of the resolution is no longer tenable because it has been held by this Court in Life Insurance Corporation of India vs Municipal Corporation for Greater Bombay and Others, [1985] Supp. 2 SCR 927 that the ground for rejecting the plan submitted by the respondent no 5 has all been considered and taken into account by the High court. In view of the matter, there is no merit in the appeal challenging the legality or otherwise of the order giving exemption to the Respondent NO.

The appellant Union, a public utility service, was engaged in the manufacture of various kinds of steel ingots. The employers were guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out which under the law was illegal. The employer filed two complaints before the Industrial Court, Maharashtra, Bombay, alleging that the employers had imposed and continued a lockout and had thus committed unfair labour practice. The Labour Court framed an issue whether the employers have committed an unfair labour practices by imposing and continue a lock Out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Act. After hearing the parties, the Industrial court framed an issues whether the employer has committed an "unfair labour practice" within the meaning of section 2(L) of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act 1971 ( 'the Act ' for short). The appellant Union filed two special civil applications in Bombay High Court under article 226 of the Constitution questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Courts. Both the applications were dismissed in limine. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the employers that there was a closure of the industrial undertaking and it was not a case of lock out. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Industrial Court before which the action of the employer is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the time of closure decide and determine whether the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employee. [661C] 2. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the appellant employer at the date of closure but is not decisive of the matter. To accept the view taken by the Industrial Tribunal would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device Or pretence. Therefore the correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the employer had resorted to closing down of industrial activity, the industrial court before which action of tho employer is challenged must keep In view all these circumstances at its discretion and the true test is that when the industry is claimed to have resorted to close down, bonafide request to continue to employ workmen employed by him even though the business activity was not closed down. The essence of lockout is the refusal of the workman to continue in employment. There may be several reasons which may have necessitated closure. But the duration of closure may not necessarily be temporary or for a period. [678C D] 3.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which are set out in cl. III of the memorandum of association and other documents relating to the business of which the assessee company is a registered company, were set out therein. In 1930 the assessee made a claim every year being treated as a dealer in investments and properties but this claim was rejected by the Income Tax authorities on the ground that it was not a dealer 'in investments and property. The Appellate Tribunal held that in the case of the assessee the assessee could not be treated as an investor and therefore the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities and immovable properties were not liable to be taxed as business profits. On reference the High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant that (1) the assessee 's case could not have been treated as one of pure points of law; (2) the Tribunal had wrongly made a reference under section 66(1) of the Act to the High court and (3) since no question of law arose out of its order, it was open to the Appellate Tribunal to examine whether the Tribunal bad applied the relevant legal principles correctly or not in reaching its final conclusion; and (4) that the profits of shares securities and properties could be taxed only as business profit. HELD: The High Court must be directed to make a fresh statement of the case. [73 G] (1)(a) The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law, has to be decided on the basis of the facts found by the Tribunal. In dealing with findings on such questions of mixed law and fact the High Courts must not only be bound by the answers given at the last occasion but also by the considerations of the relevant circumstances in which the transactions both of purchase and sale had been brought about. [74 C D] (b) The proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and therefore, the claim of the assesee that the profit and losses arose from the sales of shares or securities and property could be assessed as business Profits.

The appellant was appointed as Subordinate Judge in 1935 and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate judge of Masulipatnam. On July 27, 1950 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge of Masilipatnam and on September 16, 1950. He was then transferred to the Subordinate Court of Amalapuram in East Godavari District. Thereafter he was transferred to Madras State. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the ground that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953, enquiry into the conduct of Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above could be held only by a Tribunal to which the Government might refer the same for enquiry. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that under r. 4 of the Madras Civil Services Rules, the Government had ceased to have jurisdiction over the Andhra State until July 1, 1954 when a separate High Court was established therefor. Held, that the order in question fell within the rule making power conferred by section 5(1)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Act, 1951 and was not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311 of the Constitu tion. The Government had no authority under the rules to suspend a judicial officer pending final orders of the Government. The order in the present case fell within r.4(1) (a) and was therefore valid.

The assessee, a registered holder of 2674 shares of the company, was assessed to income tax on the dividend received by it on August 14, 1946. The Income tax Officer included the dividends deemed to have been distributed and after processing the amount under section 18(5) included it in the total income of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment but the Tribunal held that the dividend was not distributed as the administrator had not been appointed by the company. In reference, the High Court held that since the shares were allotted to a shareholder on August 13, 1946, the dividend could be distributed only in accordance with section 18 (5) and not under section 24B of the Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal to this Court, HELD : The expression "shareholder" in section 2(2) of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953, means a person by whom income tax or any other sum of money has been paid or is payable and not a person on whose estate income is payable. By the incorporation of section 24 B the Legislature has extended the legal personality of a deceased person for the duration (1) [1960] 1 S.C.R. 312, followed. The expression 'assessee ' in section 12B means a shareholder registered in the books of the Company and such shareholder alone is liable to be taxed as his income in the hands of the legal representative of a person to whom the assets are transferred. The liability of the tax payer to pay tax on dividend so deemed to be distributed arises only when he has not died. [602 D E] Amarchand Shroff vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City I.L.R., , approved.

The appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. The said Instrument was signed by the Government of India and it was signed in token thereof. On December 15, 1947 he entered into an agreement with the Dominion Government whereby he agreed to pay a certain sum of money to the Government as compensation for the lands which were exempt from payment of rent or tax. The appellant contended that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler and that the said properties had been exempted from the payment of land revenue by the Dominion Legislature. The expression "maufidar" as defined in article 366(22) of the Indian Constitution means any person who for the time being is recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler. The word "maui" in section 2(j) of Act 1 of 1951, includes a person who was the holder of land which was exempted from payment Of rent or revenue. The definition of "proprietor" in article 3(1) of that Act includes an ex ruler and therefore, the appellant could not claim to be a Ruler for purposes outside the Constitution as he had no right to recover rent or Revenue from persons holding land in such villages. Held further, that under article 366 (22) the appellant certainly came within the expression "amaufidar ' and was within the class of persons who were by name specifically included in the definition of proprietor and therefore clearly within the scope of the Act.

The respondent, a Garden Curator in the office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong, was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, Office of the Director General, National Circle, Meghalaya. As many as 19 persons were transferred under the said order including the respondent. The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the order of transfer on the following grounds: (i) that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the central Government, that his children are studying there and also because his health had suffered a set back some time ago; (ii) that he should not be transferred because his wife was working at shillong, his children were studying there, and also that he has suffered back bone fracture injuries some time previously. He submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. The Tribunal dismissed the application holding that the transfer was ordered on administrative grounds and is unexceptionable. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines issued by the Government ofIndia O. M. dated March 3, 1986 do not confer upon the government employee a legally enforceable right. The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is akin to the jurisdiction of High Court under Article 226 of the constitution of India in service matters. This is evident from a persual of article 323 A of the Constitution. [431E F] 1.2 In the instant case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by transfer. [ 431F G] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; , referred to. 1.3 The guidelines require the two spouses to be posted at one pi" as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authori ties should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouse to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of Jawahar. The Trial Court convicted them under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34 I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Believing the prosecution evidence, the Sessions Judge convicted A4 under Section 498A I.p.c. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The High Court confirmed the acquittal of A2, A3 and A4. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of the deceased was beyond doubt. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The intention of the accused to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34 I P.P., and instead convict them under section 325, I P C. read with Sec tion 34, I PC. [11D] 1.2 A person is to cause death or injury to a person who has caused grievous hurt, if it causes such bodily injury as is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause the death, and that the offence should be committed by him by him, by himself, but not by his own individual, and he must have been aware of the fact that the act was done in the deceased. [12E F] 1:3 A person who is to give such a blow as would be sufficient in ordinary course would cause death, if no intention of his individual is shown, they would have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing simple and grievous injuries to him. [13F G] 2. The intention to cause hurt and also as such, the offence was committed by A1, A2 and A3 who were set them on Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The fact that A2 had a stab wound with aruval (bill hook) and A6 inflicted an injury on the deceased, be it he himself or his individual, was not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners for recovery of a sum of Rs.18,14,817/ being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs,3,00,000/ being in respect of certain transactions made in its favour to secure repayment of the aforesaid amount of loan. The respondents filed a written statement and contended that the appellant Bank was not formed in pursuance of any `special Indian law ', but by or under a `special ' law '. The appellant Bank also pleaded that the said partner, the respondent No. 1, had been declared an insolvent on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1951. The trial court decreed the suit holding that in addition to the hypothecation of the A and Schedule properties made in favour of the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively, the other partner, respondent No 1 had been created under the said Ordinance VIII of 1969 promulgated on July 19, 1969 and the present Banking Companies Act was a special law enacted by the Indian Parliament. The High Court held that the Bank was entitled to recover the entire amount without the same being scaled down as provided in section 13 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant bank that (i) the words `special I Indian Law ' are placed after the words 'an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom or any special Indian law or Royal Charter or Letters Patent, and (ii) the expression should be interpreted in the light of the setting up of the same in the words of the provision of section 4(e). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words `any special Indian Law" are placed before a special Indian legislature for the purpose of interpreting the provisions of the statute. [966D] 2.1 The intention of the Legislature is very clear in that the provision has been made by the Parliament to provide for a special I Indian law and the provision is applicable to the appellant, Bank. It is not a corporation within the meaning of section 2(e) of the . [967F G] Krishna Murthy 's case (supra), distinguished.

The appellants were dealers in sugar factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. The Central Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1950, fixing ex factory prices for sugar produced by them at a percentage of their production in the country. By section 3(1) of the Act the Central Government was given the power to fix the price of any essential commodity at which any essential commodities might be bought or sold. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it contravened article 19 (1)(g) of Constitution and was, therefore, bad as it violated articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31(2) and 31(3). Held, that the impugned notification was not invalid because it infringed articles 19(i)(g), 31 (ii) and (iii) of Part III of the Constitution. The object of the impugned Act is to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of general public, so that the price for the commodity may be fixed at a reasonable price. The preamble shows that it has been passed in the interest of the general public by providing for controlling prices of sugar in the larger interest of securing equitable distribution of the commodity. It is well known that there are three kinds of prices prevalent in the market for a commodity like sugar, namely, ex factory price, wholesale price and retail price. In the present case the appellants were not able to sell at any price; they had no other way of achieving it. The impugned notification did not contravene article 19(l)(f) of India as it was discriminatory because it fixes ex factory rates only for factories in which the factories were compelled to sell their products. The prices fixed by the impugned Notification could, therefore be said to have been proved to be below the cost of production.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 26, 1956, transferred the dispute from the file of the Second Industrial Tribunal to that of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. The Company challenged the award on the ground that it was not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the , and therefore the reference was bad in law. Held, that the order of transfer was invalid as it did not refer to the working class cost of living index in the year 1957. The Tribunal had rightly relied upon the evidence of the Company 's witness, who was examined after the Tribunal came to the conclusion that there was change of circumstances which entitled the employees to claim an increase in their dearness allowance. The finding given by the Tribunal was one on fact and it did riot call for interference with it in this appeal. The award of the Tribunal is a composite and fair reading of the provisions, it is clear that the Tribunal has taken into account all the relevant factors including the working classes cost of food and other amenities to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis of the rise in the cost of live index. The evidence given by State Government before the Tribunal shows that there were no surplusage in the living index for the year 1954 and 1957. It was not suggested that any such surplusage had been made out. The fact that the cost was taken as the basis, did not indicate so much increase as in the case of menial class. The workmen were entitled to claim enhanced dearness allowance only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which the workmen would have been otherwise entitled on that basis.

The appellant was the Mataduct of Sri Gavi Mutt, which is a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The principal question for determination in this appeal was whether the appellant 's property was the property of the Mathadhip of Sri Kari Mutt. Held, that the scheme framed under section 63 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, is valid and does not contravene article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The scheme has been framed in 1939 and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If it is found that any of the provisions of the said schemes are inconsistent with the relevant provisions of this latter Act, it has so provided. If the scheme is valid, then it is open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme on the ground that it contravenes article 19 (1) (f). The fact that the order was not implemented till 1952 could not be considered as a valid order under section 103(d) of Act XIX of 1951. The effect of this provision merely is to make the schemes in question operative as though they were framed under the provisions Of the latter Act; the intention was not to examine the said scheme once again by reference to the relevant sections of the latter enactment and re framing them so as to make them consistent with those provisions. Held further, that when the scheme was framed and a challenge made by the appellant in the High Court against its validity failed in courts of law, his property rights had been taken away.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. He was not paid the salary for the period of summer vacation during all these years. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to be regularised in terms of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. The State Government preferred a Letters Patent Appeal before the Division Bench which dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [995B] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, A.I.R. 1987 S.C. 478; Rattan Lal v State of Punjab, AJ.R., 1987 S C.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Vidhan Sabha from a constituency in the General Election of 1967. The respondent, who was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti, challenged the election on the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the various questions involved were of considerable importance and should be settled by a larger Bench; (ii) the Act did not convert the office of Chairman into an office or profit, and (iii) the appellant had failed to establish that he had incurred any pecuniary gain. HELD: The appeal must fail. (i)(a) The expression "office" in r. 3 means the office which is held by a member, Vice Chairman or Member of a District Parishad. The word "profit" connotes the idea of pecuniary gain and there is really a gain, its quantum or amount would not be material; but the amount of money receivable by a person in connection with the office he holds may be material in deciding whether the office really carries any profit. [427 B C] (b) The Act does not convert an office into an Office under the Government. It is only when the journey is performed for attending meetings held within a radius of five miles from his place of residence or he performed the journey in a transport provided at the expense of the District Magistrate/Panchayat Samiris or any other local authority or Government. [426 B C, D] (c) The appellant had not established that he incurred any expenditure on travelling allowance or daily allowance. He was therefore entitled to claim the allowances for expenses incurred by him in connection therewith.
