The appellant was the tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in the erstwhile State of Meerut, a year later, on a rent of Rs 93 per mensem. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963, a month later, they filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on a number of grounds including the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without the consent of the landlord. The trial court decreed the suit and dismissed the respondents ' suit on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under section 13(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction Act, 1947. On appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the trial court 's order and dismissed respondents ' appeal on the finding that no suit shall be instituted for eviction of a tenant without obtaining permission of the District Magistrate but if the tenant, without the landlords permission made or permitted to make construction which in the opinion of the Court has materially altered the accommodation, or is likely substantially to diminish its value, substantial ly, substantial 'l y the landlord was free to file suit for tenant 's ejectment without obtaining the permission of tho District Magistrate. The Additional Civil judge held that the tin shed shown by letters CDCDH on the Eastern side of the tin sheds did not constitute material alteration and that the respondents were in fact resting on the pucca wall of the premises, and on that findings the trial Court decreed the eviction suit. On second appeal, a Single Judge of the High Court set aside both the judgments of the courts below and dismissed their appeals. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A permanent construction tends to make changes in the accommodation on a permanent basis while a temporary construction is on temporary basis which does not ordinarily affect the form or structure of the building, as it can easily be removed without causing any damage to the building. The nature of the constructions whether they are permanent or temporary, is a relevant consideration in determining the question of 'material alteration '. [975B C] 1.2 In deciding this question the Court must address itself to the nature, character and character of the construction and the extent to which they make changes. It has to be seen whether the constructions have been made with the consent or not. The question whether disputed constructions constitute material alterations is a mixed question of fact and law. [981C D] 1:3 A permanent constructions tends to making changes in accommodation on the a permanent footing while a permanent construction is an opening or closing a verandah by temporary structure or replacing of a damaged roof which may be leaking or placing partition in a room or making similar minor alterations for the convenient use of the accommoda tion do not materially alter the building as in spite of such constructions, the front and structure of tho accommodation. [980D E] 1 :4 A permanent construc tion tends to makes changes in it on a temporary basis while the temporary construction does not affect the question as to whether the construction materially alteres is as to what the constructions are permanent and important. The material alterations contemplated by the two clauses show that the landlord has made substantial alterations in the form, front and structures of the tenanted shop. [978E F] 2:1. In deciding the question whether a disputed construction constitutes material alteration, the Court should not interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the High court. The High Court committed error in interfering with the finding of fact. [979F G] 2.2. The contention that the nature of construction whether permanent or tempo rary is not relevant for determining the 'material alterations ' made by a tenant, cannot be accepted. The facts of this case show that there was no material alteration in the building and the portion shown by letter ABGH had been constructed by the appellant after obtaining permission from the Cantonment Board and the erstwhile landlord.

The appellant company had filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain goods. The respondent filed a civil suit against it claiming damages to the tune of Rs. 26,000/ on account of alleged non delivery of certain documents. Summons in the suit was sent to the registered office of the company in Calcutta and was said to have been served on one Shri Navlakha on 17 3 1975 asking the company to appear at Indore on 25 3 1975 for settlement of issues. Since the company did not appear in Court, the ex parte decree was passed on 22 4 1975. The appellant filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aside the ex motion order and for setting it aside. The trial court held that summons in the plaint was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975 only when its constituted attorney Shri Mukhiram was examined as a witness on behalf of the respondent. The Trial Court also held that since the company had no knowledge of the ex earlier decree, the application filed by the appellant under Order IX Rule 13 was not maintainable. The High Court in revision set aside the judgment of the trial court and upheld the order of the Trial Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellant that the respondent had not applied his mind to the provision of law contained in clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 9 of C. P.C., and that the application made by the company under Order9 Rule 13 of the Code was about a week 's time thereafter, was held to be within time. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment by the Trial court setting aside ex parte decrees is correct. [1031D] 2.1 The High Courts were wrong in upsetting the judgments of the courts below. There was no error of jurisdiction committed by it. The order of this Court setting aside a decree was correct. In any event no error or error of law was committed by the High Court. [ 1032F G] 2:2 No error of Jurisdiction was committed in the instant case. The appeal is allowed and the judgment passed by the trial Court set aside. [1103G] 3.1 There was a clear violation of clause (a) of rule 2 of order 9, Rule 13, C.p.C.; and hence the application for setting the ex decree was not barred by limitation. [1132H; 1033A] 3:2 The High court went wrong in interfering with it.

The Magistrate, after passing a preliminary order on 29th July, 1976, recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of the peace existed. The Magistrate passed an order under section 145(5) Cr. P.C., declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the said order on the ground that the final order was vitiated in absence of a finding by the Magistrate in the final report that there was an apprehension of breach of peace. The High Court held that as there was no clear finding by him in the preliminary order that there existed an apprehension, the final orders were bad and the High court accordingly set aside the order of the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts erred in holding that the preliminary orders were vitiated in the absence of any finding that breach of a peace existed at the time when the order was passed, nor was such a case set up by any party before the Magistrate or before the High Curt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the High COurt is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [94C] 2. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach or an error of procedure. Once he records his satisfaction in the judicial order, he has to direct the parties concerned in such dispute to attend his court in person or by pleader and put in written statements of their respective claims as regards the fact of actual possession of subject of dispute. The enquiry under section145 is limited to the question to who was in actual possession on the date of preliminary order irrespective of the rights of the parties. [95F G] 3. In a proceeding under section 144, it is not for the magistrate to be satis fied regarding the nature of a dispute likely to cause a breach Of peace. It is for him to be satisfy about the existence or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the magistrate is based. [96G] 4. The contradictory stands taken by the parties clearly show that there were no question of the dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under sub section (5) of section 145 nor was it such a plea set up in the written statement could be allowed. [97A B] 5. If the Magistrate had given a finding on this aspect of the matter also but in the circumstances, it can be safely presumed that apprehension of the breach of law was not necessary at the stage when a final order is passed nor is there any provision in the Code requiring such a finding in the order. Once a preliminary Order drawn up by the magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a dispute has been raised, it cannot be said that no dispute existed as contemplated under section 146(5). [97B C] 6. The objection to the maintainability of the complaint on a purely technical ground when the aggrieved party had a clear remedy in the civil court. For these reasons therefore, the order passed is legally unsustainable and cannot stand. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The appellant, a public limited company, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer under section 66(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant contended that the transactions in favour of the intermediaries were genuine and that the sales in favour Of the intermediaries constituted genuine and so the question whether the intermediaries had been benami or not must be decided on the facts of each case. Held, that the finding of the Tribunal was correct and must be upheld. The decision of the High Court was based on a misapprehension of the law as to the legal effect of those findings. It is well settled that in cases where there are two inferences from one of fact, one which is not supported by evidence or perverse, one pointing towards the other, the finding is liable to be set aside on the ground that there was no evidence to support it or that on the evidence it was perverse. The question whether a transaction is genuine or not depends upon the facts found and circumstances of each particular case. In the present case the Tribunal had held that the intermediaries, firms and companies were benamidars for the appellant and that they paid the price therefor to the appellant. The finding of fact based on such findings was binding on the High Courts under section 11(1). Commissioner of Income tax vs B. N. Sen, (1955) 1 S.C.R. 869, referred to. Commissioner of Incometax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., , distinguished. Commissioner Of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmed Bhai Umarbhai & Co., ; , explained.

The appellant, a manufacturer of blankets and other woollen cloth, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49. The assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 75465 as commission paid to him by the General Manager, who had been allowed a sum of Rs 4,063 as commission. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to the General manager who was given the charge of the conduct of business after his death. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that Rs. 5,000 were not sufficient and it was reasonable to allow the payment of commission at the rate of 121/2% on the profits. The Tribunal also rejected the contention of the assessee that the entire amount of Rs 75465 paid to Shri J.P. Vaish was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of business of the appellant and was wrongly disallowed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. On reference, the High Court held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was giving the charge on the profit. The High Court also held that in applying the test of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out for the purposes of business, reasonableness of the expenditure had to be adjudged from the point of view of the businessman and not (1) of the Income tax Department. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out Or expended wholly and solely for the purpo se of business profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(Xv) of Income Tax Act has to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each particular case. But as observed by this Court in Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; , the final conclusion on the admissibility of an allowance is one of law. In the present case, both the Appellate Tribunal and the High Courts have applied the proper legal test in this case. [529 G H] Swadesha Cotton Mills Company Ltd. V. C. I.T. Bombay, ; , followed.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of which he was a member. On January 13, 1954, the management of the company served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the Company. The appellant submitted his written statement denying the charge and asking for an opportunity to be heard. The Tribunal held that the appellant could not be allowed to represent his case before the Tribunal instead of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union and thereafter in making an award on the basis of the reference. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the dispute between the employer and a workman cannot be an industrial dispute as defined in section 2(k) of Industrial Disputes Act unless it is taken up by a Union of workmen or by a considerable number of workmen. The question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken upto the Tribunal under the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, he is a party to the industrial dispute is not a matter which cannot be allowed at this stage. The ordinary rule should in our opinion be that such representation by an officer of the trade union should continue throughout the proceedings in the absence of excep tional circumstances which may justify the Tribunal to permit other representation of the workman concerned. In the present case, there were no such exceptional circumstances. It has been suggested that the Union 's Secretary was not taken up his cause and that the compromise was collusive and mala fide.

The appellants were the tenants of a portion of a house in which they had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2. The suit for ejectment was decreed against both the defendants and their original plaintiffs. On appeal by defendant No, 2 the District judge set aside the decree holding that the entire appeal had abated. The High Court on appeal held that the appellants were competent to continue the appeal even after the death of defendant No 2 as no application for bringing his legal representatives on record was made within the prescribed time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the deceased appellant and the surviving appellants constituted a joint Hindu family and other members of the family were already on the record and that the suit had abated so far as he was concerned, that the death in question had not been proved by any evidence and that there was no evidence to show that the family was separate. HELD: (i) The appeal by defendants No. 1 and 2 was incompetent. The abatement of an appeal means not only that the decree between the appellant and defendant No2 had become final but also as a necessary corollary that the appellate court cannot in any way modify that decree directly or indirectly. It is immaterial whether the modification which the Court will do is one to which exception can or cannot be taken. [554 B C] (ii) The High Courts have taken the correct view of the matter viz., that the Appellate Court has no power to proceed with the appeal and to reverse and vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants under O. XLI, r. 4 when the decree proceeds on a ground common to all the appellants or defendants, if all the plaintiff or the defendants appeal from the decree and any of them dies and the appeal abates so faras he is concerned under O, XLI, rr. 33 and 34. [555 E F] (iii) The appellate court has no powers to proceed in the appeal against the entire decree in certain circumstances. When the legal representatives of the deceased appellants and the respondents were negligent in not taking steps for substitution, the Court is not to exercise its discretion in favour or to reverse or vary the decrees in favour. [556 G H] (iv) The discretion conferred on the appellate Court by section 5 of the Limitation Act is not a judicial power but a discretionary power which cannot be exercised to nullify the effect of the abatement of the appeal so far it affects the rights of the appellant. When an appeal has been filed against all the defendants, the provisions of 0. XLI of r. 3 of O. XXII and those of r, 4 of 0 XLI have become final. [557 B C; 556 A] (v) The order of the appellate authority is not only to exercise his discretion in the matter of abatement but also to the Court below. It does not give any indication as to how the appellate courts exercised their discretion in disposing of the appeals so far, as it affects them. [558 E F].

The appellant tenant fell back on certain defences raised by the respondent landlord in the eviction petition filed under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The Rent Controller found that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 108 was needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g). The Rent Control Tribunal held that the lessee had expired without any notice as required by section 106. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the decision of the Rent Controller and restored the order of eviction passed against the appellant. In this appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant tenant that the respondent 's lease had lapsed by efflux Of time limited by efflux and therefore section 111 could not apply to the tenancy in question and, therefore, a forfeiture giving rise to a determination of the lease under section III(g), because, the respondent had failed to comply with the requirements of section 106, and that the principles of justice, equity and good conscience were not violated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Act which are but a statutory recognition of the rules of justice equity and bad faith do not require any further notice to determine, is a well settled principle of law that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111 of the act does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture. [917C D] 2. The principles of equity and natural good will apply to notions of good conscience in India notwithstanding, there is no absolute rule that a tenant has reasonable notice of termination even though it does not expire with the end of the month of tenancy. It is also not disputed that in the present case no notice whatever was sent to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the ground that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux or by efflux. [951D E] 3. The requirement of law which are, but a statute, is not based on any well established principles of Equity and good faith, must be construed in the light of the rule laid down in section III (g) as it stands. If, therefore. the appellant 's case was that the document did not contain a notice of terminating the lease, there being no such requirement, the lease would have to be decided in accordance with the rule which, though in express terms, has not been made applicable to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force. [952D E; 918A] 4. The question whether a particular provision introduced in sub section (g), of section 111, is but a Statutory recognition of a principle of justice and good consciousness, or whether it is merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and is not founded on any principle of equity or good conscience, must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [948C D; 919A] 5. The requirements of law as laid down by this Court in section 11(g)(1) of the POCA are that notice should be given in writing to the lessee of an intention to determine the lease. Once it is assumed that the intention is to terminate the tenancy, it must be presumed that the lessor has knowledge of the fact that the formality is merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of equity. [947E F] 6. The appellant ' s case was not one of mere technical pleas but one of a legal plea based on no evidence. It was not a case of statutory tenancy as it had been contended before this Court that the renewal of the license could not be claimed by the lessor.

The Governor of Assam, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, framed a rule called the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission Rules, 1936. Rule 3 of the said rules provided that the Governor shall not dismiss or remove from service any person who was dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge; and under sub clause (c) of this rule the Governor is empowered to dismiss or reduce him in rank. The appellant, a Superintendent, was dismissed from service with effect from June 30, 1965. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the order was passed in violation of article 311(2) of Constitution and quashed it as having been passed in contravention of article 31(2). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Governor 's satisfaction under sub cl. (c), of the proviso to clause (2) Of Article 311, is recorded in the language in which the provision in article 311 has been made. It is not mandatory and that it should be held that he must have used these words in the sense in which they were used in the Constitution prior to its amendment. [488 B C] (ii) The expression "it is not expedient to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him" in article 31 (2). What was required to be done was that a reasonable opportunity of show cause should be given to the government servant concerned, and under the proviso, the Governor ' s satisfaction required was that in the interest of security of the State it was not expedient. [490 C D] (iii) The word "shall" used in cl. 2(c) must mean "may" or "shall". If a person is dismissed or reduced to a lower grade on the grounds of conduct, which has lead to his guilt on a charge of misconduct, he may be given a reasonable opportu nity of showing sufficient cause for doing so and that opportunity should not be given in a case where the order proposed to have been passed is that it was "not reasonably practicable to give him such an opportunity". [490 E F] (iv) The words "it shall not apply" in cl.(c) are wide enough to include all cases which may lead to disciplinary action. The word 'shall ' has been used in a wider sense than the word 'may ' and it is not necessary that the word should be construed as 'shall be '. [491 G H] (v) The order of the Governor did not satisfy the requirements of cl. 3(c). The expression 'it shall be expedient to do so ' in cl, 2(e) must be interpreted in a broad and general sense. It was not mandatory that it must be complied with before an order is passed by the Governor. [489 G H; 490 A] (vi) The satisfaction under cl. 4 of the Uttar pradesh Public Service (Conduct) Rules, 1955, that the appellant had been dismissed or remove ed from service on a charges of misconduct was not justified. The order was therefore invalid. [486 B C].

The petitioners and the Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi are alleging that the respondents 5 and 6 as representing the Sunni Community of Mohalla Dohipura were basing their customary rights to perform their religious ceremonies and functions on the said nine plots and structures thereon. The petitioners and their Shia Community of the Mohalla Dorshipura filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act, and the Rules framed thereunder, and also the notification dated 15th January 1954 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to challenge the impugned order passed by the City Magistrate, Varanasi on 24th November, 1979 prohibiting both the respondents and the members of the Shias community from holding their Majlises and imposing other restrictions on the occasion of celebration of the said religious ceremonies. The State Government preferred an appeal against the judgment of the High court which was dismissed in limine. Hence this petition under article 32 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners have also claimed that the aforesaid plots and structure thereon had been registered as Shia Wakfs for purposes of performing their religious rites and functions under section 38 of the U.P. Sunni Muslim Waqfs Act 1936. [1110G] 1.2 The petitioners are not entitled, on the basis of the judgment in Civil Appeal No. 961 of 1976, to challenge that order passed in the appeal by the State Government on 24.11.1979. [1106B C] 2.1 It is only in an extremely extraordinary situation when other measures are bound to fail, that a total prohibition or suspension of their rights may be resorted to as a last measure. [111D E] 2:2 The notification dated 26th February 1944 issued under Section 5( 1) of 1936 Act was issued by the Shian Sabha on 23rd January 1954 and published in Official Gazette on 23nd January 1954, and it is now common ground that the mosque on Plot No. 1 is a Sikh minority which is desirous of freely practising their religious faith and perform their rites, practices, observances, ceremonies and function without let or hindrance by members belonging to the majority sect of the community namely Sunni Muslims, and as such a positive approach is called for on the part of the local authorities, and every time instead of exercising the power in aid of their right it is being exercised in suppressing their rights under the pretext of imminent danger to peace and tranquility of the locality. [112F G] 2 :3 The petitioners ' case that plots and buildings thereon had become a religious minority and performing their rites and duties on the property in question and structures on those plots and constructions thereon, which had been admitted by them in the writ petitions, is one where the entitlement of the Sunni community to perform its religious ceremonies, practices and observances has been established and is the subject matter of a judicial pronouncement and decree of Civil Court of competent jurisdiction as also by reason of these properties having been registered under the 1960 Act. [114A B] 2 .4 The petitioners who have filed their respective affidavits in the matter and have been heard through respective counsel, have not challenged the rights of the parties on merits but the Court took the view that the parties should be relegated to a civil suit on the assumption that the petitions were maintainable under Article 32.

The assessee, a limited company, was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling shares. The assessee, in its return for the assessment year 1957 58, claimed set off of capital loss of Rs.3,10,200 but claimed setoff of capital losses of Rs 3,17,500 sustained by it during the assessment years 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. It was maintained by the Income Tax Officer that the loss was a capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no justification to hold that the claim was not genuine. The Tribunal held that there was no genuine loss and set off could not be allowed. In reference, the High Court held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of set off under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the provisions in Section 24 (3) regarding intimation of losses as notional when he really meant that it was an estimate. It agreed with the conclusion of the Tribunal and found against the Revenue. [1165D] 1.2 In the instant case, the assessee had made the claim and he took note of it. his failure to comply strictly with the requirement of sub section (3), should not be permitted to be taken advantage of by the Revenue nor should it be used to the prejudice of the assessee. Since set off has been claimed in the assessment Year 1965 66 to which the Act of 1961 applied, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. [1106F G] 1:3 The High court was right that the benefit conferred under Section 7 of 1961 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the same portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following assessment year and so on. [111A] 1 :4 The benefit conferred by Section 24 of 1922 Act continued in force even after the assessee 's claim and took note thereof. The failure to do so would not make any difference. [112B] 2.1 In the present case, there was a loss of profit or gains which had taken place which he was entitled under the 1922 act and notwithstanding that his failure had resulted in the loss, failure to carry forward the loss for the year 1957 could be said to have been determined for the purpose of assessment year 1966 66. [113C] 2:2 The benefit granted under Section 4 of 1922 act continued to remain given effect from the 1st day of April 1961 and notwithstanding its wordings. there was nothing more, this is not a case where the assessee has made the claims and took notes note of the same.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), which post he held earlier. The Department of Defence Research & Development by an Office Memorandum dated 24.12.85 decided that Scientific and technical personnel (GD) were entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 60 years and those in the lower grade for which flexible complementing scheme was applicable would also retire at the age of 58 years provided they had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age Of 58 years within the preced ing five years. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, claiming that he was entitled to be retired at the said age of sixty years and was not liable to be superannuated at the alleged superannuation age. The Tribunal held that the re spondent was not entitled to any amount so paid to him as he had been appointed in the post of Deputy Chief Scientific Officer. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question involved in the present case is not whether the Government had such power. The question is whether the respondent was also entitled to the benefit of the power so exercised in the facts and circumstances of the case. [22E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had been recruited initially to the Defence science Service and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of service in any of the said three units. The service conditions of the employees belonging to the different units were the same and their services were inter changeable between the three units, and the service conditions were inter changed. However, at that time admittedly no option was given to the employees working in the different unit to opt for one or the other of the units. It appears that those who were already working in either of the three unit were deemed to belong to the respective newly constituted service. This being so, their service conditions will have to run parallel and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to us by the respondent appearing for the appellants. [23F G] 1:3. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid. There is no substance in the appeal. The order of the Central Administrative Tribunal is, both proper as well as valid, and there is no merit in the Appeal. [24G H; 25A] 2.1 In the circumstances, the denial of the benefit to the members of one 24 unit while the same is granted to the member of the other unit amounts to discrimination violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [25B] 2:2 The decision in the instant appeal is both valid and valid, but there is not a dispute that the Government has power to vary the service condition of the members. The classification made between them further has no rational basis and no relationship of such classifications to the objects sought to he achieved has also no rational justification.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant before the High Court on several grounds, including that he had been guilty of publication of two pamphlets and distributed them amongst the voters in a newspaper which cast serious aspersions on his character and conduct and prejudiced him materially in the eyes of the voters as a result whereof he lost the election. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the trial Judge was right in allowing them to be called as court witness. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant would have had a real cause for grievance if he had asked for an opportunity to rebut the evidence of these two witnesses and had been denied the same but this has nowhere been alleged. On the evidence no exception can be taken to the course adopted by the Judge in deciding the issue against the appellant on the facts and circumstances of this case. But it cannot be said that there was no evidence on which the Judge could have come to the conclusion he did, The first point therefore fails. [968 C D] (ii) The High court was right when it held that the three election petitions were not maintainable. The appellant had been found guilty of publishing two pamphlets and distributed the same amongst the electors and the petitioner had come across the first pamphlet during the process of distribution. The evidence adduced by the appellant was that he was guilty of the publication of the pamphlet only. The trial Judge, therefore, framed the issues in a manner which leaves much to be desired. Evidence was adduced about the publication and distribution of the pamphlets by the petitioner and contradicted by the respondent. [948 E F] (iii) The allegations of corrupt practice were of a serious nature and if the appellant had asked the election judge to do so on the 21st August, 1968 he would certainly have gone into the matter and found out why there were two Gazette Publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period of limitation prescribed by section 21(1) of the Act. There was no error apparent on the face of the record before the trial judge in deciding issue against him on the evidence.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State Government imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged the validity of this notification by a petition under article 32 of the Constitution. It was contended that (i) the Validation Act was ultra vires as it had not been validated and because the Act itself was ultra rites, (ii) the levy was illegal as it imposed a duty on the purchaser to pay sales tax at the rate of one annas per rupee on sale proceeds; (iii) the validation Act was not ultra vires the State Legislature under Entry 54, List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and (iv) the impugned notification was invalid because it was issued before section 3 A was in operation. Held, that the Validation act was not a law which sought to tax it, treating it as a sale, but was an essential characteristic of a sales tax that the seller must have the right to pass it on to the consumer, and that the validation was not in any way inconsistent with the true character of the tax which, by the express provisions of the law, is cast upon the seller. The State Legislature derives its authority from section 3A and the impugned Act is not ultra rites. Firm Bangali Mal vs Sales Tax Officer, (1959) Supp. 1 S.C.R. 489, referred to. Held further, that a sales Tax was leviable on the supply of materials in a contract for the construction of works simpliciter on the footing of a sale was held to be outside the entry and the tax could not be imposed with retrospective operation. Firm Bangalore Mal vs The State of Mysore, ; , followed.

The appellant, a young man of 22 years, overpowered by sex stress under thezoological 's prescription under the Act and was sentenced to imprisonment for 4 years R.I. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. In prison treatment must be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation, apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. [591B] Sunil Batra 's case and later on that decision, rendered by this Court in Sunil Batra vs State of Delhi, ; , referred to. 1.2. The current efforts of Governments, Central and State, to reform jail regimen, are not bound to follow the correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [592C D] Sunil, Batra ' s case and another decision rendered by the High Court, rendered in Sunil, though deplore the sex violence is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and sexually victimised. [593D E] Sunil was a young girl of 22 year old age for rape and her parents have forgiven the criminal. The extreme penalty of death must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart, from training and rehabilitation to devalue their credibility. [594F G] Sunil has a good felonious antecedents except this fugitive punishment is bad sufficient in a Society where women were often socially advanced. [595G H] Sunil had a young wife and a farm to look after. The victim and her family have forgened, and mating by unwed students, sex explosion in celluloid and book stalls and corrupt morals reaching a new 'high ' in high places. The circumstances of the case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. [596H; 593A] Sunil. Batra 'Silva, wife of the appellant has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a balanced person, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or of reformatory self expression. In this background, it is not safe to substitute our criminal justice by stamping out voluptuous meat markets by merciless criminal action.

The respondent assessee, a limited company dealing in land, was requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal under section 5 of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the said Defence of Pakistan Act, 1939. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded compensation at Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the assessee. The assessee deposited the amount in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956, the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum of Rs.7,24,914 which was assessed by him as compensation under section 6 of the Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951. The respondent assessee deposited Rs. 7,36,691 in the suspense Account on April 25, 1956 without furnishing security bond for refunding the amount. The Income Tax officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesee on the date of the award. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In second appeal by the assessee before the IncomeTax Appellate Tribunal, two contentions were raised by it: (1) that the amount of compensation received by the respondent was not a receipt of a revenue nature; and (2) that in any event the amount did not accrue to the respondent as its income during the relevant previous year ended 31st March 1956. The High Court answered both the questions in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sum of compensation which was received by it related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the respondent, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assesses, and therefore a receipt under section 4(1)(b)(i) of the Act could not be said to have accrued to it as income during that previous year. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The payment made by the Land Acquisition officer, by his award, if not accepted by a claimant would not result automatically in a liability to pay additional compensation as claimed by the owner of the land. [395C] 2. The very foundation of the claim made by assessee was in serious jeopardy and nothing would be due if the appeal was decided against him. [397F] 3.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the respondent on the ground that they had been in occupation of the shop for non residential purposes. The appellants contended that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. The High Court allowed the appeal of the respondents and set aside the order of the executing court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that (i) in spite of the fact that there was no express provision in the Bombay Rent Act prohibiting contracting out, such a prohibition would have to be read by implication consistently with the public policy underlying this welfare measure; and (ii) the provisions in the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language of section 12(1)(f) of the Act is somewhat different from many similar State Statutes. Section 12(2) says that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no suit shall be filed in any civil court against a tenant for his eviction from any accommodation except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in section 12 (1). A Bench of the High Court in Smt. Chandan Bai vs Surja Ram, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 872, held that the provisions Of section 12 of the Code were not applicable to eviction proceedings governed by that provision of the Rent Restriction Act and that the protection of the tenant was inherent in the language of the said provision. [882 D E; 883 A B] 2. The expression "in any suit" occurring in section12(1) (f) means a proceeding in which the Court is empowered to grant relief under any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act. The protection of tenant is inherent in tho language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". If however, parties choose to enter into a compromise due to any reason such as to avoid the risk of protracted litigation, it is open to them to do so. The Court can pass a decree on the basis of the compromise. [888 D E] 3. In the instant case, the appellant 's necessity was pleaded both in the positive and negative aspects of clause (f). Both were denied in paragraph 3 of the written statement of the appellants. Paragraph 1 of the plaint is clear and definite especially in the background of the pleadings of the parties and in our opinion it squarely makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of section12 (1)(f)of the Act on admission of the appellant.

The assessee company was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs, 91,116/ . The Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs,. 11,88,COO/ as a loss in the value of the shares held by the company in its investment account. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal it was contended that the assessee had not declared any dividend because of the loss referred to earlier. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The assessee had suffered a capital loss of Rs 12,00,000/ and this was due to the loss of the value at the time of declaration of dividends. [8 4 C] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. , applied. (ii) The loss in question was not a capital one. In view of the fact that the Directors were naturally more interested in the stability of their concern rather than in increasing the tax payable to the Government, the provisions must be worked not from the standpoint of the tax collector but from that of a businessman. [884 D] Commissioner Of Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., , referred to. (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the loss incurred being a capital expenditure the same cannot be taken into consideration in the application of section 23A(1). This very contention was examined and rejected by the Judicial Committee in Commissioner of Incometax, WestBengal vs Gangadharar Banners Ltd., ; , referred.

The appellant filed objections to the award of the Civil Judge, Aligarh. The Civil Judge overruled the objection and set aside the order modifying the award. The High Court in appeal held that an appeal lay under section 39 of the , which was pending before the District judge, Aligarh, and therefore, the provisions of section 15 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, were not applicable to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 37 of the Act applied only to arbitrations referred to in section 37 and not to arbitrations as provided by section 15. HELD : (i) Section 12(6) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of holdings Act, 1954, provides for a statutory arbitration and section 37 is not applicable because the appellants had apparently applied under section 15 Of the U P. Consolidation Of Holdings Act. [37 C] (ii) The effect of section 46 and section 47 of the is that all the provisions Of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations. Section 37 of Act does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15, of the . [37 D] Attar Singh vs The State of U. P., ; , followed. (iii) Section 37 is applicable only to awards under the consolidation of Holdings. It is not necessary to rely on section 12(1) for construing section 37.

The petitioner, diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation, was promoted as Superintending Engineer on 31st October 1990. The promotion was challenged by him by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post, as they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proposition that in the absence of rules or regulations the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution the petitioner who was senior to respondent No. 2 would have been promoted to the said post on 31 st October 1990, cannot be accepted. [711C D] 2.1 The High Courts of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , referred to. In State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao, ; , a Constitution Bench of this Court has clearly held that such a classification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [372F G] 2:2 The contention that if at all such a discrimination was permissible, it could be done only by carving out two classes in the same category of junior Engineers, cannot also be accepted since the impugned Resolution dated 31st Octo ber, 1990 is not a law or regulation framed under Section 64 of the said Act. [373F G; 374A] State of Haryana & Ors. vs Dr. (Mrs.) S.B.

The petitioners in the two writ petitions were appointed as Judges of the Supreme Court by an order dated 15th September, 1987. The appointment was made on the basis of a petition filed by the Advocate General of the State for filling up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme court and the several High Courts of the country. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said order before the Supreme Bench which dismissed their writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court it was contended that the appointment of a person as a Judge had nothing personal either to the Chief Justice or the Chief Minister of the States concerned, and that the Division Bench of the High Court had no jurisdiction to reopen the matter merely because there has been a change in the personnel of the Chief justice or the State concerned. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Chief Justice of India, the Chief Justices of the various High Courts and the Supreme Courts as the Central Government may deem it neces sary to consult, are merely constitutional functionaries having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Govern ment. [445C] 2.1 The primacy of the position of the institution of the chief Justice of the India is not justiciable should be re considered by a larger bench. It will be difficult for an appropri ate selection to be made. [441E] 2:2. The primacy has to be given due weight, the Central and State Governments have been given finality in regard to the appointment. [442G] 2 :3. The responsibility of the administration of the judiciary is that of the executive. It is not necessary for the Court to examine the views of the majority, but it will be open to an appropriato ry body to make a proper assessment of the opinion of the Judges. [443A B] 2 .4. The importance of the primacy of a Chief Justice in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered by any larger bench.[444C D] 2 5.1 It is clear on a plain reading of Article 124(1) that the Chief Judge of the Union or the Governor of the state who consulted in the matter also came to be known as the head of the office of the President of India. [444D E] 2 2.2 The primacy and responsibility of administration of justice are not, however, entitled to primacy but after considering the opinion expressed by each of the constitutional functionaries and giving it due weight and the Central government is entitled to come to its own decision as to which opinion it should accept in deciding whether or not to appoint the particular person as Chief Justice. [44H; 45A B C] 2 3.3 The primacy, of the situation of the institutional functioning of the judicial system in the country require consideration and there is an element of immediacy in the matters. It would be difficult to hold that the final say is the exclusive proroguous of the Executive Government. There are preponderant and com pliance on the constitutional obligation for the executive to adopt and apply the standard.

The respondent was serving as a Reve nue Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the appellant Bank, availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting a bill for Rs.2,800 on May 5, 1978. He submitted a bill on May 6, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/s. Shri Manju Travels of Bangalore and claimed reimbursement of the amount paid. The respondent did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Shri U.B. Menon. The appellant Bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the order of discharge passed on January 14, 1980. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal preferred by the appellant bank. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of punishment has to be quashed not because the merits of the case so demand but because the technical plea of incompetence is not cure the defect as to his compensa tion. [201B] 1.2 In the facts and circumstances of this case, the course suggested by Shri Shetye can be usefully adopted. The High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of removal from service on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the High court for the first time and, therefore, the High COurt ought not have ordered payment of all consequential reliefs flowing from the declaration that the impugned orders were bad in law. [202C D] 1:3 The respondent was then served with a second show cause notice on the question of punishment and thereafter the impugned orde r has been passed on a merely technicality. An officer who was due to retire within a few days only was chosen to act as an Enquiry Officer and Disciplinary Authority by the order dated January 9, 1979. [203E] 1 :4 The respondent succeeded in getting the order quashed on a purely technicality, and that is why too on his part could not be prejudiced on account of the said Enquiry Officer conducting him domestic enquiry but he was still in the superannuation age. [204F] Pulin 's case, followed.

The respondents were owners of a building in the main Chawri Bazar, Delhi. As the building was an old construction and required urgent repairs, they submitted to the appellant plans for sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions and alterations to the said building. The plan was prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Development Act 1957 and it was approved by the Government. The appellant 's application for approval was rejected on the grounds that the proposal was under acquisition and also that the plan submitted by them did not conform to bye laws and contravened section 336(2) (a). The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the rejection of their application. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had failed to establish that the proposed building or the use of the site for the building, by the respondents, would contravene the provisions of section 336 (2)(a), and that the grounds on which the sanction of a build ing authority was refused were not germane to the Master Plan. The appeal to this Court was filed with certificate granted by the High court. HELD: (i) The appellant had to establish, as it seeks to, that the building or work or use of any site in that zone has been dealt with in a particular manner by the Master plan and that it is proposed to be used in a different manner. If a Zonal Development Plan is prepared for the area, before it comes into operation in the Zone, the procedure indicated in section 10 will have to be followed and parties will have a right of placing any objections or making representations or offering any suggestions. So far as the appellant can question the rejection by the Commissioner under section 33(2), he has to establish as it sought to be justified under this provision. [171 E F] (ii) The High court was in error in holding that there would be no violation of section 14 of the Development Act if the respondents were permitted to use the land, as asked for by them. [172 G H] (iii) The object of the development Act is to freeze new buildings which will be inconsistent with the Master plans and also to provide for the better management of such buildings in a proper manner. It is not possible to accept the contention that there will be any violation of the provisions contained in section 14 if the respondent is permitted to do so. [173 G H; 173 A] (iv) The respondents ' lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of the proposed road, mentioned in the Master Plans and, if that is so, there is no violation or infringement of section 15(2)(b).

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the Chief Industries Officer of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No, 2 was the Secretary to the Government of India in charge of the Department of the Government. On the day of the occurrence the appellant No 1 was found in possession of certain Government currency notes which were recovered from his house. The trial court acquitted both the appellants but convicted them under section 120 B I.P.C. and sentenced them to various terms of imprisonment. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentences passed on the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1) the evidence as to the recovery of the currency notes from the top drawer of the dressing table in the bedroom of the appellant no. 1 could not be accepted as true; (2) the statement made by the appellant to the police authorities that he had brought these moneys from his home were inadmissible in evidence and could not, therefore, bring the guilt home to the appellant; (3) the statements made by him to the two officers were inadmissible under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or because they were made by a Police Officer who was not competent to make such statements; and (4) the conviction of the appellants No. 2 and 3 under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code was illegal. HELD : (i) The evidence as regards the recovery from the appellant 's house was worthy of credit and could be brought home to them. [253 B] (ii) The statement made to the Police authorities by the two accused persons that they had brought those moneys from their home were admissible in evidence under section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The statements made to them being admissible in proof of the fact that they were not his and he would have been able to bring the whole Affair to its culmination, were admissible under section 165 of the Evidence Act. [252 C] (iii) The statements were inadmissible as they did not relate to the commission of any offence by the appellants nor did they amount to any abetment in respect of that offence. The evidence was therefore inadmissible and could have been brought home only to the accused persons.

The respondent plaintiff was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the appellant along with the Head Constable, who was also a constable. The charge made against him was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the order of dismissal was void on the ground of arbitrariness and, there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. On appeal by the respondent plaintiff, the High Court held that the impugned order of dis missal was void as it was passed without giving any reasons for invoking the doctrine of laches. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question involved in the suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High court in limine. It is clear from the record that only two questions were pressed by the parties, namely, whether the suit was barred by limitation and whether the order was illegal on the grounds that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned orde r was passed. [825D E] 2. The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [826E F] 3. In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the question involved is a different. The possibility that "the other police officials convicted with him" (that is, the plaintiff might have been later punished), is recognised. It has been further urged on behalf of the appellants that the finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation was applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The respondent entered into certain transactions of sale of tea gardens and broth sacks with two parties M/s. Raghunath Prasad Poddar & Co., for the purchase of gunny bags from various parties after paying full price of the goods covered by the delivery orders and transferred those P.D.Os. to buyers after receiving the price fixed for the goods. The appellant paid the price realised on sale to M/S. 98,534/ to the respondent and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax officer held that the transactions involving mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the good were of a speculative character as contemplated by Explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Act, and that the transaction was not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that this case came within the scope of section 24 (1) and set aside the order of the Income tax Officer. The Tribunal however allowed the appeal holding that the sales in question were speculative transactions within the meaning of Explanation 2, to section 4(1). In the reference following its earlier decisions, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The Explanation to section 25 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, provides that where an assessee sustains a loss under any of these heads in any year, he shall be entitled to have the loss set off against his income, profits or gains under any other head in that year. This general provision is qualified by the first proviso which permits the set off of a loss in speculative business against the assessee 's profits and gains, i any, in a similar business only. Explanation 1 says that where the speculative transactions are of such a nature as to constitute a business, the business shall be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. [183B C] (b) The explanation does not invalidate speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery or the commodity or the scrips have taken place; on the other hand, a transaction which is not otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative according as there is an actual delivery and the stock of goods are so as to put them in a special category for income tax purposes. This rule is qualified under the first Proviso which permits a set off only where the transactions are not completed by actual delivery but only laid down that if there was no actual or physical delivery, the loss, if any would be a loss. [184D E] (c) The question whether on the facts of the case there were two separate transactions of sales so that tax was payable at both the points under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, and the High Courts answered it in favour. [185E F] Raghunath Prasad Agarwal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; , followed. (d) The law on the point was correctly stated in D. M.

The first respondent was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination paper was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage. The appellant filed an election petition challenging the rejection of the second respondent 's nomination papers on the ground that the Returning officer had wrongly rejected the nomination papers. The Election Tribunal decided in favour of the appellant and declared the whole election void. On appeal, the High Court held that the first respondent had not been validly nominated but that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice under section 33(1) (b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the first appellant that : (i) the Returning Officers were wrong in rejecting the nomination paper and (ii) the rejection was improper because the nomination had been improperly rejected. HELD: The Returning Officer rightly rejected the second Respondent 's election. [486 B] (1) The word "subscribe" is not defined but it is used in various senses to indicate different modes of signing and that it includes the placing of a mark. The words "sign" and "subscribes", are used interchangeably with the word "sign". The General Clauses Act also says that "signs" means "to sign". The word 'subscribe ' is not used in several senses to convey an intention, but it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by the Rules. [488 B C] (2) The words 'sign ' and 'subscribe ' are of a substantial character. They are intended to indicate the different modes by which the signature may be read as 'to give assent to or to attest ' or 'written upon '. The word is not restricted to writing but it should be used in both senses, namely, that it must mean signing, so called, and the word can be used only in the sense of making a signature and not to "sign", in the ordinary way. [487 C D] (3) The Returning officer has not been able to reject any nomination paper on the grounds of any technical defect which is not of substantial character but he cannot remedy the defect. He must leave it as it is. If he does so, he can be set right.

The appellants were employees of the respondent company. During the pendency of the reference, the respondent workmen raised a dispute before the Labour Court under section 33(A) of the , claiming wages for the period during which they had abandoned their service and also claimed that they should be reinstated in service with full back wages. The appellants contended that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary, that the appellants had not abandoned the company 's service, that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the company "s standing orders" and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service, they were liable to disciplinary action. The Industrial Tribunal held that the respondent 's action was manifestly illegal and invalid and dismissed the appeal. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision of the Labour Appellate Court in dismissing the appeal against the order removing the name of the appel lants from its roll was manifestly wrong, that there was nothing in the surrounding circumstances or the conduct of the parties indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case could be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undo or untie the binding knot or link which holds one to the office and the obligations and privileges that go with it. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there had been no abandonment of service on the part of the respondents. [616G] 2.1 The failure to perform the duties pertaining to the officer must be with actual or imputed intention, on the contrary, on his part, and is a question of fact which has to be determined in the light of the surrounding circumstance of each case. [625H; 618A B] 2:2. The failure of the workmen to return to work by a notified date clearly implied abandonment of their employment. It was not necessary for them to have abandoned the service, and the respondents were entitled to relief. [613B C] 3.1 There was nothing on record to indicate that the company could terminate the services of the employees on the ground of abandonment of the service because of their going on strike in enforcement of their demands.

The appellant mortgaged a house belonging to the trust. The trustees of the trust executed a mortgage deed in favour of the appellant. The appellant did not pay the instalments due under the mortgage and the entire amount remaining unpaid was paid by him. The respondents filed an application for execution of the decree which was dismissed by the District Court. The High Court held that the sale of the mortgaged property which belonged to a public trust without the sanction of the Charity Commissioner being prohibited by section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, was invalid and on that view remanded the case to the District Judge for decision on all the points correctly arising out of the matter. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the provisions of 0. 21 r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure were not complied with and the Subordinate Judge had no power to set aside the sale held in execution of a decree; (ii) that section 56B of the Act which provides that "in any suit or legal proceedings in which it appears to the Court that any question affecting a public religious or charitable purpose is involved, the Court shall not proceed to determine such question until after notice has been given to the Charity Commis sioner and that if that officer desires to be joined as a party, he may be joined by him as a defendant to the suit; (iii) that in the present case the claim of the mortgagee was not satisfied by that deposit. HELD: (i ) The High Courts have no power under 0.21 r.89 of the Civil Procedure Code to set down any time for payment of the amount for which the property is sold, and on such a view it would be impossible to hold that a judgment delivered by a Full Bench of a High Court after due consideration of the points before it is liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the Full Bench. [459 E] (ii). The power of the Supreme Court under 0, 21 r 89 of Civil procedure Code to interfere with an order passed by a subordinate court or of the Charter of the High Court is not excluded by the Judges ' jurisdiction of the Letters Patent. [460 G] (iii). The judgment of the Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court was binding upon the appellant and the District judge. [461 C] (iv) The decision of the Allahabad High Court will be regarded a relevant paper before the Chief Justice of the City Civil Court, who will act according to law.

The appellant joined the Post and Telegraph Department as clerk on June 4, 1935. He was compulsorily retired from service under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of retirement by way of a writ in the nature of mandamus. The learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) and that it was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. On appeal, the Division Bench held that Rule 2 of the Pension Rules was ultra rites Articles 14 & 16 of Constitution of India. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of Rule 2 is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 2 has been interpreted in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) of Indian Railway Establishment Code, which is identical to Fundamental Rule 56(j). Para 620 of the Manual being executive instructions issued in the names of President and General Administration, it is not capable of being used arbi trarily and with an un even hand. [801C D] 2. The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitu tion of India and as such cannot be statutory. The Memorandum is in the form of executive instructions. [800D] 3. Rule 2046 is a statutory rule and is identical with Fundamental Rule, 56(1). Para 619 is in nature of executive instruction but is similarly worded as Rule 2. A Division Bench of the Madras High Court came to the conclusion that Rule 20 46 having been framed under Article 311 of the Consti tution and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover ned by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative. This Court while setting aside the judgment of the High court held as under: (1) The memorandum dated November 30, 1962 is in substance executive instructions and has no parity with Rule 2.(2)of Pension Rules which is a stat ute. [701D] (2)(a) Para 620 is in tact as per Rule 2 and para 621 was void. [ 800F] (b) The words "weed out unsuit able employees" can only be read qua the power to retire under para 6 and not under Rule 1 of Pension Rules.

The assessee firm carried on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1944. During the assessment year 1949 41, the sales of katsechu were effected by M/s Biharilal Balkishan at their shops in Kanpur. The sales of Katechu made by M /s Bihari Lal Balkrit at their shop in Kanpur were effected on 26th July, 1943 and 29th September, 1941 respectively. The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/S Biharilal. The Sales Tax Officer did not set off the deficiency of profits that accrued in respect of the period 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st December, 1941 to 31th March, 1946. The claim of the assessee was rejected by the Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal held that no profits accrued unless sale was effected and therefore there could be no deficiency of profit during the chargeable assessment period ending 31 st March, 1942 and as such there could not be any deficiency of the profit during those periods. In reference the High Court held that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable account periods ending 30th May, 1941 and 31st October, 1942 would have to be set off when computing the excess profits for that year under consideration. The High Court also held that there was no profit attributable to the said chargeable accounting years and therefore the assessee could not claim a set off of the deficiency. In appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that as provided in the Act, the provisions of the Act would apply to every business of which any part of profits was made during the relevant assessment year, is chargeable to income tax. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The assessee was carrying on the same business from 28th October, 1941 onwards and there were no sales effected thereafter. It could not therefore be said that there had been any deficiency in the profits during those years. [608 D] (2) The High Courts were right in holding that the loss suffered by the assessee is a business to which the Act applied when the profits of a business charge able with excess profits tax was made, but a necessary pre condition was that profit must be made in the accounting period to which it relates. [613 E F] (3) The method of computation under section 7 of the Income Tax Acts must be on the basis of 'accounting period ' and after that the balance sheet and the deficiency are only of loss or expense entered into the year to which enquiry refers; and in like manner, only those elements of loss of profit or gain, and those only enter into the computation which are earned or ascertained in the year, to which an assessment relates. The method is the true excess profits, if any, as contemplated by the Act be deter mined. [508 G] (4) The accounting period is the twelve months proceeding just on the assumption that there is no deficiency in during those three periods but where the profits arose during the account ing period and as a result of the computation of the income for the relevant chargeable accounting year ending 31th, March,1944, it must be held that it was not necessary to redetermine what part of the loss from the business carried on in 1940 41 to which that enquiry refers. [625 G] Haji Rahmat Ullah & Co. vs Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., ; , referred to. (5) The question whether the activity which the assessee carried on at Raichur was part of their business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5 of the Indian Act, that the profits in respect thereof were added to the amount of the standard profits, did not arise for consideration.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the State Government (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Civil engineering and in Category II, questions relating to Civil Engineering and in category III, questions of seniority. In the case of any category for which the number of options is more than the appointment by transfer aud the junior persons will be admitted to the services as and when vacancies arise. The Kerala Public Services Commission, however, did not finally publish the rank list. On receipt of information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service Commis sioner issued a notification inviting applications for the post of Junior Engineer in the Kerala Engineering Service (Mechanical Branch) as per the notification published in the Gazette dated 16 5 1978. In response to the said notification, the Kerala Government and the K PSC published two lists one for the Civil Judge and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted.
