The respondents who had qualified in Civil Engineers in Civil Engi neers ' category filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the above mentioned two lists. The learned Single Judge allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare two separate rank lists one after another for the civil judge and the Mechanical branch on the strength of examination earlier conducted. He also held that some of the aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petition filed appeals before the Division Bench. The Division Bench dismissed all the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Kerala Government or the K.PSC was not directed to prepare a common list. Common list was referred to in the earlier orders in this Court through certain misapprehensions. The KP SC was not asked to prepare separate lists for Civil Engineering selected by transfer to the respective service. [747C] 1.2 In view of the difficulties faced by the Kerala Public Sector Undertakings and the Government of Kerala it is necessary to clarify the position and give necessary directions. Clause 4 gave unconditional options to those in the KpSC who had submitted unconditional option and who possess the required qualifications prescribed in the rules will be appointed by transfer. [750D] 1:3 The K P Service Commission, constituted the Kerala Engineers (Mechanical) Branch, with posts prescribed therein. It is open to him to choose which wing, Civil or Mechanical, suits him most. In that view, the Division Benches of the High Courts were right in dismissing the writ appeals. But in view of difficulties faced in giving effect to the directions given by the High court, the State of Kerala filed a petition before this Court for clarification and directions. [751E] 1 :4 The K. P. Public Service Commissioner was not directing prepare a Common list. common list was refer ed to in that order in the later orders in the present cases. The judgment of the Single Judge and Division Bench is set aside and the special leave petitions are dismissed.

The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts. The appellant defendant No. 1, the respondent No. 2, and the other defendants Nos. 1 and 2, contended that they were partners in the firm. The trial court passed an order on 26th December 1981 holding that the plaintiff was entitled to a larger share in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch, solely and absolutely '. The defendant No 2 filed an appeal against the order of the trial court which was dis missed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff respondent No 2 has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under estimates the relief the court is entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation given by the plaintiff and to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. [512C D] 1.2 The High Court while repelling the argument that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the appellant in the suit, has not taken into consideration the statement in the plaint that the court was powerless to challenge the valuation put by the defendant on the relief claimed in the Suit. It is true that in a suit of accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. The plaintiff is, therefore, allowed to give his own tentative valuation. Ordinarily the Court shall not examine the correct valuation of a valuation chosen, but the plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. [511D E] 1:3 The High Courts while replying to the argument of the defendant No 1 that relief could be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only, have not taken any decision to the contrary. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, AIR 1932 Madras 626, the plaintiff non applicant before the High court filed a Suit for dissolution and accounts valuing at Rs 150 as has been done in the case before this Court. The High court while reputing the argument on behalf of the plaintiff that relief cannot be tentative or arbitrary, has held that when the valuation placed by the defendants is arbitrary and unreasonable the court may reject it and leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. [ 512E G] 2.1 In a suit under Article for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore. put a tentative valuation upon the suit but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At the same time it is also not uniform.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of manu facture and manufac turing industrial units, filed two writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of sales tax on its products. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the exemption sought for was originally granted but subsequently revoked by the State Government. However, the High court held that the respondent assessee could not be allowed to avail of the concession under paragraph 20 of the Notification dated 23.10.1981. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the exemption was initially granted but later revoked, the view taken by the Division Bench in the case of G.S. Dhall & Sons and others vs State of Orissa, ; that the earlier scheme and the exemption now proposed are total ly different in their object and scope and that while the former scheme was intended as an incentive to any one who set up a new industry in the State so that "traditional" industries did not get any benefit, the notification dated 23 10 1981 had no application. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that since it was not the intention or effect of the notification, it could not have been given retrospective operation. Allowing the appeals and setting aside the judgment of the High Courts, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Government has not intended to give the exemption of deferment of payment of tax on the date of the tax can be deferred. It is not necessary for the rules of deferring the exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect of the industries mentioned by it. [609C D] 1.2 In view of this interpretation, the 1987 amendment has the effect of rescinding the exemption conferred by the 1982 notifica tion.

The Delhi Higher Judicial Service was constituted in the year 1965. The Rules were amended by the Delhi High Court (Amendment) Act, 1976 with retrospective effect from 1st April, 1977. Rule 5(2), which is in the nature of a non obstante provision provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the rules, the Administrator may, in consultation with the High Court, fill substantive vacancies in the Service by making temporary appointments thereto from amongst the members of the Delhi Judicial Service. The proviso to rule 7(b) states that no person shall be appointed to the service unless he is appointed in a substantive capacity to a post in the service. Rule 17 provides for appointment of promotees to the Service on probation, while Rule 17 prescribes for appointment by promotion to the Indian Administrative Service. Rule 18 provides for the appointment of direct recruits to the Services and, under sub rule (2), such appointments are to be made by the Administrator on the recommendation of the High court. The petitioners who were members of Delhi Judicial service in the Delhi Higher judicial Service filed a writ petition before the High Courts challenging the validity of the seniority list prepared by the High Commission. The High Court dismissed their petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the inter se seniority between promotees and direct recruits is governed by Rule 7(a), (ii) the seniority of direct recruit vis a vis promotees shall be determined in the order of rotation of vacancies between the direct recruits and promotees based on the quota of vacancies reserved for both categories by Rule 8(1); (iii) the principle of "quota and rota" ceases to apply when appointments are made under Rules 16 and 17; (iv) the ratio of 1:3 between promotees, and direct recruit is that while direct recruits are appointed to temporary posts in the Services, the promotees are appointed on a regular basis to posts in a permanent capacity to be created by a temporary appointment; (v) Rule 17 which provides for recruitment to temporary post in case there were recruitment from Bar as well as by promotion, is not in the context of inter se merit between promotees who are appointed in substantive capacity and those appointed to posts on a temporary basis; (vi) Rule 18 which prescribes a quota of one third for direct recruits, does not prescribe a quota for direct recruit; it only enables the appointment to substantive vacancies so that they shall not hold more than 1/3rd of the total number of substantive posts in service; and (vii) Rule 16(1) which empowers the Administrator to create temporary posts is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The seniority of promotees vis avis promotees is governed not by Rule 17 but by Rule 18 of the Rules. [395F] 2. The inter se Seniority of members of Parliament and State Legislatures is governed in accordance with Rule 7 of the Central Civil Service (Cadre) Rules, 1966. Rule 16 provides for appointments to temporary vacancies in service on a permanent basis. Rule 8 prescribes that seniority of the members appointed to permanent posts shall be the same as in the Central Government Service. Sub rule (1) of Rule 8 stipulates that inter se between promotees appointed to substantive posts and by promotion in such a case, the seniority is to be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the State Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in regular vacancies to be filled in a temporary capacity. The combined effect of the proviso to Rule 7 is that seniority shall be fixed in accordance, with the dates of direct recruitment. [396H 396A] 3. The principle of 'quota ' has been laid down by this Court in the case of Shri C.D. Sharma vs Union of India and Ors., ; , and Shri C D. Sharma & Anr.

The appellant was a partner in a trading venture conducted by the respondent. The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51, and the Income tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of assessment. In appeals by the Commissioner of Income tax, the High Court held that the income belonged to a stranger in respect of the income tax proceedings against the Ambala Cloth Mills. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The expression 'any person ' in section 34(3) proviso 2 at p. 346 means a person intimately connected with the assessment of the year under appeal. The words 'any other than an order of assess under section 23 to which clause (c) of sub section (1) of section 28 applies or an order or assessment or reassessment in cases falling within cl.(a) of subsection (1), or sub section(IA) of this section, are not confined to a person intimationately connected in the aforesaid sense with the assessments of the years under appeal.[392 H] Commissioner of income tax U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndicate and others, ; , followed. (ii) The words "any person" in the setting in which it appears must be confined to the person intimally connected in such sense with his assessment of income. ' In making a direction against Debi Parshad the Tribunal did not exercise its powers qua a stranger to the assessment proceeding. [392 B C] Commissioner off Income tax U P vs Kanpur Sugar Syndicate and Others, , followed, (iii) The word "any" in section 31(3), proviso 2, at p., 346, referred to an assessment made against the assessee or any person in consequence of or to give effect to any finding or direction contained in an order under section 31.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by him. The respondent, who was the son of the appellant, filed a memorandum of appeal under section 7(iv)(b) of the Madras High Court (Four Judges ' Bench), Act, 1953, against the order passed by the learned single judge on the merits of the case. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal holding that section 7 (iv)(a) was not applicable to the appellant 's claim for partition as he had valued his relief in the suit for purposes of court fees under section 8(v)(b). On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The question about the levy of court fee on a memorandum filed on the Original Side of the High Court and also on the memorandum of appeals was not raised before the Division Bench. The decision of the Division bench in Krishnaswamy Naidu J. vs C. P. Sarathy, , distinguished. (ii)The question about valuation for purposes Of jurisdiction under section 10(iv) (b) is governed by section 3 of the Act and it cannot be reopened at this stage. In the present case the memorandum was filed on behalf of the respondent who had valued the relief sought for in the plaint. The court fees paid on the plaint were not only on the memo of appeal but also on his memorandum of Appeal. The question regarding the levy or determination of court Fees under section 6(iv), (b), (c) and (d) of Act, is governed not by article 17 B of Schedule II to the Act but by article 18 B of Sch. II of the Indian Limitation Act.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee sought special sanction of the building plans submitted by the respondent No. 1 and 2 for construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road, New Delhi, of which the first respondent is the lessee. The appellant, a lessee, filed an application in the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the sanction of its plan for construction. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of building plans on or before 5th May, 1989. The NDMC challenged the decision of the High court by way of a Writ Petition in this Court. The respondent No 1 and the 2nd respondent contended that the proposed build ing did not have any right to occupy the plot of land as it was leased out to them for construction purposes; that the permission from the Chief Fire Officer, Delhi Fire Service envisaged in Bye law 16.4.8.1, though so defined in bye law 16(2), was in addition to the requirements of bye laws 16.

The joint family carried on business of grocery shop, liquor shops and a ration shop. The family consisted of two brothers and the plaintiff respondent. The suit was decreed for partition against the appellant defendant. On appeal the High Court held that the decree was not barred by res judicata or by Order II, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the cause of action in the two suits was different from the cause in the first suit and the suit was therefore barred under 0. II, r. 2(1) of C.P.C.; (ii) the suit in the previous suit was not one for partition but only a mere declaration of title to the property; (iii) the claim was barred by limitation as it was not based on any mistake or misunderstanding and that the parties had agreed to confine the taking of all accounts upto March 31, 1946. HELD : The cause of actions in the subsequent suit was different than the cause for action in both the suits being the same. The cause Of action in a subsequent suit is the desire of the plaintiff to separate from his brothers and to divide the joint family property. That suit embraced the entire property without any reservation and was compromised, the plaintiff having abandoned his claim to account in respect of the motor business subsequent to March 31 1946. His subsequent suit to enforce a part of the claim is founded on the same cause of Action which he deliberately relinquished. [103 D E] The cause for the action in two suits being one the desire to separate the joint Hindu family property after the first of April, 1946, and the second by the plaintiff 's father, the latter having abandoned the claim to accounts in respect thereof, the subsequent suits to enforce the part of his claim are barred under Order II rule 2 (3) Of the Code.

The appellant was engaged in the manufacture of sea water. The salt works were being carried on in the open air and not in building, but in buildings, which were let out to the appellant for residence. The appellant was prosecuted under section 92 of the , for his working the salt works. The defence of the appellant was that the salt work was carried on by the salt Works in the area where the salt water was being carried for the purpose of working a factory and therefore it was not a factory within the meaning of the Act. The trial court held that the application of the provisions of the Indian Factories Act, 1948, to the Salt Works was maintainable. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one under section 2 of the . In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the expression " premises" in the definition of the word " factory" in el. (k) of section 2 Of the Act must be restricted to buildings and that the words " premises " occurring in cl. (m) of s 2 of that Act should be confined to buildings alone. Held, that the word 'factory ' is not restricted in scope to buildings only but also includes buildings which are used for building purposes. The expression "premises" in cl.(k) must be read as including buildings and it means any premises used for working or were working on any day of the preceding twelve months. The definition of " factory " in el., (k), of section2 Of the , is not confined to factories only but includes factories engaged in such a process as would bring them within the definition. The word " premises ' in cl, (k ) of section 1 of the Bombay Act means buildings and does not include buildings which do not come within the purview of the expression. The words "premises " occurring at the time of the commencement of the present case, are used to indicate that the building must be a factory as defined by the respective Factory Acts and that it is only those buildings which can be said to have been manufactured from the sea water that would fall within the term " premises ". The expression 'factory" in cls. (p) and (q) of cl. 2 of section I of the Factories Act means any building or part thereof which is used for the work of a manufacturing process. The process carried out in the Salt works, and described as "fire water" is not an activity of manufacture within the scope of the definition and therefore the expression ' premises ' must be confined only to buildings which were used for carrying on the manufacturing process and not for sale.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, three occupational Institutes (Polytechnics) at Hassan were started in the State. The respondent continued to make representations to the Government for his absorption in the department of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949. On May 17, 1965, the State Government issued orders reverting him to his parent department. He was absorbed in that Department on November 28. The appellant filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of reversion and also the consequential reliefs. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent had been invidiously discriminated against in the matter of absorption and appointment while his junior K. Narayanaswamy Chetty was similarly situated, and that he could not be discriminated against and treated differently from K. N. Chetty who was junior to him in the parent Department and came on deputation to the Polytechnics establishment subsequently. The State Government appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) In the matter relating to absorption of a person initially brought on deputation from another department and he stayed on that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption was not justified. [260B] (2) It is well settled that in the case of an employee who was admittedly junior to the respondent, and was identically situated, the Government had acted arbitrarily and in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [261C D] (3) In view of the fact that K.N. Chetty was junior, he could be absorbed as Tailoring Instructor from the dates on which he initially joined duty after deputation to a Polytechnic Department and he continued on deputation till the date on which his counterparts were promoted to that post. [262D] (4) The High court was right in holding that his "impermissible reversion" for a short while in 1955 to the parent department was no ground to hold that he was not similarly situated as K.V. Chetty.

The petitioner, a foreign parent, filed an application under section 9 of the , praying for appointment of his guardian as guardian of the child. The Court held that the petitioner was not entitled to be appointed guardian of her child and directed the petitioner to file a child in adoption. The petitioner challenged this order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the Court had no jurisdiction to appoint the petitioner as guardian. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Court has no power to appoint a foreigner as guardian unless it is satisfied that the application of the foreigner for taking a child is sponsored by such social or child welfare agency recognised or licensed under the Government of India Act, 1935; and (ii) the court has in most cases where an application for taking the child in adopt is made directly without the intervention of a social or a child welfare Agency recognised or approved by the government of the country in which the foreigner resides and the application is accompanied by a home study report prepared by such Social or child Welfare agency. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The court has, in most instances, where an adoption proposal from a foreign parents is sponsored, by a social Or child welfare agencies recognised or recognised by the Government, processing the application for guardianship is processed and that one copy can be filed in court and the other can remain with the social or the child welfare authority in India. [842C D] 2. The Indian Council of Social Welfare has in many cases where the application made by a foreign father for taking his child in Adoption is made, directly without intervention of the social agency agencies, there would be no authority or agency in the country of the foreigners who could be made responsible for supervising the progress of the case and ensuring that the child is adopted at the earliest in accordance with law and grows up in an atmosphere of warmth and affection with moral and material security assured to it. [852E F] 3. The recognised social or children welfare agency through which an application of a foreigner for take a child, is routed must, before offering a child to be taken in adoption, make sure that the juvenile or child would be adopted at a later stage of making an atmosphere in an environment of wormth and understand the child, if he decides to adopt it as also to assist the court in coming to a decision whether it will be for the welfare of the children to be given in adoption to the foreigner desiring to adopt. [850E G] 4. The recognition of the foreign parents who have taken a child under the guise of maintenance charges and medical expenses or otherwise, would be almost eliminated. It is also necessary to point out that the recognised social/ child welfare organisation through which the foreign parent has taken a son in adoption must, therefore, undertake while forwarding the application to the social/child welfare agency in India, that it will ensure adoption of the juvenile by the foreigner according to the law of his country within a period not exceeding two years and as soon as the adoption is effected, it will send two certified copies of the adoption order to the Social or Child Welfare Agency in India through which such child is proposed to be made available in inter country adoption. [851G H; 843A] 5. The recognized social or/ child Welfare Agency through which a foreigner has taken an Indian child in adopted, may make sure, that the children are free to be adopted. Since an application by a foreigner who has taken the child into adoption is required to be routed through a recognised social Or Child welfare agency, the possibility of any so called social or labour welfare agency being recognised by it cannot be ruled out. [853B] 6. The Government of West Bengal should make sure the child being free to he adopted. [ 844C] 7.

The appellant company was a very prominent position in the Cable Industry of India having its Head Office at Calcutta and its factory at Jamshedpur. It had branches in Bombay, Madras, Bangalore, Bangalore and Bangalore. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year were Rs. 23,68,706. The Company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employes in accordance with the provisions of the . The Central Government by an order dated June 23, 1967 referred the claim for additional bonus for adjudication to a Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the claim was not admissible as it had been made out of the gross profits for the accounting year 1965 66 and allowed the claim of Rs. 24,61,176. The appellant company filed an appeal before the High Court against the award of the Tribunal. It contended that the computation of allocable surplus by the Company has not been properly made in accordance to the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure have to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits. The High Court rejected this contention. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that under the Re tirement Gratuity Scheme which is in force, a workman retires at the age of 60 and normally during the year 1965 67, the payment of gratuity to persons so retired would have come to Rs. 1,46,252. The claim for deduction of certain items from gross profits was rejected by the Tribunal on the ground that the amount of Rs, 21,06,576 being bonus due to him under the Act for the year 1964 65 on the basis that his salary is only Rs. 3,715 and not Rs. 20,000, it should have been added back as allocable.

The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954. In 1969 he was promoted as an assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954 and later as a Joint Commercial Tax officers in 1957. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member, Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. He was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) on September 28, 1975. His service book showed that he had an excellent record of service. The appellant 's service book shows that he has an excellant record of services. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him during the period from May to September, under the rule which enables the Government to retire a Government servant in the public interest after he has attained the age of SO years or after he had completed 25 years of qualifying service. One such adverse entry was knocked out by the order dated November 29, 1974 of the A Government and the effect of the entry was blotted out by promotion of the appellant as Deputy Commissioned Commercial Tax Officers in 1954, next as a Deputy Commissioner. The Government accepted the report of the Full Board and dropped the charges making the following order on 29 11 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against the appellant. The Enquiry Officer considered all the charges framed against him in respect of allegations substantiated, obtained his explanation and sent its report thereon. The Full Board considered that all the charge framed against the Appellant were dropped. " The appellant challenged the validity of the order of November 29 1974 before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appel lant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 which was not considered by the Promotion Committee and with nothing of the sort, it was impossible to sustain the order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Government retiring the appellant from service is bound to perplex any right thinking man and make him wonder whether the right hand knows what the left hand has done. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion but before his promotion one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But with nothing more suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter it is impossible to uphold the order passed by the Government compulsorily retiring the appell lant from service. [771G H] 2. The High Court was right in dismissing the petition on the ground that the appellant had not been able to prove his innocence beyond a few months, and that with nothing whatsoever that he could have disappeared from his utility as a Govt. servant. If the appeal is allowed, it would be impossible to maintain the order for the Govern ment retiring the petitioner from service [772A B] 3. The State Government was not entitled to taking into consideration entire history or the entry. All that it could find was some stray mildly deprecating entries such as the one in 1964 which said: "He is sincere and hard working". [773B C] 4. The question of previous history of a Government Servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. Sometimes past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, it is no justification for needless digging into the past. [703C D] 5. The appeal is dismissed.

The appellants were the owners of certain areas in the Kumool District of Andhra Pradesh. The scheme was framed under section 68 C of the , and published by the Corporation on November 4, 1962. The appellants challenged the validity of the schemes on the grounds that they violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they had not been given an opportunity to make representations against them before the proposed nationalisation. The High Court dismissed their petitions holding that the scheme was vitiated by non compliance with section 68C and rule 4 of the Rules regarding particulars to be embodied in the schemes and that in consequence the core of the scheme being in violation of Rule 68 C, the entire scheme was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the scheme framed under s 68 C was not in conformity with the requirements of section 68 D and rule 5 of the rules regarding particulars required by section 68D(1); (2) the provisions of section 69C were not complied with; (3) the schemes were vitiated by mala fides; and (4) the appellants had been given a totally different question whether the scheme in question was valid. HELD: (i) The scheme framed by the State Government was not invalid because it was not published as a result of which the scheme could not be assailed as not in accordance with section 69 C. [368 E] (ii) The schemes were also vitiated by violation of rule 4. The validity of Rule 5 was challenged on the ground that it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution. It was contended for the appellants, inter alia, that the provisions in the scheme were invalid because they had to be quashed as not warranted by law and since the scheme had been vitiated by noncompliance with section68 D(1), the scheme itself could not he assailed as invalid. [369 E F] (iii) The contention of the respondents was that the schemes framed under sections 68 C were formulated by them in pursuance of the directions given by the Chief Minister and the direction given to the Corporation that the Schemes now impugned were formulated must be held to be invalid. The policy decision taken by the Government was taken as a whole and it was as a consequence of its decision that the Scheme framed by it could not, therefore, be assailed. [370 E F; 371 A] (iv) The appellants had no right to challenge the scheme on the basis of the provisions contained in section 68F(1). The scheme is vitiated by failure to comply with the requirement of section68C and the Rules made thereunder. [372 B C] (v) The Scheme was not vitiated by any mala fides or violation of any provision of law. The schemes are vitiated by the non compliance of section 67F(l). The schemes have to be set out in the Scheme so that they can be challenged as invalid only if they are found to be violative of section 70 C. The respondents had also been given liberty to file objections under section 69 D(2) before the State Transport Undertaking. [373 E F, 371 A B] (vi) The High Courts have held that the appellants were not justified in challenging the scheme as not only did they violate article 14 but also the provisions relating to particulars required to be incorporated in the Schemes and that the impugned schemes were invalid. It is well settled that if a statute gives a particular authority what it has to do, the action must be taken by it within the limits prescribed by the statute. [371 E F]. (vii) The State Government had no power under section 70C to issue a permit to the transport undertaking "notwithstanding anything contained in Ch. IV". The scheme itself was not a statutory one and could not therefore be assailed on the plea of mala fides.

The appellant was a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed him to sales tax for the year 1954 54 and deposited the tax in the treasury. The appellant contended that the assessment was illegal because he had not filed the returns as required by section 5(2)(a)(ii). Held, that the substantive clause gives the exemption and the proviso qualifies the substantive clauses of section 5 (2) (a) (ii) of the Act. Section 5(1) of Act 1 of 1941 provides for exemption in respect of certain sales to a registered dealer of goods of the class or classes specified in the certificate of registration of the dealer as being intended for the purposes mentioned therein. The proviso does not give any help to the appellant because, it is well settled that "the effect of an excepting or qualifying proviso, according to the ordinary rules of construction, is to except out of the preceding portion of the enactment, or to qualify something enacted therein which but for the proviso would be within it": see "Craies on Statute Law", 6th Edn., p. 780; and "The general rule that a dealer cannot get the exemption unless he furnishes the declaration in the prescribed form is furnished". The expression "on demand" only fixes the point of time when the declaration forms are to be produced, but does not enable him to ignore a statutory condition to claim exemption. The object of section 6(2) is to save the tax payable by a dealer if the sales are made to a registra tion dealer for the purpose mentioned therein and that is to avoid fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax.

The Bihar State Legislature enacted the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Section 3 of the said Act provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or liberty except in accordance with the procedure established by law. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for seven years under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that it violated article 21 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of the Bihar Act were not complied with in as much as the State had no authority to obtain release on bail and that the requirement of the proviso to section 167(2) was complied with. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right to free legal services is a fundamental right of every accused person who is unable to engage a lawyer and secure legal services on account of reasons such as poverty, indigence or incommunicado situation and the State is under a mandate to provide a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail. [539C D] 1.2 The right of one charged with crime to counsel may not be deemed fundamental and essential to fair trial in some countries but is in ours. These are quite distinct offences which are punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term of ten years. They are offences involving moral turpitude and, therefore, they have to be dealt with under the provisions contained in Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [540D E] 1:3 The right conferred by section 167 (2) is not absolute but is subject to certain restrictions imposed by law, it must be held implicit in the guarantee of Article 21. This is a constitutional obligation of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trial to the accused. [541E F] 1 :4 In order to enable the Court to discharge this constitutional obligation, it is necessary that the Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. The State is also under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy Trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It is also the constitutional obligation to issue to the State which may include taking of positive action with a view to securing enforcement of the fundamental right to speedy trial. [542F G] 1 5 2 The right under section 167 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not an absolute one and it is the constitutional responsibility of the Court as the guardian of the Fundamental Rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to enforce the fundamental rights to speedy trials by issuing necessary directions to the state which may included taking of negative action such as augmenting and strengthening the investigative machinery, setting up new courts, building new court houses, providing more staff and equipment to the courts, appointment of additional judges and other measures calculated to ensure expeditious trial. The Court in the last mentioned case asserted that it "has the duty of fashioning a decree that will require defendants to eliminate the conditions and practices at particulasis and also explaining why it has not been possible to dispose of such of those cases as have been pending for more than six months, and explaining why the same had not been done.

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The appellant contended that the notice was not given within the meaning of section 34(2 A) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, as it was given in December 1951 before the Amending Act came into force. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the provisions of section34(2A) were applicable to notices issued before the amending Act came in force. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the amendment made by the Amending act did not affect any vested right of the landlord and the amendment was only a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the respondent to terminate the tenancy. The notice under section 34 (1) is merely a declaration of the tenant 's intention to terminate tenancy and no further proceedings may be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof. The legislature could not have intended that the benefit of this beneficent measure should not be extended to tenants in whose cases the tenancy had not yet terminated, though notices had been given when the further restrictions were being put on the right to terminate. Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai, (1933) I.L.R. LX Cal. 1037, approved. Durlavdas Fakir Bhai vs Jhaffbhai Bhikbhai, , disapproved. Durrabbhai Gafurti vs Abdul Kader Chaudhuri, (1930) L.R . 70 I.A. 1038 and Durlabaheb Fakiribhai vs Jhatabhai Bhikubhai, (1932) Lloyds. I. L. R. LX All.

The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan and the property of one Khadim Ali who had never been declared an evacuee. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian, but the respondents contended that the male petitioner was not entitled to declare the entire property as evacuee property. Held, that the act of the custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property could not be upheld. The acts of the respondent in so respect which he had acquired under the , were not in dispute and therefore the petitioners had no longer any claim to them. The act of taking possession of the houses was a quasi judicial decision. The action of an evacuee in so as to deprive the petitioner of their right to property could be upheld, but it was not necessary that the person should have been given notice under section 7 of the Act. A notification mentioned in section 8 of the , had been issued and the rights of the petitioners in the properties were already acquired under that section. The orders of January 10, 1952, were without jurisdiction so far they affected the rights. The proceedings of the evacuee in respect of the house never vested in the Custodian. The Act did not affect the petitioners ' right to hold property. The order was without jurisdiction as it had been passed by the Custodian under section 8 and therefore no question as to the right of the evacuees in the house could arise. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, , applied.

The assessee company had two departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool and (2) for weaving yarn from imported wool tops by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The assessee company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agent for the worsted yarn on payment of 2% commission. The agreement provided that the agents were to get 6% interest on all the advances made by them and further agreed to pay 2% interest in case of default. The commission was to be paid at 3% per annum on the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. The company appointed another agent for each of the two departments. One of the departments was known as M/S. Agarwal Pat Woollen Mills, Kharar and the other was known M/ s. Navin Woollen & General Mills. The firm was registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. It had a plant at Kanpur. It entered into an agreement with the assessee company for the manufacture of worsted cotton yarn from which it was to get 2% of the sale price. The agency was to got 6% commission on net sales and 50% commission in respect of the net profits of the firm. The first department was to start a joint venture for distributing the net profit, after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses which were to be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agents. The second department was also to carry on the business of manufacturing yarn from indigenous raw materials and to manufacture the same. The assessees claimed that the two amounts mentioned above being in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents would be deemed expenses incurred by them in order to earn profits and would, therefore, fall within the ambit of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax. The Tribunal held that the agreement amounted to a joint arrangement for distribution of profit between the assessee Company and the selling agent after being determined between themselves, and that was why there were two separate agreements in respect thereof. On reference the High Court answered both the questions in favour of the assessee. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the amounts in question were not legally deductible under section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax, 1922, as it was not incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits. The High Court held that though the agreement was a contract of agency and not a joint transaction, it was clear from the terms of the agreement that there was no such agreement in existence. It further held that there being an express provisions in the agreements dated October 20, 1955, unmistakably revealed that in the garb of an agency the parties entered into a joint obligation for distributing net profits after being ascertain between themselves. The question whether or not the agreement dated October, 20,1955 read as a whole amounts to a Joint venture for distribution was a matter which was essentially a mixed question of law and fact. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The view taken by the High court that the payments in question are not legally allowable under section10(2) (xv) appears to be legally erroneous. [200B] 1.2 In the instant case, the agreement between the parties was a joint contract for distribution and on being ascertained whether the expenses incurred could be said to have been laid out for the purposes of the partnership or not, it could not be said that the amount set apart for the pur pose of distribution amongst the consumers is not chargeable to tax on the ground that it represents over charge. [201C] 1:3 The view of the High Courts that the agreements amounted to joint venture was erroneous cannot be upheld. For the reasons given above, the appeals must fail and the same are dismissed.

The assessee, a non applicant for the assessment year in which loans were advanced to the assessee, was withdrawing moneys from the company and in the belief that those amounts were liable to be treated as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) of that Act could not include current profits but only those current profits which were included within the accumulated profits of the company. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In second appeal, the Tribunal held that the accumulated profit would not include " current profits" and therefore, the assessee was entitled to raise a question before it. The High Court answered the first question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The expression "accusation" in Section 2(7) of Income Tax, 1961, means "any distribution made to the shareholders by a company on its liquidation, to the extent to which the distribution is attributable to the accumulated Profits". [949B] 2. The words "current profits" are used for convenience) to ask for a reference of questions of law on the application made by the assessee. In either case, the party who is aggrieved and who desires a reference to the High Court must file a reference application for that purpose. It is not open to him to make a reference applications filed by the other party the basis of his claim that a question of law sought by him should be referred. The second category consists of cases where the order made by an Appellate Tribunal under section 254 operates entirely in favour or one party, although in the course of making the order the Appellate Tribunal may have negatived some points of law raised by that party. [950C D] 3. The language of the statute does not require that the assessee should state the questions of Law which he desires to be referred to the Appellate Court. It requires it to draw up a statement of the case and refer it to the court.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan. He instituted suits against the respondents for recovery of possession of certain plots of land in their occupation, or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. The defendants pleaded that they had been in possession without payment of rent for a long time without payment and that they were entitled to assess the fair and reasonable rent. Held, that the suit lands formed part of a zamindari assessed to revenue and the title of the Asthal was lost by adverse possession for long over the statutory period. The suits were within time under article 131 of the Limitation Act as the final settlement of records was published on 16 6 1931, and the present suits were filed within 12 years thereof for establishing the right of the institution to assessment of rent. J. K. Das vs D. N. Mukherjee, (1923) L.R. 58 I.A. 65, referred to. Held further, that a presumption of lost grant could be made in favour of the defendants and that the plaintiff was entitled to assessment on the holdings in their possession. The suit properties formed part Of Mauza Nala within the Zamindari assessed to Revenue and in view of that finding there was no question of adverse possession. J, K. Dass vs D, C. Das, (1933) L I.L.R, , referred to and held inapplicable. Held also, that on the facts found, no presumption of a lost grant can be made against the defendants.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965, which was dismissed by the trial Court and the plaintiff 's first appeal was also dismissed by a single Judge of the High Court. The plaintiff ' suit was decreed by the Trial Court and his first appeal to the Bombay High Court was dismissed. In the second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if the Court does not take note of the fact that the plaintiff is an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy Act, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court would be ousted because the issue is not required to be decided or dealt with under the Tenancy act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a civil court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the tenancy Act required to he settled, decided or deal With by any authority under the Act is totally ousted. Therefore, it an issue arises in a civil suit whether a person is an agriculturalist within the definition of the ' Tenancy Act ', the Mamlatdar alone would have exclusive jurisdiction under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 to decide the same and the jurisdiction is ousted. [595D E] 2. The High Court has rightly held that if an issue arose in a properly constituted civil suit which the Civil court is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of the tenancy law, then notwithstanding the fact whether such an issue is required to fall to be settled, decide and dealt with by the competent authority under section 70(a) of the Act. [596F G] 3. The legislative scheme that emerges from a combined reading of sections 70, 85 and 85A appears to be that when in a suit properly instituted, an issue arise on rival contentions between the parties which is required by the Tenancy law to be settle, decided, or dealt With by a competent authority, then it would have to be referred to the competent authori ty under the provisions of Tenancy Act for determination. [597G] 4. The trial court came to the conclusion that an issue would arise whether the defendant was an agriculturist or not and therefore, the civil court will have jurisdiction to decide it. It is only when a question arises in such a suit that the jurisdiction to settle the issues is ousted by the provisions contained in section 85A of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. [598B] 5. The Civil Court as required by a statutory provision contained in Section 85A will have to frame the issue and refer it to the Mamlatdar and on the reference being answered back, to dispose of the suit in accordance with the decision of the competent au thority under the Maharashtra Tenancy Act. If there is an issue which has to be determined by the civil Court, then the jurisdiction would be barred and it will have no jurisdiction to deal with that question. [599D E; 600A] 6. The provisions contained therein are not mandatory in character. [600E] 7. The suit as required under Section 70(b) of Tenancy and Agriculture Act is a suit which is a competent civil court having jurisdiction to try the same. It would have no jurisdic tion to decide or dispose of it treating it as a subsidiary or incidental issue, but to refer the same to the authority constituted under the Abolition Act.

The assessee, a heavy engineering concern manufacturing steam pipes, machinery parts, wagons etc. entered into an agreement with the respondent assessee company for manufacturing steam tubes, spare parts, etc. The assessee company was purchasing spare parts and forgings from outside. Ltd., and others who were also doing the same work as those of the assessee company. The question arose whether the steel Foundry Division set up by the assessee Company was an industrial undertaking to which section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 applied. The Tribunal held that the steel plants, machinery, parts, wagon, wagons, etc., were not formed by reconstruction of the business already in existence and therefore the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 15 C. On reference, the High Court held that even though the manufactured products of the new industrial undertakings were mostly used in the assessee 's other business of manufacture and for that purpose the benefit of section 15D would be available to the assessee. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (1) the two steel plants were not forming part of the original business since they were new industrial units; (2) the manufacturing process of the raw materials was only ancillary activity to the main business of the assesses and since the articles produced in these two supplemental undertakings help in producing the identical article which had been the end product of the asses see 's main business, section 15B(2)(i) cannot come to the aid of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1 ) The High Court was not right in holding that the two undertakings as formed by the reconstruction of a business already having been separate and independent production units in the sense that the commodities produced or the results achieved were commercially tangible products and the undertakings could be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old business. [776B C] (2)(a) The new industrial undertaking of the assessees is a heavy Engineering concern which would not weigh against holding that these are new and separate undertakings. Use by the assesses of the articles manufactured or produced in its existing business or the concept of expansion are not decisive tests in construing section 15A. [764C D] (b) The High court was not justified in answering two questions in the negative and against the assessee.[775B C]. Commissioner of Income tax vs Gangs Sugar Corpora tion Ltd., ; Commissioner of Incometax vs Gangals Sugar Corporation Ltd., , Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Wynare, [1924] A.C. 109, Commissioner of lncome Tax vs Gangades Sugar Corporat ion Ltd., [1955] 1 S.C R. 869 and Commissioner of income tax vs G.M. Gangs, ; , referred to. (c) The fact that an assessee by establishment of a new industrial concern expands his existing business which he certainly does not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section15C cannot be a different question in the course of practical application of the section. [774D E] Commissioner of Wealth Tax vs GM Gangs Ltd., A.I.R. , approved. (d) The Tribunal was right in answering the two questions against the Department.

The inam title deeds, the entries in the Inam fair register prepared at the time of confirmation of the inams by the Inams Commissioner in 1863 and the contemporaneous statement made by the inamdars were of the same pattern in respect of all the inams. The inam title deed was not personal inams burdened with services and was not resumable under section 44 B(2)(a)(i). The Inam title deeds were not personal inam burdened with service and were not resuscitated. The Inam titles were granted to the inamdar as remuneration for services to be rendered by them in connection with the temple. The inams were granted on the basis of a statement made before the Inamdars that they were personal inams. In 1934, the Inam title deed, the Entries in the inam fair register, prepared at time of the confirmation of inams by Inams Commissioner, was amended and it was stated that in fasli 1272 corresponding to 1862 63, Veerabadra Mudali, Periasami Mudaliar and Arumugam, the inam were granted a permanent lease for the performance of services connected therewith. The lands were resumed under section 43 B(1) (a)(ii). The inams in the present case were not Personal inams burdened by the Inamdar but were personal inamdars. The question whether an alienee from the inam was entitled to the grant of resumption of an inam fell within the purview of section 44B(2) (b) (i). Held, that the inam title, if any, of all persons claiming through the inamholders to any subordinate interest in the inams stood determined. Kunjanna Ayyar and his successors in title were lessees of the inam lands under the inamdaridars. During the continuance of the tenancy, their possession was not adverse to the Government under whom the inamants held the inam land. The grantees were not entitled to any prescriptive title to the kudiwaram rights either against the inam proprietors or against the Government.

The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. Under section 76 of the Act the Municipality had imposed a tax on houses and buildings or lands within the municipal limits at a rate not exceeding 12 1/2% of the gross annual letting value. The appellant Corporation levied house tax on the basis of gross annual rent at the rate of 7% of such value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. This was objected to by the respondents on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the annual letting values less 10% of a rateable value in respect of the financial year. The objection was rejected by the respondent Corporation. In appeal, the High Court held that the appellant Corporation could not levy the house tax at 7% on the gross yearly letting value as such imposition was inconsistent with sec. 73 of the 1954 and therefore the rate was saved by section 2(c) and therefore it was not bound to deduct 10% allowance provided by sec. 75 and section 76. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant corporation was entitled to levy the tax on gross annual tenancy at 7%. [131 E] (ii) Section 76 provides that where a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year the provisions of sections 75 and 76 shall be applicable as if it was a new assessment list. The scheme of the section shows that when such a previous list is adopted it becomes the list for such subsequent year subject to the procedure laid down in secs. 73 and 74. [131 G] (iii) The saving and deeming provisions in section 2 (c) can only apply if the tax is assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions Of section 73, that is, if it is assessed on a net and not the gross profits of any other account whatsoever. In order to prevent such a result the legislature has provided by sub sec. 2 of sec. 79 that where the assessment list prepared in accordance with the provision of secs 75 or 76 is adopted, it becomes its list for that subsequent year, subject to procedure laid prescribed in section 76(6) after disposing of the objections if any and it is then only that it becomes conclusive evidence of the valuation and tax assessed thereon for that particular official year. If it were otherwise, the annual tenancy value or the value estimated on a particular building or house would be static for 4 years during which the Corporation can go on adopting the assessment lists prepared in an earlier year and the owner or occupier of the building would be deprived of the right to object to the valuation or the annual rent assessed thereon.

The assessee company carried on the business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. The profits from the business became less and less due to War conditions and the assessee company began to manufacture plywood chests for tea, paints and lemon grass oil. These were contemplated by cl. (3) of the Memorandum of Association of the company which provided that the price would not include manufactured goods, chemicals and other raw materials necessary for the manufacture of matches and had sold the concern for a lesser price, that in the past it had sold chemicals and some other raw material necessary for manufacture of match factory for a smaller price, and that the sale was therefore a revenue sale. The assessee company claimed that the stock in trade could only be that which was the subject of trade, and not that of the assessee Company. Held, that the transaction was not one of sale of the entire stock as part of trading activity but on a winding up sale. It was not an accretion to capital but a profit on the sale of its stock in business. The fact that the clause in the Memorandum gave power to the company to sell the chemicals and raw materials for match manufacture was something more than a windingup sale, not with a view to trading in chemicals and the fact that raw materials were sold in the ordinary way of business or that the assessee was carrying on a trading busi ness. The profit making apparatus was not evidence of a trading activity. The essence of the matter however, was not that an extra amount had been gained by the selling out or the exchange but whether it could fairly (1) [1923] A.C. 327, 965 864 be said that there was a trading from which alone profits can arise in business and that this was impossible to infer that the chemicals were sold as part only of trading profits. The question whether the transaction of sale was one of sales of the whole stock as a part of the trading activity or not was irrelevant for the purpose of determining the true character of the transaction. Doughty vs Love, , referred to.
